questions.question: A 58-year-old with metabolic syndrome has fasting labs: TG 340 mg/dL, HDL-C 32 mg/dL, LDL-C 152 mg/dL, waist 118 cm, BP 148/92, HbA1c 6.8%. What MOST explains his lipid pattern?
options: A. Decreased intestinal cholesterol absorption
B. Reduced hepatic bile acid synthesis
C. Genetic LDL receptor mutations
D. Increased hepatic VLDL with impaired lipolysis
questions.explanation: Atherogenic dyslipidemia mechanism: Insulin resistance → lipolysis → excess free fatty acids → hepatic TG synthesis → VLDL secretion. Apo C-III on VLDL inhibits lipoprotein lipase. CETP exchanges TGs for cholesterol creating atherogenic remnants and low HDL-C. A, B, C wrong: Not primary mechanisms in metabolic syndrome.

questions.question: A 45-year-old with familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C 285 mg/dL) takes atorvastatin 80 mg for 8 weeks. LDL-C drops to 145 mg/dL. Liver enzymes normal. What is the BEST next step?
options: A. Add ezetimibe for complementary absorption blockade
B. Switch to rosuvastatin monotherapy
C. Stop statin, start PCSK9 inhibitor
D. Add fenofibrate to lower LDL-C
questions.explanation: High-intensity statin achieved ~50% reduction but LDL-C still elevated. Ezetimibe blocks intestinal NPC1L1 protein, reducing absorption ~50% with complementary mechanism. Adds 15-20% additional LDL-C lowering. Maximize oral therapy before PCSK9 inhibitor. B wrong: Minimal added benefit. C wrong: Premature. D wrong: Fibrates don't lower LDL-C substantially.

questions.question: A 62-year-old with ASCVD on atorvastatin 80 mg plus ezetimibe has LDL-C 95 mg/dL. Insurance requires justification for PCSK9 inhibitor. What scenario BEST supports addition?
options: A. Any ASCVD patient warrants PCSK9 therapy
B. Recent ACS with LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL on max statin
C. Only familial hypercholesterolemia qualifies
D. Patient must have diabetes diagnosis
questions.explanation: ODYSSEY Outcomes studied recent ACS patients (within 1-12 months) with LDL-C ≥70, nonHDL ≥100, or apo B ≥80 mg/dL despite statins. Showed 15% CV event reduction. Represents highest-risk group with strongest evidence. A wrong: Too broad. C wrong: Not only indication. D wrong: Diabetes not required.

questions.question: A 55-year-old develops severe myalgias on atorvastatin 40 mg (CK 850 U/L, baseline 120). After stopping, symptoms resolve and CK normalizes. She has ASCVD and LDL-C 165 mg/dL off therapy. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Avoid all statins permanently
B. Rechallenge with low-dose or different statin plus ezetimibe
C. Use only ezetimibe monotherapy
D. Start PCSK9 inhibitor without statins
questions.explanation: Statin intolerance management: ~30% tolerate different statin. Try lower doses, alternate-day dosing, or hydrophilic statins (pravastatin, fluvastatin). Add ezetimibe to reach goal with lower statin dose. Complete avoidance last resort given strong CV benefit. A, C wrong: Premature. D wrong: Should attempt statin rechallenge first.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 25%) takes furosemide 40 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg, spironolactone 25 mg daily. Labs: K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cr 1.9 (baseline 1.4), BUN 45. Euvolemic. What is BEST management?
options: A. Stop spironolactone and lisinopril permanently
B. Continue all medications, give IV calcium
C. Reduce spironolactone, lower ACEI dose, recheck labs
D. Stop only ACEI, keep spironolactone
questions.explanation: Goal: Maintain RAAS blockade (mortality benefit) while managing hyperkalemia. Reduce spironolactone to 12.5 mg, consider reducing ACEI dose, ensure adequate diuresis, dietary K+ restriction. Recheck 3-5 days. Consider K+ binders if persistent. Complete discontinuation loses mortality benefit. A, B, D wrong: Too aggressive or inadequate response.

questions.question: A 72-year-old hypertensive on amlodipine 10 mg has controlled BP (128/78) but develops bothersome bilateral ankle edema. What is the MOST appropriate intervention?
options: A. Add furosemide for edema control
B. Increase amlodipine to 15 mg daily
C. Add ACEI/ARB for balanced venous dilation
D. Continue with compression stockings only
questions.explanation: CCB edema results from arterial vasodilation WITHOUT venous dilation → capillary pressure gradient → fluid extravasation. ACEIs/ARBs cause balanced arterial AND venous vasodilation, reducing gradient and edema. Diuretics ineffective (not volume-mediated). A wrong: Diuretics don't work. B wrong: Worsens edema. D wrong: Symptomatic only.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with bilateral renal artery stenosis (confirmed imaging) has BP 168/98. Which antihypertensive has HIGHEST acute kidney injury risk?
options: A. Amlodipine 5 mg daily
B. Chlorthalidone 12.5 mg daily
C. Lisinopril 10 mg daily
D. Metoprolol 50 mg twice daily
questions.explanation: Bilateral stenosis causes kidneys to depend on angiotensin II for efferent arteriole vasoconstriction maintaining glomerular pressure. ACEIs/ARBs remove this compensation → GFR drops → AKI. Monitor Cr within 1-2 weeks; >30% rise suggests hemodynamically significant stenosis. A, B, D wrong: Don't affect glomerular hemodynamics same way.

questions.question: A 60-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 30%) on lisinopril 40 mg and furosemide 40 mg BID is stable and euvolemic. You initiate beta-blocker. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Start metoprolol succinate 200 mg immediately
B. Start atenolol 50 mg daily
C. Wait until LVEF >40% before starting
D. Start carvedilol 3.125 mg BID, titrate slowly
questions.explanation: 'Start low, go slow': Use proven beta-blockers (carvedilol 3.125 mg BID, metoprolol succinate 12.5-25 mg daily, or bisoprolol). Patient must be stable and euvolemic. Titrate by doubling dose every 2-4 weeks. Monitor HR, BP, fluid retention. Target: carvedilol 25 mg BID. A wrong: Target dose causes decompensation. B wrong: Atenolol lacks HFrEF mortality data. C wrong: Indicated regardless of LVEF.

questions.question: A 65-year-old with HFrEF on optimal GDMT plus digoxin 0.125 mg develops nausea, yellow-green halos, ECG shows atrial tachycardia with 2:1 AV block. Digoxin level 2.8 ng/mL, K+ 3.2 mEq/L. What MOST contributed to toxicity?
options: A. Hyperkalemia increasing toxicity risk
B. High dietary potassium intake
C. Hypercalcemia from vitamin D
D. Hypokalemia from loop diuretic
questions.explanation: Hypokalemia MAJOR risk for digoxin toxicity: K+ and digoxin compete for Na+/K+-ATPase binding; low K+ increases digoxin binding. Also displaces digoxin from skeletal muscle increasing free drug. Other factors: elderly, renal dysfunction, drug interactions (spironolactone, amiodarone). Atrial tach with AV block pathognomonic. A wrong: Hyperkalemia protective. B wrong: High K+ reduces toxicity. C wrong: Less significant than hypokalemia.

questions.question: A 58-year-old hypertensive on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg and lisinopril 20 mg has BP 142/88. Which addition provides BOTH BP lowering AND may reduce ACEI cough if it develops?
options: A. Enalapril 10 mg adds complementary effect
B. Metoprolol 50 mg twice daily
C. Amlodipine 5 mg via different mechanism
D. Spironolactone 25 mg for resistant HTN
questions.explanation: Adding CCB to ACEI + thiazide is common triple therapy. CCB works via different mechanism (calcium channel blockade) providing additive BP lowering. Evidence suggests CCBs may reduce ACEI cough. If cough intolerable, switch ACEI to ARB. A wrong: Another ACEI adds no benefit, doubles cough risk. B wrong: Not preferred add-on. D wrong: Increases hyperkalemia risk with ACEI.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with COPD (FEV1 55%) and hypertension needs BP medication. If beta-blocker necessary, which property is MOST important?
options: A. Non-selective blocks both β1 and β2
B. Beta-1 selective reduces bronchospasm risk
C. Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity essential
D. Long half-life most important factor
questions.explanation: In COPD/asthma, avoid non-selective beta-blockers that block β2-receptors causing bronchoconstriction. Beta-1 selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol) have less β2 activity. Carvedilol's alpha-1 blockade may offset β2 blockade. However, CCBs, ACEIs, or ARBs generally preferred first-line. A wrong: Highest bronchospasm risk. C, D wrong: Not relevant to bronchospasm prevention.

questions.question: A 52-year-old with atherogenic dyslipidemia (TG 380 mg/dL, HDL-C 34 mg/dL, LDL-C 142 mg/dL) asks about treatment. What is PRIMARY target and initial therapy?
options: A. HDL-C primary target, start niacin
B. LDL-C remains primary, start statin first
C. Triglycerides only, start fenofibrate monotherapy
D. All parameters equal, start combination immediately
questions.explanation: Even in atherogenic dyslipidemia, LDL-C remains PRIMARY target. Statins first-line: lower LDL-C substantially, moderate TG reduction (20-40%), modest HDL-C increase (5-10%), proven CV benefit. High-intensity preferred. If TG >500 mg/dL, fibrate first to reduce pancreatitis. A wrong: HDL-raising drugs lack CV benefit. C wrong: TG not high enough for primary fibrate. D wrong: Start statin monotherapy.

questions.question: A 48-year-old on atorvastatin 80 mg has asymptomatic ALT 185 U/L, AST 158 U/L (ULN 40 U/L). Bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase normal. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Immediately stop statin permanently now
B. Hold statin, recheck in 2-4 weeks, consider rechallenge
C. Continue statin, add hepatoprotective agent
D. Switch to highest dose different statin
questions.explanation: Transaminases ~4-4.5x ULN (≥3x threshold): Hold statin, investigate other causes, recheck LFTs 2-4 weeks. If normalize, rechallenge with lower dose same statin OR different statin. If progress or >10x ULN, discontinue permanently. Mild elevations (<3x) often transient. A wrong: Can often rechallenge. C wrong: No evidence for hepatoprotective agents. D wrong: Should hold first.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with acute decompensated HFrEF (bilateral rales, JVP 14 cm, BNP 1850) is not on medications. What is CORRECT therapy sequence?
options: A. Start all GDMT simultaneously immediately
B. Diuretics first → ACEI stable → BB stable → MRA
C. Beta-blocker first priority, then others
D. Wait for LVEF improvement before any therapy
questions.explanation: Correct sequence: (1) IV diuretics for euvolemia first, (2) ACEI once stable with adequate BP, (3) Beta-blocker after stable on ACEI and euvolemic (NEVER during acute decompensation), (4) MRA if persistent Class II-IV symptoms. Beta-blockers during acute HF worsen hemodynamics. A wrong: Beta-blocker during acute HF dangerous. C wrong: Beta-blocker first causes shock. D wrong: Delays proven therapy.

questions.question: A 62-year-old with HFrEF on lisinopril 40 mg, metoprolol 200 mg, spironolactone 25 mg has recurrent volume overload despite furosemide 80 mg BID. What explains diuretic resistance?
options: A. Medication non-adherence is only factor
B. Furosemide dose too low to be effective
C. Distal tubule hypertrophy, low GFR, neurohormonal activation
D. Beta-blocker causing all fluid retention
questions.explanation: Diuretic resistance mechanisms: (1) Distal tubule hypertrophy from chronic loop diuretic → compensatory Na+ reabsorption, (2) Reduced GFR → less drug delivery, (3) Neurohormonal activation → Na+ retention, (4) Gut edema → poor absorption. Strategies: Increase dose/frequency, add thiazide, IV diuretics. A wrong: Multiple factors. B wrong: 160 mg substantial. D wrong: Not primary cause.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation and HFrEF takes warfarin (INR goal 2-3), metoprolol, lisinopril, furosemide, spironolactone. Today INR is 5.2 without bleeding. Which drug MOST likely increased INR?
options: A. Furosemide has major warfarin interaction
B. Lisinopril commonly elevates INR significantly
C. Metoprolol known to increase INR
D. Spironolactone inhibits warfarin metabolism
questions.explanation: Spironolactone increases warfarin effect via CYP enzyme interference and reduced vitamin K synthesis by gut bacteria. Amiodarone (major - reduce warfarin 30-50%), certain antibiotics, NSAIDs also interact. Management INR 5-6 without bleeding: Hold 1-2 doses, recheck INR, resume lower dose. A, B, C wrong: Minimal warfarin interaction.

questions.question: A 75-year-old with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 35%) has persistent NYHA Class III on ACEI, beta-blocker, MRA. QRS 155 ms with LBBB. Besides medications, what has mortality benefit?
options: A. Increased diuretic dose provides mortality benefit
B. CRT improves synchrony in wide QRS LBBB
C. Immediate heart transplant is only option
D. Add calcium channel blocker for symptoms
questions.explanation: CRT (biventricular pacing ± ICD) indicated for LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB ≥150 ms, NYHA II-IV on GDMT. Corrects dyssynchrony → reduced mortality, HF hospitalizations, improved symptoms. Best response LBBB ≥150 ms. A wrong: Symptomatic only. C wrong: CRT may improve function. D wrong: CCBs avoided in HFrEF.

questions.question: A 50-year-old with small dense LDL and TG 320 mg/dL on atorvastatin 40 mg asks about omega-3 fatty acids. Which formulation/dose has CV evidence?
options: A. Over-the-counter fish oil 1000 mg daily
B. Any omega-3 supplement at any dose
C. Cod liver oil from health stores
D. Icosapent ethyl 2g BID or omega-3 4g daily
questions.explanation: Prescription omega-3: (1) Icosapent ethyl (EPA only) 2g BID reduced CV events in REDUCE-IT for TG 135-499 on statin, (2) Omega-3 ethyl esters 4g daily reduces TG 20-50%. OTC doses insufficient. Mechanism: Reduces hepatic VLDL synthesis, increases lipoprotein lipase. A, B, C wrong: Insufficient dose/formulation.

questions.question: A 45-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and prednisone 10 mg develops hypertension (BP 152/96). Which antihypertensive needs caution with her medications?
options: A. Amlodipine safe, no interactions
B. NSAIDs reduce ACEI/ARB/diuretic effectiveness
C. Metoprolol safe for this patient
D. Hydralazine preferred in RA patients
questions.explanation: NSAIDs (often in RA) + RAAS inhibitors: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin vasodilation → reduced ACEI/ARB/diuretic efficacy, increased BP, AKI risk ('triple whammy' with diuretics). ACEIs may increase methotrexate levels. Prednisone causes HTN via sodium retention. Best: CCB (amlodipine) its safe but don’t need caution in this patient . A, C, D wrong: Miss key interactions.

questions.question: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes, albuminuria (300 mg/g), hypertension (BP 146/92) needs therapy. Which provides BOTH BP control AND renal protection?
options: A. Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg monotherapy
B. Amlodipine 10 mg alone sufficient
C. ACE inhibitor or ARB for renoprotection
D. Clonidine is preferred agent
questions.explanation: ACEIs/ARBs PREFERRED in diabetic patients with albuminuria >30 mg/g: Reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating efferent arteriole, decrease proteinuria, slow CKD progression to ESRD (RENAAL, IDNT trials). Use even if BP normal. Monitor Cr (up to 30% increase acceptable) and K+. A, B, D wrong: Lack specific renoprotection in diabetic nephropathy.

questions.question: A 65-year-old with PAD (claudication at 100 meters) and hypertension starts aspirin 81 mg daily. After 3 months, no walking improvement. What explains this?
options: A. Aspirin dose too low for PAD
B. Aspirin reduces CV events but not claudication symptoms
C. Patient definitely non-adherent to therapy
D. Aspirin contraindicated in PAD patients
questions.explanation: Important distinction: Aspirin reduces CV events (MI, stroke, vascular death) ~20% in PAD but does NOT improve claudication or walking distance. Cilostazol improves symptoms 50-67% but contraindicated in HF. Exercise therapy most effective for symptoms. Revascularization for severe claudication. A wrong: Higher dose doesn't improve symptoms. C wrong: Assumptions. D wrong: Indicated in PAD.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with stable angina on metoprolol 100 mg BID, lisinopril, atorvastatin, aspirin has 2-3 anginal episodes weekly. What is PRIMARY anti-anginal beta-blocker mechanism?
options: A. Direct coronary artery vasodilation
B. Reduce MVO2 via decreased HR, contractility, BP
C. Increase oxygen delivery to myocardium
D. Prevent platelet aggregation at plaques
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers first-line anti-anginal: Block β1-receptors → decreased HR (MOST important - increases diastolic coronary perfusion time), decreased contractility, decreased BP. All reduce myocardial oxygen demand. Goal HR 55-60 bpm. Also reduce cardiac events. A, C wrong: Don't vasodilate coronaries. D wrong: Aspirin mechanism.

questions.question: A 62-year-old with variant (Prinzmetal's) angina has rest pain with ST-elevation relieved by nitroglycerin. Which medication is CONTRAINDICATED and worsens his condition?
options: A. Diltiazem prevents vasospasm
B. Amlodipine appropriate for variant angina
C. Non-selective beta-blockers worsen vasospasm
D. Long-acting nitrates are first-line
questions.explanation: Variant angina = coronary vasospasm (rest, early morning). Treatment: CCBs first-line, longacting nitrates. AVOID non-selective beta-blockers - block β2 vasodilation leaving α1 vasoconstriction unopposed → severe vasospasm. Beta-1 selective safer but CCBs preferred. Smoking cessation critical. A, B, D wrong: Appropriate treatments.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with acute STEMI receives fibrinolytic (alteplase), aspirin, heparin, clopidogrel. What is MOST concerning risk during transfer?
options: A. Hypotension from nitroglycerin infusion
B. Major bleeding from antiplatelet/fibrinolytic/anticoagulant combination
C. Headache from aspirin adverse effects
D. Cough from ACE inhibitor therapy
questions.explanation: Fibrinolytic + antiplatelet + anticoagulation creates substantial bleeding risk: Intracranial hemorrhage (0.5-1% - most feared), major bleeding (GI, retroperitoneal). Contraindications: recent surgery/trauma/stroke, active bleeding, severe uncontrolled HTN >180/110. Monitor neuro status, access sites, hematocrit. A, C, D wrong: Less immediately life-threatening than hemorrhage.

questions.question: A 48-year-old with acute NSTEMI refuses angiography. He starts aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, metoprolol. How does ticagrelor differ from clopidogrel?
options: A. COX-1 inhibition like aspirin mechanism
B. Direct reversible P2Y12 antagonist, no metabolism required
C. GP IIb/IIIa inhibition at receptor
D. Direct thrombin inhibition mechanism
questions.explanation: Ticagrelor: Direct-acting (no CYP2C19 metabolism needed unlike clopidogrel), reversible binding, faster onset/offset, BID dosing. Superior to clopidogrel in ACS but higher bleeding. Causes dyspnea (10-15%) and bradyarrhythmias. Prasugrel also superior but more bleeding. Duration: 12 months post-ACS. A, C, D wrong: Different mechanisms.

questions.question: A 67-year-old on warfarin for atrial fibrillation (baseline INR 2.5) starts amiodarone 400 mg for rhythm control. What warfarin change is REQUIRED?
options: A. No dose adjustment needed currently
B. Reduce warfarin 30-50%, recheck INR 3-7 days
C. Increase warfarin dose for synergy
D. Stop warfarin, use heparin only
questions.explanation: Amiodarone-warfarin MAJOR interaction: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9 (metabolizes Swarfarin). Effect begins days but full impact takes weeks (long half-life 40-55 days). REDUCE warfarin 30-50% when starting amiodarone, recheck INR 3-7 days and weekly. Also increases digoxin (reduce 50%). A, C, D wrong: Dangerous or unnecessary.

questions.question: A 72-year-old with persistent atrial fibrillation, HFrEF (LVEF 30%), CHA2DS2-VASc=5 takes apixaban 5 mg BID. Why are DOACs often preferred over warfarin?
options: A. More effective at stroke prevention
B. No monitoring, fewer interactions, lower ICH risk
C. Cheaper cost than warfarin therapy
D. Can use with any GFR level
questions.explanation: DOAC advantages: No routine monitoring, fewer drug-food interactions, predictable doseresponse, lower intracranial hemorrhage risk, similar or better efficacy, rapid onset/offset. Disadvantages: Cost, adherence critical, renal dosing needed, limited reversal, contraindicated CrCl <15-30. A wrong: Similar not superior efficacy. C wrong: More expensive. D wrong: Renal dosing required.

questions.question: A 65-year-old on apixaban 5 mg BID presents with major GI bleeding (Hgb 7.2 from 14 g/dL). Hemodynamically stable after fluids. What is MOST appropriate anticoagulation management?
options: A. Continue apixaban, bleeding worse without it
B. Hold apixaban, supportive care, andexanet alfa if severe
C. Give vitamin K 10 mg IV
D. Start heparin infusion immediately
questions.explanation: Major DOAC bleeding: (1) Hold anticoagulant, (2) Supportive care - fluids, transfusion (Hgb >7-8), control source, (3) Reversal if life-threatening - andexanet alfa for Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban), idarucizumab for dabigatran, (4) Short half-life ~12 hours, recovery in 12-24 hours. A wrong: Must hold. C wrong: Vitamin K for warfarin only. D wrong: Worsens bleeding.

questions.question: A 58-year-old with DVT starts rivaroxaban. CrCl is 28 mL/min. What is the concern in renal impairment?
options: A. No renal elimination, safe any GFR
B. Renally eliminated, accumulates in CKD increasing bleeding
C. Completely contraindicated at CrCl <60
D. No dose adjustment ever needed
questions.explanation: DOAC renal considerations: Dabigatran 80% renal (avoid CrCl <30), rivaroxaban 33% renal (reduce/avoid CrCl <30), apixaban 27% renal PREFERRED in CKD (dose reduce 2.5 mg BID if CrCl 15-29 or 2 of 3: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, Cr ≥1.5), edoxaban 50% renal (reduce CrCl 30-50). Monitor renal function. A, C, D wrong: Mischaracterize dosing requirements.

questions.question: A 70-year-old on warfarin (INR goal 2-3) eats large amounts of kale, spinach, broccoli daily in new diet. INR drops from 2.5 to 1.4. What is the mechanism?
options: A. These foods contain tyramine
B. High vitamin K antagonizes warfarin effect
C. These foods induce CYP2C9 metabolism
D. Protein binding displacement occurs
questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1). High dietary vitamin K (green leafy vegetables, liver) overcomes warfarin inhibition → increased clotting factors → LOWER INR. Counsel CONSISTENT vitamin K intake (not eliminate). Recheck INR 3-7 days after diet changes. Antibiotics, CYP2C9 inhibitors, NSAIDs also interact. A, C, D wrong: Not the mechanism.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 28%) post-IV diuresis starts lisinopril 5 mg. Day 3: Cr 1.2→1.7 mg/dL (42% rise), K+ 5.4, BP 118/76. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Stop lisinopril permanently for safety
B. Continue lisinopril, monitor K+ with diet restriction
C. Double lisinopril dose for renal perfusion
D. Emergency dialysis for acute kidney injury
questions.explanation: Up to 30% Cr rise acceptable with ACEI - hemodynamic effect not AKI. This 42% borderline but continue if stabilizes. Monitor K+/Cr in 5-7 days. Manage hyperkalemia: diet, adequate diuresis. Stop only if >35% progressive rise or K+ >5.5-6.0. Longterm renal protection outweighs initial rise. A wrong: Loses mortality benefit. C wrong: Worsens renal function. D wrong: Not indicated.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with HFrEF on GDMT has NYHA III. QRS 165 ms LBBB, LVEF 28%, sinus rhythm. Besides meds, what reduces mortality?
options: A. Regular permanent pacemaker only
B. Temporary pacing during optimization
C. CRT-D synchronizes in LBBB ≥150 ms
D. No device indicated at this time
questions.explanation: CRT-D (biventricular pacing + ICD) for LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB ≥150 ms, NYHA IIIV on GDMT. Corrects dyssynchrony → 25% mortality reduction, 40% fewer hospitalizations. Best response LBBB ≥150 ms. A wrong: Regular pacing doesn't resynchronize. B wrong: Temporary only. D wrong: Clearly indicated.

questions.question: A 72-year-old with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%) on GDMT ≥4 months has no arrhythmia history. What justifies ICD?
options: A. Primary prevention - LVEF ≤35% on GDMT ≥3 months
B. Only if syncope occurs first
C. Not indicated without prior cardiac arrest
D. Wait until LVEF improves to normal
questions.explanation: Primary prevention ICD: Ischemic LVEF ≤35% on GDMT ≥3 months AND ≥40 days post-MI. Life expectancy >1 year. Reduces mortality ~30% by terminating VT/VF. Non-ischemic: LVEF ≤35% on GDMT ≥3 months. B wrong: Syncope not required. C wrong: Primary prevention indicated. D wrong: Persistent low LVEF is indication.

questions.question: A 45-year-old with dilated cardiomyopathy switches from lisinopril to sacubitril/valsartan. What washout prevents angioedema?
options: A. No washout required for transition
B. 12 hours sufficient for safety
C. 36 hours prevents dual bradykinin accumulation
D. 7 days minimum waiting period
questions.explanation: MANDATORY 36-hour ACEI washout. Neprilysin inhibitor + ACEI both increase bradykinin → severe angioedema with airway risk. Never combine. Contraindicated if prior ACEI/ARB angioedema. Indications: HFrEF LVEF ≤40%, NYHA II-IV. A, B wrong: Insufficient/dangerous. D wrong: Unnecessary delay.

questions.question: A 58-year-old HFrEF develops symptomatic hypotension (BP 88/54) on lisinopril 40 mg, metoprolol 200 mg, spironolactone 25 mg. Euvolemic. Which adjustment is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Reduce ACEI, maintain beta-blocker and MRA
B. Stop all three medications immediately
C. Increase all doses for better output
D. Add midodrine for vasopressor support
questions.explanation: Priority: Maintain beta-blocker and MRA (proven mortality benefit). First: Reduce/hold ACEI/ARB, ensure not volume depleted. Many tolerate systolic 80-90s asymptomatically. Strategies: Split doses, bedtime dosing. B wrong: Too aggressive. C wrong: Worsens hypotension. D wrong: Rarely needed.

questions.question: A 65-year-old HFrEF admitted for decompensation was on carvedilol 25 mg BID. During hospitalization for IV diuresis, what should be done?
options: A. Continue carvedilol if tolerated hemodynamically
B. Always stop beta-blockers during admission
C. Double dose for better control
D. Switch to different beta-blocker now
questions.explanation: Continue if tolerated - abrupt withdrawal causes rebound. Hold only if: shock, symptomatic hypotension, severe bradycardia, requiring inotropes. Resume before discharge when stable. Continuing reduces mortality/rehospitalization. B wrong: Routine discontinuation harmful. C, D wrong: Inappropriate during acute illness.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with HFpEF (LVEF 58%) and hypertension has persistent dyspnea. BP 156/88. Which has STRONGEST evidence for HFpEF outcomes?
options: A. Digoxin for inotropic support
B. Amlodipine monotherapy alone
C. Milrinone infusion continuously
D. SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalizations
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin EMPEROR-Preserved, dapagliflozin DELIVER) reduced CV death/HF hospitalizations in HFpEF (LVEF >40%). Class I recommendation. Also control BP, promote diuresis. HFpEF: BP control, diuretics, treat comorbidities. No proven ACEI/ARB/BB mortality benefit specifically for HFpEF. A, B, C wrong: No proven benefit.

questions.question: A 62-year-old with DM2 and HFrEF (LVEF 32%) on GDMT has recurrent hospitalizations. Which reduces HF hospitalizations regardless of diabetes?
options: A. Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin independent of glucose
B. Sulfonylureas for glucose control
C. Metformin for insulin sensitization
D. Regular insulin for glycemic control
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin DAPA-HF, empagliflozin EMPEROR-Reduced) reduced HF hospitalizations/CV death in HFrEF regardless of diabetes. Benefits independent of glucose-lowering. Mechanisms: Natriuresis, reduced preload, improved energetics. Class I in HFrEF. B, C, D wrong: Don't reduce HF outcomes.

questions.question: A 48-year-old on atorvastatin 40 mg for 6 months has bilateral calf pain/weakness. CK 1250 U/L (baseline 150). What defines this?
options: A. Normal expected statin response
B. Statin myopathy requiring management
C. Unrelated orthopedic issue, continue
D. Increase statin for better control
questions.explanation: Statin myopathy with CK >10x ULN or symptomatic with elevation. Stop immediately. Monitor CK until normalizes. Rechallenge with different statin at lower dose OR non-statin therapy. Rhabdomyolysis risk if continue. A wrong: Pathologic. C, D wrong: Dangerous.

questions.question: A 67-year-old with PAD (ABI 0.65) has lifestyle-limiting claudication at 75 meters. On aspirin, atorvastatin, BP meds. What improves walking?
options: A. Cilostazol 100 mg BID improves 50-67%
B. Increase aspirin to 325 mg daily
C. Add clopidogrel dual antiplatelet
D. Switch to warfarin anticoagulation
questions.explanation: Cilostazol (PDE-III inhibitor) improves walking distance 50-67%, QOL. CONTRAINDICATED in HF (increases mortality). Aspirin/clopidogrel reduce CV events but don't improve symptoms. Exercise therapy most effective. Revascularization for severe. B, C wrong: Don't improve symptoms. D wrong: Not indicated.

questions.question: A 58-year-old takes amlodipine 10 mg with BP 124/76 but develops ankle edema without dyspnea. What is pathophysiology?
options: A. Arterial vasodilation exceeds venous creating capillary gradient
B. Volume overload from HF decompensation
C. Allergic reaction to CCB
D. Renal sodium retention primary
questions.explanation: CCB edema: Arterial vasodilation WITHOUT venous → increased capillary hydrostatic pressure → fluid extravasation. Dose-dependent. Add ACEI/ARB (balanced vasodilation), reduce CCB, or switch. Diuretics ineffective (not volume-mediated). B wrong: No HF signs. C wrong: Not allergic. D wrong: CCBs don't retain sodium.

questions.question: A 75-year-old HFrEF with AF (HR 110-120) starts metoprolol. After 2 weeks: HR 70, BP 102/64, weight +4 kg, worsening dyspnea. What occurred?
options: A. Optimal beta-blocker response achieved
B. Unrelated pneumonia causing symptoms
C. Beta-blocker induced HF decompensation
D. AF progressed despite therapy
questions.explanation: Beta-blocker can cause temporary fluid retention/decompensation during initiation. Signs: Weight gain, dyspnea, edema. Management: Increase diuretic temporarily, DON'T stop beta-blocker if possible. If severe, reduce beta-blocker, increase diuretics, restart lower when stable. A wrong: Weight gain not optimal. B, D wrong: Don't explain weight.

questions.question: A 52-year-old hypertensive (BP 168/98) has gout with recent flare. On allopurinol and prednisone taper. Which antihypertensive is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Hydrochlorothiazide plus losartan combination
B. Chlorthalidone monotherapy volume control
C. Amlodipine plus losartan avoiding thiazide
D. Spironolactone plus furosemide diuresis
questions.explanation: Thiazides increase uric acid → gout flares. In gout history, prefer: CCB, ACEI, ARB. ARBs (especially losartan) may have mild uricosuric effect. Avoid loop/thiazide unless essential. Prednisone causes HTN via sodium retention. A, B wrong: Thiazides worsen gout. D wrong: Both increase uric acid.

questions.question: A 60-year-old HFrEF (LVEF 30%) on lisinopril 40 mg, metoprolol 200 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, furosemide 40 mg BID remains NYHA III. What represents appropriate escalation?
options: A. Stop beta-blocker, increase diuretics
B. Add ivabradine if sinus rhythm HR ≥70 despite max beta-blocker
C. Add verapamil for rate control
D. Triple furosemide dose immediately
questions.explanation: Ivabradine (If channel inhibitor): HFrEF LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, NYHA II-III, HR ≥70 on max beta-blocker or contraindicated. Reduces HF hospitalizations. Dose: 5-7.5 mg BID. Side effects: Phosphenes, bradycardia. A wrong: Don't stop beta-blocker. C wrong: Non-DHP CCBs contraindicated HFrEF. D wrong: Gradual better.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with DM2, CKD Stage 3 (GFR 45), hypertension (BP 152/94) starts lisinopril. What monitoring is MOST critical?
options: A. Creatinine and potassium within 1-2 weeks, periodically
B. Only blood pressure measurements
C. Liver enzymes weekly initially
D. No monitoring required for ACEIs
questions.explanation: Critical ACEI monitoring in CKD: Cr and K+ within 1-2 weeks of initiation/dose changes. Accept up to 30% Cr rise if stable. Hold if Cr >30-35% or K+ >5.5-6.0. CKD patients higher risk hyperkalemia, AKI. B wrong: Insufficient. C wrong: LFTs not primary. D wrong: Monitoring essential.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with resistant HTN on lisinopril 40 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, chlorthalidone 25 mg has BP 156/94. Labs: K+ 3.2, normal renal function. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Increase chlorthalidone to 50 mg
B. Stop all, start different class
C. Add spironolactone 25 mg, monitor K+
D. Add clonidine fourth-line agent
questions.explanation: Resistant HTN (uncontrolled on ≥3 drugs including diuretic): Spironolactone effective fourthline. Corrects volume retention, aldosterone escape. Check K+ baseline, 1 week, 4 weeks, regularly. Contraindications: K+ >5.0, severe CKD (CrCl <30). Current hypokalemia will improve. A wrong: Adequate dose already. B wrong: Premature. D wrong: Not preferred fourth-line.

questions.question: A 62-year-old with long-standing HTN develops new HF (LVEF 35%). Takes amlodipine 10 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg. What change is MOST important?
options: A. Initiate ACEI and beta-blocker, transition to furosemide PRN
B. Continue current regimen for familiarity
C. Add digoxin immediately for support
D. Double amlodipine dose for control
questions.explanation: New HFrEF requires GDMT: ACEI + beta-blocker mandatory for mortality benefit (start ACEI first, add beta-blocker when stable). Amlodipine/felodipine safe in HFrEF if needed. Switch thiazide to loop if volume overload. Add MRA if persistent symptoms. B wrong: Misses life-saving therapy. C wrong: Not first-line. D wrong: Wrong priority.

questions.question: A 70-year-old on warfarin (INR 2.5) for AF takes amoxicillin 500 mg TID for dental infection. Day 5, INR 4.8 without bleeding. What mechanism?
options: A. Amoxicillin induces hepatic metabolism
B. Antibiotics kill gut flora reducing vitamin K synthesis
C. Direct drug interaction at protein binding
D. Amoxicillin has intrinsic anticoagulant properties
questions.explanation: Antibiotics (especially broad-spectrum) reduce gut bacteria synthesizing vitamin K → decreased vitamin K → enhanced warfarin effect → increased INR. More frequent INR monitoring during antibiotics. INR 4.5-10 without bleeding: Hold 1-2 doses, recheck, resume lower dose. A wrong: Opposite. C, D wrong: Not primary mechanisms.

questions.question: A 58-year-old HFrEF with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 4) needs anticoagulation. CrCl 35 mL/min. Which DOAC is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Apixaban 2.5 mg BID adjusted for renal
B. Dabigatran 150 mg BID standard
C. Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily unchanged
D. Edoxaban 60 mg daily standard
questions.explanation: Apixaban PREFERRED in moderate-severe CKD (least renal 27%). Dose: 2.5 mg BID if CrCl 15-29 OR 2 of 3 (age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, Cr ≥1.5). CrCl 30-50 can use 5 mg BID unless meets reduction criteria. B wrong: Dabigatran 80% renal, avoid CrCl <30. C wrong: Needs reduction. D wrong: Reduce to 30 mg.

questions.question: A 65-year-old post-MI (3 weeks) on aspirin 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg BID develops melena, Hgb 14→10 g/dL. Endoscopy shows duodenal ulcer. What antiplatelet management is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Continue dual antiplatelet unchanged despite bleeding
B. Temporarily hold, treat ulcer with PPI, resume when healed (ideally 3-5 days if low-risk)
C. Hold both permanently, avoid all antiplatelets
D. Switch to warfarin monotherapy instead
questions.explanation: Post-MI DAPT balance bleeding vs thrombotic risk: (1) Hold temporarily during active GI bleed, (2) Treat ulcer: High-dose PPI (omeprazole 40 mg BID→daily), H. pylori eradication, (3) Resume DAPT as soon as safe (ideally 3-5 days low-risk, 7-14 days highrisk), (4) Continue PPI. Early post-MI has high ischemic risk. A wrong: Active bleeding requires holding. C wrong: Increases MI risk. D wrong: Inappropriate

questions.question: A 48-year-old with Prinzmetal angina uses SL nitroglycerin PRN. He starts sildenafil for ED. What is PRIMARY concern?
options: A. Severe hypotension from additive vasodilation - nitrates contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitors
B. No interaction concerns exist
C. Increased coronary vasospasm risk
D. Reduced nitrate efficacy for angina
questions.explanation: ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION: PDE-5 inhibitors + nitrates → severe life-threatening hypotension. Both increase cGMP vasodilation. Hypotension can last 24-48 hours. Wait 24 hours after sildenafil, 48 hours after tadalafil before nitrates. Educate patients. B wrong: Major interaction. C, D wrong: Not primary concerns.

questions.question: A 55-year-old develops rash, fever, eosinophilia, elevated Cr 3 weeks after starting allopurinol for gout. What represents this?
options: A. Normal allopurinol response, continue
B. Unrelated viral infection needing antibiotics
C. DRESS syndrome - stop allopurinol immediately
D. Gout flare requiring prednisone increase
questions.explanation: Allopurinol hypersensitivity (DRESS): Rash, fever, eosinophilia, multi-organ involvement (hepatitis, nephritis, vasculitis). Potentially fatal. Risk: CKD, thiazide, HLA-B*5801. STOP allopurinol immediately, supportive care, systemic corticosteroids if severe. Alternative: Febuxostat (cross-reactivity possible). A wrong: Serious adverse reaction. B, D wrong: Misdiagnosis.

questions.question: A 67-year-old HFrEF on digoxin 0.125 mg starts amiodarone 400 mg for AF. What digoxin management is REQUIRED?
options: A. Reduce digoxin 50%, monitor level closely
B. No dose change needed
C. Increase digoxin for synergy
D. Stop digoxin, continue amiodarone
questions.explanation: Amiodarone-digoxin interaction: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein → reduces renal digoxin clearance → doubles levels. REDUCE digoxin 50% (0.125 mg → 0.0625 mg or every other day) when starting amiodarone. Monitor level 1-2 weeks, target 0.5-0.9 ng/mL. Watch toxicity signs. B wrong: Will cause toxicity. C wrong: Dangerous. D wrong: Can continue with adjustment.

questions.question: A 72-year-old with persistent AF, HFrEF wants to stop warfarin. CrCl 42 mL/min, weight 68 kg, no prior bleeding. Which DOAC regimen is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Dabigatran 150 mg BID standard
B. Apixaban 5 mg BID without adjustment
C. Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily unchanged
D. Apixaban 2.5 mg BID dose reduction
questions.explanation: Apixaban dosing: Standard 5 mg BID UNLESS 2 of 3: (1) Age ≥80, (2) Weight ≤60 kg, (3) Cr ≥1.5 mg/dL. This patient: Age 72, weight 68 kg, CrCl 42. Only CrCl reduced but doesn't meet 2 of 3 → use 5 mg BID. A wrong: Dabigatran avoid CrCl <50 for AF. C wrong: Rivaroxaban reduce 15 mg if CrCl 30-49. D wrong: Doesn't meet criteria.

questions.question: A 58-year-old with severe AS (area 0.7 cm², gradient 52 mmHg) and hypertension (BP 168/92) needs BP control pre-valve replacement. Which is SAFEST?
options: A. Dihydropyridine CCB - gentle BP reduction
B. Aggressive high-dose furosemide diuresis
C. Potent vasodilators for afterload reduction
D. Aggressive beta-blockade primary treatment
questions.explanation: Severe AS: Avoid excessive preload/afterload reduction (fixed CO dependent on preload, compensatory LVH needs afterload). CCBs allow gentle BP control. Avoid: Aggressive diuretics (reduce preload), potent vasodilators (excessive afterload reduction), aggressive beta-blockade (reduce compensatory tachycardia). ACEIs/ARBs cautiously if tolerated. Definitive: Valve replacement. B, C, D wrong: Compromise hemodynamics.

questions.question: A 45-year-old marathon runner with hypertension (BP 156/94) has resting HR 48 bpm. Which antihypertensive should be AVOIDED?
options: A. Beta-blockers further reducing low HR
B. Amlodipine causing reflex tachycardia
C. Lisinopril with minimal HR effects
D. Hydrochlorothiazide for volume control
questions.explanation: Athletic bradycardia common in endurance athletes. Beta-blockers further reduce HR → excessive bradycardia (<50), fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance. Preferred in athletes: CCBs (amlodipine), ACEIs, ARBs, thiazides. Non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) also reduce HR - use cautiously. B, C, D wrong: Appropriate choices.

questions.question: A 68-year-old HFrEF starts sacubitril/valsartan. Week 1: BP 92/58, lightheadedness standing. No volume overload. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Temporarily reduce dose, ensure hydration, reassess
B. Stop sacubitril/valsartan permanently now
C. Add midodrine for vasopressor support
D. Increase dose for better efficacy
questions.explanation: Sacubitril/valsartan frequently causes initial hypotension. Management: (1) Reduce dose temporarily (97/103 mg BID → 49/51 mg BID), (2) Ensure hydration, (3) Reduce other vasodilators, (4) Reassess 1-2 weeks - many accommodate. Target 97/103 mg BID for optimal benefit. Complete discontinuation premature. B wrong: Too aggressive. C wrong: Rarely needed. D wrong: Worsens hypotension.

questions.question: A 52-year-old HFrEF post-MI has LVEF 32%. Intolerant to ACEIs (angioedema) and ARBs (severe cough). What alternative RAAS modulation?
options: A. Hydralazine-isosorbide dinitrate combination provides vasodilation
B. No alternative exists, avoid RAAS
C. Calcium channel blocker sufficient
D. Spironolactone alone for RAAS blockade
questions.explanation: ACEI/ARB intolerance: Hydralazine-ISDN alternative. Proven in: (1) African Americans with HFrEF added to ACEI + BB (A-HeFT), (2) ACEI/ARB-intolerant (V-HeFT). Dose: Hydralazine 75 mg + ISDN 40 mg TID, titrate to 75-100 mg/40 mg TID. Side effects: Headache, lupus-like syndrome. B wrong: Alternative exists. C, D wrong: Insufficient alone.

questions.question: A 60-year-old with new AF (HR 140) and mild HFrEF (LVEF 40%) needs immediate rate control. Which agent provides rate control WITHOUT worsening HF?
options: A. Metoprolol IV for rate and rhythm
B. Diltiazem IV bolus then infusion
C. Verapamil IV push immediate effect
D. Amiodarone IV loading both rate/rhythm
questions.explanation: AF with HFrEF rate control: Beta-blockers (metoprolol, esmolol) or amiodarone PREFERRED. Avoid non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) in HFrEF - negative inotropes worsen hemodynamics. Digoxin option for stable patients. Emergency cardioversion if unstable. Metoprolol IV: 2.5-5 mg over 2 min, repeat Q5min PRN (max 15 mg). B, C wrong: Non-DHP CCBs contraindicated HFrEF. D wrong: Acceptable but slower onset.

questions.question: A 70-year-old on warfarin (INR 2-3) for mechanical mitral valve takes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for UTI. Day 4, INR 6.2 with epistaxis (minor). What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Hold warfarin 1-2 doses, give vitamin K 2.5 mg PO, recheck 24 hours
B. Continue warfarin, bleeding minor
C. Give fresh frozen plasma immediately
D. Stop warfarin, switch to DOAC
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim inhibits CYP2C9 → increased warfarin. INR 6-10 with minor bleeding: Hold 1-2 doses, give low-dose vitamin K (2.5 mg PO or 1-2 mg IV), recheck 24 hours. Resume lower dose when therapeutic. Major bleeding or INR >10: vitamin K 5-10 mg IV + consider 4-factor PCC or FFP. B wrong: Must address elevated INR. C wrong: Reserved for life-threatening. D wrong: DOACs contraindicated mechanical valves.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with CAD stable angina takes metoprolol 100 mg BID, amlodipine 10 mg, aspirin, atorvastatin. Angina persists with exertion. What is MOST appropriate addition?
options: A. Long-acting nitrate for additional vasodilation
B. Short-acting nifedipine for symptom relief
C. Increase beta-blocker to 200 mg BID
D. Stop amlodipine, start diltiazem instead
questions.explanation: Stable angina on beta-blocker + CCB: Add long-acting nitrate (isosorbide mononitrate). Mechanism: Coronary vasodilation, reduced preload. Triple therapy: Beta-blocker + CCB + long-acting nitrate. Avoid short-acting DHP alone (reflex tachycardia worsens angina). If symptoms persist, consider revascularization. B wrong: Reflex tachycardia. C wrong: Already on adequate dose. D wrong: Combining non-DHP CCB + beta-blocker increases bradycardia/AV block risk.

questions.question: A 48-year-old develops acute MI. He took sildenafil 100 mg 18 hours ago. He has chest pain. What is the PRIMARY concern with nitroglycerin?
options: A. Can use nitroglycerin safely now - 24 hours passed
B. Severe hypotension - wait 24 hours after sildenafil before nitrates
C. Increased coronary vasospasm from combination
D. Reduced analgesic effect of nitroglycerin
questions.explanation: ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours tadalafil). PDE-5 inhibitors + nitrates → severe prolonged hypotension (both increase cGMP vasodilation). This patient 18 hours post-sildenafil → CANNOT use nitrates. Alternative pain management: Morphine. Manage MI with antiplatelet, anticoagulation, beta-blocker. A wrong: Must wait full 24 hours. C, D wrong: Not primary concerns.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with chronic stable angina on ranolazine 1000 mg BID, metoprolol, aspirin, statin develops QTc prolongation to 510 ms. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Continue ranolazine - QTc prolongation expected effect
B. Reduce ranolazine dose or discontinue; avoid other QT-prolonging drugs
C. Add amiodarone for rhythm control benefits
D. Increase ranolazine for better anti-anginal effect
questions.explanation: Ranolazine (late sodium current inhibitor) causes dose-dependent QTc prolongation. QTc >500 ms increases torsades risk. Reduce dose (500 mg BID) or discontinue. Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, azole antifungals, macrolides). Use ECG monitoring. Alternative anti-anginals if needed. A wrong: This degree concerning. C wrong: Amiodarone worsens QTc. D wrong: Increases QTc further.

questions.question: A 62-year-old post-CABG (2 weeks ago) has new-onset AF with RVR (HR 135). He's hemodynamically stable, BP 128/78. What is MOST appropriate rate control strategy?
options: A. Metoprolol IV then oral for rate control
B. Immediate DC cardioversion for all post-op AF
C. Diltiazem drip for rapid rate control
D. Observation only without intervention needed
questions.explanation: Post-cardiac surgery AF common (20-40%). Hemodynamically stable → rate control first-line. Beta-blockers preferred (metoprolol IV 2.5-5 mg, then oral). Alternative: Amiodarone. Often self-terminates within days-weeks. Anticoagulation if persists >48 hours or high stroke risk. DC cardioversion if hemodynamically unstable. B wrong: Not first-line if stable. C wrong: Beta-blockers preferred post-op. D wrong: Rate control needed for symptoms.

questions.question: A 58-year-old with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and LVOT obstruction develops AF with RVR (HR 145). Which rate control agent should be AVOIDED?
options: A. Beta-blockers are first-line in HCM
B. Verapamil appropriate in HCM for rate control
C. Dihydropyridine CCBs worsen LVOT obstruction
D. Amiodarone safe alternative for rhythm control
questions.explanation: HCM with LVOT obstruction: AVOID dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine) - potent vasodilation reduces afterload worsening obstruction. Preferred: Beta-blockers (first-line), verapamil, diltiazem (reduce contractility and HR). Disopyramide for refractory symptoms (negative inotrope). Avoid vasodilators (ACEIs, ARBs, nitrates, DHP CCBs). A, B, D wrong: These are appropriate choices.

questions.question: A 45-year-old marathon runner develops palpitations. ECG shows SVT (HR 180). Vagal maneuvers fail. What is first-line pharmacologic treatment?
options: A. Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push followed by saline flush
B. Metoprolol 5 mg IV slowly over 5 minutes
C. Verapamil 10 mg IV over 2 minutes
D. Amiodarone 150 mg IV loading dose
questions.explanation: SVT first-line pharmacologic: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push + saline flush. If no response, 12 mg (can repeat once). Mechanism: Transient AV block terminates reentry. Contraindications: Asthma (bronchospasm), 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sick sinus. Side effects: Transient flushing, dyspnea, chest discomfort (<10 seconds). If ineffective: Verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers. B, C wrong: Second-line. D wrong: Not for acute SVT termination.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with permanent AF, LVEF 35%, CHA2DS2-VASc 5 refuses warfarin due to monitoring. He wants DOAC. CrCl 25 mL/min. Which is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Apixaban 2.5 mg BID adjusted for severe CKD
B. Dabigatran 150 mg BID standard dosing
C. Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily without adjustment
D. No DOAC option - must use warfarin only
questions.explanation: Severe CKD (CrCl 15-29): Apixaban ONLY DOAC approved - 2.5 mg BID. All other DOACs contraindicated or not studied: Dabigatran (avoid CrCl <30), rivaroxaban (avoid CrCl <30), edoxaban (avoid CrCl <30). CrCl <15: Warfarin preferred. Apixaban least renally eliminated (27%). B, C wrong: Contraindicated this GFR. D wrong: Apixaban option exists.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with paroxysmal AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 2) prefers rhythm control over rate control. He's on metoprolol, apixaban. What is MOST appropriate rhythm control strategy?
options: A. Amiodarone for most effective rhythm control
B. Flecainide or propafenone if no structural heart disease
C. Digoxin provides effective rhythm control in AF
D. Sotalol first-line for all AF patients
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal AF rhythm control without structural disease: Flecainide or propafenone (Class IC) first-line. Effective, well-tolerated. CONTRAINDICATED in structural disease (CAD, HF, LVH). Alternative: Sotalol (requires QT monitoring), dofetilide (requires 3-day inpatient initiation). Amiodarone reserved for refractory cases (toxicity concerns). A wrong: Too toxic for first-line. C wrong: Digoxin only rate control. D wrong: Not first-line.

questions.question: A 60-year-old starts amiodarone for AF. What monitoring is REQUIRED due to multi-organ toxicity?
options: A. Only ECG for QT monitoring needed
B. Thyroid function, liver enzymes, pulmonary function, ophthalmologic exams
C. No monitoring required for amiodarone
D. Just annual chest X-ray sufficient
questions.explanation: Amiodarone monitoring: (1) Thyroid (TSH, free T4) baseline, 3-6 months - hypo/hyperthyroidism, (2) LFTs baseline, 6 months - hepatotoxicity, (3) Pulmonary (CXR, PFTs) baseline, annually - pulmonary fibrosis, (4) Ophthalmologic baseline, annually - corneal deposits, optic neuropathy, (5) ECG for QTc. Half-life 40-55 days - toxicity can occur/persist after discontinuation. A, C, D wrong: Insufficient monitoring.

questions.question: A 52-year-old on flecainide for paroxysmal AF develops wide-complex tachycardia. ECG shows very wide QRS (>180 ms). What occurred?
options: A. Normal expected flecainide effect continue
B. Flecainide toxicity causing 1:1 AF conduction with extreme widening
C. Unrelated ventricular tachycardia event
D. Beneficial rhythm control achieved successfully
questions.explanation: Flecainide toxicity/overdose: Extreme QRS widening (sodium channel blockade), 1:1 atrial flutter conduction (paradoxically rapid ventricular rate). Management: Stop flecainide, sodium bicarbonate IV (reverses sodium channel blockade), supportive care. Prevention: Must use with AV nodal blocking agent (beta-blocker, CCB) to prevent 1:1 conduction. A, D wrong: This is toxicity. C wrong: Drug effect not separate VT.

questions.question: A 65-year-old starts dofetilide for AF. What is REQUIRED for safe initiation?
options: A. Can start outpatient with oral loading
B. 3-day inpatient monitoring with continuous telemetry and QT monitoring
C. Single dose at home then follow-up
D. No special precautions needed for dofetilide
questions.explanation: Dofetilide initiation REQUIRES: 3-day inpatient stay with continuous telemetry. Baseline QTc <440 ms, CrCl-based dosing. Monitor QTc 2-3 hours post each dose. Stop if QTc >500 ms or increases >15%. High torsades risk during initiation. Also adjust for renal function, avoid QT-prolonging drugs. Most effective rhythm control drug but complex initiation. A, C, D wrong: Dangerous - must be inpatient.

questions.question: A 58-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 28%) needs rhythm control for persistent AF. Which antiarrhythmic is SAFE in systolic heart failure?
options: A. Flecainide highly effective in HFrEF patients
B. Propafenone safe first-line in HFrEF
C. Amiodarone or dofetilide - only safe options
D. Sotalol preferred in heart failure patients
questions.explanation: AF in HFrEF rhythm control: ONLY amiodarone or dofetilide safe. Class IC (flecainide, propafenone) CONTRAINDICATED in structural heart disease (increase mortality). Sotalol contraindicated in decompensated HF. Dronedarone contraindicated in NYHA III-IV HF (increases mortality). Ablation increasingly used. A, B, D wrong: Contraindicated in HFrEF.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with AF on dabigatran 150 mg BID for 2 years presents with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). What is the SPECIFIC reversal agent?
options: A. Vitamin K 10 mg IV for reversal
B. Andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors
C. Idarucizumab (Praxbind) - specific dabigatran reversal
D. Fresh frozen plasma provides adequate reversal
questions.explanation: Dabigatran reversal: Idarucizumab (Praxbind) - monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity. Dose: 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials). Rapid complete reversal. For Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban): Andexanet alfa. If reversal unavailable: Supportive care, hemodialysis for dabigatran (removes ~60%). A wrong: For warfarin only. B wrong: For Xa inhibitors not dabigatran. D wrong: Inadequate for DOACs.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with unprovoked PE needs anticoagulation. No active cancer, normal renal function. Which duration of anticoagulation is MOST appropriate?
options: A. 3 months then stop for all PEs
B. 6 months minimum then reassess bleeding/clot risk
C. Indefinite anticoagulation always required for any PE
D. 4 weeks sufficient for pulmonary embolism
questions.explanation: Unprovoked VTE (PE/DVT): Minimum 3-6 months, then reassess bleeding risk vs recurrence risk. Unprovoked has ~10%/year recurrence → many candidates for indefinite anticoagulation if low bleeding risk. Provoked (surgery, trauma, temporary risk): 3 months sufficient. Cancer-associated: Indefinite (or until cancer resolved). Reassess periodically. A wrong: May need longer. C wrong: Not always indefinite. D wrong: Insufficient.

questions.question: A 48-year-old with acute PE is hemodynamically stable (BP 118/72, HR 95). Which anticoagulation strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Rivaroxaban 15 mg BID x21 days then 20 mg daily or apixaban 10 mg BID x7 days then 5 mg BID
B. Warfarin monotherapy without bridging required
C. Thrombolytic therapy for all PEs regardless
D. Low-dose aspirin sufficient for stable PE
questions.explanation: Acute PE hemodynamically stable: DOACs first-line (easier than warfarin, no bridging). Rivaroxaban: 15 mg BID x21 days → 20 mg daily. Apixaban: 10 mg BID x7 days → 5 mg BID. Edoxaban/dabigatran require parenteral bridging 5-10 days. Thrombolytics only if massive PE with shock. B wrong: Warfarin requires bridging. C wrong: Only massive/submassive. D wrong: Inadequate.

questions.question: A 62-year-old with active metastatic cancer develops DVT. What is PREFERRED anticoagulation for cancer-associated thrombosis?
options: A. Warfarin standard therapy for all DVT
B. LMWH or DOAC (rivaroxaban, edoxaban) for cancer-associated VTE
C. Aspirin monotherapy sufficient in cancer
D. No anticoagulation needed in cancer patients
questions.explanation: Cancer-associated VTE: LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin) preferred traditionally - lower recurrence vs warfarin. Recent data: Rivaroxaban, edoxaban, apixaban non-inferior with caution in GI/GU cancers (higher bleeding). Avoid warfarin (drug interactions, unstable INR). Duration: Indefinite while active cancer or until resolved. A wrong: Warfarin inferior. C, D wrong: Inadequate/dangerous.

questions.question: A 70-year-old on warfarin for DVT has INR 8.5 without bleeding. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Hold warfarin; give vitamin K 2.5-5 mg PO; recheck INR in 24 hours
B. Continue warfarin at same dose unchanged
C. Give fresh frozen plasma immediately now
D. Stop warfarin permanently, never restart
questions.explanation: INR 5-10 without bleeding: Hold 1-2 doses, give LOW-dose vitamin K 2.5-5 mg PO (or 1-2 mg IV if rapid reversal needed), recheck INR 24 hours. Resume warfarin at lower dose when therapeutic. Avoid high-dose vitamin K (causes warfarin resistance for days). If bleeding or INR >10: Higher vitamin K doses ± clotting factors. B wrong: Must address elevated INR. C wrong: Reserved for active bleeding. D wrong: Can restart after correction.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with unprovoked DVT completes 6 months anticoagulation. He has low bleeding risk (HAS-BLED 1). What determines if anticoagulation should continue?
options: A. Always stop after 6 months for all DVTs
B. Consider indefinite if male gender, proximal DVT, elevated D-dimer
C. Only continue if recurrent DVT occurs first
D. Duration never exceeds 1 year maximum
questions.explanation: Extended anticoagulation decision: Unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk → consider indefinite. Risk factors for recurrence: Male gender (2x risk vs female), proximal DVT/PE vs distal, persistently elevated D-dimer post-treatment, thrombophilia. Reassess bleeding risk periodically. Aspirin if stop anticoagulation (modest protection). A wrong: Many benefit from longer. C wrong: Prevention better than waiting. D wrong: Can continue indefinitely.

questions.question: A 45-year-old develops heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Platelet count drops from 250K to 60K on day 5 of UFH. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Continue heparin - thrombocytopenia will resolve spontaneously
B. Stop all heparin; start alternative anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux)
C. Switch to LMWH for safer alternative
D. Give platelet transfusion to increase count
questions.explanation: HIT (Type II): Immune-mediated, day 5-10 of heparin, platelet drop >50%, HIGH thrombosis risk (30-50%). Management: (1) STOP all heparin (including flushes, LMWH), (2) Start alternative: Argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor), bivalirudin, or fondaparinux, (3) Screen for thrombosis. AVOID platelet transfusion (increases thrombosis). Transition to warfarin only after platelet recovery. A wrong: Dangerous - thrombosis risk. C wrong: LMWH cross-reacts. D wrong: Increases thrombosis.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with AF on warfarin (INR 2.5) needs hip replacement surgery in 5 days. What is MOST appropriate perioperative anticoagulation management?
options: A. Continue warfarin through surgery for stroke prevention
B. Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op; bridge with LMWH; resume post-op when hemostasis achieved
C. Stop warfarin permanently before any surgery
D. Switch to aspirin for perioperative period only
questions.explanation: Perioperative warfarin: Stop 5 days pre-op (INR <1.5 by surgery). High stroke risk (mechanical valve, AF with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5-6, recent VTE) → bridge with therapeutic LMWH (stop 24h pre-op). Resume warfarin evening of surgery if hemostasis OK, restart LMWH 24-48h post-op until INR therapeutic. DOACs: Stop 1-3 days pre-op based on CrCl, usually no bridging needed. A wrong: Excessive bleeding risk. C, D wrong: Inadequate stroke protection.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with new DVT asks about compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS). What is the evidence?
options: A. Compression stockings strongly prevent PTS - Class I recommendation
B. Recent trials show no benefit from compression stockings for PTS prevention
C. Only use if symptoms develop later
D. Compression increases DVT recurrence risk
questions.explanation: Compression stockings for PTS prevention: Previously recommended but recent SOX trial showed NO benefit vs placebo. Current guidelines don't routinely recommend for PTS prevention. Use for symptom relief if PTS develops (leg pain, swelling, heaviness). Early ambulation encouraged. Focus on adequate anticoagulation. A wrong: Evidence changed. C wrong: Not proven preventive. D wrong: Don't increase recurrence.

questions.question: A 50-year-old develops proximal DVT. Doppler shows extensive clot burden with phlegmasia cerulea dolens (leg severely swollen, cyanotic, painful). What intervention beyond anticoagulation may be considered?
options: A. Anticoagulation alone always sufficient for all DVTs
B. Catheter-directed thrombolysis for limb-threatening extensive DVT
C. Immediate amputation is standard treatment
D. No additional intervention ever indicated
questions.explanation: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens: Massive iliofemoral DVT causing venous gangrene risk. Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis (or pharmacomechanical thrombectomy) to rapidly reduce clot burden, preserve venous valves, reduce PTS risk. Reserved for extensive DVT with limb-threatening features in patients with low bleeding risk. Most DVTs treated with anticoagulation alone. A wrong: Limb-threatening cases may need intervention. C wrong: Thrombolysis may save limb. D wrong: Intervention sometimes indicated.

questions.question: A 60-year-old with CAD takes aspirin 81 mg daily. He develops upper GI bleeding from gastric ulcer (Hgb 9.2 g/dL, hemodynamically stable). What antiplatelet management is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Continue aspirin - benefits outweigh bleeding risk always
B. Hold aspirin temporarily; treat with high-dose PPI; resume aspirin with PPI when healed
C. Stop aspirin permanently after any bleeding
D. Switch to clopidogrel which doesn't cause GI bleeding
questions.explanation: Aspirin + GI bleeding: (1) Hold temporarily during active bleed, (2) Treat ulcer: High-dose PPI (omeprazole 40 mg BID initially → daily), H. pylori eradication if positive, (3) Resume aspirin with PPI when healed (typically 1-2 weeks). For secondary prevention (established CAD), benefit of aspirin usually outweighs bleeding risk with PPI co-therapy. A wrong: Must hold during active bleeding. C wrong: CAD risk high. D wrong: Clopidogrel also causes GI bleeding.

questions.question: A 65-year-old on aspirin plus clopidogrel (DAPT) post-PCI needs urgent cholecystectomy. Last DES placed 8 months ago. What is MOST appropriate perioperative antiplatelet management?
options: A. Stop both aspirin and clopidogrel 7 days before surgery
B. Continue aspirin; hold clopidogrel 5 days pre-op; resume post-op ASAP
C. Stop both permanently before any surgery
D. Continue both through surgery regardless of bleeding
questions.explanation: Perioperative DAPT: Continue aspirin if possible (low bleeding risk procedures). Hold P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel 5 days, ticagrelor 3-5 days, prasugrel 7 days) pre-op. Resume P2Y12 inhibitor post-op as soon as hemostasis adequate (ideally within 24-48 hours). Complete ≥6 months DAPT post-DES before elective surgery if possible. For very high-risk surgery or <6 months post-DES, defer surgery if possible. A, C wrong: Stent thrombosis risk. D wrong: Excessive bleeding.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 4), CAD s/p PCI 2 years ago needs anticoagulation. He's on aspirin 81 mg daily. What is MOST appropriate antithrombotic regimen?
options: A. Warfarin or DOAC monotherapy (stop aspirin) for chronic stable CAD
B. Triple therapy indefinitely (aspirin + clopidogrel + anticoagulant)
C. Aspirin alone sufficient for both indications
D. Clopidogrel alone without anticoagulation adequate
questions.explanation: AF + stable CAD (>1 year post-PCI): Anticoagulation monotherapy sufficient. Adding antiplatelet increases bleeding without additional benefit for stable CAD. Triple therapy (anticoagulant + aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) only for: Immediately post-PCI (1-4 weeks) then transition to DOAC + P2Y12 inhibitor (up to 12 months) then DOAC alone. B wrong: Excessive bleeding risk chronically. C, D wrong: Inadequate stroke prevention.

questions.question: A 58-year-old post-ACS on DAPT (aspirin + ticagrelor) for 6 months develops significant epistaxis requiring ENT cauterization. What is MOST appropriate antiplatelet adjustment?
options: A. Stop both agents permanently after bleeding
B. Continue both unchanged - bleeding unrelated
C. Consider de-escalation to aspirin + clopidogrel (less potent P2Y12 inhibitor)
D. Stop aspirin, continue ticagrelor alone
questions.explanation: DAPT bleeding complications: Consider de-escalation strategies. Ticagrelor/prasugrel → clopidogrel (less potent, lower bleeding). Still maintains DAPT benefit with reduced bleeding. Alternative: Shorten DAPT duration if approaching 12 months. Balance ischemic vs bleeding risk. Complete discontinuation increases thrombotic events. A wrong: Thrombotic risk. B wrong: Bleeding likely related. D wrong: Need dual therapy post-ACS.

questions.question: A 72-year-old with severe AS (valve area 0.6 cm²), LVEF 60%, develops dyspnea. Physical exam shows pulmonary rales. What medication should be used CAUTIOUSLY?
options: A. Aggressive IV furosemide diuresis for pulmonary edema
B. ACE inhibitors or vasodilators with caution - avoid excessive preload/afterload reduction
C. Increase fluids to maintain cardiac output
D. Beta-blockers for rate control primarily
questions.explanation: Severe AS with pulmonary edema: Cautious diuresis - patients preload-dependent. Gentle diuresis (avoid excessive preload reduction causing CO drop). Avoid aggressive vasodilators. Definitive: Valve replacement (SAVR or TAVR). Medical management temporizing. Can use low-dose ACEIs/ARBs cautiously if tolerated. B wrong: Can use cautiously but A more acutely relevant. C wrong: Has pulmonary edema. D wrong: Not primary issue.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with severe chronic AR (aortic regurgitation) is asymptomatic with LVEF 62%. Which medication may help delay surgery?
options: A. Beta-blockers slow heart rate worsening regurgitation
B. Vasodilators (ACEIs, ARBs, dihydropyridine CCBs) reduce afterload and regurgitant volume
C. Aggressive diuresis as primary therapy
D. Digoxin for contractility enhancement
questions.explanation: Chronic AR: Vasodilators (ACEIs, ARBs, dihydropyridine CCBs) reduce afterload → decrease regurgitant volume, reduce LV dilation. May delay surgery in asymptomatic patients. Avoid beta-blockers (bradycardia increases regurgitant time per beat). Surgery indicated for: Symptoms, LVEF <50%, severe LV dilation. A wrong: Beta-blockers worsen AR. C wrong: Not primary strategy. D wrong: Limited role.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with severe symptomatic MS (mitral stenosis, valve area 1.0 cm²) develops AF with RVR (HR 140). Which rate control agent addresses BOTH AF rate AND MS symptoms?
options: A. Beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs slow HR allowing more diastolic filling time
B. Digoxin alone provides adequate rate control
C. Dihydropyridine CCBs for vasodilation benefits
D. No rate control needed in MS
questions.explanation: MS pathophysiology: Fixed obstruction limits LV filling. Need LONGER diastole for filling across stenotic valve. AF with RVR → short diastole → worsening symptoms. Beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem): Slow HR → longer diastolic filling time → improved CO and symptoms. Definitive: Valve intervention (balloon valvotomy or surgery). B wrong: Less effective rate control especially with exertion. C wrong: Don't control HR. D wrong: Rate control crucial.

questions.question: A 45-year-old IV drug user develops acute severe MR (mitral regurgitation) from endocarditis. He's in cardiogenic shock. What medication provides temporary hemodynamic support?
options: A. IV nitroglycerin or nitroprusside reduce afterload and regurgitant volume
B. Aggressive IV fluids for preload augmentation
C. Beta-blockers for rate control primarily
D. Digoxin for inotropic support alone
questions.explanation: Acute severe MR: IV vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside) reduce afterload → decrease regurgitant fraction, increase forward CO. May need inotropes (dobutamine) ± IABP if shock. Definitive: Urgent surgical repair. Chronic compensated MR different (ACEIs/ARBs, diuretics). B wrong: Worsens pulmonary edema. C, D wrong: Inadequate for cardiogenic shock.

questions.question: A 58-year-old post-MI on aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin 80 mg has CK 450 U/L (baseline 120), mild myalgias. Ticagrelor started 3 days ago. What is MOST likely cause?
options: A. Statin-induced myopathy requiring discontinuation
B. Normal post-MI enzyme elevation from cardiac injury
C. Ticagrelor side effect unrelated to muscles
D. Combination drug interaction causing myopathy
questions.explanation: Post-MI: CK elevation expected from myocardial injury. CK peaks 24h, normalizes 3-4 days. Troponin more specific for cardiac vs skeletal muscle. This modest CK (450 U/L, 3.75x baseline) likely residual cardiac injury. True statin myopathy: CK >10x ULN or symptomatic with >5x. If concerned, recheck when further from MI. A wrong: Premature diagnosis. C wrong: Ticagrelor doesn't cause myopathy. D wrong: No significant interaction.

questions.question: A 62-year-old with NSTEMI receives eptifibatide (GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor) during PCI. Post-procedure platelet count drops from 180K to 35K. What complication occurred?
options: A. Drug-induced thrombocytopenia from GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor
B. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
C. Dilutional thrombocytopenia from IV fluids
D. Bone marrow suppression from contrast dye
questions.explanation: GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor thrombocytopenia: Occurs in 0.5-1% (eptifibatide, tirofiban, abciximab). Acute onset (hours), severe (<20K possible). Mechanism: Antibody-mediated. Management: Stop drug, platelet transfusion if bleeding/severe, avoid re-exposure. HIT typically days 5-10, less severe drop. B wrong: Wrong timeline. C wrong: Not this severe. D wrong: Contrast doesn't cause this.

questions.question: A 55-year-old undergoes PCI with drug-eluting stent (DES). What is MINIMUM recommended duration of dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor)?
options: A. 1 month sufficient for all DES
B. 6 months minimum, often 12 months for ACS
C. 3 months then stop P2Y12 inhibitor
D. Lifelong dual antiplatelet always required
questions.explanation: DAPT duration post-DES: Minimum 6 months (stable CAD), 12 months if ACS. Longer (>12 months) if high ischemic risk, low bleeding risk. Aspirin lifelong. Premature P2Y12 inhibitor discontinuation increases stent thrombosis risk (peaks month 1, elevated through 12 months). A, C wrong: Too short. D wrong: Not always lifelong DAPT.

questions.question: A 68-year-old develops acute stent thrombosis 10 days post-PCI with DES placement. He admits stopping clopidogrel 3 days ago for dental procedure. What is mortality risk?
options: A. Stent thrombosis has 5% mortality similar to stable CAD
B. Stent thrombosis 20-45% mortality, often presents as STEMI or sudden death
C. Stent thrombosis is benign, easily treated
D. No mortality risk from stent thrombosis
questions.explanation: Acute/subacute stent thrombosis: Catastrophic complication, 20-45% mortality. Presents as acute STEMI or sudden cardiac death. Risk factors: Premature DAPT discontinuation (MOST important), underexpansion, malapposition. Treatment: Emergent PCI. Prevention: Complete recommended DAPT duration, patient education. Never stop DAPT without cardiology consultation. A, C, D wrong: Underestimate severity.

questions.question: A 70-year-old needs elective colonoscopy. He's on aspirin + clopidogrel post-DES placement 4 months ago. Gastroenterologist requests stopping all antiplatelet therapy 7 days before. What should you recommend?
options: A. Stop both aspirin and clopidogrel as requested
B. Continue aspirin, hold clopidogrel 5 days; defer procedure if possible until 6-12 months post-DES
C. Stop all permanently before any procedure
D. Continue both through procedure regardless
questions.explanation: Elective surgery <12 months post-DES: DEFER if possible. If urgent: Continue aspirin if feasible, hold P2Y12 inhibitor minimum time (clopidogrel 5 days, ticagrelor 3-5 days). Resume immediately post-procedure. Colonoscopy can often be done on aspirin. Communicate stent thrombosis risk to proceduralist. A wrong: Dangerous - stent thrombosis risk. C wrong: Never appropriate. D wrong: Excessive bleeding risk for colonoscopy.

questions.question: A 65-year-old with three-vessel CAD, LVEF 35%, diabetes has chest pain on maximal medical therapy. Which revascularization strategy has better outcomes?
options: A. PCI with multiple stents provides equivalent outcomes
B. CABG superior for multivessel disease with diabetes and reduced LVEF
C. Medical therapy alone preferred over revascularization
D. Both strategies completely equivalent in all patients
questions.explanation: CABG vs PCI in multivessel CAD: CABG superior for: (1) Three-vessel disease, especially with diabetes (FREEDOM trial), (2) Left main disease, (3) Reduced LVEF. PCI reasonable for: 1-2 vessel disease, no diabetes, preserved LVEF, high surgical risk. Heart Team approach for complex CAD. A wrong: PCI inferior in this scenario. C wrong: Symptomatic despite medical therapy. D wrong: Outcomes differ based on anatomy.

questions.question: A 58-year-old post-CABG (day 2) develops new-onset AF with RVR (HR 135). He's hemodynamically stable. What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. Immediate DC cardioversion for all post-op AF
B. Beta-blocker (metoprolol) for rate control, correct electrolytes (K+, Mg2+)
C. Amiodarone loading for rhythm control immediately
D. Observation only without any intervention
questions.explanation: Post-cardiac surgery AF (20-40%): Rate control first-line if stable. Beta-blockers preferred (resume if held perioperatively). Correct electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia). Often self-terminates within days-weeks. Anticoagulation if persists >48h or stroke risk factors. DC cardioversion if hemodynamically unstable. A wrong: Not first-line if stable. C wrong: Rate control before rhythm. D wrong: Rate control needed.

questions.question: A 72-year-old post-CABG has mediastinal chest tube output 400 mL/hour for 2 consecutive hours. What is concerning about this drainage?
options: A. Normal expected post-operative drainage amount
B. Suggests excessive bleeding, may need re-exploration if continues
C. Too little drainage, tube likely occluded
D. No clinical significance, continue observation
questions.explanation: Post-cardiac surgery bleeding: >200 mL/h for 2 hours or >100 mL/h for 4 hours suggests excessive bleeding. Causes: Surgical bleeding, coagulopathy, platelet dysfunction. Evaluate: Coags, platelet count/function, consider re-exploration. Transfusion thresholds: Hgb <7-8 g/dL, platelets <50K if bleeding. A wrong: This is excessive. C wrong: High not low output. D wrong: Requires intervention.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with chronic systolic HF (LVEF 25%) on GDMT develops progressively worsening dyspnea, fatigue. He's euvolemic on exam but symptomatic at rest (NYHA IV). What stage of HF?
options: A. Stage A - at risk but no structural disease
B. Stage B - structural disease, no symptoms
C. Stage C - structural disease with symptoms
D. Stage D - refractory HF despite optimal GDMT
questions.explanation: ACC/AHA HF stages: A (risk factors, no disease), B (structural disease, asymptomatic), C (structural disease with symptoms), D (refractory requiring advanced therapies). Stage D: NYHA III-IV despite optimal GDMT, frequent hospitalizations, refractory symptoms. Options: Inotropes, mechanical support (LVAD), transplant, palliative care. A, B wrong: Earlier stages. C wrong: Stage C is symptomatic but not refractory.

questions.question: A 48-year-old with Stage D HF (LVEF 18%), refractory symptoms despite GDMT is being evaluated for heart transplant. What is ABSOLUTE contraindication?
options: A. Age 48 years (too young for transplant)
B. Active malignancy or recent cancer (<5 years remission)
C. Diabetes mellitus with good control
D. History of treated hepatitis C
questions.explanation: Transplant absolute contraindications: Active infection, active malignancy (most require 5-year remission), irreversible pulmonary hypertension (PVR >5 Wood units unresponsive to vasodilators), severe peripheral vascular disease, active substance abuse, medical non-adherence, inadequate social support. Relative: Age >70, diabetes with end-organ damage, obesity (BMI >35). A wrong: Age 48 appropriate. C, D wrong: Not absolute contraindications.

questions.question: A 67-year-old African American woman presents to cardiology clinic for medication optimization. PMH: HTN (8y), T2DM (12y), Stage 3a CKD (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m²), hyperlipidemia, anterior STEMI 14 months ago (primary PCI with DES to LAD). Current meds: ASA 81mg daily, clopidogrel 75mg daily, atorvastatin 80mg HS, metoprolol succinate 200mg daily, lisinopril 40mg daily, ezetimibe 10mg daily, metformin 1000mg BID. VS: BP 138/84 mmHg, HR 58 bpm. Labs: Na 138, K 4.8, BUN 28, SCr 1.4 (baseline 1.3), glucose 142, TC 142, LDL-C 58, HDL-C 48, TG 180, HbA1c 7.2%, Hgb 11.8, CK 145 U/L (ULN 200). Reports mild bilateral leg cramping started 3 weeks ago. Denies chest pain, dyspnea. Metoprolol increased from 100mg to 200mg six weeks ago. What is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Discontinue atorvastatin, check CK in 2 weeks, rechallenge with rosuvastatin 20mg after symptom resolution
B. Discontinue clopidogrel after >12 months DAPT post-DES; continue ASA monotherapy
C. Add cilostazol 100mg BID for peripheral arterial disease symptoms
D. Reduce metoprolol to 100mg daily for beta-blocker peripheral vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: - DAPT duration post-DES for ACS is minimum 12 months. After 14 months, transition to ASA monotherapy reduces bleeding risk without loss of ischemic protection. The cramping may be DAPT-related (normal CK argues against statin myopathy). A wrong: CK normal (145 U/L), symptoms started recently despite >14mo on same statin dose. C wrong: Cilostazol contraindicated in HF (PDE-3 inhibitor increases mortality). D wrong: Post-MI patients need target-dose beta-blockers indefinitely; symptoms began 3wk ago but dose change 6wk ago.

questions.question: A 58-year-old male with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%, diagnosed 4mo ago after anterior MI) presents to ED with worsening dyspnea x1 week. Meds: Sacubitril/valsartan 97/103mg BID (started 6wk ago after ACEI washout), metoprolol succinate 25mg daily (started 4wk ago), spironolactone 25mg daily, furosemide 40mg daily, ASA 81mg, atorvastatin 40mg HS. VS: BP 88/54 mmHg sitting, 78/48 standing, HR 110 bpm, RR 24, weight 81kg (up 4kg from 2wk ago), O2 sat 91% RA. Exam: JVP 12cm, bilateral crackles, 2+ edema to knees, S3 gallop, hepatomegaly. Labs: Na 132, K 5.6, BUN 48, SCr 2.1 (baseline 1.3 six weeks ago, was 1.5 two weeks ago), BNP 1240 (was 420 six weeks ago), Mg 1.9, TnI 0.04 (negative). Lightheaded when standing, adherent to meds/low-salt diet. What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. D/C sacubitril/valsartan and spironolactone; IV furosemide 80mg bolus then infusion; hold metoprolol; treat hyperkalemia with insulin/dextrose and kayexalate
B. Reduce sacubitril/valsartan to 49/51mg BID; continue metoprolol and spironolactone; switch to IV furosemide and add metolazone 5mg daily
C. D/C metoprolol; reduce sacubitril/valsartan to 49/51mg BID; continue spironolactone; IV furosemide and optimize volume before adjusting GDMT
