D. Hold sacubitril/valsartan; reduce spironolactone to 12.5mg daily; continue metoprolol; start dobutamine infusion with IV diuresis
questions.explanation: - In acute decompensated HFrEF with hypotension: (1) Hold beta-blocker FIRST (most contributes to hypotension), (2) Reduce (don't stop) sacubitril/valsartan dose, (3) Continue spironolactone (K 5.6 manageable with diuresis), (4) Aggressive IV diuresis. A wrong: Complete d/c of sacubitril/valsartan excessive (hard to restart); kayexalate unnecessary for K 5.6. B wrong: Continuing metoprolol with BP 88/54 and orthostatic hypotension dangerous. D wrong: Dobutamine not first-line for "cold and wet" - needs diuresis primarily.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman presents to ED with sudden severe chest pain 2 hours ago while swimming. Describes sharp, tearing pain radiating to back between shoulder blades, 10/10 severity. PMH: Bicuspid aortic valve (diagnosed 5y ago on echo), HTN diagnosed 3mo ago (untreated). VS: BP right arm 182/98 mmHg, left arm 146/82, HR 108, RR 26, O2 sat 94% RA. Exam: Severe distress, diaphoretic. Cardiac: Regular rhythm, early diastolic murmur LSB. Pulses: Right radial 2+, left radial 1+, both femorals 2+. Neuro: A&Ox3;, no deficits. Labs: TnI 0.08 (ULN 0.04), D-dimer 2800. ECG: Sinus tach, no ST changes. CT angiography: Stanford Type A aortic dissection 2cm above aortic valve extending through ascending aorta into arch, dissection flap in right brachiocephalic artery, no pericardial effusion, aortic root 4.2cm. Cardiothoracic surgery consulted, estimated 2-3h to OR. What is MOST appropriate initial pharmacologic intervention?
options: A. Labetalol IV 20mg bolus over 2min, then infusion titrated to HR <60 and SBP 100-120; avoid vasodilator monotherapy
B. Esmolol IV loading 500mcg/kg over 1min, then infusion 50-300mcg/kg/min; once HR <60, add nitroprusside 0.3mcg/kg/min for BP control
C. Diltiazem IV 0.25mg/kg over 2min for rate control, then nicardipine 5mg/hr for BP control
D. Morphine 4-8mg IV for pain; nitroglycerin infusion 10mcg/min for BP management
questions.explanation: - Acute Type A dissection requires BETA-BLOCKADE FIRST to reduce dP/dt (force of contraction), THEN vasodilation for BP. Esmolol preferred (ultra-short t½, rapid titration). Target HR <60 BEFORE adding nitroprusside for SBP 100-120. A wrong: Labetalol (combined α/β) less precise - simultaneous alpha blockade can cause reflex tachycardia before adequate beta-blockade. C wrong: DANGEROUS - diltiazem inadequate beta-blockade; nicardipine without prior beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia, increased dP/dt, risk of dissection propagation. D wrong: Vasodilator without beta-blocker absolutely contraindicated - causes reflex sympathetic activation and increased shear stress.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with permanent AF (CHA2DS2-VASc=6), LVEF 42%, and mechanical mitral valve on warfarin (INR goal 2.5-3.5) needs urgent hip replacement for displaced femoral neck fracture. Surgery scheduled in 5 days. Current meds: Warfarin 5mg daily (INR today 2.8), metoprolol 50mg BID, apixaban recently switched TO warfarin 3 weeks ago. PMH: HTN, T2DM, prior ischemic stroke 2y ago, CKD stage 3 (eGFR 48). No active bleeding. What is MOST appropriate perioperative anticoagulation strategy?
options: A. Continue warfarin through surgery at current dose for stroke prevention given high thromboembolic risk
B. Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op; bridge with therapeutic enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC Q12h (last dose 24h pre-op); resume warfarin evening of surgery; restart enoxaparin 24-48h post-op until INR therapeutic
C. Stop warfarin 3 days pre-op; no bridging needed since CHA2DS2-VASc <5 indicates low risk
D. Stop warfarin permanently; switch to apixaban 5mg BID long-term starting day after surgery
questions.explanation: - Mechanical mitral valve = HIGH thromboembolic risk requiring bridging. Protocol: (1) Stop warfarin 5d pre-op (allows INR <1.5 by surgery), (2) Start therapeutic LMWH when INR <2.0, (3) Last LMWH dose 24h pre-op, (4) Resume warfarin evening of surgery if hemostasis adequate, (5) Restart LMWH 24-48h post-op, (6) Continue LMWH until INR therapeutic. A wrong: Continuing warfarin through surgery = excessive bleeding risk. C wrong: CHA2DS2-VASc irrelevant - MECHANICAL valve status determines bridging need (very high thrombosis risk); 3 days insufficient for INR normalization. D wrong: DOACs contraindicated with mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN trial showed increased thrombosis/bleeding).

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman with recently diagnosed non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 32% on echo 8 weeks ago, etiology unclear) presents for HF clinic follow-up. Started on GDMT 7 weeks ago. Current meds: Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51mg BID, carvedilol 6.25mg BID, spironolactone 25mg daily, furosemide 40mg daily. NYHA class III symptoms (dyspnea with minimal exertion). VS: BP 102/64, HR 68, weight stable. Labs: Na 136, K 4.2, BUN 24, SCr 1.1 (baseline), BNP 890 (down from 1450 at diagnosis). No ischemic symptoms. She asks about ICD for sudden death prevention. What is MOST appropriate recommendation regarding ICD?
options: A. Implant ICD now - meets criteria with LVEF ≤35% and NYHA III on optimal medical therapy
B. Defer ICD decision; continue optimizing GDMT for at least 3-6 months total to allow LV reverse remodeling; reassess LVEF
C. ICD not indicated in non-ischemic cardiomyopathy regardless of LVEF or symptoms
D. Proceed with CRT-D implantation for combined resynchronization and defibrillation therapy
questions.explanation: Primary prevention ICD in non-ischemic CMP requires LVEF ≤35% on optimal GDMT for ≥3 months (some recommend 6-9mo) to allow reverse remodeling. This patient only 7-8 weeks on GDMT with recent diagnosis - must defer ICD and reassess LVEF after adequate trial of medical therapy. BNP improving suggests potential for recovery. A wrong: Too early - insufficient time on GDMT. Many patients with new non-ischemic CMP improve LVEF with medical therapy. C wrong: ICD indicated in non-ischemic CMP if LVEF ≤35% after adequate GDMT trial (SCD-HeFT showed benefit). D wrong: No indication for CRT (need LBBB with QRS ≥150ms or QRS ≥120ms with LBBB to benefit; not mentioned in case).

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with history of anterior STEMI 11 months ago (treated with PCI and DES) presents for cardiology follow-up. Post-MI echo showed LVEF 33%. Currently on: ASA 81mg, ticagrelor 90mg BID, metoprolol succinate 200mg daily, lisinopril 40mg daily, atorvastatin 80mg, eplerenone 50mg daily. NYHA class II symptoms, tolerates medications well. Repeat echo today shows LVEF 34%, no wall motion abnormalities beyond prior infarct territory. VS: BP 118/72, HR 62. Labs: Na 139, K 4.4, Cr 0.9, BNP 180. What is MOST appropriate next step regarding device therapy?
options: A. No ICD indicated - must wait until 12 months post-MI before considering primary prevention ICD
B. Implant single-chamber ICD for primary prevention
C. Implant CRT-D for biventricular pacing benefit in addition to defibrillation
D. Defer ICD indefinitely - LVEF too close to 35% cutoff and patient only NYHA class II
questions.explanation: - Primary prevention ICD criteria (ischemic CMP): LVEF ≤35%, ≥40 days post-MI (or ≥3mo post-revascularization), NYHA II-III on optimal GDMT ≥3 months, life expectancy >1y with good functional status. This patient 11 months post-MI with LVEF 33-34% on stable GDMT meets all criteria. MADIT-II and SCD-HeFT showed 30% mortality reduction. A wrong: 40 days sufficient, not 12 months (would delay beneficial therapy 1 month). C wrong: No CRT indication - needs LBBB with QRS ≥150ms or QRS ≥120-149ms with LBBB for benefit (not mentioned). D wrong: LVEF 33-34% clearly ≤35%; NYHA II qualifies (NYHA I doesn't, NYHA IV only if transplant candidate).

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (valve area 0.7cm², mean gradient 52mmHg, peak velocity 4.8 m/s) and LVEF 55% is being evaluated for intervention. PMH: HTN, CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38), COPD (FEV1 55% predicted), frailty (slow gait speed, recent 10-lb weight loss). STS risk score 14% (high surgical risk). She has exertional dyspnea limiting ADLs, denies syncope/angina. Cardiology and cardiac surgery consulted. What is MOST appropriate intervention?
options: A. Surgical AVR remains standard of care regardless of surgical risk in symptomatic severe AS
B. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) - now approved for high, intermediate, and low surgical risk; preferred given STS score 14%
C. Medical management with diuretics and beta-blockers; defer intervention due to prohibitive risk
D. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy for this high-risk patient
questions.explanation: - TAVR now approved for severe symptomatic AS across all surgical risk categories. For high-risk patients (STS >8-10%), TAVR preferred over SAVR due to lower perioperative mortality, shorter recovery. PARTNER trials showed non-inferiority to surgery even in low-risk patients. STS 14% = high risk. A wrong: TAVR has replaced SAVR as preferred option in high/prohibitive surgical risk patients. C wrong: Symptomatic severe AS has 50% 2-year mortality without intervention - medical management inadequate. This patient not prohibitive risk (would require inability to survive procedure). D wrong: Balloon valvuloplasty palliative only (rapid restenosis 6-12mo) - reserved for bridge to TAVR/SAVR or destination palliation in prohibitive-risk patients.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease and severe mitral stenosis (valve area 1.1cm², mean gradient 14mmHg) has progressive dyspnea NYHA III. Echo shows: Pliable valve leaflets, minimal calcification, no/mild mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus on TEE, Wilkins score 6. Atrial fibrillation (chronic, rate-controlled on metoprolol). What is MOST appropriate definitive intervention?
options: A. Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty (PMBV)
B. Surgical mitral valve replacement required for all severe symptomatic MS
C. Medical management with diuretics and rate control sufficient for MS
D. Mitral valve repair via surgical commissurotomy as first-line
questions.explanation: - PMBV first-line for symptomatic severe MS with favorable anatomy: (1) Pliable non-calcified valve, (2) Minimal MR, (3) No LA thrombus, (4) Wilkins score ≤8. Results comparable to surgery with less morbidity. Contraindications: Heavy calcification, moderate-severe MR, LA thrombus, Wilkins score >8. B wrong: Surgery reserved for unfavorable anatomy, failed PMBV, or concomitant severe MR. C wrong: Symptomatic severe MS needs mechanical relief - medical management temporizing only (rate control helps but doesn't address obstruction). D wrong: Open surgical commissurotomy largely replaced by PMBV due to lower morbidity; surgery reserved for unsuitable PMBV candidates.

questions.question: A 45-year-old IV drug user presents with fever (39.2°C), new systolic murmur, and multiple septic pulmonary emboli on chest CT. Blood cultures: 4/4 bottles growing Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible). TEE shows 1.4cm vegetation on tricuspid valve with severe tricuspid regurgitation. Started on IV nafcillin. Infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery consulted. What is recommended DURATION of IV antibiotic therapy for right-sided native valve endocarditis with MSSA?
options: A. 2 weeks IV nafcillin sufficient for uncomplicated right-sided MSSA endocarditis
B. 4-6 weeks IV nafcillin standard for native valve endocarditis regardless of valve location
C. 6-8 weeks required for all endocarditis cases involving IV drug users
D. Oral antibiotics can replace IV after 2 weeks if blood cultures negative
questions.explanation: - Native valve endocarditis requires 4-6 weeks IV antibiotics. MSSA: Nafcillin or oxacillin 12g/day divided Q4-6h. Right-sided IE (tricuspid) in IVDU: Some data support 2-week short-course for UNCOMPLICATED cases (no extracardiac complications, vegetation <2cm, rapid defervescence, no immunosuppression), BUT this patient has SEVERE TR and large 1.4cm vegetation - NOT uncomplicated. Standard 4-6 weeks appropriate. A wrong: Only for truly uncomplicated right-sided IE; this case has severe TR. C wrong: 6-8 weeks for prosthetic valve IE, not native valve. D wrong: Must complete full IV course; oral step-down not validated for IE.

questions.question: A 52-year-old with known mitral valve prolapse (MVP) with moderate mitral regurgitation needs dental extraction for infected tooth. No prior history of endocarditis. No prosthetic valves, no cardiac devices. Otherwise healthy. Asks about antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedure. What is MOST appropriate recommendation per current guidelines?
options: A. Amoxicillin 2g PO 30-60min before procedure - all MVP patients need prophylaxis for dental procedures
B. No antibiotic prophylaxis needed - MVP with MR not an indication; only prior IE, prosthetic valve, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, or cardiac transplant with valvulopathy qualify
C. Clindamycin 600mg PO if penicillin allergic, required for any valvular disease
D. Prophylaxis required for extraction but not routine dental cleaning
questions.explanation: - 2007 AHA guidelines RESTRICTED IE prophylaxis to highest-risk only: (1) Prior IE, (2) Prosthetic cardiac valve, (3) Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, (4) Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy. Prophylaxis NO LONGER recommended for: Acquired valvular disease (including MVP with MR), bicuspid aortic valve, most CHD. Procedures requiring prophylaxis (in high-risk patients): Dental with gingival manipulation, respiratory tract involving incision/biopsy. A, C wrong: MVP not an indication even with MR. D wrong: Type of dental procedure irrelevant since patient doesn't meet high-risk criteria.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation with known severe mitral stenosis (valve area 0.9cm²) from rheumatic heart disease presents with acute dyspnea, orthopnea, and pulmonary edema. HR 130 bpm (atrial fibrillation with RVR), BP 138/88, O2 sat 88% on RA. Exam: Bilateral rales, elevated JVP. Echo: Same severe MS, elevated PA pressure 65/35 mmHg. Fetus doing well per OB. What is MOST appropriate acute management strategy?
options: A. Immediate delivery via C-section to relieve cardiovascular stress
B. Aggressive IV diuresis, IV metoprolol for rate control; if refractory, consider percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty during pregnancy
C. Start nitroprusside infusion for afterload reduction in acute pulmonary edema
D. Initiate ACE inhibitor therapy for heart failure management
questions.explanation: - Acute decompensation of MS in pregnancy: (1) Aggressive rate control (betablocker/digoxin - slow HR to maximize diastolic filling time across stenotic valve), (2) Diuretics for pulmonary edema, (3) If refractory to medical therapy: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty (PBMV) can be performed during pregnancy (preferably 2nd trimester, minimize radiation). AF with RVR dramatically worsens MS (short diastole → inadequate LA emptying). A wrong: Premature delivery at 28 weeks increases neonatal morbidity/mortality; optimize mother first. C wrong: Nitroprusside contraindicated in pregnancy (cyanide toxicity to fetus). D wrong: ACEIs contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic - renal agenesis, oligohydramnios).

questions.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 34 weeks gestation with chronic hypertension develops new-onset severe headache, visual disturbances (blurry vision, scotomata), and epigastric pain. VS: BP 172/108 mmHg, HR 98, RR 18. Previously well-controlled BP on methyldopa 500mg TID. Exam: 3+ reflexes, mild periorbital edema. Labs: Platelets 89,000 (baseline 220,000 two weeks ago), AST 156 U/L, ALT 142 U/L, LDH 520 U/L, Cr 1.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), urine protein/Cr ratio 0.8. Fetal monitoring reassuring. What is MOST likely diagnosis and appropriate acute management?
options: A. Chronic hypertension exacerbation; increase methyldopa dose and monitor closely
B. Preeclampsia with severe features; IV magnesium sulfate, IV antihypertensives (labetalol/hydralazine), plan for delivery
C. HELLP syndrome variant; expectant management until 37 weeks for fetal maturity
D. Eclampsia; immediate delivery regardless of gestational age without seizure prophylaxis
questions.explanation: - Preeclampsia with severe features: New HTN (≥140/90) after 20 weeks with proteinuria OR end-organ dysfunction. Severe features: BP ≥160/110, thrombocytopenia (<100K), elevated transaminases (>2x ULN), renal insufficiency, cerebral/visual symptoms, pulmonary edema. Management: (1) IV MgSO4 4-6g load then 1-2g/h (seizure prophylaxis), (2) Acute severe HTN treatment (labetalol/hydralazine, target SBP 140-150), (3) Delivery (definitive cure - timing based on severity and gestational age; ≥34 weeks with severe features → deliver). A wrong: This is preeclampsia with severe features, not simple chronic HTN. C wrong: HELLP present (hemolysis=LDH, elevated LFTs, low platelets) but requires delivery, not expectant management at 34 weeks with severe features. D wrong: Not eclampsia (no seizures); MgSO4 needed for seizure prophylaxis.

questions.question: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 36 weeks gestation with preeclampsia (BP 168/102, proteinuria) is started on IV magnesium sulfate 4g loading dose over 20 minutes, followed by maintenance infusion at 2g/hour for seizure prophylaxis. Two hours into infusion, she develops absent deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate 8/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. What is MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: A. Continue magnesium - these are expected therapeutic effects indicating adequate levels
B. Stop magnesium immediately; administer calcium gluconate 1g IV slowly over 3-5 minutes as antidote
C. Reduce magnesium infusion rate to 1g/hour and continue monitoring
D. Intubate patient immediately before administering any antidote
questions.explanation: - Magnesium toxicity! Therapeutic Mg level 4-7 mEq/L. Toxicity signs: (1) Loss of DTRs (8-10 mEq/L), (2) Respiratory depression (10-15 mEq/L), (3) Cardiac arrest (>15 mEq/L). Management: STOP magnesium immediately, give calcium gluconate 1g (10mL of 10% solution) IV over 3-5min as antidote (antagonizes Mg effects at neuromuscular junction and myocardium). Monitor: Reflexes, RR, UOP, Mg level. A wrong: Absent reflexes and respiratory depression = TOXICITY not therapeutic effect. C wrong: Must stop completely and give antidote - reducing rate insufficient for acute toxicity with respiratory compromise. D wrong: Give calcium first (may reverse respiratory depression); intubate if no improvement.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with new-onset atrial fibrillation (HR 142 bpm) and LVEF 58% presents to ED. Symptom onset 8 hours ago per patient (palpitations, lightheadedness). Hemodynamically stable (BP 132/78, alert, no chest pain). PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia. CHA2DS2-VASc score = 3 (age 62-74, male, HTN). TEE not performed. What is appropriate management regarding anticoagulation and cardioversion?
options: A. Immediate electrical cardioversion without anticoagulation since symptom onset <12 hours

B. Start therapeutic anticoagulation; cardiovert after 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation OR perform TEE to exclude LA thrombus, then cardiovert; continue anticoagulation ≥4 weeks post-cardioversion
C. Rate control only; cardioversion not indicated for first AF episode
D. Cardiovert immediately with heparin bolus; no need for post-cardioversion anticoagulation
questions.explanation: - AF >48h (or unknown duration, which includes this 8h by patient report - often unreliable): Two options: (1) 3 weeks therapeutic anticoagulation → cardioversion → ≥4 weeks anticoagulation post-cardioversion, OR (2) TEE to exclude LA/LAA thrombus → if negative, cardiovert on therapeutic anticoagulation → ≥4 weeks post-cardioversion. Continue long-term anticoagulation per CHA2DS2-VASc (score 3 → anticoagulate). Post-cardioversion anticoagulation essential due to atrial stunning (delayed thrombus formation risk). A wrong: Patient report of 8h unreliable; actual duration often longer. C wrong: Cardioversion reasonable in new-onset symptomatic AF. D wrong: Heparin bolus insufficient; need ≥4 weeks post-cardioversion.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (frequent episodes despite metoprolol 100mg BID) desires rhythm control. She has no structural heart disease (normal LVEF, no CAD, no LVH). CHA2DS2-VASc score 2 (age, female gender). On apixaban 5mg BID. What is MOST appropriate first-line antiarrhythmic for rhythm control?
options: A. Amiodarone 400mg daily - most effective antiarrhythmic for AF rhythm control
B. Flecainide 100mg BID or propafenone 225mg TID
C. Sotalol 80mg BID - dual class II/III effects provide superior efficacy
D. Dofetilide 500mcg BID after appropriate monitoring
questions.explanation: - Rhythm control in paroxysmal AF WITHOUT structural heart disease: Class IC agents (flecainide, propafenone) first-line. Well-tolerated, effective. ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION in structural heart disease (CAD, HF, significant LVH) due to increased mortality. Must use with AV nodal blocking agent (beta-blocker/CCB) to prevent 1:1 atrial flutter conduction. A wrong: Amiodarone very effective but reserved for refractory cases due to multi-organ toxicity (thyroid, pulmonary, hepatic, ocular, skin). C wrong: Sotalol requires QT monitoring; not preferred first-line. D wrong: Dofetilide requires 3-day inpatient initiation with continuous telemetry and QTc monitoring - too intensive for first-line.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with persistent atrial fibrillation and HFrEF (LVEF 28%) is being considered for rhythm control. Currently on sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, furosemide, apixaban. NYHA class II-III despite GDMT. Which antiarrhythmic agent is SAFE to use in this patient with systolic heart failure?
options: A. Flecainide 100mg BID - well-tolerated with good efficacy
B. Propafenone 225mg TID - Class IC with beta-blocking properties
C. Amiodarone 200mg daily or dofetilide (with appropriate initiation)
D. Dronedarone 400mg BID - designed as safer alternative to amiodarone
questions.explanation: - AF rhythm control in HFrEF: ONLY amiodarone or dofetilide safe. All other antiarrhythmics contraindicated or increase mortality in structural heart disease/HF. Dofetilide requires 3-day inpatient initiation with telemetry and QTc monitoring. Catheter ablation increasingly used as alternative. A, B wrong: Class IC agents (flecainide, propafenone) CONTRAINDICATED in structural heart disease - increase mortality (CAST trial). D wrong: Dronedarone CONTRAINDICATED in NYHA III-IV HF or recent decompensation - increases mortality, hospitalizations (ANDROMEDA trial). Also contraindicated in permanent AF (PALLAS trial).

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman on dabigatran 150mg BID for atrial fibrillation presents with acute intracranial hemorrhage (subdural hematoma after fall). CT shows significant bleeding with mass effect. Neurosurgery consulted for urgent evacuation. Last dabigatran dose 6 hours ago. CrCl 58 mL/min. What is MOST appropriate strategy for dabigatran reversal?
options: A. Vitamin K 10mg IV - reverses all oral anticoagulants including DOACs
B. Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5g IV
C. Andexanet alfa 800mg IV - reverses factor Xa inhibitors
D. Fresh frozen plasma 4 units - provides clotting factors for hemostasis
questions.explanation: - Idarucizumab (Praxbind) is specific dabigatran reversal agent: Humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with >350x higher affinity than thrombin. Dose: 5g IV (two 2.5g vials). Provides rapid, complete reversal. For Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban): Andexanet alfa. If specific reversal unavailable: Supportive care, hemodialysis for dabigatran (removes ~60% in 2-3h). A wrong: Vitamin K only for warfarin (vitamin K antagonist). C wrong: Andexanet alfa for Xa inhibitors, not dabigatran. D wrong: FFP ineffective for DOAC reversal - doesn't provide factors targeted by DOACs.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with unprovoked proximal DVT (left leg, extending to iliac vein) completed 6 months of rivaroxaban therapy. Repeat ultrasound shows resolution. CHA2DS2-VASc score 1, HAS-BLED score 1 (both low). No family history of VTE. D-dimer obtained 4 weeks after stopping anticoagulation: 680 ng/mL (elevated, upper limit 500). Genetic thrombophilia testing negative. What is MOST appropriate recommendation regarding anticoagulation duration?
options: A. Discontinue anticoagulation - 6 months sufficient for all unprovoked DVT
B. Consider extended/indefinite anticoagulation
C. Switch to aspirin 81mg daily for indefinite VTE prevention
D. Repeat course of 3 months anticoagulation then stop permanently
questions.explanation: - Unprovoked VTE: ~10%/year recurrence risk. Factors FAVORING extended anticoagulation: (1) Male gender (2x recurrence vs female), (2) Proximal DVT/PE (vs distal), (3) Elevated D-dimer off anticoagulation, (4) First unprovoked event, (5) Low bleeding risk. Factors AGAINST extended: Distal DVT, provoked VTE, high bleeding risk. This patient: Male, proximal, unprovoked, elevated D-dimer, low bleeding risk → strong candidate for indefinite anticoagulation. Reassess periodically. A wrong: 6 months minimum but many benefit from longer. C wrong: Aspirin provides modest protection (30% reduction) but inferior to anticoagulation; consider if patient refuses anticoagulation. D wrong: Arbitrary duration without reassessment inappropriate.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman with newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer (stage IV, liver and bone metastases) develops symptomatic DVT in right leg. Started on rivaroxaban 15mg BID for acute VTE treatment. Oncologist planning to start chemotherapy (doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide). Platelet count 185,000, Cr 0.9. What is preferred LONGTERM anticoagulation strategy for cancer-associated thrombosis?
options: A. Warfarin - standard therapy for all VTE regardless of etiology
B. LMWH (enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC Q12h or 1.5mg/kg daily) preferred alternatively rivaroxaban or edoxaban; avoid warfarin
C. Aspirin 325mg daily sufficient for cancer-associated VTE
D. Stop anticoagulation after 3 months - same as non-cancer VTE
questions.explanation: - Cancer-associated VTE: LMWH traditionally preferred over warfarin (CLOT trial: lower recurrence). Recent trials: Rivaroxaban (SELECT-D), edoxaban (Hokusai-VTE Cancer), apixaban (CARAVAGGIO) shown non-inferior to LMWH. Caution: Higher bleeding with DOACs in GI/GU malignancies. Avoid warfarin (drug interactions with chemotherapy, unstable INR, dietary changes). Duration: Indefinite while cancer active or until resolved. A wrong: Warfarin inferior to LMWH in cancer VTE. C wrong: Aspirin inadequate. D wrong: Need indefinite anticoagulation while cancer active (very high recurrence risk ~15-20%/year).

questions.question: A 55-year-old man on warfarin for AF (INR goal 2-3) has INR checked routinely: Result 9.2. He feels well, no bleeding symptoms, no falls/trauma. Exam unremarkable, vital signs stable. Hgb/Hct stable compared to baseline. Takes warfarin 5mg daily, no recent dose changes or new medications. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Continue warfarin at same dose - INR will self-correct in few days
B. Hold warfarin 1-2 doses; give oral vitamin K 2.5-5mg; recheck INR in 24 hours; resume warfarin at lower dose when INR therapeutic
C. Admit to hospital for IV vitamin K 10mg and fresh frozen plasma administration
D. Stop warfarin permanently - patient unreliable with dosing
questions.explanation: - INR 5-10 WITHOUT bleeding: (1) Hold warfarin 1-2 doses, (2) Give LOWdose oral vitamin K 2.5-5mg (or 1-2mg IV if rapid reversal needed but no active bleeding), (3) Recheck INR 24h, (4) Resume warfarin at lower dose once INR therapeutic. Avoid high-dose vitamin K (causes prolonged warfarin resistance for days-weeks). If INR >10 or active bleeding: Higher vitamin K doses ± clotting factors. A wrong: INR 9.2 carries bleeding risk - must intervene. C wrong: No active bleeding - outpatient management appropriate with oral vitamin K; FFP reserved for active bleeding. D wrong: Single elevated INR doesn't indicate non-adherence - can restart at adjusted dose.

questions.question: A 45-year-old healthcare worker develops heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) after 7 days of unfractionated heparin for DVT treatment. Platelet count dropped from 245,000 to 68,000. 4Ts score: 7 (high probability). Heparin stopped immediately. Patient currently has DVT requiring anticoagulation. No active bleeding. Cr 1.0 mg/dL. What is MOST appropriate alternative anticoagulation?
options: A. Switch to LMWH (enoxaparin) - safer alternative with lower HIT risk
B. Start direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban) or fondaparinux; avoid all heparin products including LMWH
C. Start warfarin immediately to bridge off heparin
D. Hold all anticoagulation until platelets recover to normal
questions.explanation: - HIT Type II: Immune-mediated, platelets drop >50% day 5-10, HIGH thrombosis risk 30-50% (arterial/venous). Management: (1) STOP all heparin (including flushes, LMWH - cross-reacts ~90%), (2) Start alternative anticoagulant: Argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor, hepatically cleared), bivalirudin, or fondaparinux (no cross-reactivity), (3) Screen for thrombosis (ultrasound, CT), (4) Transition to warfarin ONLY after platelet count recovers >150K and overlap ≥5 days (warfarin alone initially increases thrombosis risk via protein C depletion), (5) AVOID platelet transfusion (increases thrombosis). A wrong: LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies. C wrong: Starting warfarin before platelets recover and without alternative anticoagulant increases thrombosis (warfarin-induced limb gangrene). D wrong: Thrombosis risk very high need alternative anticoagulation.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc=5) and chronic stable CAD s/p PCI with DES 2 years ago presents for medication review. Current: Apixaban 5mg BID, aspirin 81mg daily, metoprolol 50mg BID, atorvastatin 40mg HS. No angina, functionally active. What is MOST appropriate antiplatelet/anticoagulation regimen for this patient?
options: A. Continue both apixaban and aspirin indefinitely - dual therapy needed for AF + CAD
B. Anticoagulation monotherapy (apixaban) without aspirin - for chronic stable CAD >12 months post-PCI
C. Triple therapy (apixaban + aspirin + clopidogrel) for optimal protection
D. Stop apixaban; aspirin monotherapy sufficient for both AF and CAD
questions.explanation: - AF + stable CAD (>1 year post-PCI): Anticoagulation monotherapy sufficient - adding antiplatelet increases bleeding without ischemic benefit. Triple therapy (anticoagulant + aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) only immediately post-PCI (1-4 weeks) → transition to anticoagulant + P2Y12 inhibitor (up to 12 months) → anticoagulant alone. This patient 2 years post-PCI → anticoagulation monotherapy. A wrong: Adding aspirin increases major bleeding 1.5-2x without benefit in stable CAD. C wrong: Triple therapy increases bleeding dramatically; only for immediate post-ACS/PCI period. D wrong: Aspirin alone inadequate stroke prevention for AF with CHA2DS2-VASc 5.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man 8 months post-ACS (STEMI with PCI and DES) on DAPT (aspirin 81mg + ticagrelor 90mg BID) develops severe recurrent epistaxis requiring ENT cauterization twice in past month. Hgb dropped from 14.2 to 11.8 g/dL. He's adherent, no other bleeding. Needs to continue DAPT to complete 12 months. What is MOST appropriate DAPT de-escalation strategy?
options: A. Stop both agents temporarily until bleeding resolves, then restart
B. Switch from ticagrelor to clopidogrel 75mg daily (less potent P2Y12 inhibitor); continue aspirin
C. Stop aspirin; continue ticagrelor monotherapy
D. Continue current regimen unchanged - bleeding unrelated to DAPT
questions.explanation: - DAPT de-escalation for bleeding: Switch potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor/prasugrel) to clopidogrel (less potent, lower bleeding risk) while maintaining DAPT benefit. TROPICAL-ACS and POPular-Genetics trials support guided de-escalation. Alternative: Shorten DAPT duration if approaching 12 months. Goal: Balance ischemic vs bleeding risk. A wrong: Stopping DAPT completely 8 months post-DES/ACS increases stent thrombosis risk (still within critical 12-month window). C wrong: Need dual antiplatelet therapy; monotherapy insufficient post-ACS with DES. D wrong: Recurrent severe bleeding with Hgb drop clearly related to DAPT.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (valve area 0.6cm², mean gradient 58mmHg, LVEF 60%) develops acute pulmonary edema in ED. BP 156/88, HR 108, RR 28, O2 sat 86% on RA. Crackles bilateral, JVP elevated. Cardiothoracic surgery consulted for urgent SAVR but OR not available for 6 hours. What is appropriate acute medical management while awaiting surgery?
options: A. Aggressive IV furosemide 80mg bolus then infusion for rapid diuresis
B. Cautious diuresis with careful monitoring - severe AS patients preload-dependent; avoid excessive preload reduction
C. IV nitroglycerin infusion for rapid afterload reduction
D. IV esmolol for heart rate control to improve diastolic filling
questions.explanation: - Severe AS with pulmonary edema: CAUTIOUS diuresis - patients preload-dependent (fixed obstruction requires adequate preload to maintain cardiac output). Gentle diuresis (avoid dropping preload dramatically → can precipitate cardiogenic shock). Avoid aggressive vasodilators (sudden afterload reduction → hypotension). Definitive treatment: Valve replacement. Can use nitroprusside/nitroglycerin VERY cautiously with invasive monitoring in ICU if needed. A wrong: Aggressive diuresis can precipitate shock in severe AS - stroke volume fixed, rely on preload. C wrong: Nitrates can cause profound hypotension in severe AS. D wrong: Beta-blockade not primary issue; rate 108 reasonable compensatory response.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with severe chronic aortic regurgitation (AR), asymptomatic, LVEF 58%, LV end-systolic dimension 52mm presents for cardiology follow-up. Echo unchanged from 6 months ago. Currently not on any cardiac medications. What medication may help delay need for surgical intervention?
options: A. Beta-blockers to reduce heart rate and regurgitant volume per beat
B. Vasodilators (ACEIs, ARBs, or dihydropyridine CCBs) to reduce afterload and regurgitant volume
C. Digoxin to increase contractility and forward flow
D. No medical therapy proven beneficial in chronic AR
questions.explanation: - Chronic AR: Vasodilators (ACEIs, ARBs, nifedipine/amlodipine) reduce systemic vascular resistance → decrease regurgitant volume, reduce LV dilation progression. May delay surgery in asymptomatic patients. Surgical indications: (1) Symptoms, (2) LVEF <50%, (3) LV end-systolic dimension >50mm (this patient at threshold), (4) Severe LV dilation (LVESD indexed >25mm/m²). A wrong: Beta-blockers WORSEN AR - bradycardia increases diastolic time per beat → more time for regurgitation; avoid unless specific indication. C wrong: Digoxin limited role. D wrong: Vasodilators have benefit in chronic AR.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with severe symptomatic mitral stenosis (valve area 1.0cm²) and atrial fibrillation develops acute decompensation with dyspnea and pulmonary edema. HR 145 bpm (irregular), BP 142/86. What rate control medication addresses BOTH atrial fibrillation rate AND mitral stenosis pathophysiology?
options: A. Digoxin 0.5mg IV load - provides both rate control and positive inotropy
B. Beta-blocker (metoprolol) or non-dihydropyridine CCB (diltiazem) - slow HR to prolong diastolic filling time across stenotic valve
C. Dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine) for vasodilation and rate control
D. Amiodarone for rhythm and rate control
questions.explanation: - MS pathophysiology: Fixed valve obstruction limits LV filling. Need LONGER diastole for adequate filling across stenotic valve. AF with RVR → shortened diastole → inadequate LA emptying → pulmonary congestion. Beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) slow HR → longer diastolic filling time → improved hemodynamics and symptoms. Target HR 60-80 bpm. A wrong: Digoxin provides some rate control but less effective (especially with exertion) than beta-blockers/CCBs; positive inotropy not beneficial in MS (problem is filling not contractility). C wrong: DHP CCBs don't control heart rate effectively. D wrong: Amiodarone not first-line for acute rate control in MS.

questions.question: A 45-year-old IV drug user develops acute severe mitral regurgitation from infective endocarditis (large vegetation destroying posterior leaflet). Presents in cardiogenic shock: BP 82/48, HR 118, cold extremities, pulmonary edema. What medication provides temporary hemodynamic stabilization while awaiting urgent surgical repair?
options: A. IV dobutamine for inotropic support as primary therapy
B. IV nitroglycerin or nitroprusside to reduce afterload and regurgitant fraction, increase forward cardiac output
C. IV fluids for volume expansion to increase preload
D. IV metoprolol for rate control to reduce regurgitant volume
questions.explanation: - Acute severe MR: IV vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside) reduce afterload → decrease regurgitant fraction (more blood forward, less backward into LA), increase forward CO, reduce pulmonary congestion. May add inotropes (dobutamine) if persistent low output. May need IABP in refractory shock. Definitive: Urgent surgical repair. Note: Chronic compensated MR different (ACEIs/ARBs, diuretics). A wrong: Inotropes alone don't address regurgitation; afterload reduction primary strategy. C wrong: Volume expansion worsens pulmonary edema in acute MR. D wrong: Rate control not primary issue; reducing afterload key.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes) while hospitalized for pneumonia. Medications: Levofloxacin 750mg daily, ondansetron 4mg Q6h PRN nausea, sotalol 80mg BID (for AF). Labs: K 3.1 mEq/L, Mg 1.4 mg/dL. ECG baseline: QTc 520ms. What is MOST important immediate intervention?
options: A. Amiodarone 150mg IV bolus to suppress ventricular arrhythmia
B. Magnesium sulfate 2g IV bolus (even if Mg normal); stop sotalol/levofloxacin/ondansetron; replete K >4.0 and Mg >2.0; isoproterenol or overdrive pacing ifrecurrent
C. Lidocaine 100mg IV bolus for ventricular arrhythmia suppression
D. Immediate defibrillation only if patient becomes pulseless
questions.explanation: - Torsades de pointes management: (1) IV magnesium 2g bolus (FIRST-LINE even if Mg normal - stabilizes myocardial membrane), (2) Stop ALL QT-prolonging drugs (sotalol, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron, many others), (3) Correct hypokalemia (K >4.0) and hypomagnesemia (Mg >2.0), (4) If recurrent: Isoproterenol infusion (increases HR, shortens QT) or temporary overdrive pacing, (5) Avoid class IA and III antiarrhythmics (prolong QT further). A wrong: Amiodarone prolongs QT contraindicated. C wrong: Lidocaine not first-line for torsades. D wrong: Magnesium prevents recurrence; defibrillation only if sustained VF.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman with newly diagnosed hypertension has office BP readings 168/98, 164/96, 162/94 mmHg over 2 visits. She purchased home BP monitor and reports average home BP 128/76 mmHg over 2 weeks (multiple readings morning and evening). BMI 26, no other cardiac risk factors, exam unremarkable. What is MOST likely diagnosis and appropriate next step?
options: A. Stage 2 hypertension; start two-drug combination therapy immediately based on office readings
B. White coat hypertension - elevated office BP with normal home BP; no immediate pharmacotherapy; annual monitoring with home BP/ABPM
C. Masked hypertension requiring aggressive treatment
D. Normal blood pressure - ignore office readings completely
questions.explanation: - White coat hypertension: Elevated office BP (≥130/80 mmHg) with normal out-of-office BP (<130/80 home or <125/75 daytime ABPM). Prevalence 15-30%. Management: (1) No immediate medications (not entirely benign - some progress to sustained HTN), (2) Annual monitoring with home BP or ABPM, (3) Aggressive lifestyle modification, (4) Treat if progresses to sustained HTN or very high CV risk. Out-of-office BP more predictive of CV outcomes than office BP. A wrong: Would over-treat based on office readings when home BP normal. C wrong: Masked HTN is opposite (normal office, elevated home). D wrong: Should monitor - not completely ignore.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed Stage 1 hypertension (office BP 142/88 mmHg confirmed by home monitoring average 138/86) has 10-year ASCVD risk 6% (low risk). No diabetes, CKD, or cardiovascular disease. BMI 31, sedentary lifestyle. What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. Start thiazide diuretic immediately - all Stage 1 HTN requires medication
B. Lifestyle modifications (weight loss, DASH diet, exercise, sodium restriction) for 3-6 months; add medication if BP remains >130/80 or if ASCVD risk ≥10%
C. Start two-drug combination for faster BP control
D. No intervention needed - BP close to goal
questions.explanation: - Stage 1 HTN (130-139/80-89) with LOW CV risk (<10% ASCVD): Lifestyle modifications first-line. Interventions: (1) DASH diet (8-14 mmHg reduction), (2) Weight loss (5-20 mmHg per 10kg), (3) Exercise ≥150 min/week (4-9 mmHg), (4) Sodium <1500-2300 mg/day (2-8 mmHg), (5) Limit alcohol (2-4 mmHg). Add medication if: ASCVD ≥10%, DM, CKD, known CVD, or BP remains elevated after 3-6 months lifestyle therapy. Stage 2 HTN (≥140/90) → start medication immediately. A, C wrong: Stage 1 with low CV risk → try lifestyle first. D wrong: BP 138/86 above goal <130/80 - needs intervention.

questions.question: A 58-year-old African American man with T2DM (8y), CKD stage 3a (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m²), and untreated obstructive sleep apnea presents to hypertension clinic with BP 168/98 mmHg despite amlodipine 10mg daily, lisinopril 40mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25mg daily x6 months. Home BP monitoring: average 162/94 mmHg over 2 weeks. 24h ABPM: daytime 158/92, nighttime 152/88 (non-dipper). Reports poor HCTZ adherence due to polyuria. Diet: frequent fast food, high sodium. Drinks 2-3 beers daily. Non-smoker. Family history: HTN both parents, father MI age 54. Exam: BMI 33.3, BP 168/98, HR 78. Labs: Na 142, K 3.7, BUN 24, Cr 1.4, glucose 142, HbA1c 7.8%, aldosterone 18 ng/dL, plasma renin 0.4 ng/mL/hr, aldo/renin ratio 45. ECG: LVH by voltage. Renal US: no stenosis. What is MOST appropriate next step?
options: A. Add spironolactone 25mg daily and refer for sleep study
B. Increase HCTZ to 50mg daily and add metoprolol succinate 50mg daily
C. Discontinue lisinopril, start valsartan 320mg daily
D. Refer for renal denervation procedure
questions.explanation: - Resistant HTN defined as BP above goal despite 3 agents including diuretic. Aldo/renin ratio 45 (>20-30 suggests primary aldosteronism), low-normal K, CKD 3a support spironolactone. PATHWAY-2 trial: spironolactone 25-50mg most effective 4th agent. Safe in CKD 3 with close K monitoring (target K<5.0). Additionally, untreated OSA major contributor - obesity (BMI 33.3), documented OSA, non-dipper pattern indicate need for sleep study. B wrong: HCTZ >25mg minimal additional benefit; JNC-8/ACC-AHA recommend 25mg max. Betablockers less effective than spironolactone as 4th agent; can worsen glucose control. C wrong: No indication to switch ACE-I to ARB. Dual RAAS blockade contraindicated (ONTARGET: increased hyperkalemia, hypotension, AKI). D wrong: Renal denervation not standard - SYMPLICITY HTN-3 failed. First optimize medical management.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with newly diagnosed stable angina after positive stress test (ST-depression II,III,aVF at 7 METS with chest pain). PMH: HTN, dyslipidemia on statin, hypothyroidism, postmenopausal. Presented 3wk ago with exertional chest pressure walking 2 blocks, relieved with rest 5-10min. Angiography: 70% mid-RCA stenosis (non-dominant), 40% LAD, 30% LCx. Cardiology recommended initial medical management. Never smoked. Father died MI age 72. Meds: ASA 81mg, atorvastatin 80mg, levothyroxine 88mcg, amlodipine 5mg, lisinopril 10mg daily. VS: BP 128/76, HR 82. Labs: Na 140, K 4.2, Cr 0.9, glucose 94, HbA1c 5.4%, LDL-C 68, HDL-C 58, TG 130. ECG: NSR rate 78. Echo: LVEF 60%, no WMA. What provides GREATEST mortality benefit and symptom control?
options: A. Add metoprolol succinate 25mg daily, titrate to target HR 55-60 bpm
B. Add ranolazine 500mg BID, titrate to 1000mg BID
C. Add sublingual NTG 0.4mg PRN for chest pain only
D. Add isosorbide mononitrate 30mg daily
questions.explanation: - Beta-blockers first-line for stable angina - provide mortality benefit and superior symptom control. Reduce myocardial O2 demand. Target HR 55-60 optimal (BEAUTIFUL trial: HR>70 worse outcomes). Patient HR 82 indicates room for titration. Metoprolol succinate preferred: once-daily dosing, proven post-MI mortality benefit. B wrong: Ranolazine second-line - NO mortality/MACE reduction (MERLIN-TIMI 36). Side effects: QTc prolongation. Cost $200-300/month vs $4-10/month. C wrong: Sublingual NTG essential for acute relief but NO chronic prevention or mortality benefit. D wrong: Long-acting nitrates NO mortality benefit, less effective than beta-blockers. Nitrate tolerance develops.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents to rural ED with severe substernal chest pain started 90min ago while shoveling snow. Pain crushing 9/10, radiating to left arm and jaw, with diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea. PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia, 30-pack-year smoking. Meds: ASA 81mg, atorvastatin 40mg, lisinopril 20mg. VS: BP 168/95, HR 102, RR 22, O2 sat 94% RA. Exam: diaphoretic, anxious, lungs bibasilar crackles, S4 gallop. ECG: ST-elevation 3-4mm in II,III,aVF with reciprocal ST-depression I,aVL,V1-V3. Troponin I 0.8 ng/mL (normal <0.04). Nearest PCI hospital 120min away. PCI center has 30min door-to-balloon. Hospital can give fibrinolytics in 15min. No contraindications. What is MOST appropriate reperfusion?
options: A. Immediate transfer for primary PCI without fibrinolysis
B. Administer tenecteplase immediately, then transfer for possible rescue PCI
C. Administer tenecteplase, ASA, clopidogrel, UFH, transfer after 6h
D. Start tirofiban infusion and transfer for primary PCI
questions.explanation: - Inferior STEMI 90min from onset at non-PCI hospital. Expected first medical contact-to-device: 90min + 120min + 30min = 240min or 150min from first contact. ACC/AHA: fibrinolysis when onset <3h, expected PCI delay >120min. Patient meets criteria. Tenecteplase preferred: single bolus, easier. Most effective <2-3h (GUSTO-I). After fibrinolysis, transfer for rescue PCI if failed or routine angiography 3-24h. TRANSFER trial: early angiography improves outcomes. A wrong: Primary PCI generally preferred but advantage diminishes when delays >120min. CAPTIM: fibrinolysis <2h similar outcomes. C wrong: Waiting 6h delays potential rescue PCI. Should transfer immediately. STREAM: early routine PCI reduced recurrent ischemia. D wrong: Routine GP IIb/IIIa not recommended. FINESSE, ASSIST: no benefit, increased bleeding.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman presents to ED with 4h of crescendo chest discomfort at rest, worse than prior stable angina. PMH: CAD s/p PCI with DES to LAD 2y ago, T2DM, HTN, hyperlipidemia, CKD stage 3 (eGFR 48). Meds: ASA 81mg, metoprolol 50mg BID, lisinopril 20mg, atorvastatin 80mg, metformin 1000mg BID. VS: BP 152/88, HR 96, RR 20, O2 sat 96% RA. Exam: mild diaphoresis, S4 gallop, lungs clear. ECG: ST-depression 1-2mm V2-V5, T-wave inversions V2-V4. Troponin I 0.15 ng/mL at 0h, 0.28 at 3h (ULN 0.04). GRACE score 142 (high risk). Started on ASA 325mg, ticagrelor 180mg load then 90mg BID, heparin, metoprolol, nitrates. Pain resolved after 2h. What is MOST appropriate invasive strategy timing?
options: A. Immediate invasive strategy (<2h) - high-risk requires urgent cath
B. Early invasive strategy (within 24h) - high GRACE score, dynamic ECG, rising troponins
C. Ischemia-guided strategy - defer cath unless recurrent ischemia
D. Delayed invasive (48-72h) - allow platelet inhibition
questions.explanation: - NSTEMI/UA invasive strategy timing per GRACE and high-risk features. Immediate (<2h): Hemodynamic instability, refractory ischemia, life-threatening arrhythmias, shock. Early (within 24h): High-risk - GRACE >140, dynamic ECG changes, elevated troponins, DM, CKD, prior CAD. This patient: GRACE 142, dynamic ECG, rising troponins, DM, CKD, prior PCI - warrants early invasive. TIMACS, ABOARD: early invasive reduces death/MI. A wrong: Immediate reserved for very high-risk - instability, refractory ischemia, shock. Pain resolved, now stable. C wrong: Ischemia-guided only for low-risk. Multiple highrisk features mandate early invasive. D wrong: Delaying increases events. Ticagrelor achieves inhibition within 2-4h.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man develops cardiogenic shock 6h after anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI to proximal LAD (TIMI 3 flow). Now: BP 78/52, HR 118, cool extremities, oliguria <20mL/h x2h, altered MS. Exam: JVP elevated, S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles, hepatomegaly. Labs: lactate 4.2 mmol/L, Cr 1.9 (baseline 1.1), troponin I 48 ng/mL. Echo: LVEF 28%, anterior/apical akinesis, no mechanical complications. PA catheter: CO 3.2 L/min, CI 1.7 L/min/m², PCWP 22mmHg, SVR 1680. On dopamine 10mcg/kg/min, furosemide 40mg IV given. Persistent hypotension. What is MOST appropriate next step?
options: A. Increase dopamine to 20mcg/kg/min
B. Switch to norepinephrine 0.1mcg/kg/min; consider adding dobutamine
C. Start milrinone 0.375mcg/kg/min
D. Emergent IABP placement
questions.explanation: - Cardiogenic shock: CO<2.2, PCWP>18, SBP<90, end-organ hypoperfusion. This patient: CI 1.7, PCWP 22, BP 78/52, lactate 4.2. Dopamine ineffective. Norepinephrine first-line vasopressor to restore perfusion pressure. Add dobutamine for inotropy if CO remains low. Goal: MAP >65, CI >2.2, lactate clearance. A wrong: Dopamine >10mcg/kg/min increases tachycardia (HR 118), arrhythmias. OptimaCC: norepinephrine superior. C wrong: Milrinone causes vasodilation - DANGEROUS with BP 78/52. Appropriate in "cold-wet" with NORMAL/elevated BP. Contraindicated in severe hypotension. D wrong: IABP-SHOCK II showed NO mortality benefit. Not routine. Consider advanced MCS if refractory.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man day 3 post-anterior STEMI (primary PCI with DES to LAD) develops sustained monomorphic VT (rate 180 bpm) on telemetry. BP 92/58, alert but lightheaded. Meds: ASA, ticagrelor, metoprolol 25mg BID, lisinopril 5mg, atorvastatin 80mg. Labs: K 3.8, Mg 1.8, Cr 1.1. Echo: LVEF 32%, anterior akinesis. What is MOST appropriate acute management?
options: A. Immediate electrical cardioversion - hemodynamically unstable VT
B. Amiodarone 150mg IV over 10min; correct K>4.5, Mg>2.0; cardiovert if persists
C. Lidocaine 1-1.5mg/kg IV bolus
D. Increase metoprolol to 100mg BID
questions.explanation: - Sustained monomorphic VT post-MI: Patient conscious, BP 92/58 (marginal but not pulseless). ACLS: Hemodynamically STABLE → trial of antiarrhythmic before cardioversion. UNSTABLE → immediate cardioversion. Amiodarone 150mg IV first-line, can repeat to 300mg. Correct electrolytes: K>4.5, Mg>2.0 (both low-normal). If persists or becomes unstable → synchronized cardioversion. Consider ICD after 40 days if LVEF ≤35%. A wrong: Patient conscious with marginal but adequate BP - trial of amiodarone reasonable. Immediate cardioversion if: unconscious, pulseless, severe hypotension, pulmonary edema. C wrong: Lidocaine less effective than amiodarone. D wrong: Increasing beta-blocker won't acutely terminate VT. Important for chronic prevention but acute VT requires amiodarone or cardioversion.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman with HTN, T2DM, obesity (BMI 38), AF presents with progressive dyspnea NYHA III. Echo: LVEF 58%, LV wall thickness 1.4cm, severe LA enlargement, Grade II diastolic dysfunction, elevated E/e' 18, estimated RVSP 52mmHg. BNP 420 pg/mL. Restrictive mitral inflow pattern. No valvular disease. Meds: metoprolol 50mg BID, lisinopril 20mg, furosemide 40mg, apixaban 5mg BID, metformin 1000mg BID. VS: BP 148/82, HR 76 (AF), weight 105kg. Labs: Na 138, K 4.1, Cr 1.2, eGFR 48, HbA1c 8.2%. What is MOST appropriate medication change for HFpEF?
options: A. Add sacubitril/valsartan 24/26mg BID - proven mortality benefit in HFpEF
B. Add spironolactone 25mg daily - improves diastolic function
C. Add empagliflozin 10mg daily - SGLT2 inhibitor with proven HF hospitalization benefit
D. Increase lisinopril to 40mg daily and add digoxin 0.125mg
questions.explanation: - HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%, symptoms, diastolic dysfunction, elevated natriuretic peptides). EMPEROR-Preserved: Empagliflozin reduced CV death/HF hospitalization 21% in HFpEF. Mechanism: natriuresis, improved remodeling, reduced inflammation. Also benefits DM (HbA1c 8.2%). SGLT2 inhibitors now CLASS I for HFpEF. eGFR 48 safe. A wrong: PARAGON-HF: sacubitril/valsartan neutral primary endpoint (p=0.06). NOT Class I like HFrEF. B wrong: TOPCAT: spironolactone neutral primary outcome in HFpEF. Not definitively proven. D wrong: Increasing ACE-I hasn't shown HFpEF benefit. Digoxin not indicated.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with NSTEMI underwent angiography showing severe 3-vessel disease. Cardiac surgery recommends CABG in 3-5 days. Loaded with ticagrelor 180mg in cath lab, started 90mg BID. PMH: HTN, dyslipidemia, prior TIA 18mo ago. VS: BP 138/82, HR 78. Labs: Cr 1.0, Hgb 13.8, platelets 220K. No active bleeding. Cardiac surgery concerned about bleeding with potent P2Y12 inhibitor. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Continue ticagrelor through surgery - benefits outweigh bleeding
B. Hold ticagrelor 5 days before CABG; restart 24h post-op; no bridging
C. Switch to clopidogrel now; hold 5 days before CABG
D. Discontinue all antiplatelet including ASA 7 days before
questions.explanation: - P2Y12 inhibitor management for CABG post-ACS: Ticagrelor half-life 7-9h. Platelet recovery: ~5 days. Guidelines: Hold ticagrelor ≥5 days before CABG. ASA continued through surgery. Resume P2Y12 inhibitor 24-48h post-op. PLATO: ticagrelor superior to clopidogrel - should resume post-CABG. No bridging needed - surgery within days, low thrombotic risk with ongoing ASA. B wrong: Switching to clopidogrel doesn't allow earlier surgery - also requires 5-day washout. Clopidogrel inferior (PLATO). C wrong: Switching provides no advantage. D wrong: ASA should be CONTINUED. Studies show continuing lowdose ASA reduces graft thrombosis without significantly increasing bleeding.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with anterior STEMI underwent primary PCI with DES to proximal LAD. Cardiology wants potent P2Y12 inhibitor for DAPT. PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia only. No prior stroke/TIA. Weight 92kg. VS: BP 132/76, HR 82. What is MOST appropriate P2Y12 inhibitor?
options: A. Clopidogrel 600mg load then 75mg daily
B. Prasugrel 60mg load then 10mg daily
C. Ticagrelor 180mg load then 90mg BID
D. Either prasugrel or ticagrelor - equivalent
questions.explanation: - STEMI P2Y12 selection: Both prasugrel and ticagrelor superior to clopidogrel. TRITON-TIMI 38: prasugrel reduced CV death/MI/stroke vs clopidogrel, particularly in STEMI. Prasugrel contraindications: prior stroke/TIA, age ≥75y, weight <60kg, active bleeding. Prasugrel advantages in STEMI: faster onset (30min vs 60-90min), more predictable inhibition. Ticagrelor: reversible binding, no active metabolite. This patient: age 54, weight 92kg, no stroke - NO contraindications. Prasugrel or ticagrelor appropriate. Slight preference prasugrel in STEMI. A wrong: Clopidogrel inferior. D wrong: Prasugrel has MORE bleeding (especially prior stroke, age ≥75, weight <60kg). Not equivalent safety.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man 13mo post-NSTEMI (PCI with DES to RCA) on DAPT (ASA 81mg + ticagrelor 90mg BID) presents for follow-up. Tolerating well, no bleeding. PMH: HTN, dyslipidemia, T2DM. Currently taking metoprolol, atorvastatin, lisinopril, metformin. No recurrent chest pain, functionally active. Echo: LVEF 52%. What is MOST appropriate DAPT management?
options: A. Continue DAPT indefinitely
B. Transition to ASA monotherapy
C. Continue DAPT for 36mo total
D. Switch ticagrelor to clopidogrel, continue DAPT 12mo
questions.explanation: - DAPT duration post-ACS with DES: Minimum 12mo (Class I). After 12mo, assess bleeding vs ischemic risk. This patient 13mo post-NSTEMI, uncomplicated, no high ischemic risk features - transition to monotherapy reasonable. PEGASUS-TIMI 54: extended DAPT beyond 12mo reduced ischemic events but increased bleeding. High ischemic risk features: DM, prior MI, multivessel CAD, CKD. This patient has DM but no bleeding risk factors. Guidelines support transitioning after 12mo in standard-risk. A wrong: Indefinite not standard - increases bleeding. C wrong: Extended DAPT reduces ischemic but increases bleeding. Not routine. D wrong: No benefit switching at 13mo.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman 2wk postpartum with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, edema x5 days. Pregnancy complicated by gestational HTN. Delivered healthy baby via vaginal delivery. No cardiac history. VS: BP 102/68, HR 112, RR 24, O2 sat 92% RA. Exam: JVP 10cm, S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles, 2+ edema. CXR: cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion. Echo: LVEF 28%, LV dilation, global hypokinesis. BNP 1840. Labs: Na 136, K 4.2, Cr 0.9. What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. Furosemide, metoprolol, lisinopril, spironolactone - standard HFrEF
B. Furosemide, metoprolol, hydralazine/nitrates (avoid ACE-I if breastfeeding); consider bromocriptine 2.5mg BID x8wk
C. Furosemide, digoxin, carvedilol - avoid ACE-I/ARBs entirely
D. Immediate listing for transplantation
questions.explanation: - Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM): HF in last month pregnancy or within 5mo postpartum, LVEF <45%. Management: Standard HFrEF therapy with breastfeeding considerations. ACE-I/ARBs: Safe postpartum even if breastfeeding (minimal breast milk excretion). If strongly breastfeeding: hydralazine/nitrates alternative. Beta-blockers: metoprolol, labetalol safe. Diuretics: furosemide safe. Bromocriptine: blocks prolactin, may improve recovery. BOARD trial suggested benefit. Dose: 2.5mg BID x2wk then daily x6wk. Cautions: suppresses lactation, theoretical thrombosis risk. Consider if LVEF <30% or LV thrombus. Prognosis: 50% recover. A wrong: If breastfeeding, counsel about ACE-I safety or use hydralazine/nitrates. C wrong: Digoxin not first-line. D wrong: Many recover.

questions.question: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 35wk gestation with severe headache, blurred vision, RUQ pain x6h. Prenatal care uncomplicated until 2wk ago when BP 142/88. Today VS: BP 178/112 (repeated 172/108, 180/110), HR 92. Exam: 3+ reflexes, 2+ edema. Labs: Platelets 92K (baseline 240K), AST 168, ALT 154, LDH 580, Cr 1.4 (baseline 0.7), urine protein/Cr ratio 0.9. Fetal monitoring: reassuring. What is MOST appropriate acute management?
options: A. Expectant management until 37wk
B. IV magnesium for seizure prophylaxis, IV labetalol/hydralazine for severe HTN, deliver within 24-48h
C. Immediate C-section regardless
D. Oral nifedipine and methyldopa, continue pregnancy
questions.explanation: - Preeclampsia with severe features: BP ≥160/110, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, renal insufficiency, cerebral symptoms, RUQ pain. Management: (1) IV MgSO4 4-6g load then 1-2g/h (seizure prophylaxis), (2) Severe HTN treatment: IV labetalol/hydralazine or oral immediate-release nifedipine. Target SBP 140-150. (3) Delivery: definitive cure. ≥34wk with severe features → deliver within 24-48h. Give betamethasone if <34wk. A wrong: Expectant inappropriate with severe features - risks eclampsia, stroke, HELLP, abruption. C wrong: Stabilize first then deliver. Vaginal preferred unless obstetric indications. D wrong: Oral agents insufficient for acute severe HTN.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman at 36wk gestation with preeclampsia on IV magnesium (4g load, 2g/h x3h) develops absent DTRs, RR 8/min, O2 sat 88% RA. Drowsy but arousable. VS: BP 148/92, HR 76. UOP 20mL/h past 2h. What is MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: A. Continue magnesium - reflexes and respiratory depression expected
B. Stop magnesium immediately; calcium gluconate 1g IV over 3-5min; support ventilation
C. Reduce magnesium to 1g/h
D. Intubate before antidote
questions.explanation: - Magnesium toxicity! Therapeutic 4-7 mEq/L. Toxicity: Loss of DTRs (8-10) - FIRST sign, Respiratory depression (10-15), Cardiac arrest (>15). Management: (1) STOP magnesium, (2) Calcium gluconate 1g (10mL 10%) IV over 3-5min as antidote, (3) Support ventilation, (4) IV fluids if not anuric. Calcium reverses toxicity within minutes. Risk factors: renal insufficiency, excessive dosing. Oliguria (20mL/h) contributed. A wrong: Absent reflexes + RR 8 = TOXICITY. C wrong: Must STOP and give antidote. D wrong: Give calcium FIRST.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with new AF (HR 138, symptom onset "this morning" per patient - ~10 hr ago) presents to ED. Hemodynamically stable: BP 128/76, no chest pain, no dyspnea. PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia, T2DM. CHA2DS2-VASc 4. No TEE. What is appropriate anticoagulation and cardioversion management?
options: A. Immediate cardioversion without anticoagulation since <12h
B. Start therapeutic anticoagulation; cardiovert after 3wk OR TEE to exclude thrombus then cardiovert; continue ≥4wk post
C. Rate control only; defer cardioversion
D. Cardiovert with heparin bolus only
questions.explanation: - AF cardioversion anticoagulation: AF >48h OR unknown duration: Two options: (1) 3wk therapeutic anticoagulation → cardioversion → ≥4wk post, OR (2) TEE exclude thrombus → cardiovert on anticoagulation → ≥4wk post. Continue long-term per CHA2DS2-VASc (score 4 → anticoagulate). Post-cardioversion anticoagulation ESSENTIAL - atrial stunning. Patient report "8h" unreliable. A wrong: Patient-reported timeline unreliable. Thrombus can form within hours. C wrong: Cardioversion reasonable for symptomatic new AF. D wrong: Heparin insufficient. Need ≥4wk post due to atrial stunning.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman evaluated for TAVR. Cardiologist asks about frailty assessment. What defines frailty?
options: A. Age alone
B. Frailty
C. All elderly are frail
D. No clinical significance
questions.explanation: - Frailty: Clinical syndrome of decreased reserve. Fried criteria: 5 components (weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow gait, low activity). 3+ = frail. Predicts post-procedural outcomes. Important for TAVR risk assessment.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman on dabigatran 150mg BID for AF with acute ICH after fall. CT: large subdural with midline shift. Neurosurgery for urgent evacuation. Last dabigatran 5h ago. CrCl 62. What is MOST appropriate reversal?
options: A. Vitamin K 10mg IV
B. Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5g IV (two 2.5g vials)
C. Andexanet alfa 800mg IV
D. FFP 4 units
questions.explanation: - Idarucizumab is specific dabigatran reversal: Humanized monoclonal antibody fragment binds dabigatran with >350x affinity. Dose: 5g IV (two 2.5g vials). Rapid, complete, sustained reversal. For Xa inhibitors: Andexanet alfa. If unavailable: 4-factor PCC 50 units/kg. Hemodialysis removes ~60% dabigatran. A wrong: Vitamin K only for warfarin. C wrong: Andexanet for Xa inhibitors, NOT dabigatran. D wrong: FFP ineffective for DOAC reversal.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with unprovoked proximal DVT (left femoral-iliac) completed 6mo rivaroxaban. Repeat US: resolution. CHA2DS2-VASc 1, HAS-BLED 1. No family VTE. D-dimer (4wk after stopping): 720 ng/mL (elevated; ULN 500). Thrombophilia testing: negative. What is MOST appropriate recommendation?
options: A. Discontinue - 6mo sufficient
B. Consider extended/indefinite anticoagulation
C. Switch to aspirin 81mg daily
D. Repeat 3mo then stop
questions.explanation: - Unprovoked VTE: ~10%/year recurrence. Factors FAVORING extended: Male gender (2x recurrence), Proximal DVT/PE, Elevated D-dimer off anticoagulation, First unprovoked, Low bleeding risk. This patient: male, proximal, unprovoked, elevated D-dimer, HAS-BLED 1 → strong candidate. Reassess annually. A wrong: 6mo minimum but many benefit from longer. C wrong: Aspirin provides modest protection (~30%) but inferior. ASPIRE, WARFASA trials. D wrong: Arbitrary duration inappropriate.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer (stage IV, liver mets) develops symptomatic PE (segmental bilateral PEs). Started rivaroxaban 15mg BID x21d. Oncology planning FOLFIRINOX. Platelets 165K, Cr 0.8, Hgb 11.2. What is MOST appropriate LONG-TERM anticoagulation for cancer VTE?
options: A. Warfarin dose-adjusted INR 2-3
B. LMWH
C. Aspirin 325mg daily
D. Stop after 3mo
questions.explanation: - Cancer-associated VTE: LMWH traditionally preferred. CLOT trial: dalteparin reduced VTE recurrence vs warfarin (9% vs 17%). Recent trials: rivaroxaban (SELECT-D), edoxaban (Hokusai-VTE Cancer), apixaban (CARAVAGGIO) non-inferior. Caution: Higher GI bleeding with DOACs in GI/GU malignancies. Recommendations: LMWH OR DOACs first-line. Avoid warfarin - drug interactions with chemo, unstable INR. Duration: INDEFINITE while cancer active. A wrong: Warfarin inferior, problematic interactions. C wrong: Aspirin inadequate. D wrong: Need indefinite while cancer active - recurrence 15-20%/year.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man on warfarin for AF (INR goal 2-3) has routine check: INR 9.2. Feels well, no bleeding, no falls/trauma. Exam unremarkable, VS stable. Hgb/Hct stable. Takes 5mg daily, no recent changes. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Continue same dose - will self-correct
B. Hold warfarin 1-2 doses
C. Admit for IV vitamin K 10mg and FFP
D. Stop warfarin permanently
questions.explanation: - INR 5-10 WITHOUT bleeding: (1) Hold 1-2 doses, (2) Consider low-dose oral vitamin K 2.5-5mg (or 1-2mg IV if more rapid but no active bleeding), (3) Recheck INR 24h, (4) Resume at LOWER dose. Avoid high-dose K (causes prolonged warfarin resistance). INR >10 WITHOUT bleeding: K 5-10mg PO. INR any level WITH major bleeding: K 10mg IV + 4-factor PCC 25-50 units/kg OR FFP. A wrong: INR 9.2 carries bleeding risk. B correct balances reversal with avoiding over-correction. C wrong: No active bleeding - outpatient appropriate. D wrong: Single elevated INR doesn't indicate non-adherence.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman develops HIT on day 7 of UFH for DVT. Platelet count 245K to 72K. 4Ts score 7 (high). Serotonin release assay pending. Heparin stopped. Currently has DVT requiring anticoagulation. No active bleeding. Cr 1.0. What is MOST appropriate alternative?
options: A. Switch to LMWH (enoxaparin)
B. Start direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban) or fondaparinux; avoid ALL heparin including LMWH
C. Start warfarin immediately
D. Hold all anticoagulation until platelets recover
questions.explanation: - HIT Type II: Immune-mediated, platelets drop >50% day 5-10, HIGH thrombosis risk 30-50%. Management: (1) STOP all heparin (including flushes, LMWH - crossreacts ~90%), (2) Start alternative: Argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor, hepatic), Bivalirudin, or Fondaparinux (synthetic pentasaccharide, NO cross-reactivity), (3) Screen for thrombosis, (4) Do NOT start warfarin until platelets >150K and overlap ≥5d (warfarin alone increases thrombosis via protein C depletion - warfarin-induced limb gangrene), (5) AVOID platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding. Duration: ≥3mo. A wrong: LMWH has ~90% cross-reactivity - CONTRAINDICATED. C wrong: Warfarin should NOT be started before platelets recover. D wrong: High thrombosis risk mandates anticoagulation.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman with permanent AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 5) and stable CAD s/p PCI with DES 18mo ago on apixaban 5mg BID, aspirin 81mg, metoprolol 50mg BID, atorvastatin 40mg. No angina, functionally active, no bleeding. What is MOST appropriate antithrombotic regimen?
options: A. Continue both apixaban and aspirin indefinitely
B. Anticoagulation monotherapy (apixaban alone)
C. Triple therapy (apixaban + aspirin + clopidogrel)
D. Stop apixaban; aspirin monotherapy
questions.explanation: - AF + stable CAD (>12mo post-PCI): Anticoagulation monotherapy sufficient - adding antiplatelet increases bleeding 1.5-2x without ischemic benefit. Triple therapy duration: (1) Immediate post-PCI: triple x1-4wk, (2) 1-12mo: dual (anticoagulant + P2Y12, STOP aspirin), (3) >12mo: anticoagulant MONOTHERAPY. This patient 18mo post-PCI, stable → stop aspirin. PIONEER AF-PCI, RE-DUAL PCI, AUGUSTUS: rivaroxaban/dabigatran + P2Y12 (without aspirin) non-inferior with less bleeding. A wrong: Adding aspirin increases bleeding without benefit. C wrong: Triple dramatically increases bleeding. D wrong: Aspirin alone inadequate for stroke prevention with CHA2DS2-VASc 5.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman with severe symptomatic AS (valve area 0.6cm², mean gradient 58mmHg, LVEF 60%) develops acute pulmonary edema. Scheduled for TAVR in 3 days. BP 162/86, HR 102, RR 26, O2 sat 88% RA. Crackles bilateral, JVP elevated, S4. What is appropriate acute management?
options: A. Aggressive IV furosemide 80mg bolus then infusion
B. Cautious diuresis with careful monitoring
C. IV nitroglycerin for rapid afterload reduction
D. IV esmolol for rate control
questions.explanation: - Severe AS with pulmonary edema: CAUTIOUS management - preloaddependent due to fixed obstruction. Adequate preload required to maintain CO across stenotic valve. Gentle diuresis (furosemide 20-40mg initially). Avoid aggressive diuresis → hypotension/shock. Vasodilators: Use VERY cautiously or avoid - sudden afterload reduction causes profound hypotension. If needed, use in ICU with invasive monitoring. Nitroprusside preferred if vasodilator needed. Beta-blockade: Generally avoid. Definitive: Valve replacement. A wrong: Aggressive diuresis can precipitate shock - stroke volume fixed, depends on preload. C wrong: Nitrates/vasodilators can cause profound hypotension. D wrong: Beta-blockade may worsen HF.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with severe chronic AR, asymptomatic, LVEF 56%, LV end-systolic dimension 51mm, LV end-diastolic dimension 68mm. Echo unchanged from 6mo. Currently not on cardiac medications. What medication may help delay surgical intervention?
options: A. Beta-blockers to reduce HR and regurgitant volume
B. Vasodilators (ACE-I, ARB, or DHP CCB like nifedipine/amlodipine) to reduce afterload and regurgitant volume
C. Digoxin for contractility
D. No medical therapy proven beneficial
questions.explanation: - Chronic AR: Vasodilators (ACE-I, ARB, nifedipine, amlodipine) reduce SVR → decrease regurgitant volume, reduce LV dilation progression. May delay surgery in asymptomatic patients. Surgical indications: (1) Symptoms, (2) LVEF <50%, (3) LVESD >50mm or indexed >25mm/m², (4) LVEDD >70mm or indexed >35mm/m². This patient: asymptomatic, LVEF 56%, LVESD 51mm (AT threshold), LVEDD 68mm - borderline. Vasodilator may help postpone progression. A wrong: Beta-blockers WORSEN AR - bradycardia prolongs diastole → MORE regurgitation time. Contraindicated unless specific indication. C wrong: Digoxin limited role. D wrong: Vasodilators demonstrated benefit.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with severe MS (valve area 1.0cm²) from rheumatic disease and AF develops acute dyspnea and pulmonary edema. HR 142 bpm (irregular), BP 138/82, O2 sat 89% RA. Exam: JVP elevated, bibasilar crackles, diastolic rumble. What rate control addresses BOTH AF and MS pathophysiology?
options: A. Digoxin 0.5mg IV load
B. Beta-blocker (metoprolol IV) or non-DHP CCB (diltiazem IV)
C. DHP CCB (amlodipine)
D. Amiodarone
questions.explanation: - MS pathophysiology: Fixed obstruction limits LV filling. Require LONGER diastole for adequate filling across stenotic valve. AF with RVR → shortened diastole → inadequate LA emptying → LA pressure elevation → pulmonary congestion. Beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs slow HR → prolong diastolic filling → improved hemodynamics. Target HR 60-80. IV metoprolol: 2.5-5mg Q5-15min. IV diltiazem: 0.25mg/kg over 2min, then 5-15mg/h. Also: diuretics, anticoagulation. Definitive: PBMV if favorable anatomy. A wrong: Digoxin provides some rate control but LESS effective, especially with exertion. Slower onset. Inotropy NOT beneficial - problem is filling. C wrong: DHP CCBs don't effectively control rate. D wrong: Amiodarone not first-line for acute rate control.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with IE (S. aureus) develops acute severe MR from posterior leaflet destruction. Cardiogenic shock: BP 84/52, HR 122, cool extremities, pulmonary edema, altered MS. Echo: severe MR with flail leaflet, LVEF 45%. Surgery consulted for urgent repair. What provides temporary hemodynamic stabilization?
options: A. IV dobutamine alone
B. IV vasodilators
C. IV fluids for volume expansion
D. IV metoprolol for rate control
questions.explanation: - Acute severe MR: Sudden volume overload → pulmonary edema, reduced forward CO. Key: Reduce afterload → decrease regurgitant fraction (more forward, less backward). IV vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside): Reduce SVR → easier for blood to go forward → increase forward CO, reduce pulmonary congestion. If persistent low output: add dobutamine. If refractory: IABP. Definitive: Urgent surgical repair. Chronic MR different: ACE-I/ARB, diuretics. A wrong: Inotrope alone doesn't address high afterload driving regurgitation. B includes inotrope if needed. C wrong: Volume worsens pulmonary edema - already overloaded. D wrong: Rate control not primary issue.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman hospitalized for pneumonia on levofloxacin 750mg develops polymorphic VT (torsades) on telemetry. Also taking sotalol 80mg BID (for AF), ondansetron 4mg Q6h. Labs: K 3.2, Mg 1.5, Cr 0.9. Baseline ECG: QTc 512ms. Episode self-terminated after 15sec. What is MOST important immediate intervention?
options: A. Amiodarone 150mg IV bolus
B. Magnesium sulfate 2g IV bolus
C. Lidocaine 1-1.5mg/kg IV
D. Immediate defibrillation preparation only
questions.explanation: - Torsades management: (1) IV magnesium 2g bolus FIRST-LINE (even if normal) - stabilizes membrane, effective ~90%. Can repeat to 4-6g. (2) STOP ALL QTprolonging drugs: sotalol, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron. (3) Correct K>4.5, Mg>2.0. (4) If recurrent: Isoproterenol 2-10mcg/min (increases HR → shortens QT) OR overdrive pacing (HR 90-120). (5) Identify cause. (6) AVOID class IA/III antiarrhythmics (prolong QT). (7) Defibrillate if sustained VF. A wrong: Amiodarone prolongs QT - CONTRAINDICATED. C wrong: Lidocaine not first-line. D wrong: Magnesium prevents recurrence.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with office BP 166/94, 162/96, 168/98 mmHg over 2 visits. Home monitor reports average 128/78 mmHg over 2wk (multiple readings morning and evening). BMI 27, no other CV risk factors, exam unremarkable. What is MOST likely diagnosis and management?
options: A. Stage 2 hypertension - start two-drug combination immediately
B. White coat hypertension
C. Masked hypertension requiring treatment
D. Normal BP - ignore office readings
questions.explanation: - White coat hypertension: Elevated office BP (≥130/80) with normal out-ofoffice on home (<130/80) or daytime ABPM (<125/75). Prevalence 15-30%. Not entirely benign - some progress to sustained HTN (5-10%/year). Management: (1) Confirm with home BP or ABPM, (2) Do NOT start medications, (3) Annual monitoring, (4) AGGRESSIVE lifestyle modifications, (5) Treat if progresses or very high CV risk. Out-of-office BP more predictive. Masked HTN (opposite): Normal office, elevated home - HIGHER CV risk, requires treatment. A wrong: Would over-treat. C wrong: Masked is opposite. D wrong: Should not ignore - monitor annually.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with Stage 1 HTN (office 144/88, home average 138/84) has 10-year ASCVD risk 6% (low). No DM, CKD, CVD. BMI 32, sedentary. What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. Start thiazide diuretic immediately
B. Lifestyle modifications
C. Start two-drug combination
D. No intervention
questions.explanation: - Stage 1 HTN (130-139/80-89) with LOW CV risk (<10% ASCVD): Lifestyle modifications FIRST-LINE. Interventions: (1) DASH diet (lowers BP 8-14mmHg), (2) Weight loss (5-20mmHg per 10kg), (3) Exercise ≥150min/week (4-9mmHg), (4) Sodium <1500-2300mg/day (2-8mmHg), (5) Limit alcohol (2-4mmHg). Add medication if: ASCVD ≥10%, DM, CKD, known CVD, or BP remains elevated after 3-6mo. Stage 2 (≥140/90): Start medication immediately. A, C wrong: Stage 1 with low CV risk → trial lifestyle first. D wrong: BP 138/84 above goal - needs intervention.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with newly discovered HTN. Office BP 178/106, confirmed. Home average 172/102. No family HTN. BMI 22, active. Exam: systolic-diastolic abdominal bruit. Labs: K 3.1 (repeat 3.0), Cr 1.4 (eGFR 48), glucose 92. UA: protein 2+. Renal US: right kidney 8.2cm, left 11.4cm (asymmetric). What is MOST likely diagnosis?
options: A. Primary (essential) hypertension
B. Renal artery stenosis
C. Primary aldosteronism
D. Pheochromocytoma
questions.explanation: - Renal artery stenosis clinical clues: (1) Onset <30 or >55, (2) Severe/resistant HTN, (3) Abdominal bruit (systolic-diastolic specific), (4) Asymmetric kidney size (>1.5cm - stenotic atrophies), (5) Rise in Cr >30% after ACE-I/ARB, (6) Flash pulmonary edema, (7) Hypokalemia (secondary hyperaldosteronism from RAAS). This patient: age 28, severe HTN (178/106), bruit, asymmetric kidneys (right 8.2, left 11.4 - 3.2cm difference), hypokalemia (K 3.0), elevated Cr - CLASSIC. Etiology: Young: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) - "string of beads". Older: Atherosclerotic. Workup: CTA or MRA. Treatment: Medical vs revascularization. CORAL: revascularization didn't improve outcomes in atherosclerotic. FMD more likely benefits from angioplasty. A wrong: Unlikely given age <30, severity, secondary features. C wrong: Primary aldo possible but bruit + asymmetric kidneys point to RAS. D wrong: Lacks paroxysmal symptoms.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with ASCVD (prior MI 3y ago) on atorvastatin 80mg x2y develops new bilateral proximal muscle pain/weakness x4wk. Denies dark urine. Adherent. Labs: CK 880 U/L (ULN 200), AST 52, ALT 48 (mildly elevated), Cr 1.0, TSH 2.4. LDL-C on treatment: 62 mg/dL. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Continue atorvastatin - mild CK elevation acceptable
B. Hold atorvastatin
C. Switch to fenofibrate
D. Stop all lipid-lowering - already at goal
questions.explanation: - Statin-associated muscle symptoms: Spectrum from myalgias (no CK elevation) to myositis (pain + CK elevation) to rhabdomyolysis (CK >10x ULN + myoglobinuria, renal injury). This patient: myalgias + CK 880 (4.4x ULN), AST/ALT mildly elevated - statin myopathy.
