Management: (1) Hold statin, (2) Check CK weekly until normalizes (2-6wk), (3) Evaluate contributing factors: hypothyroidism (TSH normal), vitamin D deficiency, drug interactions, (4) Rechallenge: Lower-intensity statin, Different statin (pravastatin/fluvastatin least likely - hydrophilic, less muscle penetration), Alternate-day dosing (atorvastatin/rosuvastatin long t½), (5) If recurrent: Non-statin - ezetimibe 10mg (lowers LDL ~18%), PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab - SC, very effective), bempedoic acid (oral, lowers LDL ~18%, not activated in muscle). In high-risk ASCVD, maintaining lipid therapy crucial. A wrong: CK 4.4x ULN with symptoms = myopathy requiring discontinuation. C wrong: Fenofibrates also cause myopathy. D wrong: Patient has ASCVD - high-intensity statin indicated. Try rechallenge strategies or non-statin alternatives.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 18%) on maximal GDMT (sacubitril/valsartan 97/103mg BID, carvedilol 25mg BID, spironolactone 50mg, torsemide 100mg BID) has progressive NYHA IV symptoms refractory to medical therapy. Recent: 3 HF hospitalizations past 3mo requiring IV inotropes. Cardiac cath: severe 3-vessel CAD not amenable to revascularization. RHC: CI 1.6 L/min/m², PCWP 28mmHg, PA 58/28mmHg, PVR 2.8 Wood units. CPX test: peak VO2 10 mL/kg/min. BMI 28, Cr 1.8 (eGFR 38), no active infection. Listed for transplant. What is MOST appropriate advanced HF therapy?
options: A. Continue current medical therapy, wait for transplant
B. LVAD implantation as bridge to transplant
C. CRT-D implantation
D. Palliative care only
questions.explanation: - LVAD indications: Bridge to transplant (BTT), bridge to candidacy, or destination therapy for advanced HF refractory to GDMT. This patient meets BTT criteria: NYHA IV despite maximal GDMT, peak VO2 <12-14 mL/kg/min, CI <2.0, recurrent hospitalizations requiring inotropes, listed for transplant but decompensating. INTERMACS profile 3-4 (inotrope-dependent). Contraindications screened: no infection, adequate BMI, acceptable renal function. MOMENTUM 3: HeartMate 3 LVAD survival benefit. A wrong: Patient decompensating - NOT compensated. C wrong: CRT-D for LBBB with QRS ≥120-150ms, LVEF ≤35%. Advanced HF requiring inotropes needs more. D wrong: Appropriate transplant candidate (age 52, listed).

questions.question: A 32-year-old man with sharp substernal chest pain x2 days, worse lying flat, improved sitting forward. Recent URI 1wk ago. Pain radiates to trapezius ridges. Low-grade temps at home. No cardiac history. VS: BP 128/76, HR 94, temp 37.8°C. Exam: Friction rub at left sternal border. Lungs clear. ECG: Diffuse ST-elevation I,II,aVL,V2-V6 with PR-depression. No reciprocal ST-depression. Troponin I 0.12 ng/mL (mildly elevated; ULN 0.04). CRP 48 mg/L (normal <3). Echo: Small circumferential pericardial effusion, no tamponade, LVEF 60%. CXR: Normal. What is MOST appropriate initial therapy?
options: A. Aspirin or ibuprofen alone
B. Aspirin 750-1000mg TID or ibuprofen 600-800mg TID PLUS colchicine 0.6mg BID x3mo
C. Prednisone 0.5mg/kg daily - corticosteroids first-line
D. Urgent pericardiocentesis
questions.explanation: - Acute pericarditis diagnosis: 2 of 4 criteria - Chest pain (pleuritic, positional), Friction rub, Diffuse ST-elevation or PR-depression, New/worsening effusion. This patient has all. Treatment: NSAID + Colchicine combination. NSAIDs: Aspirin 750-1000mg TID, Ibuprofen 600-800mg TID, or Indomethacin 25-50mg TID until symptom/CRP resolution, then taper. Colchicine: 0.6mg BID (or 0.6mg daily if <70kg) x3mo for first episode. COPE, ICAP trials: Colchicine reduces recurrence from ~30% to ~10-15%. Gastroprotection: PPI if GI bleeding risk. Avoid strenuous activity until resolution. A wrong: NSAID alone higher recurrence (~30%). B correct per ESC 2015 guidelines. C wrong: Corticosteroids INCREASE recurrence (~50%) vs NSAID+colchicine (~10-15%). Reserved for contraindications to NSAIDs/colchicine, pregnancy, autoimmune disease. D wrong: Small effusion without tamponade - NO pericardiocentesis.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with progressive dyspnea x1wk. Reports fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance. Recent chemotherapy. VS: BP 88/62, HR 118, RR 22, O2 sat 94% RA. Exam: JVP 14cm, clear lungs, distant heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus 18mmHg. No peripheral edema. ECG: Sinus tach 118 bpm, low voltage, electrical alternans. CXR: Enlarged cardiac silhouette. Echo: Large circumferential effusion, diastolic collapse RA and RV, respiratory variation mitral inflow >25%. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. IV furosemide for volume overload
B. Urgent pericardiocentesis - clinical and echo findings of tamponade
C. NSAIDs and colchicine
D. Admit for observation, repeat echo 24h
questions.explanation: - Cardiac tamponade: Pericardial effusion causing hemodynamic compromise. Beck triad: Hypotension, Elevated JVP, Muffled heart sounds. Additional: Tachycardia, Pulsus paradoxus >10mmHg, Low voltage, Electrical alternans (pathognomonic). Echo: RA/RV diastolic collapse, Respiratory variation >25%, Plethoric IVC. This patient: hypotension (88/62), JVP 14cm, distant sounds, pulsus 18mmHg, electrical alternans, echo with RA/RV collapse, respiratory variation - DEFINITE tamponade. Management: Urgent pericardiocentesis. Temporizing: IV fluids (increase preload), avoid diuretics/vasodilators. Approach: Subxiphoid most common. Post-drainage: Monitor, drain catheter, treat underlying cause (malignant - may need pericardial window, sclerotherapy). A wrong: Tamponade is OBSTRUCTIVE shock. Diuretics WORSEN by reducing preload. Contraindicated. C wrong: Tamponade requires immediate drainage. D wrong: Life-threatening emergency.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man with remote TB (treated 15y ago) presents with progressive dyspnea, abdominal distension, leg swelling x6mo. Early satiety. VS: BP 118/82, HR 88. Exam: JVP 12cm with prominent x and y descents, Kussmaul sign (JVP rises with inspiration), pericardial knock, hepatomegaly, ascites, 2+ leg edema. Lungs clear. ECG: Low voltage. Echo: LVEF 60%, small effusion, septal bounce, biatrial enlargement, dilated IVC. Cardiac cath: RA mean 18mmHg, RV 48/18mmHg, PA 48/22mmHg, PCWP 20mmHg. Dip-and-plateau (square root sign). RVEDP and LVEDP equalized (~18mmHg). CT: Pericardial thickening 4-6mm with calcification. What is diagnosis and treatment?
options: A. Restrictive cardiomyopathy - diuretics
B. Constrictive pericarditis - pericardiectomy definitive; medical therapy (diuretics) if poor surgical candidate
C. Cardiac tamponade - urgent pericardiocentesis
D. RV failure from pulmonary HTN - pulmonary vasodilators
questions.explanation: - Constrictive pericarditis: Rigid, thickened pericardium restricts filling. Causes: Idiopathic, post-cardiac surgery, TB, radiation, viral. Clinical: Right HF symptoms, Kussmaul sign, Pericardial knock, Friedreich sign (rapid y descent). Hemodynamics: Equalized diastolic pressures (RA, RV, PA, PCWP within 5mmHg), Dip-and-plateau (square root sign), Prominent x/y descents. Echo: Septal bounce, Respiratory variation, IVC plethora. CT/MRI: Pericardial thickening >4mm, calcification. Definitive: Pericardiectomy (complete stripping). Surgical mortality 5-15%. Medical: Diuretics for symptoms (caution - may reduce CO). This patient: classic constriction post-TB. Differentiate from restrictive CM: Constriction has equalized pressures, septal bounce, pericardial thickening. Restrictive has elevated BNP, LV dysfunction, no pericardial thickening. A wrong: Constrictive, not restrictive. C wrong: No large effusion, no diastolic collapse. D wrong: No pulmonary HTN - PA only mildly elevated proportionate to filling pressures.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman with progressive dyspnea NYHA III x8mo. PMH: Scleroderma (limited cutaneous) diagnosed 3y ago. No lung disease, PE, cardiac disease. VS: BP 118/68, HR 88, O2 sat 91% RA. Exam: Increased P2, RV heave, TR murmur, JVP 8cm. Echo: RVSP 68mmHg, RV dilation/dysfunction, TR moderate, LVEF 60%. RHC: mPAP 52mmHg, PCWP 12mmHg, PVR 8.2 Wood units, CO 3.8 L/min. Vasoreactivity with inhaled NO: No response (mPAP decrease <10mmHg). PFTs: Mild restrictive, DLCO 58%. V/Q: Low probability PE. What is MOST appropriate initial therapy for PAH?
options: A. CCB (diltiazem or amlodipine)
B. ERA OR PDE-5 inhibitor
C. Diuretics alone
D. Immediate lung transplant
questions.explanation: - PAH: mPAP ≥20mmHg, PCWP ≤15mmHg, PVR >2 Wood units. WHO Group 1. This patient: mPAP 52, PCWP 12, PVR 8.2, CTD-associated (scleroderma). Vasoreactivity testing: Positive response = mPAP decrease ≥10mmHg AND mPAP <40mmHg AND maintained/increased CO. Only 10-15% responders. Responders: High-dose CCB (diltiazem 240-720mg or amlodipine 10-20mg). Non-responders (this patient): PAH-specific therapy. ERAs (ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan): Block endothelin, reduce PVR. LFT monitoring. PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil 20mg TID, tadalafil 40mg daily): Enhance NO-cGMP. Prostacyclin analogs (epoprostenol IV, treprostinil): For severe PAH. Riociguat (sGC stimulator): Alternative. Combination often needed WHO FC III-IV. AMBITION: Ambrisentan + tadalafil superior. Supportive: Diuretics for volume, O2 if hypoxemic. A wrong: CCB only for responders (~10-15%). Non-responder - CCB ineffective, may harm. C wrong: Diuretics insufficient - need PAHspecific therapy. D wrong: Transplant for refractory despite maximal medical therapy.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman with recurrent syncopal episodes x6mo. Episodes after prolonged standing (concerts, church), preceded by warmth, nausea, tunnel vision. Loses consciousness 5-10sec, rapid recovery, no confusion. Never during sleep/lying down. No seizure activity, tongue biting, incontinence. PMH: None. No family sudden death. VS: BP 118/72 standing, 106/68 after standing 3min. HR 78 sitting, 112 standing (increase 34 bpm). Exam: Normal cardiac, neuro. ECG: Normal. Echo: Structurally normal, LVEF 65%. What is MOST likely diagnosis and initial management?
options: A. Seizure disorder - start antiepileptic
B. Neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope - reassurance, increase fluid/salt, physical counterpressure maneuvers, avoid triggers; consider midodrine or fludrocortisone if refractory
C. Orthostatic hypotension - fludrocortisone
D. Long QT syndrome - genetic testing and beta-blocker
questions.explanation: - Neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope: Most common in young with structurally normal heart. Triggers: Prolonged standing, pain, emotion, heat, dehydration. Prodrome: Warmth, nausea, diaphoresis, tunnel vision, pallor. LOC: Brief (seconds), rapid recovery, no post-ictal confusion. Mechanism: Sudden bradycardia and/or vasodilation. Diagnosis: Clinical history, normal cardiac workup. Tilt-table can reproduce but low specificity - not always needed if classic. Initial management: Reassurance (benign), Education triggers/prodrome, Increase fluid (2-3L/day) and salt (6-10g/day), Physical counterpressure maneuvers (leg crossing, squatting, arm tensing when prodrome), Avoid prolonged standing, dehydration. Refractory: Midodrine 5-15mg TID (alpha-1 agonist, vasoconstriction), Fludrocortisone 0.1-0.2mg daily (volume expansion), Beta-blockers (may help some), SSRIs (paroxetine, sertraline). Pacemaker: Reserved for severe bradycardia-predominant with documented asystole. A wrong: No seizure features. C wrong: Orthostatic HTN = BP drop ≥20/10mmHg within 3min. This patient: 118/72→106/68 (only 12/4 drop). D wrong: ECG normal, no QTc prolongation.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man, no CV symptoms, presents for health maintenance. Family: Father MI age 42, paternal grandfather MI age 38, both on "cholesterol medications." Exam: Tendon xanthomas Achilles tendons bilaterally, xanthelasmas. VS: BP 128/78, HR 72, BMI 26. Labs: Total cholesterol 428 mg/dL, LDL-C 358 mg/dL, HDL-C 48 mg/dL, TG 110 mg/dL, glucose 92, TSH 2.1, Cr 0.9. No secondary causes identified. What is MOST appropriate diagnosis and management?
options: A. Lifestyle modification alone
B. Heterozygous FH - start high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg or rosuvastatin 40mg); add ezetimibe if LDL goal not met; consider PCSK9 inhibitor if refractory
C. Homozygous FH - immediate LDL apheresis
D. Dietary hypercholesterolemia - dietitian only
questions.explanation: - Heterozygous FH: Autosomal dominant, prevalence 1:250. LDL receptor mutation → impaired clearance → markedly elevated LDL-C from birth. Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria: LDL >190 mg/dL (untreated) PLUS Tendon xanthomas OR Family history premature CAD (men <55y, women <60y) OR Genetic mutation. This patient: LDL 358, tendon xanthomas, strong family history (father MI 42, grandfather MI 38) - DEFINITE HeFH. Untreated risk: 50% men develop CAD by age 50. Treatment: High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg or rosuvastatin 40-80mg). Goal LDL <100 mg/dL (ideally <70). Add ezetimibe 10mg if goal not met (~18% additional reduction). PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab): If LDL remains elevated despite statin+ezetimibe. SC Q2-4wk, lowers LDL 50-60%. Expensive but effective. Bempedoic acid: Oral alternative if statin intolerant. Screen first-degree relatives (50% have mutation). Genetic testing confirms. Homozygous FH: BOTH alleles, LDL >400-1000, xanthomas in childhood, CAD in teens-20s. Requires apheresis, lomitapide, evolocumab. This patient heterozygous. A wrong: Lifestyle insufficient - LDL 358 requires pharmacotherapy. C wrong: Heterozygous, not homozygous. D wrong: Genetic FH.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents to ED with severe epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea, vomiting x12h. PMH: T2DM (poor control, HbA1c 9.8%), obesity BMI 34. Drinks 6-8 beers daily. Meds: Metformin 1000mg BID (non-adherent). VS: BP 142/88, HR 108, temp 38.2°C. Exam: Epigastric tenderness, no rebound. Labs: Lipase 2840 U/L (ULN 60), amylase 680 U/L (ULN 100), glucose 342 mg/dL, Triglycerides 3200 mg/dL (milky serum), Total cholesterol 420 mg/dL, LDL-C unmeasurable, WBC 16K. CT abdomen: Pancreatic edema, peripancreatic fluid - acute pancreatitis. What is MOST appropriate management of severe hypertriglyceridemia?
options: A. Start high-dose statin immediately for TG lowering

B. NPO, IV fluids, insulin infusion to lower glucose and TG; fenofibrate when tolerating PO; address secondary causes (DM control, alcohol cessation); consider apheresis if TG >1000 despite initial therapy
C. Omega-3 fatty acids alone
D. Niacin for immediate TG reduction
questions.explanation: - Severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG >1000 mg/dL) with acute pancreatitis: TGinduced pancreatitis occurs when TG >1000-2000 mg/dL (chylomicronemia). Immediate management: NPO, aggressive IV fluids, Insulin infusion (even if not diabetic) - lowers TG by activating lipoprotein lipase, lowering glucose reduces VLDL production. Target glucose 150-200 mg/dL. Once tolerating PO: Fibrate therapy - Fenofibrate 145-160mg daily (preferred over gemfibrozil - fewer drug interactions). Lowers TG 30-50%. If TG remains >1000 mg/dL despite medical therapy: Consider plasmapheresis/apheresis. Address secondary causes: Optimize diabetes control (HbA1c 9.8% - poor control major contributor), Alcohol cessation (major cause), Weight loss, Avoid exacerbating medications (thiazides, beta-blockers, estrogen, isotretinoin). Long-term TG management: Fibrate first-line for severe TG, Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA 2-4g daily) adjunct - moderate benefit, Niacin less used (modest TG lowering, side effects), Goal: TG <500 mg/dL to prevent recurrent pancreatitis. A wrong: Statins modest TG reduction (15-30%) - insufficient for TG 3200. Fibrates first-line for severe TG. C wrong: Omega-3 alone insufficient - adjunct therapy. D wrong: Niacin modest TG lowering, side effects limit use.

questions.question: A 48-year-old Hispanic woman presents for annual physical. No CV symptoms. Family history: Mother T2DM, father MI age 58. No smoking. VS: BP 138/86 mmHg (repeated 136/88), HR 76. Exam: BMI 32, waist circumference 38 inches, acanthosis nigricans neck. Labs: Fasting glucose 112 mg/dL, HbA1c 6.2%, Total cholesterol 218 mg/dL, LDL-C 132 mg/dL, HDL-C 38 mg/dL, TG 240 mg/dL, ALT 52 U/L (mildly elevated), AST 42 U/L. What is diagnosis and MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. Normal findings - reassurance only
B. Metabolic syndrome - intensive lifestyle intervention (weight loss, exercise, diet), consider metformin; treat individual components (HTN, dyslipidemia) per guidelines
C. Start statin and antihypertensive immediately
D. Refer for bariatric surgery
questions.explanation: - Metabolic syndrome (NCEP ATP III criteria): ≥3 of 5: Abdominal obesity (waist >40" men, >35" women), TG ≥150 mg/dL, HDL-C <40 mg/dL men/<50 women, BP ≥130/85 mmHg, Fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL. This patient: Waist 38" (>35"), TG 240 (≥150), HDL 38 (<50), BP 138/86 (≥130/85), Glucose 112 (≥100) - ALL 5 criteria = DEFINITE metabolic syndrome. Increases CV risk 2x, T2DM risk 5x. Management: INTENSIVE lifestyle modification FIRST-LINE: Weight loss 7-10% (most important - improves ALL components), Exercise ≥150min/week moderate intensity, Mediterranean or DASH diet, Sodium restriction. Metformin: Consider for glucose 100-125 mg/dL (prediabetes) to prevent T2DM progression. DPP trial: Metformin reduced diabetes development 31% (lifestyle 58%). Treat individual components per guidelines: HTN: If BP ≥130/80 with ASCVD risk ≥10%, DM, or CKD → start medication. This patient ASCVD risk needs calculation. Dyslipidemia: If ASCVD risk ≥7.5-10% → statin. HDL 38, TG 240 suggest atherogenic dyslipidemia. Liver: Mildly elevated transaminases suggest NAFLD (common with metabolic syndrome). Weight loss improves. B wrong: Would immediately start statin/antihypertensive without assessing ASCVD risk or attempting lifestyle. Lifestyle first-line per guidelines. D wrong: Bariatric surgery for BMI ≥40 or ≥35 with comorbidities if lifestyle fails. This patient BMI 32.

questions.question: A 42-year-old IVDU with fever 39.2°C x1wk, new systolic murmur presents to ED. Blood cultures: 4/4 bottles growing MSSA at 12h. TEE: 1.6cm vegetation on tricuspid valve with severe TR. Septic pulmonary emboli on CT chest. No neurologic complications. No other metastatic infections. Started nafcillin 12g/day IV divided Q4h. ID and CT surgery consulted. Defervesced by day 3. Repeat blood cultures day 3: negative. What is recommended DURATION of IV antibiotic therapy for right-sided native valve IE with MSSA?
options: A. 2 weeks nafcillin sufficient for uncomplicated right-sided MSSA IE
B. 4-6 weeks IV nafcillin standard for native valve IE; 2-week regimen only for truly uncomplicated cases (vegetation <2cm, no extracardiac complications, rapid defervescence)
C. 6-8 weeks required for all IE in IVDU
D. Oral antibiotics acceptable after 2 weeks IV
questions.explanation: - Native valve IE antibiotic duration: Standard = 4-6 weeks IV from first negative blood culture. MSSA: Nafcillin or oxacillin 12g/day divided Q4-6h. Right-sided IE in IVDU: Some data support 2-week short-course IF truly uncomplicated: Vegetation <2cm, No extracardiac complications (no abscess, emboli, heart block, severe HF), MSSA (not MRSA), Rapid defervescence (<96h), No immunosuppression. This patient does NOT qualify: Vegetation 1.6cm (borderline), SEVERE TR (complication), Septic pulmonary emboli (extracardiac complication). Should receive standard 4-6 weeks. Alternative short-course (if truly uncomplicated): Nafcillin + gentamicin x2 weeks, but higher nephrotoxicity. Surgery indications right-sided IE: Refractory sepsis, Fungal IE, Recurrent emboli, Vegetations >20mm with recurrent emboli, TV dysfunction causing refractory HF. This patient severe TR + emboli → surgery may be needed if persistent sepsis. A wrong: Patient has complications - NOT uncomplicated. C wrong: 6-8 weeks for prosthetic valve, not native. D wrong: Must complete full IV course.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with bicuspid aortic valve (moderate AS valve area 1.2cm², trace AR) needs tooth extraction for infected molar. No prior endocarditis. No prosthetic valves. No cardiac devices. Otherwise healthy. Asks about antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedure. What is MOST appropriate per current AHA guidelines?
options: A. Amoxicillin 2g PO 30-60min before - all valvular disease needs prophylaxis
B. No prophylaxis needed
C. Clindamycin 600mg PO if PCN allergic - required for all valve disease
D. Prophylaxis for extraction but not routine cleaning
questions.explanation: - IE prophylaxis 2007 AHA guidelines RESTRICTED to highest-risk: Prior IE, Prosthetic cardiac valve or prosthetic material, Unrepaired cyanotic CHD OR repaired with residual defects, Cardiac transplantation with valvulopathy. NO LONGER recommended for: Acquired valvular disease (MVP with MR, AS, AR), Bicuspid aortic valve, HCM, Most CHD. Dental procedures requiring prophylaxis (in high-risk): Gingival manipulation or periapical region perforation (includes extractions, NOT routine cleaning unless these involved). Regimen (high-risk only): Amoxicillin 2g PO 30-60min before. If PCN allergic: Cephalexin 2g, Clindamycin 600mg, Azithromycin 500mg, or Doxycycline 100mg. This patient: Bicuspid aortic valve WITHOUT prior IE or prosthetic → NO prophylaxis per current guidelines. Guideline change based on: Limited efficacy data, Low absolute risk, Concerns about antibiotic resistance. A, C, D wrong: Bicuspid aortic valve not indication.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with uncontrolled HTN (non-adherent to meds x6mo) presents with sudden severe "tearing" chest pain radiating to back between scapulae x2h. PMH: HTN. Smokes 1ppd. VS: BP right arm 188/102, left arm 184/98, HR 102, RR 22. Exam: Anxious, diaphoretic. Cardiac: Regular, no murmur. Neuro: Normal. Pulses: 2+ radial bilaterally, 2+ femorals bilaterally, symmetric. CT angiography: Type B (Stanford) aortic dissection - intimal flap beginning 2cm distal to left subclavian artery extending through descending thoracic/abdominal aorta to infrarenal aorta. No malperfusion. Aortic diameter 4.8cm. No rupture. What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. Immediate surgical repair - all dissections require surgery
B. Medical management
C. Immediate TEVAR (thoracic endovascular repair)
D. Morphine for pain only
questions.explanation: - Aortic dissection Stanford classification: Type A (involves ascending) → Immediate surgery. Type B (descending only, distal to left subclavian) → Medical unless complicated. This patient: Type B (starts 2cm distal to left subclavian), uncomplicated. Medical management uncomplicated Type B: Beta-blockade FIRST (reduce dP/dt): IV esmolol 500mcg/kg load, then 50-200mcg/kg/min OR IV labetalol 20mg Q10min or infusion OR IV metoprolol 5mg Q5min. Target HR <60 bpm. THEN vasodilator (only AFTER beta-blockade): IV nicardipine 5-15mg/h OR IV nitroprusside 0.3-10mcg/kg/min. Target SBP 100-120 mmHg. Transition to PO: Beta-blocker + ACE-I/ARB/CCB. Strict BP control lifelong. Complicated Type B (requires intervention): Malperfusion (visceral, renal, limb), Contained rupture, Refractory pain/HTN, Aortic expansion, Retrograde extension to ascending. TEVAR preferred over open surgery for complicated Type B. INSTEAD trial: TEVAR + medical vs medical alone - improved remodeling but no short-term mortality benefit in uncomplicated. A wrong: Type A requires immediate surgery. Type B uncomplicated → medical. C wrong: TEVAR for complicated, not uncomplicated. D wrong: Inadequate - needs aggressive BP/HR control.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with incidental ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm on CT. Asymptomatic. PMH: HTN, bicuspid aortic valve with moderate AS (valve area 1.2cm²), trace AR. Meds: Lisinopril 20mg, atorvastatin 40mg. VS: BP 138/82, HR 72. Echo: Ascending aortic aneurysm 5.2cm diameter, bicuspid valve with moderate AS, LVEF 60%. No dissection. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Observation with serial imaging Q6-12mo - surgery only ≥6.0cm
B. Elective surgical repair indicated - diameter ≥5.5cm general population OR ≥5.0cm with bicuspid aortic valve; may need concomitant AVR
C. Immediate emergency surgery
D. TEVAR preferred over open
questions.explanation: - Thoracic aortic aneurysm surgery indications (ascending): ≥5.5cm general population, ≥5.0cm if bicuspid aortic valve (higher dissection risk), ≥4.5-5.0cm if Marfan syndrome, ≥4.0-4.5cm if rapid growth (>0.5cm/year), OR if undergoing cardiac surgery for other indication and diameter ≥4.5cm. Symptomatic aneurysm regardless of size. Dissection/rupture: Emergency. This patient: 5.2cm with bicuspid valve → MEETS threshold (≥5.0cm with bicuspid). Also moderate AS (valve area 1.2cm²) - may need concomitant AVR or valve-sparing root replacement. Surgical options: Composite graft (Bentall): Replace root, ascending, valve. Valve-sparing root replacement (David/Yacoub): Preserve native valve if minimal AS/AR. Separate ascending replacement + AVR. Medical (awaiting surgery or non-candidate): Strict BP control (target <130/80), beta-blockers preferred, avoid strenuous activity, serial imaging. A wrong: Threshold with bicuspid valve ≥5.0cm, not 6.0cm. Patient 5.2cm meets criteria. C wrong: Not emergency - asymptomatic, no dissection. Elective. D wrong: TEVAR for descending aneurysms. Ascending requires open surgery.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with 40-pack-year smoking history (quit 5y ago) presents for annual exam. No abdominal pain. PMH: HTN, COPD, hyperlipidemia. Meds: Lisinopril 10mg, atorvastatin 40mg, tiotropium inhaler. Never had abdominal ultrasound screening. VS: BP 142/86, HR 78. Exam: No pulsatile abdominal mass. What is MOST appropriate AAA screening recommendation per USPSTF?
options: A. No screening - no symptoms
B. One-time abdominal ultrasound screening
C. CT angiography annually
D. Screening only if symptoms
questions.explanation: - AAA screening USPSTF: Men age 65-75 with smoking history (ever smokers): ONE-TIME ultrasound (Grade B). Men age 65-75 never smokers: Selective - discuss (Grade C). Women: No routine screening unless family history/risk factors (Grade D). This patient: 68-year-old man with 40-pack-year history → DEFINITE indication. Screening findings/management: <3.0cm: Normal. 3.0-3.9cm: Rescreen Q3 years. 4.0-4.9cm: Rescreen Q6-12 months. 5.0-5.4cm: Rescreen Q3-6 months, refer vascular surgery. ≥5.5cm: Elective repair (open or EVAR). Repair indications: Diameter ≥5.5cm (men) or ≥5.0cm (women), Growth ≥0.5cm in 6 months or ≥1cm in 1 year, Symptomatic (pain, tenderness), Ruptured (emergency). Medical management (<5.5cm): Smoking cessation (most important), Strict BP control, Statin, Beta-blockers may slow growth. Rupture risk: 3-4cm: 0.5%/year, 4-5cm: 1-3%/year, 5-6cm: 5-10%/year, >6cm: 15-20%/year. Surgical mortality: Elective 1-5%, ruptured 40-50%. A wrong: Clear indication for one-time screening. C wrong: One-time ultrasound sufficient. CT/CTA for surgical planning if large AAA. D wrong: Screening detects asymptomatic to prevent rupture.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with newly discovered HTN. BP 168/94 both arms on multiple visits. Home BP: average 162/88. No symptoms. PMH: "Heart murmur" as child, never followed. Exam: BP right arm 168/94, left arm 166/92. Lower extremities: BP right leg 128/76, left leg 124/72 (arm-leg gradient >20mmHg). Systolic murmur left sternal border radiating to back. Weak, delayed femoral pulses vs radial (radial-femoral delay). No rib notching on CXR. CT angiography: Focal narrowing (coarctation) descending aorta just distal to left subclavian, diameter 8mm at narrowing (normal ~20mm). Peak gradient 35mmHg across coarctation. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Medical management with antihypertensives alone
B. Percutaneous balloon angioplasty ± stenting
C. Observation - mild coarctation
D. Beta-blockers alone
questions.explanation: - Coarctation of aorta in adults: Often undiagnosed until adulthood. Clinical: HTN upper extremities, arm-leg BP gradient >20mmHg, weak/delayed femoral pulses (radialfemoral delay), systolic murmur (back between scapulae), rib notching on CXR (collaterals erode ribs - longstanding). Diagnosis: CT/MR angiography shows focal narrowing. Measure gradient. Intervention indications: Peak gradient >20mmHg, HTN, LV dysfunction, Significant collaterals. This patient: Gradient 35mmHg, HTN despite young age, arm-leg gradient >20mmHg → intervention indicated. Treatment adults: Native coarctation: Balloon angioplasty + stent PREFERRED (less invasive). Recurrent coarctation (after prior repair): Balloon angioplasty ± stent. Complex anatomy or aneurysm: Surgical repair. Post-intervention: HTN often persists despite anatomic repair (50-75% remain hypertensive) - requires lifelong antihypertensive therapy. Mechanism: Chronic HTN causes baroreceptor resetting, LVH, renal changes. Complications: Aortic dissection/rupture, endocarditis, intracranial aneurysm (Berry aneurysms - circle of Willis), LV dysfunction. Lifelong follow-up required. A wrong: Coarctation with significant gradient needs mechanical relief. Medical alone insufficient. C wrong: Gradient 35mmHg and HTN - NOT mild. D wrong: Needs intervention.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer. Oncology recommends doxorubicin-based chemotherapy (AC regimen: doxorubicin 60mg/m² + cyclophosphamide Q3 weeks x4 cycles). No cardiac history. VS: BP 128/76, HR 72. Baseline echo: LVEF 62%, no abnormalities. ECG: Normal. Labs: BNP 42 pg/mL, troponin I <0.01. What is MOST appropriate cardiac monitoring strategy during anthracycline therapy?
options: A. No monitoring - baseline normal
B. Serial echocardiograms
C. ECG only before each cycle
D. Troponin monitoring only
questions.explanation: - Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: Doxorubicin, daunorubicin, epirubicin, idarubicin cause dose-dependent cardiomyopathy. Mechanism: Free radical formation, mitochondrial damage, cardiomyocyte apoptosis. Risk factors: Higher cumulative dose (>400-450mg/m² doxorubicin), Age >65 or <18, Prior chest radiation, Concurrent cardiotoxic agents (trastuzumab, cyclophosphamide), Pre-existing cardiac disease, HTN, DM. Cardiotoxicity types: Acute (during infusion): Arrhythmias, ischemia, pericarditis - rare. Early chronic (within 1 year): Asymptomatic LVEF decline or symptomatic HF - most common. Late chronic (>1 year post): Dilated cardiomyopathy - can occur decades later. Monitoring: Baseline echo with LVEF, Serial echo during treatment: After 200-250mg/m² cumulative, before each dose if high risk, at completion. Post-treatment echo: 6-12 months, then as indicated. Cardiac biomarkers (troponin, BNP): Rising levels may predict cardiotoxicity. Hold anthracycline if: LVEF drops ≥10% to <53% (ASE guidelines), OR symptomatic HF develops. Cardioprotection: Dexrazoxane (iron chelator): Reduces cardiotoxicity with cumulative doxorubicin >300mg/m². ACE-I/ARBs, beta-blockers: Some data suggest prophylactic use may prevent LVEF decline. Liposomal anthracyclines: Lower cardiotoxicity. Treatment established cardiotoxicity: Standard HF therapy. Many recover with early intervention. A wrong: Need monitoring during treatment. C wrong: LVEF monitoring essential. D wrong: Echo with LVEF key.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with HER2+ breast cancer completed doxorubicin-based chemotherapy (cumulative dose 240mg/m²). Echo post-doxorubicin: LVEF 54% (baseline 62%). Now starting trastuzumab therapy. No cardiac symptoms. PMH: HTN (controlled on lisinopril 20mg). What is MOST appropriate cardiac monitoring and management for trastuzumab?
options: A. No monitoring - LVEF 54% acceptable
B. Serial LVEF monitoring Q3mo during trastuzumab
C. Proceed without monitoring
D. Contraindicated - prior anthracycline precludes trastuzumab
questions.explanation: - Trastuzumab (Herceptin) cardiotoxicity: HER2 inhibitor for HER2+ breast cancer. Mechanism: HER2/ErbB2 signaling important for cardiomyocyte stress response. Blockade impairs adaptive response. Cardiotoxicity: Asymptomatic LVEF decline or symptomatic HF in 2-7% monotherapy, up to 20-30% with anthracyclines. Key differences from anthracyclines: NOT dose-dependent, Often REVERSIBLE with discontinuation (unlike anthracyclines), Synergistic toxicity with anthracyclines. Risk factors: Prior/concurrent anthracycline, Age >60, Pre-existing cardiac disease, HTN, Low baseline LVEF. This patient: High risk - prior anthracycline (240mg/m²), LVEF declined 62%→54% (8% drop), HTN. Monitoring: Baseline LVEF before trastuzumab, Repeat LVEF Q3 months during treatment, Continue after completion. Hold criteria: LVEF <50%, OR LVEF drops ≥10% to <53%, OR symptomatic HF. Management LVEF decline: Hold trastuzumab, Optimize HF therapy (ACEI/ARB, beta-blocker), Recheck LVEF in 4 weeks, May resume if LVEF recovers and no symptoms with close monitoring. Many can resume. Alternatives if cardiotoxicity: Adotrastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), Pertuzumab (lower cardiotoxicity), Neratinib (oral HER2 inhibitor). A wrong: Need monitoring - high-risk with baseline decline. C wrong: Monitoring essential. D wrong: Not contraindicated but requires very close monitoring.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man with schizophrenia on ziprasidone 80mg BID x2y presents for cardiac clearance before adding medication. No cardiac symptoms. PMH: Schizophrenia only. No family sudden death. VS: BP 118/76, HR 78. Exam: Normal. ECG: Sinus rhythm, QTc 468ms (prolonged; ULN men 440ms). Repeat ECG: QTc 472ms. Labs: K 4.2, Mg 2.1, Ca 9.4, TSH 2.0. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Continue ziprasidone - QTc <500ms acceptable
B. Discontinue ziprasidone
C. Add beta-blocker to shorten QTc
D. Continue and add multiple QT-prolonging drugs
questions.explanation: - Drug-induced QTc prolongation: QTc measures ventricular repolarization. Normal: Men <440ms, Women <460ms. Prolonged: Men >440ms, Women >460ms. Severe: >500ms. Torsades risk increases >500ms but can occur >460ms with risk factors. Atypical antipsychotics QTc risk (highest to lowest): Highest: Ziprasidone, thioridazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol IV. Moderate: Quetiapine, iloperidone, paliperidone. Lower: Risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole, clozapine. Management: Discontinue if QTc >500ms or >460ms with risk factors, Switch to lower-risk alternative, Correct K>4.0 (ideally >4.5), Mg>2.0, Avoid other QTprolonging drugs, Avoid combinations that inhibit metabolism. Other common QT-prolonging drugs: Antibiotics: Fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin>levofloxacin), macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin), Antifungals: Fluconazole, voriconazole, Antiemetics: Ondansetron, domperidone, Antiarrhythmics: Class IA (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide), Class III (sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide, amiodarone), Others: Methadone, SSRIs (citalopram, escitalopram). This patient: Ziprasidone (highest-risk), QTc 468-472ms (prolonged), electrolytes normal. Switch to lower-risk antipsychotic (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) recommended. A wrong: QTc 468-472ms prolonged - switch indicated. C wrong: Beta-blockers don't shorten QTc, may help prevent torsades in congenital LQTS but not drug-induced. D wrong: Absolutely avoid combining QT-prolonging agents.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson disease presents with recurrent near-syncope upon standing x3mo. Episodes within 1-2min of standing from sitting/lying. Denies palpitations, chest pain. PMH: Parkinson x5y, T2DM, BPH. Meds: Carbidopa/levodopa 25/100mg TID, pramipexole 1mg TID, tamsulosin 0.4mg HS, metformin 1000mg BID. Supine VS: BP 148/88, HR 72. Standing VS (3min): BP 106/64, HR 76. What is diagnosis and MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Neurocardiogenic syncope - increase fluid/salt
B. Orthostatic hypotension - review/reduce offending medications
C. Cardiac arrhythmia - Holter monitor
D. Dehydration - IV fluids
questions.explanation: - Orthostatic hypotension: BP drop ≥20mmHg systolic or ≥10mmHg diastolic within 3min standing. This patient: 148/88 supine → 106/64 standing (drop 42/24mmHg) - DEFINITE orthostatic hypotension. Causes: Medications: Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin), vasodilators, diuretics, antihypertensives, dopamine agonists (pramipexole), TCAs, Neurogenic: Parkinson, diabetes (autonomic neuropathy), MSA, pure autonomic failure, Volume depletion, Cardiac, Prolonged bed rest, anemia. Management: Review medications - Discontinue/reduce: tamsulosin (try alternatives: finasteride, tadalafil), pramipexole if possible, antihypertensives if excessive. Non-pharmacologic: Increase fluid (2-2.5L/day), salt (6-10g/day unless contraindicated), Physical countermaneuvers (slow rising, leg crossing, squatting), Compression stockings (waist-high 30-40mmHg), Elevate head of bed 10-20 degrees, Small frequent meals, Avoid triggers. Pharmacologic (refractory): Fludrocortisone 0.1-0.2mg daily (volume expansion, contraindications: HF, edema), Midodrine 2.5-10mg TID (alpha-agonist, vasoconstriction), Droxidopa (norepinephrine precursor) for neurogenic, Pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor). A wrong: Orthostatic hypotension, not neurocardiogenic. C wrong: No palpitations, HR change minimal. D wrong: Likely medication-induced + neurogenic from Parkinson.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with chronic fatigue, lightheadedness upon standing x8mo. Episodes within 10min of standing. Reports palpitations, "brain fog." No syncope. No cardiac disease. Supine VS: BP 118/74, HR 68. Standing VS (10min): BP 122/78, HR 122 (increase 54 bpm). Tilt-table: Confirms sustained HR increase ≥30 bpm within 10min of upright without orthostatic hypotension. What is MOST likely diagnosis and initial management?
options: A. Orthostatic hypotension - fludrocortisone
B. POTS
C. Anxiety disorder - SSRI
D. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia - sinus node ablation
questions.explanation: - POTS diagnosis: Sustained HR increase ≥30 bpm (or HR ≥120 bpm if age 12-19: ≥40 bpm) within 10min standing WITHOUT orthostatic hypotension (BP drop <20/10mmHg). Symptoms during upright: Lightheadedness, palpitations, fatigue, "brain fog," tremor, exercise intolerance. Demographics: Young women (15-50y), often post-viral. This patient: HR 68→122 standing (increase 54 bpm), BP stable (118/74→122/78), symptoms - CLASSIC POTS. Pathophysiology: Hypovolemia, Excessive sympathetic activation, Small fiber neuropathy, Deconditioning. Management: Non-pharmacologic (first-line): Increase fluid (2-3L/day), salt (6-10g/day), Graduated exercise program (recumbent initially - rowing, swimming, cycling; avoid upright initially), Compression stockings (waist-high 30-40mmHg), Small frequent meals, Avoid triggers: heat, alcohol, dehydration, prolonged standing. Pharmacologic (refractory): Beta-blockers: Propranolol 10-20mg BID-QID (low dose), bisoprolol, metoprolol. Caution: May worsen fatigue. Fludrocortisone 0.1-0.2mg daily (volume expansion), Midodrine 2.5-10mg TID (vasoconstriction), Ivabradine (If channel blocker, reduces HR without negative inotropy), Pyridostigmine. Prognosis: Many improve over time with exercise conditioning. A wrong: No orthostatic hypotension (BP stable). C wrong: POTS distinct from anxiety. D wrong: Not IST - HR increase posture-dependent in POTS.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with recently diagnosed HCM. Echo: Severe asymmetric septal hypertrophy (septum 22mm, posterior wall 11mm), LVOT gradient 68mmHg at rest, SAM of mitral valve with moderate MR, LVEF 70%. Exercise stress: Exertional dyspnea, max LVOT gradient 88mmHg. No syncope, no VT on Holter. Family: Brother died suddenly age 32 (cause unknown). What is MOST appropriate initial therapy for symptomatic LVOT obstruction?
options: A. Diuretics to reduce preload
B. Beta-blocker
C. Digoxin for contractility
D. Vasodilators (ACE-I) for afterload reduction
questions.explanation: - HCM: Asymmetric LVH, LVOT obstruction (~2/3), diastolic dysfunction. Symptoms: Dyspnea, angina, syncope, palpitations. Sudden death risk. LVOT obstruction: SAM of mitral valve → MR. Gradient ≥30mmHg at rest or ≥50mmHg with provocation = significant. This patient: Severe LVOT obstruction (rest gradient 68mmHg, exercise 88mmHg), symptomatic dyspnea, significant SAM and MR. Medical therapy: Beta-blockers (first-line): Metoprolol succinate 100-200mg daily or propranolol 120-240mg daily. Reduce contractility, HR (prolong diastole → improve filling), reduce LVOT gradient. Non-DHP CCBs (if beta-blockers contraindicated/ineffective): Verapamil 240-480mg daily. Negative inotropy, reduce HR. Caution if severe obstruction or HF. Disopyramide (added to beta-blocker if refractory): Negative inotropy. Monitor QTc. Medications to AVOID: Diuretics (reduce preload → worsen obstruction), Vasodilators (ACE-I, ARB, nitrates - reduce afterload → worsen obstruction), Digoxin (increase contractility → worsen obstruction), Nifedipine/DHP CCBs (vasodilation → worsen obstruction). Invasive therapies (if medical fails): Surgical myectomy (septal myomectomy): Gold standard. Alcohol septal ablation: Induced MI of basal septum. Dualchamber pacing: May reduce gradient. SCD risk stratification: Major factors: Prior cardiac arrest/VT, Family history SCD, Unexplained syncope, Massive LVH (≥30mm), Abnormal BP response to exercise, NSVT. This patient: Family SCD (brother age 32), severe LVH (22mm). Consider ICD. A, C, D wrong: Avoid - all worsen LVOT obstruction.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with acute chest pain and dyspnea 1h after receiving news of son's death in accident. Pain substernal, diaphoresis. PMH: HTN only. VS: BP 168/92, HR 108, RR 22, O2 sat 92% RA. Exam: Distress, JVP 8cm, S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles. ECG: STelevation V2-V6. Troponin I 2.4 ng/mL (elevated). Emergent angiography: NORMAL coronary arteries. Left ventriculography: Apical ballooning with hyperkinesis of basal segments, LVEF 35%. What is MOST likely diagnosis and management?
options: A. STEMI with spontaneous reperfusion
B. Takotsubo (stress-induced) cardiomyopathy
C. Myocarditis - corticosteroids
D. Cocaine-induced MI
questions.explanation: - Takotsubo (stress-induced) cardiomyopathy: Acute HF syndrome mimicking STEMI. Trigger: Intense emotional or physical stress. Demographics: Postmenopausal women (80-90%). Presentation: Chest pain, dyspnea, ECG changes (ST-elevation or TWI), troponin elevation (mild-moderate). Angiography: Normal or non-obstructive coronaries (KEY). Ventriculography/echo: Apical ballooning (tako-tsubo = octopus trap), basal hyperkinesis, reduced LVEF. Pathophysiology: Catecholamine surge → direct myocardial toxicity, microvascular dysfunction. Complications: Acute HF, cardiogenic shock (rare), LV thrombus (apical akinesis), MR (secondary), arrhythmias, LV rupture (very rare). Management: Supportive HF therapy: ACE-I/ARB, Beta-blockers (blunt catecholamine, reduce recurrence), Diuretics for congestion. Anticoagulation if LV apical thrombus (warfarin x3-6mo until LV function recovers). Avoid inotropes (may worsen - catecholamine-mediated). IABP if shock. Prognosis: LVEF typically recovers within days-weeks (90% completely within 1-2mo). Recurrence ~5-10%. Inhospital mortality ~1-2% (lower than STEMI). Long-term prognosis generally good. Differentiate from STEMI: Normal coronaries, Wall motion beyond single coronary territory, Emotional/physical stressor, Postmenopausal woman. This patient: CLASSIC - emotional stressor (son's death), postmenopausal woman, ST-elevation, troponin elevation, NORMAL coronaries, apical ballooning. A wrong: Normal coronaries. C wrong: Takotsubo more likely. D wrong: No cocaine use.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with known pulmonary sarcoidosis (diagnosed 2y ago, treated with prednisone) presents with palpitations and near-syncope. Holter: Frequent PVCs, episodes NSVT. Echo: Thinned basal septum, regional wall motion abnormality, LVEF 42%. Cardiac MRI: Late gadolinium enhancement in basal and mid septum (patchy, non-coronary distribution), thinned basal septum. PET: Increased FDG uptake basal septum. Angiography: Normal coronaries. Biopsy: Non-caseating granulomas. What is diagnosis and MOST appropriate treatment?
options: A. Ischemic cardiomyopathy - GDMT
B. Cardiac sarcoidosis
C. HCM - beta-blockers
D. ARVC - ICD only
questions.explanation: - Cardiac sarcoidosis: Granulomatous infiltration of myocardium. Only 5% sarcoidosis patients have clinically apparent cardiac involvement, but 20-30% on autopsy. Presentation: Arrhythmias (most common): AV block, VT, PVCs, atrial arrhythmias. HF: LV dysfunction, regional wall motion abnormalities. Sudden death. Diagnosis: MRI: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) - patchy, non-coronary distribution, typically basal and mid septum. PET: FDG uptake indicates active inflammation. Biopsy: Non-caseating granulomas (Gold standard but low sensitivity - patchy involvement). This patient: Known sarcoidosis, VT/PVCs, reduced LVEF 42%, MRI with LGE basal/mid septum, PET uptake, biopsy-proven granulomas - DEFINITE cardiac sarcoidosis. Treatment: Immunosuppression: Corticosteroids (first-line): Prednisone 40-60mg daily (or 0.5-1mg/kg) x8-12 weeks, then taper. Suppress active inflammation. Steroid-sparing agents (if refractory or steroid-dependent): Methotrexate 10-25mg weekly, Azathioprine 1-2mg/kg daily, Mycophenolate, Infliximab (TNF-alpha inhibitor). Device therapy: ICD: LVEF <35% despite therapy OR high-risk ventricular arrhythmias (VT, aborted SCD). Pacemaker: High-grade AV block. HF therapy: Standard GDMT. Monitoring: Serial MRI/PET assess treatment response, Holter for arrhythmias, Echo for LVEF. Prognosis: Variable. Corticosteroids can improve LVEF, reduce arrhythmias. High SCD risk - ICD important. A wrong: Normal coronaries, non-coronary LGE pattern. C wrong: Not HCM. D wrong: Not ARVC.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with stable exertional angina on atenolol 50mg daily, amlodipine 10mg daily, isosorbide mononitrate 60mg daily, aspirin 81mg, atorvastatin 80mg reports persistent angina 2-3 times/week despite medications. Angiography 6mo ago: 60% mid-LAD stenosis, medically managed. Adherent. VS: BP 118/72, HR 56. What is MOST appropriate next antianginal medication?
options: A. Increase atenolol to 100mg daily
B. Add ranolazine 500mg BID
C. Add diltiazem 240mg daily
D. Discontinue all antianginals
questions.explanation: - Refractory angina on beta-blocker + CCB + nitrate: Ranolazine indicated as add-on. Mechanism: Inhibits late sodium current → reduces intracellular calcium overload → improves diastolic relaxation. No effect on HR/BP. Dose: 500mg BID, titrate to 1000mg BID if tolerated. Side effects: QTc prolongation (avoid if QTc >500ms), dizziness, constipation, nausea. CYP3A4 metabolism - dose 500mg BID with moderate inhibitors (diltiazem, verapamil), contraindicated with strong inhibitors. This patient: On beta-blocker (atenolol), CCB (amlodipine), nitrate with persistent angina - ranolazine appropriate second-line. A wrong: HR 56 - already at target, increasing may cause excessive bradycardia. C wrong: Combining non-DHP CCB with beta-blocker increases bradycardia/AV block risk. Already on DHP CCB. D wrong: Angina persists.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman 32 weeks pregnant with known bicuspid aortic valve (moderate AS, valve area 1.3cm²) presents with acute dyspnea. Echo: AS now severe (valve area 0.9cm², mean gradient 48mmHg), LVEF 60%. Pregnancy increased CO worsening AS symptoms. Hemodynamically stable currently. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Immediate AVR despite pregnancy
B. Medical management with careful hemodynamics
C. Immediate C-section at 32 weeks then AVR
D. Balloon valvuloplasty during pregnancy
questions.explanation: - Severe AS in pregnancy: Increased CO worsens symptoms. Management: Hemodynamic goals: Maintain preload (avoid dehydration), Avoid tachycardia (shorten diastolic filling), Maintain afterload (avoid vasodilators). Beta-blockers for HR control if needed. Delivery planning: Vaginal preferred if hemodynamically stable (less stress than C-section). Epidural anesthesia (avoid spinal - sudden afterload drop). Continuous monitoring. Assisted second stage (minimize Valsalva). C-section if obstetric indications or severe decompensation. AVR postdelivery when stable. Emergent intervention during pregnancy (rarely needed): Balloon valvuloplasty (palliative) if maternal decompensation. AVR during pregnancy: Very high maternal/fetal risk - avoid unless life-threatening. This patient: Hemodynamically stable, 32 weeks - continue pregnancy with close monitoring, deliver at term or earlier if decompensation, AVR after delivery. A, C wrong: Stable - avoid surgery during pregnancy. D wrong: Balloon valvuloplasty reserved for severe maternal decompensation.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with lupus on chronic corticosteroids develops new dyspnea. Echo: Moderate pericardial effusion, no tamponade. Also new HTN (BP 168/98). Started amlodipine. Returns 2 weeks later with worsening edema. Labs: BUN 48, Cr 2.8 (baseline 0.9), K 5.8, bicarb 18, urinalysis: RBC casts, protein 3+. What is MOST likely diagnosis and treatment?
options: A. CHF from new HTN - increase diuretics
B. Lupus nephritis with AKI
C. Medication-induced AKI - stop amlodipine
D. Dehydration - IV fluids
questions.explanation: - Lupus nephritis presentation: New/worsening HTN, edema, AKI, hematuria (RBC casts - glomerular), proteinuria. RBC casts pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis. This patient: Lupus with new HTN, AKI (Cr 0.9→2.8), hyperkalemia, acidosis, RBC casts, heavy proteinuria - lupus nephritis. Management: Urgent nephrology referral, kidney biopsy to determine class, immunosuppression (Class III/IV proliferative): Induction: Pulse methylprednisolone 500-1000mg IV x3d, then prednisone 0.5-1mg/kg daily, PLUS Cyclophosphamide IV monthly x6mo OR Mycophenolate mofetil 2-3g daily. Maintenance: Lower-dose steroids + mycophenolate or azathioprine. Manage hyperkalemia: K 5.8 with acidosis - insulin/dextrose, kayexalate, address acidosis. Avoid ACE-I/ARBs initially with AKI. Monitor closely - dialysis if refractory. A wrong: Not simple CHF - RBC casts indicate glomerulonephritis. C wrong: Not medication-induced - RBC casts suggest intrinsic renal disease.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man with Marfan syndrome (known diagnosis) presents for routine follow-up. Asymptomatic. Echo: Ascending aortic aneurysm 4.8cm diameter (was 4.3cm 1y ago - growth 0.5cm/year). Aortic root 4.4cm. Moderate AR. LVEF 60%. No dissection. On atenolol 50mg daily. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Observation - surgery only ≥5.5cm
B. Elective aortic root replacement
C. Increase atenolol dose only
D. Emergency surgery
questions.explanation: - Marfan syndrome aortic surgery indications: Lower threshold than general population due to higher dissection risk. Aortic root replacement indicated: Diameter ≥5.0cm (some guidelines ≥4.5cm), Rapid growth: >0.5cm/year in adults OR >0.3cm/year in children, Family history aortic dissection: Consider surgery at ≥4.5cm, Aortic root ≥4.0cm if planning pregnancy, Concomitant moderate-severe AR or planning other cardiac surgery. This patient: Aortic root 4.8cm (approaching/at threshold), rapid growth (0.5cm in 1 year), moderate AR - MEETS surgical criteria. Surgical options: Valve-sparing root replacement (David/Yacoub procedure): Preferred if valve normal, Composite graft (Bentall): Replace root + valve if valve abnormal. Medical therapy: Beta-blockers (atenolol, propranolol) - reduce aortic wall stress, slow growth. Consider losartan (ARB) - may slow aortic dilation (COMPARE trial). Avoid contact sports, isometric exercise, weight lifting. Genetic counseling, family screening. A wrong: Threshold ≥5.5cm for general population. Marfan ≥4.5-5.0cm. C wrong: Approaching surgical threshold with rapid growth - needs surgery consultation. D wrong: Not emergency - asymptomatic, no dissection. Elective repair.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man post-CABG x3 (LIMA to LAD, SVG to OM, SVG to RCA) 6mo ago presents with recurrent angina. Stress test: Ischemia inferior territory. Angiography: SVG to RCA occluded, other grafts patent. Native RCA 100% occluded proximally. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Redo CABG for SVG occlusion
B. PCI to native RCA
C. Medical management only
D. Heart transplantation
questions.explanation: - SVG failure: Early (<1 year): Thrombosis (technical, hypercoagulable). 1-5 years: Intimal hyperplasia. >5 years: Atherosclerosis (accelerated). This patient 6mo post-CABG: Early SVG thrombosis. Management recurrent angina post-CABG: Optimize medical therapy: Dual antiplatelet if recent CABG, beta-blocker, statin, nitrates/ranolazine. PCI to native vessel OR PCI to SVG if patent graft: Higher success with native vessel PCI if technically feasible. Embolic protection device for SVG PCI (high atherosclerotic debris risk). Redo CABG: Higher operative risk (adhesions, prior sternotomy, limited conduits), mortality 5-10% vs 1-2% primary CABG. Reserved for: Multivessel graft failure, failed PCI, suitable anatomy. This patient: SVG to RCA occluded 6mo post-op, native RCA 100% occluded. Options: Attempt PCI to native RCA chronic total occlusion (CTO) if expertise available, or medical management. Redo CABG high risk for single-vessel. A wrong: Redo CABG high risk for single-vessel graft failure. C wrong: Symptomatic with objective ischemia - revascularization preferable if feasible. D wrong: Not indicated.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman with permanent AF (on apixaban 5mg BID), severe AS (valve area 0.7cm²), LVEF 55% scheduled for TAVR in 2 days. What is MOST appropriate periprocedural anticoagulation management?
options: A. Continue apixaban through procedure
B. Hold apixaban 48h before TAVR
C. Switch to warfarin permanently
D. Discontinue all anticoagulation
questions.explanation: - Periprocedural anticoagulation for TAVR in AF patients: Hold DOAC 48h before procedure (based on half-life), Bridge with UFH or LMWH for high-risk patients (AF, prior stroke), Intraoperative heparin for vascular access, Resume DOAC 24-48h post-procedure if hemostasis adequate. DOAC preferred over warfarin post-TAVR unless other indication for warfarin. Post-TAVR antithrombotic: AF + TAVR: Single anticoagulant (DOAC or warfarin) + aspirin 75-100mg x3-6mo, then anticoagulant monotherapy. No AF + TAVR: DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) x3-6mo, then aspirin monotherapy. Minimize bleeding while preventing thrombosis. A wrong: Hold DOAC 48h before for adequate washout. C wrong: DOACs preferred over warfarin for AF. D wrong: AF requires anticoagulation.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) presents with new ascites and lower extremity edema. No prior cardiac disease. Echo: Normal LVEF 60%, no valvular disease, no effusion. Cardiac cath for liver transplant evaluation: Normal coronaries. Hyperdynamic circulation: CO 7.8 L/min (elevated), SVR 680 dynes-sec/cm⁵ (low). What circulatory changes explain findings?
options: A. High-output heart failure from cirrhosis
B. Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy with hyperdynamic circulation
C. Normal findings
D. Restrictive cardiomyopathy
questions.explanation: - Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy: Cardiac dysfunction in cirrhosis WITHOUT other cardiac disease. Features: Hyperdynamic circulation at rest: High CO, low SVR (splanchnic/peripheral vasodilation from NO, endocannabinoids), Systolic dysfunction: Blunted contractile response to stress despite normal resting LVEF, Diastolic dysfunction: Impaired relaxation (Grade I), Prolonged QT interval, Electromechanical abnormalities. This patient: Normal resting LVEF 60%, high CO 7.8 (normal 4-8 but high-normal), low SVR 680 (normal 900-1400) - hyperdynamic state. May have impaired stress response not apparent at rest. Implications for liver transplant: Stress of transplant surgery may unmask dysfunction, Careful perioperative monitoring, Optimize volume status (significant fluid shifts). A wrong: High-output HF would have congestion symptoms. This patient's edema from portal HTN/ascites, not cardiac. C wrong: Abnormal - low SVR, high-normal CO indicate hyperdynamic state. D wrong: No evidence restrictive CM.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to ED with sudden onset palpitations, lightheadedness x30min. Reports similar episodes in past that resolved spontaneously. No cardiac history. VS: BP 108/72, HR 180 bpm (regular), RR 20. Exam: Alert, anxious, JVP normal, lungs clear, no murmurs. ECG: Narrow complex regular tachycardia rate 180 bpm, no visible P waves. What is MOST appropriate initial management for suspected AVNRT?
options: A. Immediate synchronized cardioversion
B. IV metoprolol 5mg
C. Vagal maneuvers
D. IV amiodarone 150mg
questions.explanation: - AVNRT (AV nodal reentrant tachycardia): Most common paroxysmal SVT in adults. Reentry circuit within AV node. Presentation: Sudden onset/termination, regular narrow complex tachycardia, no visible P waves or retrograde P waves (pseudo r' in V1, pseudo s in inferior leads). Acute management stable patient: Vagal maneuvers FIRST (Valsalva 15sec strain, carotid massage, ice water immersion) - success 20-30%. If unsuccessful: Adenosine 6mg IV rapid push followed by 20mL saline flush. If no response in 1-2min, give 12mg. Can repeat 12mg once more. Success rate 90-95%. Mechanism: Transiently blocks AV node → terminates reentry. Side effects: Transient (seconds): flushing, chest discomfort, dyspnea, bradycardia, brief asystole. Contraindications: Asthma/COPD (bronchospasm), 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome. Alternative if adenosine fails/contraindicated: Non-DHP CCB (diltiazem 0.25mg/kg IV or verapamil 5-10mg IV), Beta-blocker (metoprolol 5mg IV). Unstable (hypotension, altered MS, chest pain, HF): Immediate synchronized cardioversion 50-100J. Long-term management: If infrequent, brief episodes → no chronic therapy. If frequent/prolonged → catheter ablation (curative, success >95%). A wrong: Patient hemodynamically stable - try vagal maneuvers and adenosine first. B wrong: Beta-blocker can work but adenosine faster and more effective for acute termination. D wrong: Amiodarone not first-line for SVT - slower onset, more side effects.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with palpitations x2 days. PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia. VS: BP 132/78, HR 150 bpm (regular). ECG: Regular narrow complex tachycardia rate 150 bpm with sawtooth flutter waves in inferior leads (II, III, aVF), ventricular rate 150 bpm (2:1 AV conduction). CHA2DS2-VASc score 2. TEE not performed. Hemodynamically stable. What is MOST appropriate acute management?
options: A. Immediate cardioversion without anticoagulation
B. Adenosine to slow AV conduction
C. Amiodarone for rhythm control
D. Rate control with beta-blocker or CCB
questions.explanation: - Atrial flutter: Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia, typically 250-350 bpm atrial rate, usually 2:1 AV conduction (ventricular rate 150 bpm). ECG: Sawtooth flutter waves (best seen II, III, aVF, V1). Acute management stable patient: Rate control FIRST (if hemodynamically stable): Beta-blocker (metoprolol 5mg IV Q5min) or Non-DHP CCB (diltiazem 0.25mg/kg IV, then infusion). Target HR <100 bpm. Difficult to achieve rate control vs AF - often need cardioversion. Anticoagulation: Same as AF - use CHA2DS2-VASc score. This patient score 2 → anticoagulate. Cardioversion: If flutter >48h or unknown duration (this patient 2 days) → Two options: (1) 3 weeks therapeutic anticoagulation → cardioversion → 4 weeks post-cardioversion anticoagulation, OR (2) TEE to exclude thrombus → cardiovert on anticoagulation → 4 weeks post-cardioversion. Long-term management: Catheter ablation (cavotricuspid isthmus ablation) - CURATIVE for typical atrial flutter. Success rate >95%, low recurrence. Preferred over antiarrhythmic drugs. Rhythm control drugs less effective than for AF. Unstable patient: Immediate synchronized cardioversion 50-100J. A wrong: Flutter >48h requires anticoagulation strategy like AF. B wrong: Adenosine may transiently slow AV conduction revealing flutter waves but doesn't terminate flutter (only terminates AV node-dependent tachycardias like AVNRT, AVRT). C wrong: Antiarrhythmics less effective for flutter. Ablation preferred definitive therapy.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man with known WPW syndrome (delta waves on baseline ECG) presents to ED with wide complex irregular tachycardia rate 200-220 bpm, BP 98/62, chest discomfort. Exam: Anxious, diaphoretic. ECG: Irregular wide complex tachycardia, varying QRS morphology and RR intervals. Diagnosis: AF with rapid conduction down accessory pathway (pre-excited AF). What is MOST appropriate acute management?
options: A. Immediate synchronized cardioversion
B. IV adenosine to slow conduction
C. IV diltiazem for rate control
D. IV digoxin for rate control
questions.explanation: - WPW syndrome with pre-excited AF: MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Accessory pathway (AP) can conduct rapidly during AF → ventricular rates >200-300 bpm → risk degenerating to VF. Presentation: Wide complex irregular tachycardia (pre-excited QRS via AP), varying QRS morphology, very rapid rate. ECG: Irregular RR intervals, wide QRS, rate >200 bpm. This patient: Rate 200-220 bpm, BP 98/62 (borderline hypotensive), chest discomfort → cardioversion indicated. Management: Hemodynamically UNSTABLE or very rapid rate (>220 bpm): Immediate synchronized cardioversion 100-200J. Hemodynamically STABLE: Procainamide 10-15mg/kg IV over 20-60min (blocks AP and atria) OR Ibutilide 1mg IV over 10min. Medications to ABSOLUTELY AVOID in pre-excited AF: AV nodal blocking agents: Adenosine, beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil), digoxin. WHY: Block AV node → MORE conduction down AP → faster ventricular rate → VF. Digoxin particularly dangerous - shortens AP refractory period. Long-term management WPW: Catheter ablation of accessory pathway - CURATIVE, success >95%. Indications: Symptomatic arrhythmias, highrisk features (spontaneous pre-excited AF, shortest pre-excited RR interval <250ms during AF, multiple APs). This patient with pre-excited AF → high-risk, needs ablation after acute management. A correct - patient unstable with rapid rate. B, C, D wrong: NEVER use AV nodal blockers in pre-excited AF - can cause VF and death.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman with recurrent syncope x3mo. Episodes unpredictable, no prodrome, brief LOC with rapid recovery. PMH: HTN only. Holter monitor: Sinus rhythm with frequent sinus pauses up to 4.2 seconds, resulting in presyncope/syncope. No meds causing bradycardia. Echo: Normal structure and function. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Reassurance - benign finding
B. Start theophylline to increase heart rate
C. Permanent pacemaker implantation
D. Holter monitor for longer period
questions.explanation: - Sinus node dysfunction (sick sinus syndrome): Spectrum of bradyarrhythmias from sinus node disease. Manifestations: Sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses/arrest, sinoatrial exit block, tachy-brady syndrome (alternating bradycardia and tachycardia). Symptoms: Syncope, presyncope, dizziness, fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations (if tachy-brady). Pacemaker indications (Class I): Symptomatic sinus node dysfunction (syncope, presyncope, or symptoms clearly attributable to bradycardia). Sinus node dysfunction with HR <40 bpm AND symptoms. This patient: Recurrent syncope with documented sinus pauses up to 4.2 seconds on Holter → DEFINITE indication for permanent pacemaker. Pauses >3 seconds, especially if symptomatic, require pacing. Pacemaker selection: AAI/AAIR (atrial pacing): If intact AV conduction, pure sinus node disease. DDD/DDDR (dual-chamber): Preferred - allows for possible future AV block, maintains AV synchrony. Rate-responsive (R): For chronotropic incompetence. Before pacing: Exclude reversible causes: Medications (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin, antiarrhythmics), Hypothyroidism, Electrolyte abnormalities, Sleep apnea (vagal tone). This patient on no culprit medications, echo normal. A wrong: Symptomatic pauses >3 seconds require pacing. B wrong: Theophylline not standard therapy. C correct. D wrong: Diagnosis already established with documented symptomatic pauses.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with syncope. ECG: Complete (third-degree) AV block with atrial rate 75 bpm, ventricular escape rhythm rate 35 bpm, wide QRS complexes. Exam: Cannon A waves in JVP. Symptomatic with dizziness, near-syncope. No reversible cause identified. What is definitive management?
options: A. Atropine IV as long-term therapy
B. Permanent pacemaker implantation
C. Observation only
D. Isoproterenol infusion
questions.explanation: - Complete (third-degree) AV block: No atrial impulses conduct to ventricles. Atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation). Escape rhythm determines ventricular rate: Junctional escape (narrow QRS, rate 40-60 bpm) if block at AV node, Ventricular escape (wide QRS, rate 20-40 bpm) if block below His. This patient: Ventricular escape rate 35 bpm, wide QRS → infranodal block (worse prognosis). Cannon A waves: Atria contract against closed tricuspid valve → intermittent large JVP waves. Pacemaker indications complete AV block (Class I): Symptomatic (syncope, presyncope, HF, decreased exercise tolerance), Asymptomatic with: Ventricular rate <40 bpm while awake, Pauses ≥3 seconds while awake, Escape rhythm below AV node (wide QRS), Cardiomegaly or LV dysfunction. This patient: Symptomatic (dizziness, near-syncope) with ventricular rate 35 bpm → ABSOLUTE indication for permanent pacemaker. Acute management (if hemodynamically unstable): Atropine 0.5-1mg IV (may not work if infranodal block), Transcutaneous pacing, Temporary transvenous pacemaker, Dopamine or epinephrine infusion. Permanent pacemaker: DDD/DDDR (dual-chamber) preferred if atrial activity present - maintains AV synchrony, allows atrial contribution to CO (atrial kick). VVI acceptable if chronic AF. A, D wrong: Temporary measures only. B correct - definitive therapy. C wrong: Symptomatic complete AV block requires pacing.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with newly diagnosed non-valvular AF. CHA2DS2-VASc score 3 (age 65-74, HTN, DM). No history bleeding. CrCl 65 mL/min. Asks about anticoagulation options. What is MOST appropriate anticoagulation recommendation comparing DOACs vs warfarin?
options: A. DOACs
B. Warfarin always superior to DOACs
C. No anticoagulation - CHA2DS2-VASc only 3
D. Aspirin alone sufficient
questions.explanation: - AF anticoagulation: CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women) → anticoagulation. This patient: Score 3 → anticoagulate. DOACs vs warfarin: DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban): Advantages: Non-inferior or superior efficacy vs warfarin (major trials: RE-LY, ROCKET-AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48), Lower ICH risk (40-60% reduction vs warfarin), No routine monitoring (fixed dosing), Fewer drug-food interactions, Rapid onset/offset. Disadvantages: Cost ($300-500/month vs $10/month warfarin), Require renal dose adjustment (avoid if CrCl <15-30 depending on drug), No routine monitoring (adherence concerns), Reversal agents limited (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for Xa inhibitors). Warfarin: Advantages: Decades of experience, Inexpensive, Once-daily dosing, Reversible with vitamin K/FFP/PCC, Can use in severe renal impairment. Disadvantages: Narrow therapeutic window, Requires frequent INR monitoring, Multiple drug-food interactions, Higher ICH risk. Guidelines: DOACs PREFERRED over warfarin for non-valvular AF (2019 AHA/ACC/HRS). Warfarin indications: Mechanical heart valves (DOACs contraindicated), Moderate-severe mitral stenosis, CrCl <15-30 mL/min (depending on DOAC), Patient preference/cost issues. This patient: CrCl 65 mL/min, no contraindications → DOAC preferred. B wrong: DOACs preferred per guidelines. C wrong: Score 3 warrants anticoagulation. D wrong: Aspirin inferior to anticoagulation for stroke prevention.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 5), CKD stage 4 (CrCl 22 mL/min), weight 52 kg. On warfarin but INR labile. Desires switch to DOAC. Which DOAC is appropriate with correct dosing?
options: A. Dabigatran 150mg BID
B. Rivaroxaban 20mg daily
C. Edoxaban 60mg daily
D. Apixaban 2.5mg BID
questions.explanation: - DOAC dosing in renal impairment and other factors: Dabigatran: CrCl >30 mL/min: 150mg BID. CrCl 15-30 mL/min: 75mg BID (not FDA-approved, European use). CrCl <15 mL/min: CONTRAINDICATED (80% renal excretion). Rivaroxaban: CrCl >50 mL/min: 20mg daily. CrCl 15-50 mL/min: 15mg daily. CrCl <15 mL/min: Avoid. Apixaban: Standard: 5mg BID. Reduce to 2.5mg BID if ≥2 of 3: Age ≥80y, Weight ≤60kg, Serum Cr ≥1.5 mg/dL. CrCl <15 mL/min: Limited data, use with caution. Edoxaban: CrCl >95 mL/min: DO NOT USE (increased stroke risk - ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48). CrCl 51-95 mL/min: 60mg daily. CrCl 15-50 mL/min: 30mg daily. CrCl <15 mL/min: Avoid. This patient: CrCl 22 mL/min, age 78y, weight 52kg. Dabigatran: CrCl 22 → would need 75mg BID (not FDA-approved in US). Rivaroxaban: CrCl 22 → 15mg daily possible. Apixaban: Age 78y (not ≥80), weight 52kg (≤60kg - YES), Cr likely ≥1.5 (CrCl 22 suggests elevated Cr). If Cr ≥1.5 → meets 2 of 3 criteria → 2.5mg BID. If Cr <1.5 → only 1 criterion (weight) → 5mg BID. Best choice CrCl 15-30: Apixaban (has dosing for CrCl as low as 15, most data in severe CKD). Rivaroxaban also option. Avoid dabigatran (highest renal excretion 80%). A wrong: Dabigatran 150mg BID incorrect dose for CrCl 22. B wrong: Rivaroxaban 20mg incorrect - should be 15mg. C wrong: Edoxaban 60mg incorrect - should be 30mg. D correct per dose reduction criteria.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with 40-pack-year smoking history presents with bilateral calf pain with walking 2 blocks, relieved with rest. Pain reproducible. No rest pain. PMH: T2DM, HTN, hyperlipidemia. Exam: Diminished dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally, femoral bruits. ABI: Right 0.68, Left 0.72 (normal 1.0-1.4; PAD <0.9). What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. Immediate revascularization (angioplasty or bypass)
B. Warfarin anticoagulation
C. Smoking cessation
D. Observation only
questions.explanation: - Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) - claudication: Symptom: Intermittent claudication - reproducible leg pain with exertion, relieved by rest. Diagnosis: ABI (anklebrachial index) <0.9. Severity: 0.7-0.9 mild, 0.4-0.7 moderate, <0.4 severe. This patient: ABI 0.68-0.72 (moderate PAD), classic claudication. Initial management claudication (Fontaine stage II): Cardiovascular risk reduction (MOST IMPORTANT): SMOKING CESSATION - single most important intervention. Slows progression, improves outcomes. Antiplatelet therapy: Aspirin 75-325mg daily OR Clopidogrel 75mg daily. Clopidogrel slightly superior in PAD (CAPRIE trial). Statin: High-intensity regardless of LDL (reduce CV events, may improve claudication). BP control: Target <130/80. ACE-I/ARB may provide additional benefit. Diabetes control: HbA1c <7%. Exercise therapy: Supervised exercise program (walking) - FIRST-LINE for claudication. 30-45min sessions, 3-5x/week for ≥12 weeks. Improves walking distance 50-200%. Mechanism: Collateral development, improved endothelial function. Pharmacologic claudication therapy: Cilostazol 100mg BID: PDE-3 inhibitor. Improves walking distance 40-60%. Side effects: Headache, diarrhea. CONTRAINDICATED in HF (PDE-3 inhibitors increase mortality in HF). Pentoxifylline less effective, not recommended. Revascularization (angioplasty, stenting, bypass): Reserved for: Lifestyle-limiting claudication despite optimal medical therapy (≥3-6 months), Critical limb ischemia (rest pain, ulcers, gangrene - Fontaine III/IV). This patient: Initial presentation, moderate PAD → intensive medical therapy and exercise first. A wrong: Revascularization not first-line for claudication. Try medical therapy/exercise first. B wrong: Anticoagulation not indicated for claudication. Antiplatelet therapy appropriate. D wrong: Requires aggressive risk factor modification.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with known PAD presents with rest pain in right foot x2wk, worse at night, relieved by hanging foot over bed. Exam: Cool right foot, absent pulses, dependent rubor, pallor on elevation. No ulcers yet. ABI: Right 0.32, Left 0.65. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Urgent vascular surgery referral for revascularization
B. Cilostazol and exercise therapy
C. Reassurance and optimize medical therapy
D. Warfarin anticoagulation only
questions.explanation: - Critical limb ischemia (CLI): Chronic ischemic rest pain OR ischemic ulcers/gangrene. Fontaine stage III (rest pain) or IV (tissue loss). This patient: Rest pain x2 weeks, ABI 0.32 (severe PAD <0.4), physical findings (cool, pulseless, dependent rubor, pallor on elevation) → CLI. Natural history untreated CLI: 25% require major amputation within 1 year, 25% die within 1 year from CV causes. Management CLI: URGENT vascular surgery/interventional radiology referral for revascularization. Goal: Restore perfusion, prevent limb loss. Revascularization options: Endovascular: Angioplasty ± stenting - preferred for focal/short lesions, aortoiliac disease. Lower morbidity/mortality than surgery. Surgical: Bypass grafting - preferred for long/complex lesions, infrainguinal disease. Autogenous vein graft best (saphenous vein). Hybrid: Combination endovascular and surgical. Medical therapy: Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel), Statin, BP control, DM control, Pain management (opioids often needed), Wound care if ulcers, Foot protection. Amputation: If revascularization not feasible OR extensive tissue loss/infection not salvageable. Prevent CLI: Aggressive risk factor modification in all PAD patients, early intervention for worsening claudication. B wrong: Exercise therapy CONTRAINDICATED in CLI (may worsen ischemia). Cilostazol insufficient. C wrong: CLI requires revascularization - medical therapy alone inadequate. D wrong: Anticoagulation not primary therapy. Revascularization needed.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with AF (not on anticoagulation) develops sudden onset severe right leg pain, coldness, numbness x3h. Exam: Right leg pale, cold, absent pulses (femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis), decreased sensation, unable to move toes (motor deficit). Left leg: Normal pulses. What is MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: A. Observation for 24h
B. Start warfarin PO
C. CT scan first
D. Emergent vascular surgery consult for thromboembolectomy or thrombolysis
questions.explanation: - Acute limb ischemia (ALI): Sudden decrease in limb perfusion threatening viability. Usually <14 days duration. Etiology: Thromboembolism (most common) - AF, MI, LV thrombus, aneurysm, paradoxical embolus. In-situ thrombosis - underlying PAD with acute occlusion. Trauma, dissection. Clinical: 6 P's: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis (motor deficit), Poikilothermia (cold). Rutherford classification: Class I (viable): No sensory/motor deficit, audible Doppler signals. Class IIA (threatened, salvageable): Minimal sensory loss, no motor deficit, no Doppler signals. Class IIB (threatened, salvageable with urgent intervention): Sensory loss beyond toes, mild-moderate motor deficit. Class III (irreversible): Profound sensory/motor loss, muscle rigor, skin mottling. This patient: Sensory loss, motor deficit (unable to move toes), absent pulses → Class IIB (salvageable if treated urgently). Management: EMERGENT vascular surgery/interventional radiology consult. Immediate anticoagulation: UFH bolus 80 units/kg IV, then infusion 18 units/kg/h (prevent propagation). Revascularization: Surgical thromboembolectomy (Fogarty catheter) - preferred for large vessel occlusion, no lysis contraindications. Catheter-directed thrombolysis - for distal occlusion, no surgery contraindication. Hybrid approach. Supportive: IV fluids, pain control, keep limb dependent (increases perfusion pressure), protect from trauma/pressure. Reperfusion injury: After revascularization, watch for: Compartment syndrome (may need fasciotomy), Rhabdomyolysis (fluids, alkalinize urine), Hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria. Prognosis: 30-day amputation rate 10-30%, mortality 15-20% (high due to underlying CVD). Class III → amputation likely. A, B, C wrong: Class IIB ALI requires EMERGENT revascularization within 6-12h to salvage limb. Any delay worsens outcome.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman at 16 weeks gestation presents with left leg swelling, pain x2 days. Ultrasound: Left femoral-iliac DVT. No history VTE. No thrombophilia. What is MOST appropriate anticoagulation for pregnancy-associated VTE?
options: A. Warfarin throughout pregnancy
B. LMWH (enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC Q12h) throughout pregnancy and ≥6 weeks postpartum (minimum 3 months total anticoagulation); switch to UFH close to delivery or use shorteracting LMWH dosing
C. DOAC (apixaban) - safe in pregnancy
D. No anticoagulation - teratogenic
questions.explanation: - VTE in pregnancy: Pregnancy is hypercoagulable state - 5x increased VTE risk. Increased factor VIII, IX, X, fibrinogen. Decreased protein S, impaired fibrinolysis. Treatment: LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin) - drug of choice. Does NOT cross placenta (large molecule). Safe for fetus. Dose: Weight-based therapeutic dosing - Enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC Q12h OR 1.5mg/kg SC daily. Monitor anti-Xa levels 4h post-dose (target 0.6-1.0 for BID, 1.0-2.0 for daily). Adjust dose for weight changes during pregnancy. Duration: Throughout pregnancy AND ≥6 weeks postpartum (minimum 3 months total anticoagulation). Postpartum highest VTE risk period. Delivery management: Stop LMWH 24h before planned delivery (induction or C-section). Can use shorter-acting dosing near term (BID instead of daily). Alternatively, switch to UFH 36h before delivery (shorter half-life). Neuraxial anesthesia: Safe if ≥24h since last LMWH dose. Resume LMWH 12-24h post-delivery if hemostasis adequate. Can transition to warfarin postpartum if desired (safe with breastfeeding). Warfarin: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy, especially first trimester. Crosses placenta. Teratogenic: Warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) 6-12 weeks gestation, CNS abnormalities throughout pregnancy, fetal bleeding. UFH: Alternative to LMWH but less convenient (IV or SC TID), higher HIT risk, osteoporosis with prolonged use. DOACs: NO DATA in pregnancy - avoid. A wrong: Warfarin teratogenic. C wrong: DOACs no safety data in pregnancy. D wrong: VTE requires anticoagulation.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man post-total knee replacement (TKR) day 1. No prior VTE. No active bleeding. What is MOST appropriate VTE prophylaxis and duration?
options: A. Early ambulation only - no pharmacologic prophylaxis
B. Aspirin 325mg daily x2 weeks
C. LMWH (enoxaparin 30mg SC Q12h or 40mg SC daily), fondaparinux, rivaroxaban, or apixaban for ≥10-14 days, extended up to 35 days for high-risk patients
D. Warfarin with target INR 3-4
questions.explanation: - VTE prophylaxis post-orthopedic surgery: Major orthopedic surgery (THA, TKR, hip fracture surgery) = VERY HIGH VTE risk (40-60% without prophylaxis). Pharmacologic prophylaxis ESSENTIAL. Options (all equivalent efficacy): LMWH: Enoxaparin 30mg SC Q12h (starting 12-24h post-op) OR 40mg SC daily. Fondaparinux: 2.5mg SC daily (starting 6-24h post-op). Factor Xa inhibitor, no HIT risk. DOACs: Rivaroxaban 10mg PO daily (starting 6-10h post-op). Apixaban 2.5mg PO BID (starting 12-24h post-op).
