Warfarin: INR goal 2-3 (NOT 3-4). Less convenient (monitoring), slower onset - give with parenteral anticoagulant until INR therapeutic. Duration: Minimum 10-14 days for TKR. Extended prophylaxis (up to 35 days) for THA, hip fracture surgery - higher VTE risk. Consider extended for TKR if high-risk features (prior VTE, cancer, obesity, immobility). Mechanical prophylaxis: Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) devices - adjunct to pharmacologic. Used alone if bleeding contraindication to pharmacologic. Early ambulation. Contraindications to pharmacologic prophylaxis: Active major bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia (<50K), epidural catheter in place (timing restrictions for neuraxial anesthesia). Aspirin: ACCP 2012 guidelines suggested aspirin as option but less effective than other agents. Not preferred first-line. A wrong: Pharmacologic prophylaxis required for major orthopedic surgery. B wrong: Aspirin less effective than LMWH/fondaparinux/DOACs. D wrong: Warfarin target INR 2-3, not 3-4.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (prior MI 2y ago), NYHA class III despite optimal GDMT x6mo (sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, furosemide). Echo: LVEF 28%, QRS duration 155ms with LBBB morphology, LV dyssynchrony. What is MOST appropriate device therapy?
options: A. CRT-D (biventricular ICD) - meets criteria: LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II-IV on GDMT ≥3mo, LBBB with QRS ≥150ms
B. ICD only - CRT not indicated
C. CRT-P (biventricular pacemaker without ICD) - no ICD needed
D. No device - continue medical therapy
questions.explanation: - Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) indications: CRT = biventricular pacing to resynchronize LV contraction. Improves symptoms, LVEF, reduces HF hospitalizations and mortality in select patients. Class I indications (strongest evidence): LVEF ≤35%, Sinus rhythm, NYHA class II, III, or ambulatory IV on GDMT ≥3 months, LBBB with QRS ≥150ms (greatest benefit). LVEF ≤35%, NYHA III-IV on GDMT, LBBB with QRS 120-149ms (moderate benefit). LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II-IV, need ventricular pacing >40% (e.g., AV block requiring pacemaker). Class IIa (reasonable): LVEF ≤35%, NYHA III-IV on GDMT, non-LBBB pattern with QRS ≥150ms. Class IIb (may be considered): LVEF ≤30%, ischemic etiology, NYHA I, LBBB QRS ≥150ms. Non-LBBB with QRS 120-149ms - limited benefit. This patient: LVEF 28%, NYHA III on GDMT ≥6mo, LBBB with QRS 155ms → MEETS Class I criteria for CRT. CRT-D vs CRT-P: CRT-D (biventricular ICD): CRT + defibrillator function. For patients meeting BOTH CRT and ICD criteria (most patients). CRT-P (biventricular pacemaker without ICD): For CRT candidates who don't meet ICD criteria OR life expectancy <1 year. This patient: Ischemic CMP, LVEF 28%, NYHA III → also meets ICD criteria (primary prevention). Needs CRT-D. COMPANION trial: CRT-D reduced mortality 36% vs medical therapy. CARE-HF: CRT-P reduced mortality 36%. Response rate: ~70% responders (clinical improvement, LVEF increase, reverse remodeling). 30% non-responders. A correct. B wrong: LBBB QRS ≥150ms - strong CRT indication. C wrong: Also meets ICD criteria. D wrong: Strong indication for CRTD.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed 4mo ago (etiology unclear). Currently on sacubitril/valsartan 97/103mg BID, carvedilol 25mg BID, spironolactone 25mg, furosemide 40mg. NYHA class II. Echo today: LVEF 32% (improved from 25% at diagnosis). No history VT, syncope, or cardiac arrest. What is MOST appropriate recommendation regarding ICD?
options: A. Implant ICD now - meets criteria with LVEF ≤35%
B. ICD not indicated in non-ischemic cardiomyopathy
C. Wait 6 more months - already on GDMT 4mo

D. Defer ICD decision; continue optimizing GDMT for total ≥3-6 months (preferably 6-9 months for non-ischemic) to allow reverse remodeling; reassess LVEF after adequate medical therapy trial; implant ICD if LVEF remains ≤35%
questions.explanation: - ICD primary prevention: Prevents sudden cardiac death in high-risk patients without prior VT/VF. Indications: Ischemic cardiomyopathy: LVEF ≤35%, ≥40 days post-MI (or ≥3mo post-revascularization), NYHA II-III on GDMT ≥3mo, life expectancy >1y with good functional status. SCD-HeFT, MADIT-II trials: 30% mortality reduction. Non-ischemic cardiomyopathy: LVEF ≤35% on optimal GDMT ≥3 months (many recommend 6-9 months), NYHA II-III, life expectancy >1y. SCD-HeFT: benefit in non-ischemic (similar to ischemic). IMPORTANT: Must allow adequate time on GDMT for potential LVEF recovery before ICD, especially non-ischemic CMP. Many patients with new non-ischemic CMP improve LVEF with medical therapy (reverse remodeling). DANISH trial: ICD in non-ischemic CMP reduced SCD but NOT total mortality - more controversial than ischemic indication. This patient: New nonischemic CMP diagnosed 4mo ago, only on GDMT 4mo, LVEF already improved 25%→32% (reverse remodeling occurring). TOO EARLY for ICD - must give more time for potential continued LVEF improvement. Reassess LVEF after 6-9 months total GDMT. If LVEF remains ≤35% at that time → consider ICD. If LVEF improves >35% → no ICD needed. Exceptions (implant ICD earlier): Prior cardiac arrest, sustained VT, high-risk features (severe LV dysfunction despite GDMT, family history SCD, extensive late gadolinium enhancement on MRI). A wrong: Too early - only 4mo GDMT, LVEF improving. B wrong: ICD indicated in nonischemic if LVEF ≤35% after adequate GDMT trial. C wrong: 4+6=10mo total reasonable, but should specify reassessment. D correct - emphasizes need for adequate GDMT trial before ICD decision.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with inferior STEMI (ST-elevation II, III, aVF) treated with primary PCI to RCA. Post-PCI develops hypotension (BP 82/54), elevated JVP (14cm), clear lungs, no pulmonary edema. Right-sided ECG: ST-elevation in V4R (RV MI). Echo: RV akinesis, dilated RA, TR. What is MOST appropriate management of RV infarction?
options: A. IV diuretics for volume overload
B. Nitrates for afterload reduction
C. Aggressive IV fluids (1-2L NS bolus) to maintain RV preload; avoid diuretics, nitrates, morphine; inotropes (dobutamine) if persistent hypotension despite fluids
D. ACE inhibitor for afterload reduction
questions.explanation: - RV myocardial infarction: Occurs in 30-50% inferior MIs (RCA supplies RV). Occlusion proximal RCA (before RV marginal branches) → RV infarction. Clinical triad: Hypotension, elevated JVP (elevated RA pressure), clear lungs (NO pulmonary edema despite elevated JVP). Kussmaul sign may be present. Diagnosis: Right-sided ECG: ST-elevation ≥1mm in V4R (most sensitive, place V4 lead on right chest). Also V3R, V5R, V6R. Echo: RV akinesis/hypokinesis, RV dilation, RA dilation, TR. Hemodynamics: Elevated RA pressure, low cardiac output, low or normal PCWP. RV depends on preload for adequate LV filling (RV and LV in series). Management: MAINTAIN PRELOAD (most important): Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation: NS 1-2L bolus, then continue as needed. Monitor hemodynamics - may need several liters. Goal: Maintain adequate RV filling → LV preload → CO. AVOID: Diuretics (reduce preload → worsen hypotension), Nitrates (reduce preload), Morphine (vasodilation, reduce preload), Beta-blockers (may worsen bradycardia common with RV MI). ACE inhibitors (afterload reduction + may reduce preload). Inotropic support if hypotension persists despite fluids: Dobutamine 2.5-10mcg/kg/min (beta-1 agonist, increase RV contractility). Avoid pure vasopressors (increase afterload on failing RV). AV synchrony important: RV MI often has bradycardia (inferior MI affects AV node). Maintain sinus rhythm. If AV block → temporary pacing (AV sequential pacing preferred to maintain atrial kick). Prognosis: High in-hospital mortality (25-30%) if complicated. Most survivors recover RV function within weeks-months. A, B, D wrong: Diuretics, nitrates, ACE-I reduce preload or afterload - WORSEN RV MI hemodynamics. C correct - maintain preload.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman day 4 post-anterior STEMI (treated with primary PCI) develops sudden onset dyspnea, new harsh systolic murmur at left sternal border. BP 94/62, HR 108, JVP 12cm, crackles throughout lung fields. Echo: New VSD (ventricular septal rupture) with left-toright shunt. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Medical management only with diuretics
B. Urgent surgical consultation for VSD repair; temporize with afterload reduction (nitroprusside), IABP if shock; surgery within 24-48h
C. Observation for 2 weeks
D. Percutaneous VSD closure immediately
questions.explanation: - Post-MI VSD (ventricular septal rupture): Mechanical complication occurring 3-7 days post-MI (median day 4). Incidence <1% with reperfusion therapy (vs 1-3% pre-PCI era). Anterior MI → apical VSD, Inferior MI → basal/posterior VSD (worse prognosis). Presentation: Sudden clinical deterioration, New harsh holosystolic murmur at left sternal border (LSB), Acute HF (pulmonary edema, hypotension, cardiogenic shock), Left-to-right shunt → increased pulmonary blood flow. Diagnosis: Echo with color Doppler - shows defect, shunt, estimates size. PA catheter: Oxygen step-up from RA to PA (confirms left-to-right shunt). Management: URGENT surgical consultation - mortality without surgery approaches 90%. Temporizing measures (stabilize for surgery): Afterload reduction: Nitroprusside (reduce shunt fraction, increase forward CO). IABP (increase forward CO, decrease afterload). Inotropes if shock (dobutamine). Avoid excessive fluids (worsen pulmonary edema). Surgery: Timing: Previously delayed 4-6 weeks for scar formation. Current: Earlier surgery (24-48h) due to high mortality with medical therapy alone. Technique: Patch closure (Dacron, pericardium), often with CABG if needed. Mortality: 20-50% depending on timing, shock presence. Percutaneous closure: Emerging technique but surgical repair remains standard. A wrong: Medical therapy alone has 90% mortality. C wrong: High mortality risk waiting - most die within days-weeks without surgery. D wrong: Percutaneous closure investigational, surgical standard.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man day 3 post-inferior STEMI develops sudden severe dyspnea, pulmonary edema. New loud holosystolic murmur apex radiating to axilla. BP 86/58, HR 118. Echo: Flail posterior mitral leaflet, severe acute MR. Partial papillary muscle rupture. Cardiogenic shock. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Medical management with ACE inhibitor and diuretics
B. Defer surgery for 6 weeks
C. Balloon valvuloplasty
D. Emergent surgical consultation for mitral valve surgery (repair or replacement); temporize with vasodilators (nitroprusside), IABP; surgery ASAP - very high mortality without intervention
questions.explanation: - Papillary muscle rupture post-MI: Mechanical complication 2-7 days post-MI. More common with inferior MI (posteromedial papillary muscle - single blood supply from PDA). Anterolateral papillary muscle has dual supply (LAD, LCx) - less likely to rupture. Complete rupture: Catastrophic, immediate cardiogenic shock, often fatal within hours. Partial rupture: Severe MR, acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock. Presentation: Sudden clinical deterioration, New holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla, Acute severe pulmonary edema, Cardiogenic shock. Diagnosis: Echo: Flail mitral leaflet, ruptured papillary muscle (may see in LA), severe MR. PA catheter: Large V waves in PCWP tracing (severe acute MR). Management: EMERGENT surgical consultation - survival depends on urgent surgery. Temporizing (bridge to surgery): Vasodilators: Nitroprusside (reduce afterload → decrease regurgitant fraction, increase forward CO). IABP: Decrease afterload, increase forward CO. Contraindication to IABP: Severe AR. Inotropes: Dobutamine if needed. Avoid excessive preload (worsens pulmonary edema). Surgery: Timing: EMERGENT - most die without surgery within 24h. Mortality with medical therapy alone >90%. Mitral valve repair vs replacement: Repair preferred if feasible, replacement often necessary for ruptured papillary muscle. Often need CABG simultaneously. Surgical mortality: 20-40% (high-risk emergency surgery in unstable patient). Without surgery: >90% mortality. A wrong: Medical therapy alone has >90% mortality. B wrong: Cannot wait - most die within 24h without surgery. C wrong: No role for balloon valvuloplasty.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman day 5 post-large anterior STEMI suddenly develops severe chest pain, pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest despite CPR. Bedside echo during resuscitation: Large pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. What is MOST likely diagnosis?
options: A. LV free wall rupture - catastrophic complication with sudden hemopericardium and tamponade; emergent pericardiocentesis may temporize but mortality >90% even with surgery
B. Recurrent STEMI
C. Pulmonary embolism
D. Papillary muscle rupture
questions.explanation: - LV free wall rupture: Most lethal mechanical complication post-MI. Incidence <1% with primary PCI (vs 2-4% pre-reperfusion era). Timing: 3-7 days post-MI (median day 5) when necrotic myocardium weakest before scar formation. Risk factors: Large transmural MI (especially anterior), elderly women, HTN, no collaterals, first MI, late/no reperfusion, corticosteroids/NSAIDs (impair healing). Types: Acute complete rupture (>90%): Sudden hemopericardium → tamponade → PEA arrest → death within minutes. Subacute rupture with pseudoaneurysm formation (<10%): Pericardium contains rupture, may be slower presentation. Presentation: Sudden severe chest pain, Sudden hemodynamic collapse (hypotension, PEA arrest), Tamponade: elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus. Diagnosis: Echo: Pericardial effusion (hemopericardium), tamponade physiology, may see myocardial defect. ECG: Often shows PEA (organized electrical activity without mechanical cardiac output). Management: Almost universally fatal: Mortality >90% even with intervention. Emergent pericardiocentesis: May temporize (remove blood from pericardium), but bleeding continues. Emergent surgery: Patch repair, infarctectomy. Very high mortality - most patients don't survive to OR. Prevention: Early reperfusion therapy (reduces incidence). Avoid excessive anticoagulation/antiplatelet in high-risk patients? Controversial. Prognosis: Most die before reaching hospital or in ED. Survivors typically have subacute rupture/pseudoaneurysm (slower presentation allowing surgical intervention). B, C wrong: Presentation classic for free wall rupture. D wrong: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute MR, not pericardial effusion.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with acute anterior STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock post-PCI to LAD. Despite PCI, remains hypotensive. BP 78/54, HR 115, CI 1.8 L/min/m², PCWP 24mmHg. Cool extremities, altered MS, oliguria. On dopamine 15mcg/kg/min. Still hypotensive. What is MOST appropriate next step for hemodynamic support?
options: A. Increase dopamine to 25mcg/kg/min
B. Add epinephrine infusion
C. Switch to norepinephrine + add dobutamine; consider mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO) if refractory
D. Add vasopressin
questions.explanation: - Cardiogenic shock management: Definition: CI <2.2 L/min/m², PCWP >18mmHg, SBP <90mmHg, end-organ hypoperfusion. Acute MI most common cause (70-80%). Mortality 40-50% despite revascularization. Hemodynamic goals: MAP ≥65mmHg, CI >2.2, PCWP 15-18, SvO2 >60%, Lactate clearance, Urine output >0.5mL/kg/h. Pharmacologic support: Norepinephrine: FIRST-LINE vasopressor (OptimaCC trial: superior to dopamine in cardiogenic shock). Alpha-1 agonist (vasoconstriction) + beta-1 (inotropy). Dose: 0.01- 3mcg/kg/min. Dobutamine: Beta-1 selective inotrope. Add if persistent low CO despite adequate MAP. Dose: 2.5-20mcg/kg/min. Side effects: Tachycardia, arrhythmias, may worsen hypotension (vasodilation at low doses). Milrinone: PDE-3 inhibitor (inotropy + vasodilation). Use if refractory to dobutamine. CONTRAINDICATED if hypotensive (causes vasodilation). Dopamine: Mixed alpha/beta effects depending on dose. OptimaCC trial: Inferior to norepinephrine (more arrhythmias, higher mortality). Avoid high doses (>10-15mcg/kg/min). Epinephrine: Potent alpha + beta agonist. Use if refractory shock. Side effects: Tachycardia, arrhythmias, lactic acidosis, hyperglycemia. Mechanical circulatory support (MCS): IABP: Increase diastolic perfusion, decrease afterload. IABP-SHOCK II: No mortality benefit but may improve hemodynamics temporarily. Impella: Percutaneous LV assist device. Provides greater hemodynamic support than IABP. VA-ECMO: Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. For severe refractory shock. This patient: Dopamine 15mcg/kg/min failing → switch to norepinephrine + dobutamine. Consider MCS if remains refractory. A wrong: Highdose dopamine increases arrhythmias without benefit. B wrong: Epinephrine second-line if norepinephrine fails. D wrong: Vasopressin not standard in cardiogenic shock.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with inferior STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock. Post-PCI to RCA, BP improved but remains borderline 92/58. CI 2.0. Considering IABP. PMH includes severe AR (chronic, moderate-severe by echo 6mo ago). What is key consideration regarding IABP placement?
options: A. IABP always indicated in cardiogenic shock
B. IABP CONTRAINDICATED with moderate-severe AR - diastolic inflation worsens regurgitation; also contraindicated with aortic dissection, severe PVD
C. AR improves with IABP
D. Place IABP regardless of AR
questions.explanation: - Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP): Mechanical circulatory support device. 30- 50cc balloon in descending aorta. Mechanism: Inflates in diastole (after aortic valve closure) → increases diastolic pressure → improves coronary perfusion. Deflates just before systole → decreases afterload → reduces myocardial O2 demand, increases forward CO. Benefits: Increase coronary perfusion (inflate diastole), Decrease afterload (deflate systole), Increase MAP, Decrease myocardial O2 consumption. Indications (current use limited after IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit): Cardiogenic shock refractory to pharmacologic therapy (bridge to definitive therapy), Mechanical complications (VSD, papillary muscle rupture) as bridge to surgery, Refractory unstable angina/ischemia, High-risk PCI. Contraindications (ABSOLUTE): Moderate-severe aortic regurgitation: Diastolic inflation increases regurgitant volume (pumps blood back into LV). Worsens AR, worsens LV volume overload. Aortic dissection: Balloon placement/inflation could extend dissection. Severe peripheral vascular disease: Cannot access femoral artery or risk of limb ischemia. Relative contraindications: Uncontrolled sepsis, Terminal illness, Bleeding diathesis. IABP-SHOCK II trial (2012): IABP did not reduce mortality in cardiogenic shock post-MI undergoing early revascularization. Use decreased significantly posttrial. Complications: Limb ischemia (most common), Bleeding, Infection, Aortic injury, Thrombocytopenia, Hemolysis. This patient has moderate-severe AR → IABP CONTRAINDICATED. Consider other MCS (Impella, VA-ECMO) if needed. A, D wrong: Not always indicated, has contraindications. B correct. C wrong: IABP worsens AR.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man 3 weeks post-anterior STEMI (treated with PCI) presents with pleuritic chest pain, fever 38.2°C. Exam: Pericardial friction rub. ECG: Diffuse ST elevation (different from initial MI ECG). Echo: Small pericardial effusion. Labs: ESR 68 mm/hr, CRP 45 mg/L. What is MOST likely diagnosis and treatment?
options: A. Recurrent MI - urgent cath lab
B. Pulmonary embolism - anticoagulation
C. Pneumonia - antibiotics
D. Dressler syndrome (post-MI pericarditis) - NSAIDs (aspirin or ibuprofen) + colchicine; avoid corticosteroids if possible
questions.explanation: - Dressler syndrome: Post-MI immune-mediated pericarditis. Also called postcardiac injury syndrome. Incidence: <5% in modern era (much higher pre-reperfusion). Timing: 1-6 weeks post-MI (median 2-3 weeks). Distinguished from acute pericarditis (occurs within days of MI). Pathophysiology: Autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens released during MI. Presentation: Pleuritic chest pain (positional, worse lying flat, better sitting forward), Fever, Pericardial friction rub, Pericardial effusion (usually small), Pleural effusion (common), Elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP). ECG: Diffuse ST elevation (all leads), PR depression (different from localized ST elevation of acute MI). Diagnosis: Clinical - chest pain, fever, rub, effusion weeks post-MI. Exclude: Recurrent MI (troponins, ECG changes different), PE, Pneumonia. Treatment: NSAIDs: Aspirin 750-1000mg TID or Ibuprofen 600-800mg TID until symptom resolution and inflammatory markers normalize, then taper over 2-4 weeks. PLUS Colchicine 0.6mg daily or BID x3mo (reduces recurrence - COPE, ICAP trials). Corticosteroids: AVOID if possible - increase risk recurrence (50% vs 10-15% with NSAIDs + colchicine), may impair infarct healing, increased risk myocardial rupture. Use only if contraindication to NSAIDs/colchicine or refractory symptoms. Lowest dose shortest duration. Pericardiocentesis: Only if large effusion with tamponade (rare). Most effusions small and resolve with medical therapy. Prognosis: Generally benign, self-limited. Responds well to NSAIDs + colchicine. Recurrence 15-30% (reduced with colchicine). A wrong: Timing, presentation suggest Dressler, not recurrent MI. B, C wrong: Presentation classic for pericarditis.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with severe AS (valve area 0.8cm², mean gradient 52mmHg) found on routine echo. Asymptomatic, active lifestyle, walks 2 miles daily without symptoms. LVEF 62%. No CAD on recent angiography. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Close monitoring with serial echos Q6-12mo and exercise stress test
B. Immediate AVR - all severe AS requires surgery
C. Medical management with vasodilators
D. No follow-up needed
questions.explanation: - Severe AS: Valve area <1.0cm² (normal 3-4cm²), mean gradient ≥40mmHg, peak velocity ≥4.0m/s. Natural history: Asymptomatic period (may be prolonged), once symptoms develop: Average survival without AVR: Angina 5y, Syncope 3y, HF 2y. Sudden death 1-3%/year. AVR indications: Symptomatic severe AS (Class I): Angina, syncope, dyspnea. Immediate AVR. Asymptomatic severe AS (Class I): LVEF <50%, Very severe AS (valve area <0.6cm², mean gradient ≥60mmHg, peak velocity ≥5.0m/s), Undergoing other cardiac surgery. Asymptomatic severe AS (Class IIa - reasonable): Abnormal exercise stress test (symptoms, hypotension, severe ST depression), Rapid progression (velocity increase ≥0.3m/s per year), BNP >3x normal. This patient: Severe AS (area 0.8cm², gradient 52mmHg), ASYMPTOMATIC, LVEF 62%, active without symptoms. Does NOT meet Class I criteria for surgery. Management asymptomatic severe AS: Close surveillance: Echo Q6-12mo (assess progression), Exercise stress test (if genuinely asymptomatic and able to exercise safely) - unmask symptoms, assess hemodynamic response. Patient education: Teach warning symptoms (dyspnea, angina, syncope, decreased exercise tolerance). Report immediately if symptoms develop. Prompt AVR if symptoms occur. LVEF monitoring: If drops <50% → AVR indicated even if asymptomatic. Avoid: Strenuous activity, competitive sports (risk sudden death). Medications: No medical therapy prevents progression or delays need for surgery. Statins do NOT slow progression (SEAS, SALTIRE trials). Vasodilators relatively contraindicated (may cause profound hypotension). Surgery/TAVR when indicated: Surgical AVR or TAVR depending on surgical risk. B wrong: Asymptomatic patients with preserved LVEF can be observed with close monitoring. C wrong: No medical therapy effective. Vasodilators dangerous. D wrong: Requires close monitoring.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis (valve area 1.3cm²) and AF presents with dyspnea NYHA class III. HR 98 bpm on metoprolol 50mg BID. Anticoagulated with warfarin INR 2.4. What additional management would provide symptomatic benefit?
options: A. Increase metoprolol only
B. Add digoxin only
C. Optimize rate control
D. Immediate valve replacement
questions.explanation: - Mitral stenosis medical management: MS = obstruction to LV filling. Normal MV area 4-6cm². MS: Mild 1.5-2.0cm², Moderate 1.0-1.5cm², Severe <1.0cm². This patient: Moderate MS (1.3cm²), AF, symptomatic NYHA III. Hemodynamics: MS limits LV filling. Require adequate diastolic filling time across stenotic valve. Tachycardia shortens diastole → inadequate filling → elevated LA pressure → pulmonary congestion. Management: Rate control (MOST IMPORTANT): Goal HR <60-80 bpm at rest, <110 bpm with activity. Allows adequate diastolic filling time. Beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol) or non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) preferred. This patient HR 98 - suboptimal, needs better control. Digoxin: Less effective rate control, especially with activity. Not first-line. Can add to beta-blocker if inadequate control. Diuretics: For volume overload/pulmonary congestion. Careful - too aggressive diuresis reduces preload → decreased CO. Anticoagulation: Essential with AF (very high stroke risk with MS + AF). Warfarin preferred over DOACs in rheumatic MS (DOACs less studied, some guidelines recommend warfarin). AVOID: Vasodilators (nitrates, ACE-I) - reduce preload → worsen CO. Exercise: Avoid strenuous activity if moderate-severe MS. Interventions: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty (PBMV): For symptomatic moderate-severe MS with favorable valve anatomy (pliable, minimal calcification, minimal MR, no LA thrombus). Preferred over surgery if anatomy suitable. Class I if symptomatic moderate-severe MS (valve area ≤1.5cm², mean gradient >5-10mmHg) with favorable anatomy. Surgical MVR: If unfavorable anatomy for PBMV (heavy calcification, severe MR, LA thrombus). This patient: Moderate MS, symptomatic despite medical therapy. Optimize rate control and diuretics first. If symptoms persist → consider PBMV if favorable anatomy. A wrong: Rate control likely needs optimization but also need diuretics, consider intervention. B wrong: Digoxin alone less effective. D wrong: Try optimal medical therapy and PBMV before surgery.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with no CVD history. HTN controlled on lisinopril 10mg. Non-smoker. Labs: Total cholesterol 242 mg/dL, LDL-C 168 mg/dL, HDL-C 42 mg/dL, TG 160 mg/dL, glucose 96 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.6%, BP 132/78. 10-year ASCVD risk calculated: 11.2%. What is MOST appropriate lipid management?
options: A. No statin - LDL not high enough
B. Moderate-to-high intensity statin
C. Lifestyle modification only
D. Low-intensity statin only
questions.explanation: - Statin therapy primary prevention: 2018/2019 ACC/AHA guidelines. Four statin benefit groups: ASCVD (secondary prevention): High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40- 80mg or rosuvastatin 20-40mg) regardless of LDL. LDL ≥190 mg/dL: High-intensity statin. DM age 40-75 with LDL 70-189 mg/dL: Moderate-intensity statin (atorvastatin 10-20mg or rosuvastatin 5-10mg). If ASCVD risk ≥20% → high-intensity. Primary prevention without DM, LDL 70-189 mg/dL: Calculate 10-year ASCVD risk (pooled cohort equation). If risk ≥20%: High-intensity statin. If risk 7.5-19.9%: Moderate-to-high intensity statin (individualize based on risk enhancers). If risk 5-7.4%: Consider statin if risk enhancers present. If risk <5%: Lifestyle modification, consider if risk enhancers. Risk enhancers: Family history premature ASCVD, LDL persistently ≥160 mg/dL, Metabolic syndrome, CKD, South Asian ancestry, Inflammatory disorders, Early menopause, Pregnancy complications, hs-CRP ≥2.0 mg/L, ABI <0.9, Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL, apoB ≥130 mg/dL, CAC score. This patient: No ASCVD, no DM, LDL 168 mg/dL (in range 70-189), ASCVD risk 11.2% (≥7.5-10%) → Statin indicated. Moderate-to-high intensity recommended. Risk enhancers: Low HDL 42 mg/dL, family history not mentioned. Could calculate CAC score if uncertain. Statin reduces LDL ~30-50% depending on intensity, reduces ASCVD events ~25-35%. Goals: Not specific LDL target (treat to high-risk group), but generally aim for ≥50% LDL reduction with high-intensity or 30-50% with moderate-intensity. Some guidelines suggest LDL <70 mg/dL if very high risk. A wrong: Risk ≥7.5% warrants statin. C wrong: Statin indicated. D wrong: Moderate-to-high intensity appropriate for risk level.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man on warfarin (INR goal 2-3) for AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 4) needs colonoscopy with possible polypectomy. What is MOST appropriate perioperative anticoagulation management?
options: A. Continue warfarin through procedure
B. Stop warfarin permanently
C. Stop warfarin 1 day before
D. Stop warfarin 5 days before procedure
questions.explanation: - Perioperative anticoagulation management: Assess procedure bleeding risk: Low-risk (minor dental, cataract surgery, minor dermatologic) - may continue anticoagulation. High-risk (major surgery, colonoscopy with polypectomy, biopsy) - hold anticoagulation. Assess stroke/thrombosis risk: High-risk (requires bridging): Mechanical mitral valve or older mechanical aortic valve, AF with CHADS2 ≥5-6 or stroke <3mo, VTE <3mo, Severe thrombophilia. Low-moderate risk (no bridging): AF with CHADS2 <4, bioprosthetic valve, VTE >3mo. Warfarin management: Stop 5 days before procedure (allows INR to normalize - warfarin half-life 36-42h, takes 4-5 days to reach INR <1.5). Check INR day before procedure. Bridging (if high thrombosis risk): Start LMWH (enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC Q12h) or UFH infusion when INR <2.0. Last LMWH dose: 24h before procedure (hold morning dose day of procedure). UFH: Stop 4-6h before. Resume anticoagulation: Warfarin evening of procedure if hemostasis adequate. LMWH/UFH: 24h post-procedure if low bleeding risk, 48-72h if high bleeding risk. BRIDGE trial (2015): Bridging NO better than no bridging for AF patients, but increased bleeding. Routine bridging no longer recommended for most AF patients. Reserve for very highrisk (mechanical mitral valve, stroke <3mo). This patient: AF with CHADS2-VASc 4 (moderate risk), colonoscopy with polypectomy (high bleeding risk). Stop warfarin 5 days before. Likely does NOT need bridging per BRIDGE trial (moderate stroke risk). Resume warfarin evening of procedure if no bleeding. A wrong: Colonoscopy with polypectomy high bleeding risk. C wrong: 1 day insufficient - warfarin lasts days.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man 2 weeks post-CABG recovering well at home. Cardiology recommends outpatient cardiac rehabilitation. Patient asks about benefits. What are the PRIMARY benefits of cardiac rehabilitation post-cardiac surgery?
options: A. Reduces mortality 20-30%
B. No proven mortality benefit
C. Only improves exercise capacity
D. Only for emotional support
questions.explanation: - Cardiac rehabilitation: Comprehensive program - exercise training, education, counseling, risk factor modification. Class I recommendation for: Post-MI, post-PCI, postCABG, chronic stable angina, compensated HF. Benefits (strong evidence): Mortality reduction: 20-30% reduction in CV mortality. Improved exercise capacity: Increase VO2 max 11-36%, improved functional capacity. Symptom reduction: Reduced angina frequency, improved dyspnea. Quality of life: Improved physical and mental health scores. Hospital readmissions: Reduced HF rehospitalizations 30-40%. Risk factor modification: Improved lipid control, BP control, weight loss, smoking cessation, diabetes management. Medication adherence: Better adherence to GDMT. Psychosocial: Reduced depression, anxiety, improved coping. Return to work: Increased return-to-work rates. Cost-effective: $10,000-30,000 per QALY gained. Components: Phase I (inpatient): Early mobilization, education. Phase II (outpatient supervised): 36 sessions over 12 weeks typically. Monitored exercise, education sessions, psychosocial support. Phase III (maintenance): Community-based, less supervision. Exercise prescription: 3-5 sessions/week, 30-60min aerobic (walking, cycling, treadmill), Resistance training (added after 4- 6 weeks). Target HR: 50-85% HRR (heart rate reserve) or Perceived exertion 11-16 on Borg scale (6-20). Participation rates: Unfortunately low - only 20-30% eligible patients participate. Barriers: Lack of referral, distance, cost, lack of awareness. This patient post-CABG: Strong Class I indication for cardiac rehab. Proven mortality and morbidity benefits. A correct - comprehensive benefits. B, C, D wrong: Underestimate scope of benefits.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents to ED with BP 210/118 mmHg. No chest pain, dyspnea, headache, visual changes, or neurologic symptoms. No prior HTN diagnosis. Exam: Otherwise normal, no papilledema, no focal deficits. Labs: Cr 1.2 (unknown baseline), troponin negative, BNP 45 (normal). ECG: LVH. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. IV labetalol immediately
B. IV nitroprusside drip
C. Hypertensive urgency
D. Admit to ICU for IV medications
questions.explanation: - Hypertensive crisis: Severe elevation BP (usually SBP >180 mmHg or DBP >120 mmHg). Subdivided: Hypertensive EMERGENCY: Severe BP elevation WITH acute endorgan damage. Requires immediate BP reduction with IV medications, ICU admission. Target: Reduce MAP by 10-20% within 1h, then additional 5-15% over next 23h to ~160/100 mmHg. Examples: Hypertensive encephalopathy, Acute stroke, Acute coronary syndrome, Acute HF/pulmonary edema, Aortic dissection, Acute kidney injury, Eclampsia, Catecholamine crisis (pheochromocytoma, cocaine, MAO inhibitor interaction). Hypertensive URGENCY: Severe BP elevation WITHOUT acute end-organ damage. Can manage with oral medications, outpatient follow-up. NO benefit from rapid IV BP reduction - may cause harm (ischemia from hypoperfusion). Target: Gradual reduction over 24-48h. This patient: Severe HTN (210/118) but NO symptoms of end-organ damage - no chest pain (no ACS), no dyspnea/edema (no acute HF), no headache/visual/neuro (no encephalopathy, no stroke), no acute kidney injury (Cr 1.2 not clearly elevated). Diagnosis: Hypertensive URGENCY. Management: Reinitiate/start oral antihypertensive medications: Combination therapy reasonable given severity - ACE-I or ARB + CCB or thiazide. Example: Amlodipine 5mg + lisinopril 10mg. Avoid immediate IV medications or rapid reduction (risk stroke, MI, kidney injury). Observation 4-6h in ED, ensure BP improving. Close outpatient follow-up (24-48h) to titrate medications. Lifestyle counseling. Investigate secondary causes if appropriate (young age, resistant HTN). Exceptions requiring ICU even without clear end-organ damage: BP >220/140 with symptoms, Patient unreliable for outpatient follow-up. A, B, D wrong: IV medications and ICU admission not indicated for uncomplicated hypertensive urgency. Oral medications appropriate. C correct.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with CAD on aspirin 81mg daily + clopidogrel 75mg daily (s/p PCI with DES 8mo ago) presents with recurrent angina. Cath shows stent thrombosis. Compliant with medications. Platelet function testing: Elevated on-treatment platelet reactivity to clopidogrel. What genetic polymorphism is associated with reduced clopidogrel response?
options: A. Factor V Leiden
B. CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles (*2, *3)
C. MTHFR mutation
D. Prothrombin G20210A
questions.explanation: - Clopidogrel pharmacogenetics: Clopidogrel is prodrug - requires CYP450 metabolism (primarily CYP2C19) to active metabolite that irreversibly blocks P2Y12 receptor. CYP2C19 polymorphisms: Loss-of-function alleles: *2 (most common), *3, *4, *5, etc. Reduced enzyme activity → less active metabolite → reduced platelet inhibition. Gain-of-function alleles: *17 - increased enzyme activity → more active metabolite → enhanced response, increased bleeding. Prevalence loss-of-function: Caucasians ~30%, African Americans ~40%, Asians ~50- 60% carry ≥1 loss-of-function allele. Clinical impact: Carriers of loss-of-function alleles (especially *2/*2 homozygotes or *2 + *3 compound heterozygotes): Increased risk stent thrombosis, MI, cardiovascular death (TRITON-TIMI 38, PLATO subanalyses). "Poor metabolizers" have 2-3x increased risk adverse CV events. Testing: CYP2C19 genotyping available. Platelet function testing (VerifyNow, light transmission aggregometry). Guidelines: Routine genotyping NOT recommended for all patients (Class III). Consider genotyping (Class IIb): If high-risk features (history stent thrombosis, multiple/complex PCI, poor clinical outcomes on clopidogrel). If genetic testing shows loss-of-function allele → consider alternative: Prasugrel 10mg daily (not prodrug dependent on CYP2C19 - uses different enzymes). TRITON-TIMI 38: Superior to clopidogrel. Contraindications: Prior stroke/TIA, age ≥75y, weight <60kg. Ticagrelor 90mg BID (not prodrug - active drug). PLATO: Superior to clopidogrel. No genetic variability in response. This patient: Stent thrombosis on clopidogrel despite adherence. Likely poor metabolizer. Genotyping reasonable. Switch to prasugrel or ticagrelor (if no contraindications). Alternatively, consider ticlopidine (rarely used - hematologic toxicity). A, C, D wrong: Not related to clopidogrel metabolism. Factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation cause hypercoagulability. MTHFR affects homocysteine metabolism.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with HTN, DM, asks about cardiovascular risk. She mentions she had preeclampsia during both pregnancies (15 and 18y ago) and recently started having hot flashes (perimenopausal). BMI 32. What is MOST important counseling regarding CV risk?
options: A. Pregnancy complications have no long-term CV implications
B. Hormone replacement therapy will eliminate CV risk
C. Women have lower CV risk than men
D. History of preeclampsia is CV risk enhancer
questions.explanation: - Cardiovascular disease in women: Leading cause of death in women (>300,000 deaths/year in US). Often underdiagnosed and undertreated. Sex-specific risk factors: Pregnancyrelated: Preeclampsia: Doubles long-term risk HTN, stroke, IHD. Gestational diabetes: 7x increased T2DM risk, 2x increased CVD risk. Gestational HTN: Increased risk chronic HTN. Reproductive/hormonal: Early menopause (<40y): Increased CVD risk. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): Increased metabolic syndrome, DM, CVD. Traditional risk factors: Diabetes has greater relative risk in women vs men. Smoking has greater relative risk in women. Hypertension management critical. Unique presentations: Atypical symptoms more common (fatigue, nausea, dyspnea without chest pain). Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) - young women. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy - postmenopausal women. Management: Aggressive risk factor modification: Smoking cessation (if applicable), BP control, Lipid management (statins), DM control, Weight loss, Exercise. Aspirin: Same indications as men (secondary prevention, DM with risk factors). NOT routine primary prevention. Hormone replacement therapy: NOT recommended for CVD prevention. WHI trial: Increased CHD, stroke, VTE. Only for menopausal symptoms, lowest dose shortest duration. This patient: Multiple risk factors - HTN, DM, obesity, history preeclampsia (doubles risk), perimenopausal. Very high CV risk. Needs: Aggressive risk factor modification, Statin (DM + likely ASCVD risk >7.5%), Optimal BP control, Weight loss, Exercise, Consider ASCVD risk calculation. A wrong: Preeclampsia is significant CV risk enhancer. B wrong: HRT NOT for CVD prevention, may increase risk. C wrong: Women have equal or greater CV disease burden, often undertreated.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man post-MI 3mo ago asks about exercise recommendations. Completed cardiac rehab (36 sessions). LVEF 48%, no angina, no ischemia on stress test. Active lifestyle desired. What are the guideline-recommended physical activity recommendations for CV health and secondary prevention?
options: A. ≥150 min/week
B. Avoid all exercise post-MI
C. 30 min/week total sufficient
D. Only light stretching allowed
questions.explanation: - Physical activity recommendations for CVD prevention and post-MI: AHA/ACC guidelines: All adults: ≥150 min/week moderate-intensity aerobic (or ≥75 min/week vigorous-intensity, or combination). Moderate: Brisk walking, cycling <10mph, water aerobics, ballroom dancing. Vigorous: Jogging/running, swimming laps, cycling >10mph, hiking uphill. Spread over ≥3 days/week, ≥10min bouts. PLUS resistance training: ≥2 days/week (major muscle groups). PLUS reduce sedentary time (sitting, screen time). Post-MI/PCI/CABG: Same recommendations - ≥150 min/week moderate after completing cardiac rehab. May engage in vigorous activity if: Successfully completed cardiac rehab, No angina, No ischemia on stress test, LVEF adequate. Avoid: Competitive sports with high static component if LV dysfunction, Isometric exercise (heavy lifting) if very high risk. Benefits regular physical activity: Mortality reduction: 20-30% reduction CV mortality, all-cause mortality. Improved fitness: Increase VO2 max, functional capacity. Risk factor improvement: Lower BP, improved lipids (increase HDL, lower TG), improved glucose control/insulin sensitivity, weight management. Anti-inflammatory, improved endothelial function. Psychosocial: Reduced depression, anxiety, improved QOL. This patient: 3mo post-MI, completed rehab, LVEF 48% (mildly reduced but acceptable), no angina, negative stress test. Can engage in regular moderate-vigorous activity per guidelines. Avoid extreme exertion (marathons, very heavy weights) given mildly reduced LVEF. Encourage: Regular aerobic 30-60min most days, Resistance training 2x/week (light-moderate weights, higher reps), Flexibility/stretching. Monitor symptoms - stop if chest pain, dizziness, severe dyspnea. A correct - comprehensive guideline recommendations. B wrong: Exercise strongly encouraged post-MI. C wrong: Insufficient duration. D wrong: Aerobic and resistance training beneficial and safe.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with persistent AF started on amiodarone 200mg daily 6 months ago for rhythm control. Now presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion, dry cough x6 weeks. Nonsmoker. No fever. Exam: Bilateral crackles, O2 sat 92% RA. CXR: Bilateral interstitial infiltrates. CT chest: Ground-glass opacities, interstitial thickening. PFTs: Restrictive pattern, DLCO 58% predicted (decreased from baseline 88%). What is MOST likely diagnosis and management?
options: A. Pneumonia - start antibiotics
B. Heart failure exacerbation - increase diuretics
C. Continue amiodarone - pulmonary changes unrelated
D. Discontinue amiodarone immediately
questions.explanation: - Amiodarone toxicity: Multi-organ toxicity limits long-term use despite excellent antiarrhythmic efficacy. Pulmonary toxicity (most serious, 5-15% incidence): Presentation: Insidious dyspnea, cough (usually dry), hypoxemia. May present acutely (rare - ARDS-like) or chronically. Risk factors: Cumulative dose >400mg/day, duration >2mo, elderly, pre-existing lung disease. Imaging: CXR - bilateral infiltrates. CT - ground-glass opacities, organizing pneumonia pattern. PFTs: Restrictive pattern, decreased DLCO (most sensitive). Diagnosis: Clinical + imaging + PFTs. Exclude infection, HF. May need bronchoscopy/biopsy (shows foamy macrophages). Management: DISCONTINUE amiodarone IMMEDIATELY (most important). Corticosteroids if severe: Prednisone 40-60mg daily x4-12 weeks, taper slowly. Improves outcomes in severe cases. O2 supplementation. Monitor: CXR, PFTs, symptoms - improvement expected over weeks-months. Amiodarone has long half-life (40-60 days) - toxicity may persist/worsen initially after discontinuation. Prevention: Baseline CXR, PFTs (including DLCO). Monitor: PFTs every 3-6 months, CXR annually or if symptoms. Other amiodarone toxicities: Thyroid (hypo 5-10%, hyper 2-5%): Monitor TSH, free T4 every 3-6mo. Hepatic (15%): Monitor LFTs every 6mo. Ocular (corneal deposits 90%, vision changes rare): Annual eye exam. Dermatologic (blue-gray discoloration, photosensitivity): Sunscreen. Neurologic (tremor, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy). Bradycardia, QT prolongation. Drug interactions: Many via CYP3A4, P-gp inhibition. This patient: Classic amiodarone pulmonary toxicity - dyspnea, cough, bilateral infiltrates, decreased DLCO. Discontinue immediately, consider steroids. A wrong: No fever, subacute presentation - not infectious. B wrong: Presentation suggests pulmonary toxicity. C wrong: Must stop amiodarone.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with paroxysmal AF and structurally normal heart (LVEF 62%, no CAD) desires rhythm control. Cardiology recommends sotalol. CrCl 72 mL/min. Baseline QTc 420ms. What is MOST important monitoring requirement when initiating sotalol?
options: A. Inpatient initiation with continuous telemetry monitoring x3-5 days
B. Outpatient initiation acceptable - no monitoring needed
C. Only check ECG once before starting
D. Monitor liver function only
questions.explanation: - Sotalol: Class III antiarrhythmic (potassium channel blocker) with beta-blocker properties. Indications: AF rhythm control (structurally normal heart preferred), Ventricular arrhythmias. NOT for HF - negative inotrope. Proarrhythmia risk (Torsades de Pointes): QT prolongation dose-dependent. Torsades risk 1-5% (higher than other antiarrhythmics). Risk factors: Female gender, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, renal impairment, baseline QTc prolongation, structural heart disease. Initiation protocol (MANDATORY inpatient): Baseline: ECG (QTc), electrolytes (K, Mg), renal function. Admit for continuous telemetry 3-5 days. Start low dose: 80mg BID (or 40mg BID if CrCl 40-60). Check QTc 2-4h after each dose (peak effect). Escalate dose Q3 days if tolerated: 80mg BID → 120mg BID → 160mg BID (max 320mg/day). HOLD if: QTc >500ms, QTc increases >60ms from baseline, HR <50 bpm. Renal dosing: CrCl >60: Q12h dosing. CrCl 40-60: Q24h dosing. CrCl 10-40: Q36-48h dosing. CrCl <10: Avoid. Monitor: QTc, HR, BP, electrolytes. Contraindications: Baseline QTc >450ms (women) or >440ms (men), Bronchospasm, Decompensated HF, Sinus bradycardia, 2nd/3rd degree AV block, CrCl <10-30 mL/min (depending on guidelines). Side effects: Bradycardia, Fatigue (beta-blocker effects), Bronchospasm, Torsades (most serious). This patient: Structurally normal heart, CrCl 72 (adequate), QTc 420ms (acceptable) → sotalol reasonable. MUST initiate inpatient with telemetry for 3-5 days per FDA requirement. A correct - inpatient monitoring mandatory. B wrong: Outpatient initiation contraindicated due to torsades risk. C wrong: Serial QTc monitoring essential. D wrong: QTc monitoring most critical.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman with AF on digoxin 0.25mg daily presents with nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances (yellow halos), confusion x2 days. PMH: AF, HFrEF (LVEF 35%), CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38). Other meds: Metoprolol, furosemide, spironolactone. Labs: Digoxin level 3.2 ng/mL (therapeutic 0.5-2.0), K 5.8 mEq/L, Mg 1.8 mg/dL, Cr 1.9 mg/dL. ECG: AF with slow ventricular response (HR 48), frequent PVCs, bigeminy. What is MOST appropriate management of digoxin toxicity?
options: A. Continue digoxin at same dose
B. Increase digoxin dose
C. Hold digoxin
D. Hemodialysis to remove digoxin
questions.explanation: - Digoxin toxicity: Narrow therapeutic index (0.5-2.0 ng/mL for AF, 0.5-0.9 ng/mL preferred for HF). Toxicity >2.0 ng/mL. Risk factors: Elderly, renal impairment (digoxin renally cleared), Hypokalemia (enhances toxicity), Hypomagnesemia, Drug interactions (amiodarone, verapamil, diltiazem, macrolides, spironolactone - increase digoxin levels). Presentation: GI: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea (early signs). Visual: Yellow-green halos, blurred vision, scotomas. Neurologic: Confusion, delirium, fatigue, weakness. Cardiac arrhythmias (most dangerous): Ventricular: PVCs, bigeminy, VT, VF. Bradyarrhythmias: Sinus bradycardia, AV block (any degree). AF with slow ventricular response. Bidirectional VT (classic but rare - alternating QRS axis). Combination brady + tachy (pathognomonic). Labs: Elevated digoxin level, Hyperkalemia (digoxin inhibits Na-K-ATPase → extracellular K), Renal dysfunction. Management: HOLD digoxin. Correct electrolytes: Hyperkalemia management: Mild (5.0-5.5): Kayexelate, stop K-sparing diuretics. Moderate-severe (>5.5): Calcium gluconate 1g IV (if cardiac toxicity), Insulin 10 units + dextrose 50g IV, Kayexelate. Avoid calcium if hypercalcemia (may worsen arrhythmias). Hypomagnesemia: Replete Mg (enhances toxicity if low). Arrhythmia management: Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia. Avoid electrical cardioversion if possible (may trigger VF). Temporary pacing if needed. Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab/Digibind): Indications: Life-threatening arrhythmias (VF, VT, highgrade AV block), Severe hyperkalemia (>5.5 mEq/L), Hemodynamic instability, Acute ingestion >10mg, Chronic toxicity with level >6 ng/mL or level >4 ng/mL with symptoms. Dose: Calculate based on digoxin level and body weight OR empiric 10-20 vials. Works within 30min, normalizes K. Monitoring: Continuous telemetry, serial K levels, digoxin levels (unreliable after DigiFab - measures bound + free). Hemodialysis: NOT effective (large Vd, protein-bound). This patient: Digoxin 3.2 ng/mL (toxic), classic symptoms (GI, visual, confusion), arrhythmias (bradycardia, PVCs), hyperkalemia 5.8 → HOLD digoxin, treat hyperkalemia, consider DigiFab if worsens. Adjust future digoxin dose for renal function (CrCl 38) or discontinue. A, B wrong: Must stop digoxin. C correct. D wrong: Dialysis ineffective.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 28%) currently on enalapril 10mg BID, carvedilol 25mg BID, spironolactone 25mg, furosemide 40mg presents for follow-up. NYHA class II-III symptoms despite current therapy. BP 118/72, HR 68, Cr 1.2, K 4.4. Cardiology wants to switch from ACE-I to sacubitril/valsartan. What is MOST appropriate transition protocol?
options: A. Start sacubitril/valsartan immediately
B. HOLD enalapril x36 hours
C. Continue both enalapril and sacubitril/valsartan together
D. No benefit switching from ACE-I
questions.explanation: - Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto): Combination angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI). Sacubitril: Neprilysin inhibitor → increases natriuretic peptides (BNP, ANP) → vasodilation, natriuresis, inhibits RAAS. Valsartan: ARB blocks angiotensin II. PARADIGMHF trial: 20% reduction CV death, 21% reduction HF hospitalization vs enalapril in HFrEF (NYHA II-IV, LVEF ≤40%). Indications (Class I): HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), NYHA class II-IV on optimal GDMT including ACE-I/ARB, beta-blocker. Replaces ACE-I or ARB (NOT additive - don't combine). Transition from ACE-I: MANDATORY 36-hour washout: HOLD ACE-I x36 hours before starting sacubitril/valsartan. Reason: Avoid angioedema (dual inhibition ACE + neprilysin increases bradykinin). NEVER combine with ACE-I. ARB washout: Immediate switch acceptable (no mandatory washout). Dosing: Start: 24/26mg BID (if low BP, renal dysfunction, elderly) OR 49/51mg BID (if stable). Target: 97/103mg BID. Uptitration: Increase dose Q2-4 weeks as tolerated. Monitoring: BP (risk hypotension), Renal function (Cr, K), Potassium (risk hyperkalemia, especially with spironolactone). Contraindications: History angioedema with ACE-I/ARB (ABSOLUTE - 0.5% incidence with sacubitril/valsartan), Current ACE-I use (need 36h washout), Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30), Pregnancy, Severe hepatic impairment. Side effects: Hypotension (dose-limiting), Hyperkalemia, Angioedema (0.4-0.5%), Renal dysfunction, Dizziness. Drug interactions: K-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, potassium supplements (increase hyperkalemia risk). This patient: HFrEF LVEF 28%, NYHA II-III, currently on enalapril → meets criteria for sacubitril/valsartan. HOLD enalapril x36h, start sacubitril/valsartan 49/51mg BID (BP adequate), uptitrate to 97/103mg BID. Monitor closely (already on spironolactone - hyperkalemia risk). A wrong: Need 36h ACE-I washout. C wrong: NEVER combine. D wrong: PARADIGM-HF showed clear benefit.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 32%), T2DM (HbA1c 8.2%) on sacubitril/valsartan 97/103mg BID, carvedilol 25mg BID, spironolactone 25mg, furosemide 80mg BID, metformin 1000mg BID. Still has NYHA class III symptoms, recent HF hospitalization. eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m². What additional medication would provide mortality/hospitalization benefit?
options: A. Ivabradine
B. Hydralazine-isosorbide dinitrate
C. Digoxin
D. SGLT2 inhibitor
questions.explanation: - SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure: Dapagliflozin (Farxiga), Empagliflozin (Jardiance), Sotagliflozin. Originally developed for T2DM. Major HF trials showed benefit REGARDLESS of diabetes. DAPA-HF (dapagliflozin): HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), with or without T2DM. 26% reduction primary endpoint (CV death, HF hospitalization, urgent HF visit). Benefit in both diabetic AND non-diabetic patients. EMPEROR-Reduced (empagliflozin): HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%). 25% reduction CV death/HF hospitalization. EMPEROR-Preserved: HFpEF (LVEF >40%). 21% reduction CV death/HF hospitalization. DELIVER (dapagliflozin): HFpEF. 18% reduction CV death/HF hospitalization. Mechanism in HF: Natriuresis, diuresis (independent of GFR), Improved myocardial energetics, Reduced inflammation, LV remodeling, Reduced sympathetic activity, Modest BP reduction. Glucose-lowering effect (if diabetic). Indications (2022 AHA/ACC guidelines): Class I: HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%) to reduce hospitalization and CV death. Class IIa: HFpEF (LVEF >40%) to reduce hospitalization. Regardless of diabetes status. Dosing: Dapagliflozin 10mg PO daily. Empagliflozin 10mg PO daily. Can use with eGFR ≥20-25 mL/min (lower than for glucose-lowering indication). Side effects: Genital mycotic infections (10% women, 3% men), UTI, Euglycemic DKA (rare, mostly T1DM), Volume depletion, hypotension, AKI, Fournier gangrene (very rare), Amputation (canagliflozin only), Hyperkalemia (rare). Contraindications: eGFR <20-25 mL/min, T1DM (relative - DKA risk), Ketosis-prone diabetes. This patient: HFrEF LVEF 32%, symptomatic despite GDMT + recent hospitalization, T2DM (will benefit from glucose-lowering too), eGFR 48 (adequate) → SGLT2 inhibitor STRONGLY indicated. Add dapagliflozin 10mg or empagliflozin 10mg daily. A wrong: Ivabradine indicated if HR >70 on max beta-blocker. This patient HR not stated but on carvedilol 25mg BID. B wrong: Hydralazine-nitrate primarily for Black patients with HFrEF or ACE-I/ARB intolerant. C wrong: Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but NOT mortality. SGLT2i superior.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%) on sacubitril/valsartan 97/103mg BID, carvedilol 50mg BID (maximum tolerated dose), spironolactone 25mg, empagliflozin 10mg. Sinus rhythm. HR 82 bpm at rest. NYHA class II-III symptoms. What additional therapy would reduce HF hospitalizations?
options: A. Ivabradine 5mg BID
B. Increase carvedilol
C. Add second beta-blocker
D. No additional therapy beneficial
questions.explanation: - Ivabradine (Corlanor): Selective If ("funny current") channel inhibitor in SA node. Reduces HR without negative inotropy or effect on BP. SHIFT trial: 18% reduction HF hospitalization, 26% reduction CV death/HF hospitalization in HFrEF patients with HR ≥70 bpm despite max beta-blocker. Indications (Class IIa): HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%), NYHA class II-III, Sinus rhythm (does NOT work in AF - no SA node depolarization), HR ≥70 bpm despite maximum tolerated beta-blocker dose. Dosing: Start: 5mg BID with meals. Target: 7.5mg BID (if HR remains ≥60 bpm). Reduce to 2.5mg BID if HR <50 bpm or symptomatic bradycardia. Monitoring: HR (target 50-60 bpm), Symptoms (bradycardia, visual changes). Side effects: Bradycardia (10%), Visual phenomena (phosphenes - bright lights, 3%), luminous phenomena related to retinal current. AF (incidence increases). Contraindications: AF/atrial flutter (ineffective), Acute decompensated HF, BP <90/50 mmHg, Sick sinus syndrome, 3rd degree AV block (without pacemaker), Resting HR <60 bpm, Severe hepatic impairment, Pacemakerdependent, Concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (diltiazem, verapamil, azole antifungals). Drug interactions: CYP3A4 inhibitors increase levels, CYP3A4 inducers decrease levels. Avoid combining with diltiazem/verapamil (excessive bradycardia). This patient: LVEF 28%, NYHA II-III, sinus rhythm, HR 82 bpm despite carvedilol 50mg BID (max dose) → meets criteria for ivabradine. Start 5mg BID, uptitrate to 7.5mg BID, target HR 50-60 bpm. Should reduce HF hospitalizations. A correct. B wrong: Already on max carvedilol dose. C wrong: Combining betablockers not standard. D wrong: Ivabradine provides additional benefit.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman with acute PE diagnosed 2h ago. Sudden dyspnea, chest pain. CT angiography: Large bilateral PEs (saddle embolus). BP 84/58, HR 122, RR 28, O2 sat 88% on 4L O2. Altered mental status. Echo: RV strain (RV dilation, hypokinesis, D-sign), moderate TR. Troponin 0.8 ng/mL (elevated), BNP 840 pg/mL. No contraindications to thrombolysis. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Anticoagulation with heparin only
B. Catheter-directed thrombolysis
C. Systemic thrombolysis PLUS anticoagulation
D. Surgical embolectomy first-line
questions.explanation: - Pulmonary embolism risk stratification: Massive (high-risk) PE: Hemodynamic instability - SBP <90 mmHg for ≥15min OR requiring vasopressors/inotropes, Shock, Cardiac arrest. Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE: Hemodynamically stable BUT RV dysfunction (echo or CT) OR elevated biomarkers (troponin, BNP). Low-risk PE: Hemodynamically stable, no RV dysfunction, normal biomarkers. This patient: Hypotension (84/58), tachycardia, altered MS, RV strain on echo, elevated troponin/BNP → MASSIVE PE. Management massive PE: Immediate systemic thrombolysis (Class I): Alteplase 100mg IV over 2h (preferred) OR Alteplase 10mg IV bolus, then 90mg over 2h, OR Tenecteplase 30-50mg IV bolus (weight-based, easier). PLUS therapeutic anticoagulation: UFH bolus 80 units/kg IV, then 18 units/kg/h infusion. Monitor aPTT goal 60-80 sec (1.5-2.5x control). Supportive: O2, fluids (cautious - can worsen RV function), Vasopressors if needed (norepinephrine preferred). Avoid aggressive fluids (worsen RV). Outcome: Mortality without thrombolysis 30-50%. With thrombolysis 10-15%. Rapid improvement expected within 24-48h. Contraindications thrombolysis (relative): Recent surgery (<2 weeks), Active bleeding, ICH within 2mo, Ischemic stroke <3mo, Known intracranial pathology, Bleeding diathesis. If contraindications: Catheter-directed therapies: Catheter-directed thrombolysis (lower dose, direct to clot). Catheter-based fragmentation/aspiration. Surgical embolectomy: If thrombolysis contraindicated OR failed. High-risk surgery. ECMO: Bridge to intervention. Submassive PE management: Controversial. Anticoagulation alone often adequate. Consider thrombolysis if deteriorating. PEITHO trial: Thrombolysis reduced hemodynamic decompensation but increased major bleeding. Individualize decision. A wrong: Anticoagulation alone insufficient for massive PE. C correct - immediate thrombolysis indicated. B wrong: Systemic thrombolysis faster in massive PE. Catheter-directed if contraindications or submassive. D wrong: Thrombolysis first-line. Surgery if thrombolysis contraindicated/failed.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with acute PE (segmental bilateral PEs on CTA). Hemodynamically stable: BP 122/76, HR 96. Echo: RV dilation, RV/LV ratio 1.2, McConnell sign (RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing). Troponin I 0.28 ng/mL (elevated). BNP 420 pg/mL. No contraindications to anticoagulation. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Systemic thrombolysis - elevated troponin mandates thrombolysis
B. Therapeutic anticoagulation (heparin or LMWH or DOAC) with close monitoring
C. Catheter-directed thrombolysis mandatory
D. IVC filter placement
questions.explanation: - Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE: Hemodynamically STABLE but has RV dysfunction OR elevated biomarkers. This patient: Stable BP/HR, RV dysfunction (echo shows RV dilation, RV/LV >0.9, McConnell sign), elevated troponin and BNP → submassive PE. Management controversy: Anticoagulation alone (standard): Heparin, LMWH, or DOAC. Close monitoring for deterioration. Most patients do well with anticoagulation alone. PEITHO trial: Thrombolysis vs heparin in submassive PE. Thrombolysis reduced hemodynamic decompensation (2% vs 6%) BUT increased major bleeding including ICH (2% vs 0.2%). No mortality benefit. Current approach: Anticoagulation FIRST-LINE for submassive PE if hemodynamically stable. Consider thrombolysis if: Clinical deterioration (hypotension, shock developing), Severe RV dysfunction, Massively elevated biomarkers, Young patient, low bleeding risk. Catheter-directed therapies: Lower thrombolytic dose, may reduce bleeding. Consider if: Standard thrombolysis contraindicated, Submassive PE with high-risk features but want to minimize bleeding. Risk stratification tools: PESI (Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index), sPESI (simplified). Low-risk by PESI → outpatient treatment consideration. This patient: Submassive PE, stable hemodynamics → anticoagulation with close monitoring. Watch for deterioration. Reserve thrombolysis if becomes unstable. A wrong: Systemic thrombolysis not routine for stable submassive PE given bleeding risk. C wrong: Catheter-directed not mandatory. D wrong: IVC filter only if anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE despite anticoagulation.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with acute PE (lobar PE right lower lobe). Recent major abdominal surgery 5 days ago for perforated appendicitis with peritonitis. Still in hospital recovering. Active intra-abdominal bleeding noted. Hemodynamically stable. What is MOST appropriate management given anticoagulation contraindication?
options: A. Start full-dose anticoagulation - PE requires anticoagulation
B. Prophylactic-dose anticoagulation only
C. No intervention
D. Retrievable IVC filter placement
questions.explanation: - IVC filter indications: Primarily for VTE when anticoagulation contraindicated or failed. Absolute contraindications to anticoagulation: Active major bleeding (this patient), Recent major surgery with bleeding risk, ICH, Recent major trauma, Severe thrombocytopenia (<50K). Relative contraindications: Recent GI bleeding (within weeks), Recent neurosurgery/spinal surgery, Uncontrolled HTN. IVC filter types: Permanent: Older filters, not removable. Retrievable: Can be removed when no longer needed (preferred). Placed via jugular or femoral vein. Positioned in infrarenal IVC. Indications for IVC filter: Acute VTE with absolute contraindication to anticoagulation (Class I), Recurrent VTE despite therapeutic anticoagulation (Class IIa), Free-floating iliofemoral or IVC thrombus (controversial, Class IIb). NOT indicated: Prophylaxis in high-risk patients without VTE, Chronic VTE (DVT/PE months ago now on anticoagulation). Complications: Filter thrombosis, IVC occlusion (10-20% longterm), Filter migration, perforation, Increased risk recurrent DVT (especially if filter not removed). Post-thrombotic syndrome. Retrievable filters should be removed: Once anticoagulation safe (typically 2-4 weeks to 3 months). Document why filter placed, plan for removal. Follow-up essential - many filters left in inappropriately. Management this patient: Acute PE, active bleeding from recent surgery → absolute contraindication to anticoagulation. Place retrievable IVC filter to prevent further emboli from DVT. Continue monitoring, supportive care. Once bleeding resolved and surgeon approves (typically 2-4 weeks) → start anticoagulation (heparin bridge then warfarin or DOAC). Remove filter once therapeutic anticoagulation established (after at least 3-6 months anticoagulation or when DVT/PE resolved). A wrong: Active bleeding contraindicates full anticoagulation. B wrong: Prophylactic dose insufficient for acute PE. D correct.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m²), not yet on dialysis. HTN, no diabetes, no known CAD. Labs: Total cholesterol 198 mg/dL, LDL-C 124 mg/dL, HDL-C 38 mg/dL, TG 180 mg/dL. Should he be on statin therapy?
options: A. Yes - statin indicated
B. No - statins contraindicated in CKD
C. Only if LDL >190 mg/dL
D. Wait until on dialysis to start
questions.explanation: - Statins in CKD: CKD is ASCVD risk equivalent (very high CV risk). Stage 3-5 CKD has 10-30x increased CV risk vs general population. More likely to die from CVD than progress to ESRD. Guidelines (KDIGO 2013): CKD stage 3-5 NOT on dialysis: Age ≥50y → statin (or statin/ezetimibe) regardless of LDL level. Age 18-49y → statin if: Known ASCVD, Diabetes, Prior ischemic stroke, 10y ASCVD risk >10%. Do NOT routinely monitor LDL (no target) - just treat. Dialysis patients: Do NOT initiate statin if not already on one (4D, AURORA trials showed no benefit). Continue if already on statin pre-dialysis. Transplant recipients: Statin recommended (reduce CV events, may improve graft survival). Evidence: SHARP trial: Simvastatin/ezetimibe in CKD reduced major ASCVD events 17%. Meta-analyses: ~25% reduction ASCVD events in CKD stages 3-5 (not on dialysis). NO benefit once on dialysis if not already on statin. Dose considerations: Most statins safe in CKD. Atorvastatin, rosuvastatin primarily hepatic metabolism - no dose adjustment. Simvastatin, pravastatin, fluvastatin - reduce dose in severe CKD. Avoid high-intensity statins in advanced CKD (increased myopathy risk). Use moderate-intensity. Monitor for myopathy (CK) - risk increased in CKD. This patient: CKD stage 4, age 64, not on dialysis, no CAD yet but very high CV risk → statin INDICATED regardless of LDL 124 mg/dL. Start moderate-intensity statin (atorvastatin 10-20mg or rosuvastatin 5-10mg daily). Do not need to monitor LDL levels or titrate to target - just treat. B wrong: Statins beneficial in CKD stages 3-5 not on dialysis. C wrong: Age ≥50 with CKD stage 3-5 warrants statin regardless of LDL. D wrong: Should start now. Once on dialysis, less benefit.

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with no ASCVD history, HTN only. Independent, active, walks daily. Life expectancy estimated 8-10 years. Never been on statin. LDL-C 156 mg/dL. Family asking if she should start statin for primary prevention. What is MOST appropriate recommendation?
options: A. Always start statin in elderly - age alone warrants treatment
B. Never start statin in elderly - too old
C. Individualize decision
D. High-intensity statin mandatory
questions.explanation: - Statins in elderly (age >75-80y) for primary prevention: Controversial - limited RCT data in very elderly. No statin trials specifically enrolled patients >75y for primary prevention. HOPE-3, STAREE ongoing. Guidelines: 2019 ACC/AHA: Consider patient factors - life expectancy, comorbidities, functional status, patient preferences. NOT automatic. 2021 ESA/ESC: Can consider in fit elderly with high CV risk. Clinical considerations elderly patients: Benefits: CV risk increases with age. Statins reduce events ~25% at any age (extrapolated). Time to benefit: 2-5 years for primary prevention. Must have adequate life expectancy. Risks: Myopathy (increased risk in elderly), Drug interactions (polypharmacy common), Falls risk (controversial - some data suggest myopathy → falls), Cognition concerns (not proven but patient worry), Bleeding (if also on antiplatelet/anticoagulant). Individualized approach: Healthy, fit elderly with life expectancy >5-10y, high CV risk → reasonable to offer statin. Frail, limited life expectancy, multiple comorbidities, high fall risk → may not benefit. Moderate-intensity preferred (lower myopathy risk than high-intensity). Patient preferences paramount - shared decision making. This patient: Age 82y, but healthy, active, independent, life expectancy 8-10y, LDL 156 mg/dL. Reasonable to offer moderate-intensity statin with discussion of benefits/risks. Not mandatory but reasonable option. Alternatives: Intensive lifestyle modification, Close monitoring without statin if patient declines. De-prescribing: If already on statin and becomes frail/limited life expectancy → consider discontinuing (no proven harm from stopping). A wrong: Not automatic in all elderly - individualize. B wrong: Healthy elderly with good life expectancy may benefit. D wrong: Moderate-intensity preferred in elderly if used.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman at 22 weeks gestation with chronic hypertension (HTN since age 28). BP 152/96 mmHg. No proteinuria, no symptoms. Currently on lisinopril 20mg daily (started before pregnancy). What is MOST appropriate antihypertensive management?
options: A. Continue lisinopril - safe in pregnancy
B. Discontinue lisinopril immediately switch to methyldopa, labetalol, or nifedipine
C. Add hydrochlorothiazide to lisinopril
D. No treatment needed - BP not high enough
questions.explanation: - Hypertension in pregnancy: Classification: Chronic HTN: Pre-existing HTN before pregnancy or diagnosed <20 weeks gestation. Gestational HTN: New HTN ≥20 weeks without proteinuria. Preeclampsia: HTN + proteinuria ±end-organ dysfunction ≥20 weeks. Chronic HTN with superimposed preeclampsia. Medication safety: SAFE in pregnancy: Methyldopa (first-line, most data), Labetalol (beta-blocker), Nifedipine immediate/extendedrelease (CCB). Hydralazine (for severe acute HTN). CONTRAINDICATED (teratogenic): ACE inhibitors, ARBs: Fetotoxic - renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, growth restriction, neonatal renal failure, death. Risk throughout pregnancy but especially 2nd/3rd trimester. DISCONTINUE if pregnancy detected. Atenolol: Fetal growth restriction. Avoid if possible. Spironolactone: Antiandrogenic effects - avoid. Chlorothiazide relatively safe but can decrease placental perfusion. Management chronic HTN in pregnancy: BP target: <140/90 mmHg (avoid overtreatment <110-120/70-80 which may reduce placental perfusion). Medication choice: Methyldopa 250-500mg BID-TID (up to 3g/day), Labetalol 100-400mg BID-TID, Nifedipine XL 30-90mg daily. Monitoring: BP, urine protein (watch for superimposed preeclampsia), Fetal growth ultrasounds, Antepartum testing if poor control. Delivery: At term (37-39 weeks) for wellcontrolled chronic HTN. Earlier if superimposed preeclampsia or fetal concerns. This patient: 22 weeks, chronic HTN, currently on lisinopril (ACE-I) → MUST stop immediately. Switch to methyldopa 250mg BID or labetalol 100mg BID or nifedipine XL 30mg daily. Target BP <140/90. Close monitoring. A wrong: ACE-I/ARBs teratogenic - must stop. C wrong: Should not continue lisinopril. D wrong: BP 152/96 requires treatment.

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with HTN, BP averaging 158/86 mmHg. Independent, cognitively intact, no orthostatic symptoms. No prior stroke, CAD, or HF. On amlodipine 5mg daily. What is MOST appropriate BP goal and management?
options: A. BP goal <120/80 - same as younger adults
B. No treatment needed - elderly can tolerate higher BP
C. BP goal <160/90 acceptable in all elderly
D. BP goal <130/80
questions.explanation: - HTN in elderly (≥65y): BP goal: 2017 ACC/AHA: <130/80 for all adults including elderly (based on SPRINT). SPRINT: Included adults >75y - intensive BP control (<120 systolic) reduced CV events and mortality vs standard (<140). However, increased orthostatic hypotension, syncope, AKI, electrolyte abnormalities. Individualization essential: Robust, independent elderly: Target <130/80 reasonable. Frail, multiple comorbidities, limited life expectancy: Less aggressive target <140-150/90 may be appropriate. Monitor for: Orthostatic hypotension (check standing BP), Falls, AKI, Electrolytes, Cognition. This patient: Age 82y but independent, cognitively intact, no orthostatic symptoms, current BP 158/86. Reasonable to target <130/80. Increase amlodipine to 10mg or add ACE-I/ARB or thiazide. Monitor closely for adverse effects. HYVET trial: Age >80y, SBP 160-199 mmHg. Target <150/80 reduced stroke, HF, mortality vs placebo. Supports treating very elderly but target was higher than current guidelines. Key: Start low, go slow. One medication change at a time. Frequent monitoring. Avoid overtreatment causing orthostatic hypotension/falls. A wrong: <120/80 may be too aggressive in very elderly (SPRINT intensive arm had more adverse effects). B wrong: Treatment beneficial even in elderly. C wrong: 2017 guidelines recommend <130/80 if tolerated. D correct - individualized approach.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with T2DM (diagnosed 2y ago, HbA1c 7.1%), HTN (controlled on lisinopril), no known ASCVD. 10-year ASCVD risk 12%. Asks about starting aspirin for primary prevention. No history of bleeding. What is MOST appropriate recommendation per current guidelines?
options: A. Aspirin 81mg daily may be considered
B. Aspirin 325mg daily mandatory for all diabetics
C. Aspirin contraindicated in diabetes
D. Aspirin only if prior MI or stroke
questions.explanation: - Aspirin primary prevention - current evidence: Recent trials (ARRIVE, ASCEND, ASPREE): No clear net benefit for aspirin in primary prevention. Modest reduction ischemic events offset by increased bleeding. 2019 ACC/AHA guidelines: Class I (definite benefit): Secondary prevention (prior MI, stroke, PAD). Class IIa (reasonable): Selected adults 40-70y at higher ASCVD risk (≥10%) WITHOUT increased bleeding risk. Shared decisionmaking. Class IIb (may be considered): Adults 40-70y at intermediate ASCVD risk (≥10%) with LOW bleeding risk after discussion. Class III (no benefit or harm): Age >70y (ASPREE trial - increased bleeding, no CV benefit, increased mortality). Routine use not recommended. Bleeding risk assessment: High risk: Prior GI bleed, PUD, chronic NSAID use, Concurrent anticoagulation, Thrombocytopenia, Age >70y, Uncontrolled HTN. ASCEND trial (diabetesspecific): Aspirin in T2DM without ASCVD. 12% reduction serious vascular events BUT 29% increase major bleeding. No mortality benefit. Net harm-benefit unclear. Current approach diabetes: NOT routine for all diabetics. Consider if: ASCVD risk ≥10%, Age <70y, LOW bleeding risk, Patient preference after informed discussion. This patient: T2DM, ASCVD risk 12%, age 58y, no bleeding history. Aspirin 81mg daily Class IIb (may consider). Discuss: Modest CV benefit (NNT ~250 over 10y), Bleeding risk (NNH ~200 major bleed over 10y), Patient preference. Reasonable to defer or start aspirin with close monitoring. Secondary prevention (prior MI/stroke): Aspirin definite benefit - Class I. A correct - individualized decision. B wrong: Not mandatory, dose 325mg excessive. C wrong: Not contraindicated. D wrong: Can consider in primary prevention with shared decision-making.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man post-PCI with DES 2 months ago on DAPT (aspirin 81mg + clopidogrel 75mg daily). Develops dyspepsia. Endoscopy shows gastritis, no ulcer. GI recommends PPI. What is MOST appropriate PPI selection given clopidogrel interaction?
options: A. Omeprazole 20mg daily - first choice PPI
B. All PPIs equally interact with clopidogrel - avoid all
C. Pantoprazole 40mg daily preferred
D. Stop clopidogrel completely
questions.explanation: - PPI-Clopidogrel interaction: Mechanism: Clopidogrel is prodrug requiring CYP2C19 activation. PPIs (especially omeprazole, esomeprazole) inhibit CYP2C19 → reduced clopidogrel activation → potentially reduced antiplatelet effect. Pharmacodynamic studies: PPIs reduce clopidogrel-induced platelet inhibition in some studies. Clinical significance debated: Observational studies: Suggested increased CV events with PPI + clopidogrel. Confounded by indication bias (patients needing PPI sicker). RCTs: COGENT trial: Omeprazole + clopidogrel vs placebo + clopidogrel in ACS patients. No increase CV events with omeprazole. Reduced GI bleeding with omeprazole. FDA 2010 warning: Avoid omeprazole/esomeprazole with clopidogrel. Current consensus: PPI use reasonable if indicated (GI bleeding risk, active ulcer, dyspepsia). Benefits of GI protection often outweigh theoretical interaction risk. PPI selection: Least interaction: Pantoprazole, Dexlansoprazole (minimal CYP2C19 inhibition). Most interaction: Omeprazole, Esomeprazole (strongest CYP2C19 inhibition). Intermediate: Lansoprazole, Rabeprazole. Strategy: Use pantoprazole if concerned about interaction. Separate timing: Take PPI morning, clopidogrel evening (12h apart - may reduce interaction). If high thrombosis risk: Consider prasugrel or ticagrelor instead of clopidogrel (not prodrugs dependent on CYP2C19). GI prophylaxis indications with DAPT: Prior GI bleed/PUD, Concurrent anticoagulant, Age >65y, Corticosteroid/NSAID use. This patient: Post-PCI 2mo ago on DAPT, dyspepsia with gastritis. GI protection reasonable. Use pantoprazole 40mg daily (minimal interaction) OR separate dosing. Monitor for GI and CV symptoms. A wrong: Omeprazole has most interaction. B wrong: Not all PPIs equally interact - pantoprazole preferred. D wrong: Shouldn't stop clopidogrel within 12mo DES.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 4) on apixaban 5mg BID undergoes PCI with DES for NSTEMI. Now needs DAPT + OAC ("triple therapy"). HAS-BLED score 2 (moderate bleeding risk). What is MOST appropriate antithrombotic regimen and duration?
options: A. Triple therapy (OAC + aspirin + clopidogrel) indefinitely
B. Triple therapy x1-4 weeks post-PCI
C. Stop anticoagulation, use DAPT only
D. OAC monotherapy only, no antiplatelet
questions.explanation: - AF + PCI antithrombotic management: Challenge: Balance stroke prevention (OAC) vs stent thrombosis prevention (DAPT) vs bleeding risk. Triple therapy (OAC + aspirin + clopidogrel): Highest efficacy but HIGHEST bleeding risk (3-4x increased major bleeding vs dual). Minimize duration. Trials: WOEST, PIONEER AF-PCI, RE-DUAL PCI, AUGUSTUS, ENTRUST-AF PCI. Dual therapy (OAC + P2Y12 inhibitor) superior to triple therapy - reduced bleeding without increased thrombotic events. Current strategy (2021 ESC, 2021 ACC): Triple therapy: 1-4 weeks post-PCI (minimum necessary). ACS: 1 week if low bleeding risk, immediately switch to dual if high bleeding risk. Stable CAD: Immediately switch to dual (no triple). Then dual therapy (OAC + clopidogrel): Continue up to 12 months post-PCI. ACS or complex PCI: 12 months. Stable CAD or low thrombotic risk: 6 months. Then OAC monotherapy: Indefinitely for AF. Discontinue antiplatelet after 12 months. OAC selection: Prefer DOAC over warfarin (less ICH risk). Dabigatran 110mg BID or 150mg BID, Rivaroxaban 15mg daily, Apixaban 5mg BID (or 2.5mg BID if dose-reduction criteria), Edoxaban 60mg daily. Avoid prasugrel or ticagrelor in triple therapy (increased bleeding vs clopidogrel). Use clopidogrel 75mg as P2Y12 inhibitor. GI protection: PPI mandatory with triple or dual therapy. This patient: AF + ACS (NSTEMI) + PCI → Triple therapy (apixaban + aspirin + clopidogrel) x1 week → Dual therapy (apixaban + clopidogrel) x12 months → Apixaban monotherapy indefinitely. Add PPI. A wrong: Triple therapy increases bleeding - minimize duration. C wrong: Still needs stroke prevention (OAC). D wrong: Needs stent thrombosis protection initially.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with acute Type A aortic dissection diagnosed 1h ago. BP 188/102, HR 95. Awaiting cardiothoracic surgery (OR being prepared). What is MOST appropriate immediate BP and HR management while awaiting surgery?
options: A. No BP lowering - maintain perfusion
B. Nitroprusside alone for BP reduction
C. Esmolol alone
D. IV beta-blocker
