questions.explanation: - Acute aortic dissection medical management: Goals: Reduce aortic wall stress to prevent propagation/rupture. Reduce HR (reduce dP/dt - rate of change of pressure), Reduce BP (reduce peak systolic pressure). Target: HR <60 bpm, SBP 100-120 mmHg (or lowest tolerated maintaining organ perfusion). Type A dissection: SURGICAL emergency. Medical therapy temporizes pre-op. Type B dissection: Medical management unless complicated. Medication sequence (CRITICAL): ALWAYS beta-blocker FIRST: IV esmolol: 500mcg/kg load over 1min, then 50-200mcg/kg/min infusion. OR IV labetalol: 20mg over 2min, then 40-80mg Q10min or infusion 0.5-2mg/min (combined alpha/beta blocker). OR IV metoprolol: 5mg Q5min up to 15mg total. WHY beta-blocker first: Prevents reflex tachycardia from vasodilators. Reflex tachycardia increases dP/dt → worsens dissection propagation. NEVER give vasodilator alone. THEN add vasodilator (once adequate beta-blockade): IV nicardipine: 5-15mg/h. OR IV nitroprusside: 0.3-10mcg/kg/min. Analgesics: IV morphine or fentanyl for pain control (pain indicates ongoing dissection). Beta-blocker contraindications: If cannot use beta-blocker (severe asthma, decompensated HF, high-grade AV block): Non-DHP CCB: Diltiazem or verapamil IV (reduce HR + BP). Avoid hydralazine, dihydropyridine CCBs alone (cause reflex tachycardia). This patient: Type A dissection, awaiting surgery, BP 188/102, HR 95. Start IV esmolol or labetalol immediately to reduce HR <60. Then add nicardipine or nitroprusside for SBP 100-120. Monitor closely. A wrong: Must reduce BP/HR to prevent progression. B wrong: Vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia - worsens dissection. C wrong: May need vasodilator too for BP control. D correct - beta-blocker first, then vasodilator.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man presents with severe headache, confusion, visual disturbances x3h. PMH: HTN (poorly controlled, nonadherent to medications). BP 226/128 mmHg, altered mental status. Exam: Papilledema, focal neurologic deficits. CT head: No hemorrhage, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) changes. What is diagnosis and MOST appropriate BP management?
options: A. IV labetalol or nicardipine
B. Lower BP to normal (<130/80) within 1 hour
C. Oral medications sufficient
D. Observe without treatment
questions.explanation: - Hypertensive encephalopathy: Severe BP elevation with acute CNS dysfunction due to failed cerebral autoregulation. Pathophysiology: Cerebral autoregulation maintains constant blood flow across MAP 60-150 mmHg. When BP exceeds autoregulatory capacity → hyperperfusion → cerebral edema → encephalopathy. Clinical: Severe HTN (usually SBP >180 or DBP >120), Headache, confusion, visual disturbances, seizures, Papilledema, focal deficits (may mimic stroke). Imaging: PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome) - vasogenic edema, especially posterior circulation. Diagnosis: Clinical + imaging excluding other causes (stroke, SAH, ICH, mass). Management: Hypertensive EMERGENCY - requires ICU + IV medications. BP reduction: Reduce MAP by 10-20% in FIRST HOUR (not more - risk ischemia), Then reduce additional 5-15% over NEXT 23 HOURS, Target ~160/100 mmHg in first 24h, then gradual reduction to goal over days. IV medications: Labetalol 20mg IV bolus Q10min OR infusion 0.5-2mg/min, Nicardipine 5-15mg/h infusion, Esmolol infusion, Avoid: Nitroprusside (increases ICP - cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity), Hydralazine (unpredictable), Sublingual nifedipine (uncontrolled rapid drop). Avoid excessive rapid reduction: Risk ischemic stroke, MI, AKI (chronic HTN shifts autoregulation curve rightward - need higher perfusion pressure). Monitor: Continuous BP monitoring (arterial line), Neurologic exams, Transition to oral agents once stable. This patient: Classic hypertensive encephalopathy - severe HTN, confusion, visual changes, papilledema, PRES on imaging. Start IV labetalol or nicardipine, reduce MAP 10-20% over 1h. A correct. B wrong: Too rapid reduction risks ischemia. C wrong: Needs IV therapy. D wrong: Requires immediate treatment.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents with chest pain 30min after cocaine use. Pain substernal, pressure-like. BP 168/98, HR 112. ECG: ST-elevation in V2-V4. Troponin pending. What is MOST appropriate initial management?
options: A. IV beta-blocker (metoprolol) for tachycardia and HTN
B. Immediate fibrinolysis for STEMI
C. Aspirin, benzodiazepines, nitrates, consider CCB

D. Observation only - cocaine chest pain always benign
.
questions.explanation: - Cocaine-associated chest pain: Mechanisms: Coronary vasospasm (alphamediated), Increased myocardial O2 demand (tachycardia, HTN, increased contractility), Platelet activation, thrombosis, Premature atherosclerosis (chronic use). 6% have MI (STEMI or NSTEMI). ECG changes common even without MI (early repolarization, LVH). Management: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2mg IV): Reduce sympathetic surge, anxiety. Reduce HR, BP, myocardial O2 demand. FIRST-LINE therapy. Aspirin 162-325mg: Inhibit platelet activation. Nitrates (NTG SL or IV): Vasodilate coronaries, reverse vasospasm. CCB if refractory: Verapamil or diltiazem (vasodilation, reverse spasm). Phentolamine (alpha-blocker) alternative. AVOID beta-blockers: Unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation → WORSE vasospasm, HTN. Propranolol shown to worsen coronary vasoconstriction in cocaine users. Cardiac catheterization: If persistent symptoms, ST-elevation, positive troponins despite medical therapy → emergent cath. Findings: Often normal coronaries or vasospasm. May have thrombus → PCI. Fibrinolysis: Generally AVOID (higher bleeding risk). Prefer cath if available. Disposition: Persistent symptoms, ECG changes, positive troponins → admit, cath. Symptom resolution, normal ECG, negative troponins (x2 sets 3h apart) → may discharge with cardiology follow-up. This patient: Cocaine use 30min ago, chest pain, ST-elevation → cocaine-induced MI vs vasospasm. Give aspirin, lorazepam, nitrates. AVOID beta-blockers. If ST-elevation persists despite medical therapy → urgent cath. A wrong: Beta-blockers contraindicated - worsen vasospasm. B wrong: Prefer cath over fibrinolysis. D wrong: 6% have MI - not benign.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia started on clozapine 3 weeks ago. Presents with fever, chest pain, dyspnea x2 days. Tachycardia HR 118. Exam: S3 gallop, mild pulmonary edema. Labs: Troponin I 3.2 ng/mL (markedly elevated), BNP 1240 pg/mL, eosinophilia 12% (elevated). ECG: Sinus tach, diffuse ST-T changes. Echo: LVEF 38% (reduced), global hypokinesis. What is MOST likely diagnosis and management?
options: A. Viral myocarditis - supportive care only
B. Discontinue clozapine immediately
C. Continue clozapine - unrelated to cardiac symptoms
D. ACS - urgent cardiac catheterization
questions.explanation: - Clozapine-induced myocarditis: Incidence: 0.5-3% of patients starting clozapine. Timing: Typically within first 4-8 weeks of therapy (median 3 weeks). Pathophysiology: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. Direct toxic effect. Presentation: Fever, chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia (often unexplained persistent tachycardia >100 bpm), Flu-like symptoms. Labs: Elevated troponin (often markedly elevated), Elevated BNP, Eosinophilia (50% of cases - KEY clue), Elevated CRP, ESR. ECG: Tachycardia, ST-T changes, arrhythmias. Echo: Reduced LVEF, wall motion abnormalities. Diagnosis: Clinical suspicion (recent clozapine start + cardiac symptoms + eosinophilia), Elevated biomarkers, Imaging findings, Exclude other causes (ACS, viral myocarditis). Endomyocardial biopsy (rarely needed): Eosinophilic infiltration. Management: DISCONTINUE clozapine IMMEDIATELY (most important). Do NOT rechallenge - high mortality if continued. Supportive HF therapy: ACE-I/ARB, betablockers, diuretics. Corticosteroids may help if severe (controversial). Inotropes if cardiogenic shock. Monitoring: Serial troponins, BNP, ECGs, echos until resolution. Prognosis: If recognized early and clozapine stopped: Most recover (LVEF improves over weeks-months). If clozapine continued: Mortality 10-20%, risk fulminant myocarditis. Prevention: Baseline: ECG, troponin, CRP before starting clozapine. Monitoring first month: Unexplained tachycardia, fever, flu-like symptoms → check troponin, CRP. This patient: Started clozapine 3 weeks ago, classic presentation (fever, chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, elevated troponin, eosinophilia, reduced LVEF) → clozapine-induced myocarditis. STOP clozapine immediately. Start HF therapy. Switch to alternative antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone). A wrong: Eosinophilia + recent clozapine start suggests drug-induced. C wrong: Must stop clozapine. D wrong: Young age, diffuse ECG changes, eosinophilia - not typical ACS.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with breast cancer receiving doxorubicin-based chemotherapy. Cumulative dose now 420 mg/m². Oncology wants to give 2 more cycles (additional 120 mg/m², total 540 mg/m²). Baseline echo: LVEF 62%. Recent echo: LVEF 56%. No HF symptoms. What is MOST appropriate recommendation regarding anthracycline dosing?
options: A. Continue doxorubicin - no dose limit exists
B. LVEF 56% too low - stop immediately
C. Switch to different chemotherapy regardless of dose
D. consider: dexrazoxane cardioprotection, alternative regimen, or careful risk-benefit discussion
questions.explanation: - Anthracycline cumulative dose limits: Doxorubicin (Adriamycin): Dosedependent cardiotoxicity. Cumulative dose thresholds: <400 mg/m²: Low risk (<5% HF). 400- 450 mg/m²: Moderate risk (5-10% HF). 450-550 mg/m²: High risk (10-26% HF). >550 mg/m²: Very high risk (>26% HF). Traditional "safe" limit: 450-550 mg/m² (varies by institution). Risk factors (lower threshold): Age >65 or <18 years, Prior chest radiation, Concurrent cardiotoxic therapy (trastuzumab, cyclophosphamide), Pre-existing cardiac disease, HTN, diabetes. This patient: Cumulative dose 420 mg/m², planning additional 120 mg/m² → total 540 mg/m². Exceeds traditional safe threshold. LVEF already declined 62% → 56% (6% drop, still >50% but concerning). Options: Stop doxorubicin now, switch to alternative regimen. Continue with dexrazoxane cardioprotection. Use liposomal doxorubicin (lower cardiotoxicity). Careful monitoring: Serial echos, consider cardiac MRI. Dexrazoxane (Zinecard): Iron chelator, reduces free radical formation. Indicated: Cumulative doxorubicin >300 mg/m² AND continuing therapy needed. Dose: 10:1 ratio to doxorubicin (e.g., dexrazoxane 600 mg/m² for doxorubicin 60 mg/m²). Given 30min before doxorubicin. Reduces cardiotoxicity 50-80%. May slightly reduce tumor response (controversial). FDA-approved only for metastatic breast cancer. Liposomal doxorubicin: Doxil, Myocet - pegylated liposomal formulation. Reduced cardiac exposure, lower cardiotoxicity. Cumulative dose limits higher (~900 mg/m²). Consider if high cumulative dose needed. Management this patient: Cumulative dose 420 mg/m², approaching limit. LVEF declining. Discuss with oncology: If additional doxorubicin critical → use dexrazoxane. If alternative regimen available → consider switch. If proceed without dexrazoxane → very close cardiac monitoring, informed consent about increased cardiotoxicity risk. A wrong: Dose limits exist. D correct. B wrong: LVEF >50% still acceptable. C wrong: May continue with cardioprotection.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman at 36 weeks gestation with severe AS (valve area 0.7 cm², mean gradient 56 mmHg, congenital bicuspid valve). Pregnancy complicated by worsening dyspnea NYHA class III. Echo: LVEF 58%, no other abnormalities. Fetus doing well. What is MOST appropriate delivery plan?
options: A. Planned delivery at 37-38 weeks in tertiary center with cardiology/anesthesia/high-risk OB; vaginal delivery preferred if hemodynamically stable; epidural anesthesia carefully dosed; assisted second stage; continuous monitoring; avoid spinal anesthesia (sudden afterload drop)
B. Continue pregnancy to 40 weeks - no early delivery needed
C. Immediate C-section at 36 weeks regardless of stability
D. Urgent valve replacement during pregnancy
questions.explanation: - Severe AS in pregnancy: Pregnancy hemodynamics: Increase CO 30-50%, blood volume 40-50%, HR 10-20 bpm. Decreased SVR. AS physiology: Fixed CO - cannot increase to meet pregnancy demands. Preload-dependent. Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling → decreased CO. Symptoms: May worsen as pregnancy progresses. Pulmonary edema, syncope, arrhythmias. Maternal risk: Low if asymptomatic, NYHA I-II (2-5% complications). High if symptomatic, NYHA III-IV (10-25% complications). Management pregnancy: Medical: Betablockers to control HR (avoid tachycardia). Diuretics cautiously for pulmonary edema (maintain preload). Bed rest, activity restriction. Avoid: Vasodilators (ACE-I, ARB, nitrates) - reduce afterload → hypotension, decreased placental perfusion. Delivery planning: Timing: Severe AS with good control → 37-39 weeks (term). Symptomatic, worsening → 36-38 weeks (late preterm). Location: Tertiary center with cardiology, cardiac anesthesia, high-risk OB, NICU. Mode: Vaginal delivery PREFERRED if hemodynamically stable (less hemodynamic stress than C-section). C-section: Obstetric indications OR severe hemodynamic instability. Anesthesia: Epidural (slow titration, avoid sudden BP drop). Avoid spinal (sudden sympathectomy → profound hypotension). General anesthesia if emergent C-section. Labor management: Continuous hemodynamic monitoring (arterial line, pulse ox, telemetry). Assisted second stage (forceps/vacuum) - minimize Valsalva, shorten labor. Avoid: Tachycardia (beta-blockers), hypotension (fluids, phenylephrine), excessive fluid (pulmonary edema). Postpartum: High-risk period - autotransfusion from uterine contraction. Monitor 24-48h. Valve intervention: Defer until after delivery if possible. Balloon valvuloplasty during pregnancy if maternal decompensation. Surgical AVR: Very high maternal/fetal risk - only if life-threatening and valvuloplasty not option. This patient: 36 weeks, severe AS, symptomatic NYHA III but stable, fetus well. Plan delivery 37-38 weeks in tertiary center. Vaginal with epidural preferred. Close monitoring. A correct. B wrong: Symptomatic - deliver earlier. C wrong: Stable - can wait to 37-38 weeks. Vaginal preferred. D wrong: Defer surgery if possible.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation with mechanical mitral valve on warfarin throughout pregnancy (INR goal 2.5-3.5). Planned induction of labor in 3 days. What is MOST appropriate perioperative anticoagulation management?
options: A. Continue warfarin through delivery
B. Stop all anticoagulation
C. Stop warfarin, bridge with therapeutic UFH infusion; stop UFH 4-6h before delivery; resume UFH 12-24h postpartum if no bleeding; resume warfarin postpartum
D. Switch to LMWH 24h before delivery
questions.explanation: - Mechanical valve anticoagulation in pregnancy: Pregnancy management: Warfarin controversial in pregnancy (teratogenic) but often used 2nd/3rd trimester for mechanical valves due to superior efficacy vs LMWH. Some use LMWH throughout (higher thrombosis risk). This patient on warfarin - need peripartum plan. Delivery planning mechanical valve: Goal: Minimize maternal thrombosis risk AND fetal/maternal bleeding risk. Strategy: Stop warfarin 36- 48h before planned delivery (allows INR to normalize). Bridge with IV UFH: Start UFH when INR <2.0. Therapeutic dosing (aPTT goal 60-80 sec or anti-Xa 0.3-0.7). Stop UFH 4-6h before delivery/induction (allows normalization for neuraxial anesthesia). Labor/delivery: No anticoagulation during active labor/delivery. Check aPTT before neuraxial anesthesia (must be normal). Postpartum: Resume UFH 12-24h after vaginal delivery (if hemostasis adequate), 24- 48h after C-section. Resume warfarin evening of delivery (overlaps with UFH). Discontinue UFH when INR therapeutic x2 days. Warfarin safe during breastfeeding. LMWH alternative: Stop LMWH 24h before planned delivery. Neuraxial anesthesia safe if >24h since last dose. Resume 12-24h postpartum. Spontaneous labor: If on LMWH and labor starts <24h after dose → cannot do neuraxial (risk epidural hematoma). If on UFH infusion → stop, wait 4-6h, check aPTT. Risks: Warfarin at delivery: Fetal/maternal bleeding. Inadequate anticoagulation peripartum: Valve thrombosis (2-4% risk even with bridging). This patient: Mechanical mitral valve (high thrombotic risk), 38 weeks, planned induction in 3 days. Stop warfarin now (36-48h before), start UFH when INR <2.0, stop UFH 4-6h before induction, resume UFH 12-24h postpartum, restart warfarin postpartum. C correct. A wrong: Warfarin at delivery - bleeding risk. B wrong: Mechanical valve requires anticoagulation. D wrong: LMWH acceptable but UFH preferred (shorter half-life, easier to reverse, monitor).

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation with chronic HTN. BP 158/96 mmHg. Currently on no medications. PMH: HTN x3y, was on atenolol but stopped when planning pregnancy. What is MOST appropriate antihypertensive for chronic HTN in pregnancy?
options: A. Atenolol 50mg daily - resume prior medication
B. Labetalol 100-400mg BID or methyldopa 250-500mg BID-TID or nifedipine XL 30-90mg daily
C. Lisinopril 10mg daily
D. Spironolactone 25mg daily
questions.explanation: - Antihypertensives in pregnancy: Safe options: Methyldopa: First-line, most safety data. Dose: 250-500mg BID-TID (max 3g/day). Side effects: Sedation, dry mouth, elevated LFTs. Labetalol: Alpha/beta-blocker. Dose: 100-400mg BID-TID (max 2400mg/day). Well-tolerated, effective. Nifedipine: CCB (immediate or extended-release). Dose: XL 30-90mg daily or IR 10-20mg TID. Avoid combining with magnesium sulfate (profound hypotension). Hydralazine: For acute severe HTN. Dose: 5-10mg IV Q20min or 10-25mg PO QID. Avoid chronic use (tachycardia, lupus-like syndrome). Avoid/use caution: Atenolol: Associated with fetal growth restriction. AVOID in pregnancy. Other beta-blockers (metoprolol, propranolol) probably safer but less data than labetalol. ACE inhibitors, ARBs: CONTRAINDICATED (teratogenic - renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, death). Diuretics: Not first-line (reduce plasma volume → may compromise placental perfusion). Can continue if already on and well-controlled. Spironolactone: Antiandrogen effects - avoid. BP goals pregnancy: <140/90 mmHg (avoid overtreatment <120/80 → decreased placental perfusion). Severe HTN: ≥160/110 mmHg requires immediate treatment (risk stroke, eclampsia). This patient: 14 weeks, chronic HTN, BP 158/96, was on atenolol. Options: Labetalol 100mg BID, Methyldopa 250mg BID, Nifedipine XL 30mg daily. Target BP <140/90. Avoid atenolol (growth restriction risk). Monitor BP, fetal growth, watch for superimposed preeclampsia. A wrong: Atenolol associated with fetal growth restriction. B correct - safer alternatives. C wrong: ACE-I teratogenic. D wrong: Spironolactone has antiandrogen effects.

questions.question: An 84-year-old man with AF, HFrEF (LVEF 32%), HTN, CAD s/p CABG, T2DM, CKD stage 3b, chronic pain. Currently on 18 medications. Recent falls x2, orthostatic hypotension, confusion. Which approach is MOST appropriate for medication optimization?
options: A. Continue all medications - all are indicated
B. Stop all medications immediately
C. Add more medications for fall prevention
D. Deprescribing approach, use Beers Criteria, STOPP/START criteria
questions.explanation: - Polypharmacy in elderly: Definition: ≥5 medications (some use ≥10). Prevalence: 40% adults >65y on ≥5 medications. Risks: Drug-drug interactions, Adverse effects (falls, confusion, orthostatic hypotension), Medication errors (complex regimens), Decreased adherence, Increased hospitalizations. Deprescribing: Systematic process of reducing/stopping medications where risks outweigh benefits. Approach: Review ALL medications: Indication - is it still appropriate? Effectiveness - is it working? Safety - adverse effects, interactions? Patient preference - goals of care. Prioritize essential medications: GDMT for chronic conditions (HF, CAD, AF). Proven mortality benefit medications. Identify potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs): Beers Criteria (American Geriatrics Society): Medications to avoid in elderly (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, NSAIDs, etc.). STOPP/START criteria (European): STOPP - medications to stop. START - medications to start if indicated. Common PIMs to consider stopping/reducing: Anticholinergics: Diphenhydramine, promethazine, amitriptyline → confusion, falls, urinary retention. Benzodiazepines: Falls, confusion, dependence → taper slowly if stopping. Sedative-hypnotics: Zolpidem, eszopiclone → falls. Multiple antihypertensives: If orthostatic hypotension, falls → reduce to minimum needed. Tight glucose control: Relax HbA1c goal to 7.5-8.5% in elderly (avoid hypoglycemia). Sulfonylureas → consider switching to safer agents. PPIs: Long-term use → fractures, C. diff, interactions → stop if no clear indication. This patient: 84y, polypharmacy (18 meds), falls, orthostatic hypotension, confusion. Systematic review needed: Essential: Anticoagulation (AF), GDMT for HFrEF (sacubitril/valsartan or ACEI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i - but may need to reduce doses if orthostatic), aspirin (postCABG). Consider reducing/stopping: Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines/sedatives if any, Tight BP control → relax to <140/90 if orthostatic, Sulfonylureas → switch to metformin or DPP-4i. Monitor: Reassess after changes, Involve patient/family in goals of care. A wrong: Polypharmacy causing problems - review needed. D correct - systematic deprescribing. B wrong: Stop gradually, selectively. C wrong: Adding more medications worsens polypharmacy.

questions.question: An 80-year-old woman with recurrent falls. Supine BP 148/82, standing BP (3min) 104/64 (drop 44/18 mmHg). Medications: Amlodipine 10mg, lisinopril 20mg, HCTZ 25mg, tamsulosin 0.4mg HS. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Discontinue tamsulosin; reduce/stop HCTZ; reduce amlodipine or lisinopril; nonpharmacologic measures ; consider midodrine if refractory
B. Continue all medications - BP control important
C. Add fludrocortisone immediately
D. Increase all antihypertensives - supine BP too high
questions.explanation: - Orthostatic hypotension elderly: Definition: BP drop ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic within 3min standing. This patient: 148/82 → 104/64 (drop 44/18) - SIGNIFICANT orthostatic hypotension. Consequences: Falls, syncope, fractures, reduced quality of life, increased mortality. Causes elderly: Medications (most common): Diuretics, Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin), Antihypertensives (multiple agents), Nitrates, Tricyclic antidepressants, Antiparkinsonian agents (levodopa). Autonomic dysfunction: Age-related, diabetes, Parkinson's. Volume depletion: Dehydration, bleeding. Deconditioning: Bed rest, frailty. This patient: Multiple antihypertensives (amlodipine, lisinopril, HCTZ) + tamsulosin (alpha-blocker for BPH). Medication-induced orthostatic hypotension. Management: Medication review (PRIORITY): Discontinue tamsulosin: Alpha-blockers major cause orthostatic hypotension. Alternative BPH therapy: Finasteride 5mg (5-alpha reductase inhibitor, no orthostatic effect), Tadalafil 5mg (PDE5 inhibitor, less orthostatic than alpha-blockers). Reduce/stop diuretic: HCTZ 25mg may be excessive → stop or reduce to 12.5mg. Reassess need for 3 antihypertensives: Supine BP 148/82 not excessively high. Standing BP 104/64 - adequate perfusion but concerning with symptoms. Reduce to 1-2 agents (ACE-I or CCB, not both at high doses). Non-pharmacologic: Slow position changes (sit edge of bed 1-2min before standing). Increase fluid intake (2-2.5L/day if no HF). Increase salt (6-10g/day if tolerated). Compression stockings (waist-high 30-40mmHg). Elevate head of bed 10-20 degrees. Small frequent meals. Avoid prolonged standing, hot environments. Pharmacologic (if refractory): Midodrine 2.5-10mg TID (alpha-agonist, vasoconstriction). Fludrocortisone 0.1-0.2mg daily (volume expansion - caution in HTN/HF). This patient: Stop tamsulosin, stop/reduce HCTZ, reduce amlodipine or lisinopril (consider monotherapy ACE-I 10mg or amlodipine 5mg). Non-pharmacologic measures. Reassess BP supine/standing after changes. A correct. B wrong: Medications causing orthostatic hypotension - must adjust. D wrong: Standing BP already low.

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with newly diagnosed persistent AF (duration 4 months), NYHA class II HFpEF (LVEF 58%), CHA2DS2-VASc 5. Minimally symptomatic from AF. HR 88-102 bpm on metoprolol 50mg BID. What is MOST appropriate AF management strategy?
options: A. Cardioversion and rhythm control mandatory
B. No treatment needed
C. Rate control and anticoagulation
D. Amiodarone for rhythm control in all elderly
questions.explanation: - AF management elderly: Rate control vs rhythm control: AFFIRM trial: Rate control non-inferior to rhythm control for mortality. Elderly patients (mean age 70y) - no mortality difference. RACE trial: Lenient rate control (HR <110 bpm) non-inferior to strict control (<80 bpm). Rate control advantages: Simpler (fewer medications), Less toxic (avoid antiarrhythmics), Better for: Elderly, Asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic AF, Permanent/longstanding persistent AF, Multiple comorbidities. Rhythm control considerations: May be reasonable if: Younger patients (<65y), Highly symptomatic, Recent-onset AF, HFrEF (some evidence rhythm control may help). Antiarrhythmic options elderly: Amiodarone: Most effective but toxicity (pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic). Use cautiously in elderly. Dofetilide: Requires inpatient initiation, QTc monitoring. Sotalol: Beta-blocker + antiarrhythmic. Monitor QTc, renal function. Avoid: Flecainide, propafenone if structural heart disease. Dronedarone if HF. Rate control options: Beta-blockers: Metoprolol, carvedilol (first-line). Non-DHP CCBs: Diltiazem, verapamil (if beta-blockers contraindicated). Digoxin: Add-on if inadequate control (not monotherapy). Target HR: Lenient: <110 bpm at rest (RACE II - adequate for most). Strict: <80 bpm at rest (if symptomatic despite lenient control). Anticoagulation: Essential regardless of rate vs rhythm strategy. CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women) → anticoagulate. DOACs preferred over warfarin (less ICH). This patient: 82y, persistent AF x4mo, minimally symptomatic, HFpEF, CHA2DS2-VASc 5, HR 88-102 on metoprolol. Rate control appropriate: Current HR acceptable (<110 bpm lenient target). Continue metoprolol 50mg BID. Anticoagulation: CHA2DS2-VASc 5 → DOAC (apixaban 5mg BID or 2.5mg BID if dose reduction criteria). Cardioversion NOT necessary - elderly, minimally symptomatic, persistent AF x4mo (likely recurs). If becomes highly symptomatic → consider rhythm control. A wrong: Rhythm control not mandatory in elderly minimally symptomatic. C correct - rate control + anticoagulation appropriate. B wrong: Needs anticoagulation. D wrong: Amiodarone not routine in elderly.

questions.question: A 78-year-old man with severe AS (valve area 0.6 cm²), NYHA III symptoms. Cardiology recommends TAVR. Frailty assessment: Unintentional weight loss 12 lbs past year, weakness (grip strength low), slow gait speed, exhaustion, low physical activity. Lives alone, independent in ADLs but needs help with IADLs. What is significance of frailty in TAVR decision?
options: A. Frailty is contraindication to TAVR
B. Frailty assessment critical
C. Age alone determines TAVR candidacy
D. Frailty irrelevant - only surgical risk scores matter
questions.explanation: - Frailty in cardiovascular disease: Definition: Syndrome of decreased physiologic reserve, increased vulnerability to stressors. Distinct from comorbidity and disability. Prevalence: 10-15% adults >65y, 25-50% adults >85y. Components: Fried Frailty Phenotype (5 criteria, ≥3 = frail): Unintentional weight loss (≥10 lbs past year), Weakness (low grip strength), Slow gait speed (<0.8 m/s), Exhaustion (self-reported), Low physical activity. Robust: 0 criteria. Pre-frail: 1-2 criteria. Frail: ≥3 criteria. Other assessments: Gait speed alone (strong predictor), Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), Katz ADL (activities of daily living), Lawton IADL (instrumental ADLs), Timed Up and Go test. Impact on CV procedures: Frail patients: Higher mortality, complications, prolonged hospital stay, nursing home discharge, Poor quality of life improvement. TAVR/surgical AVR: Moderate frailty: TAVR reasonable, may benefit. Severe frailty: Higher mortality, less functional improvement, may favor medical management. STS/ACC guidelines: Incorporate frailty assessment in TAVR/SAVR decision. PCI: Frailty predicts worse outcomes. ACS management: Frail elderly may have less benefit from aggressive interventions. This patient: 78y, severe symptomatic AS, frailty features (weight loss, weakness, slow gait, exhaustion, low activity) - likely FRAIL (≥3 criteria). Independent in ADLs (can perform self-care), needs help IADLs (shopping, medications) - moderate functional impairment. TAVR candidacy: Not absolute contraindication. Assess degree of frailty: Gait speed, grip strength, SPPB, ADLs. If moderate frailty → TAVR reasonable (may improve symptoms, quality of life). If severe frailty → medical management may be preferable (high mortality, less benefit). Shared decision-making: Discuss realistic expectations, Goals of care, Post-procedure needs (likely need rehab, home support). A wrong: Frailty not absolute contraindication - individualize. B correct. C wrong: Age alone insufficient. D wrong: Frailty independently predicts outcomes beyond surgical risk scores.

questions.question: An 86-year-old woman with multiple falls (4 in past 6 months). PMH: HTN, AF, osteoporosis. Medications: Metoprolol 100mg BID, lisinopril 20mg, amlodipine 10mg, apixaban 5mg BID, meclizine 25mg TID. Supine BP 118/68, standing BP 92/54. Which medication changes would MOST reduce fall risk?
options: A. Increase metoprolol for better rate control
B. Add another antihypertensive
C. Stop apixaban - bleeding risk with falls
D. reduce/stop excessive antihypertensives
questions.explanation: - Falls in elderly: Epidemiology: 30% adults >65y fall annually, 50% >80y. Leading cause injury, death, disability in elderly. Medication-related falls: High-risk medications: Antihypertensives (orthostatic hypotension): 3+ agents especially risky. Benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics (impaired balance, sedation). Anticholinergics (confusion, dizziness): Diphenhydramine, meclizine, promethazine, TCAs, bladder antispasmodics. Opioids (sedation, dizziness). Antipsychotics (sedation, orthostatic hypotension, parkinsonism). This patient: 4 falls in 6mo, orthostatic hypotension (BP drop 26/14mmHg), on 3 antihypertensives + meclizine (anticholinergic). Medication optimization: Reduce antihypertensives: 3 agents (metoprolol, lisinopril, amlodipine) excessive. Causing orthostatic hypotension. Reduce to 1-2 agents: Keep metoprolol 50mg BID (for AF rate control + HTN), Stop or reduce amlodipine, lisinopril. Target BP <140/90 acceptable in elderly with fall risk. Stop meclizine: Anticholinergic, vestibular suppressant. Paradoxically WORSENS dizziness, fall risk in elderly. Beers Criteria: Avoid in elderly. Alternative vertigo management: Vestibular rehabilitation therapy (if true vertigo). Anticoagulation controversy: Falls are NOT absolute contraindication to anticoagulation. Riskbenefit: Patient must fall 295 times/year for fall-related ICH risk to outweigh stroke prevention benefit (theoretical calculation). AF with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 → anticoagulation benefits outweigh fall risk in most cases. Exception: Very frequent falls with severe head trauma, or patient/family preference. This patient: AF, likely CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 → continue apixaban. Fall prevention strategies: Medication review (done above), Home safety evaluation (remove tripping hazards, install grab bars), Vision check, Footwear (non-slip, supportive), Vitamin D supplementation (if deficient), Exercise (strength, balance training), Treat other fall risk factors (poor vision, neuropathy, arthritis). A wrong: Metoprolol already high dose, may contribute to orthostatic hypotension. B wrong: Already on 3 agents - too many. C wrong: AF anticoagulation benefits outweigh fall risk. D correct - reduce antihypertensives, stop meclizine.

questions.question: A 92-year-old man with advanced dementia, severe HFrEF (LVEF 18%), frequent HF hospitalizations. Family asks about ICD for primary prevention. Patient bed-bound, minimal verbal communication, requires assistance with all ADLs. Life expectancy estimated <1 year. What is MOST appropriate approach?
options: A. ICD NOT indicated
B. Implant ICD - all HFrEF patients need ICD
C. Defer decision to family without discussion
D. Aggressive resuscitation measures
questions.explanation: - Goals of care elderly patients: ICD indications: Life expectancy >1 year with good functional status (Class I recommendation). NOT indicated: Life expectancy <1 year from any cause, Advanced dementia, severe disability, End-stage chronic disease (cancer, HF, COPD, liver disease). This patient: Advanced dementia, bed-bound, NYHA IV HF, frequent hospitalizations, life expectancy <1 year → ICD NOT indicated. ICD would not improve quality of life or longevity. May cause distress (inappropriate shocks). Goals of care discussion: Essential in elderly with advanced illness. Assess: Patient's values, preferences (if able to communicate) OR prior expressed wishes. Quality of life vs quantity of life priorities. Family understanding of prognosis. Functional status, cognitive status. Options: Aggressive life-prolonging interventions (ICU, mechanical ventilation, resuscitation), Selective interventions (hospitalization for acute illness, antibiotics, but no ICU), Comfort-focused care (symptom management, no hospitalizations, hospice). Advance directives: Living will, Healthcare proxy/durable power of attorney, POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment). Document code status (DNR/DNI). Palliative care: NOT just end-of-life care. Appropriate anytime in serious illness. Focus: Symptom management (dyspnea, pain, anxiety), Communication, care coordination, Support for patient and family. Can be concurrent with disease-directed therapy. Hospice: For patients with life expectancy ≤6 months. Comfort-focused care, no disease-directed therapy. Provides: Medical care (medications, equipment), Nursing, social work, chaplain, Respite care for family. HF symptom management comfort-focused: Diuretics (for dyspnea, edema), Opioids (low-dose morphine for dyspnea), Anxiolytics if anxiety, Oxygen if hypoxemic. Avoid burdensome interventions (frequent hospitalizations, invasive procedures). This patient: ICD not indicated. Recommend: Goals of care discussion with family. Likely appropriate: Comfortfocused approach, Palliative care/hospice referral, Symptom management, Avoid hospitalizations unless clearly beneficial. A correct - individualized, patient-centered approach. B wrong: ICD not indicated (life expectancy <1y, poor functional status). D wrong: Advanced dementia, poor prognosis - aggressive measures not beneficial.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy with total cholesterol 680 mg/dL, LDL-C 620 mg/dL. Xanthomas on hands and Achilles tendons. Both parents have LDL 180-200 mg/dL. Echo: Mild aortic stenosis (lipid deposits on valve). Carotid ultrasound: Early atherosclerosis. What is diagnosis and MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Diet therapy alone sufficient
B. Standard-dose statin therapy
C. Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
D. No treatment until age 18
questions.explanation: - Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH): Genetics: Biallelic mutations in LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 genes. Prevalence: 1 in 160,000-300,000. Inheritance: Autosomal codominant. Presentation: LDL typically 400-1000 mg/dL (untreated). Xanthomas (tendon, tuberous) in childhood. Aortic stenosis from valvular deposits. Premature atherosclerotic CVD (MI teens-20s if untreated). Corneal arcus. Diagnosis: LDL >500 mg/dL OR LDL >400 mg/dL + both parents with hypercholesterolemia. Genetic testing confirms. Natural history: Without treatment, MI/death typically by age 20-30y. Treatment: Multi-modal aggressive therapy needed: High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg or rosuvastatin 40mg). Ezetimibe 10mg. PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab, alirocumab) - may have limited effect in HoFH with null LDLR mutations. Lomitapide (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein inhibitor): Reduces LDL 40- 50%. Oral. Side effects: hepatotoxicity, GI. Mipomersen (antisense oligonucleotide to apoB-100): Reduces LDL 25%. SC injection. Side effects: injection site reactions, hepatotoxicity. Evinacumab (angiopoietin-like 3 antibody): IV infusion monthly. Effective even in null LDLR mutations. LDL apheresis: Weekly or biweekly. Removes LDL mechanically. Burdensome but effective. Goal: LDL <100 mg/dL (ideally <70). Liver transplantation: Curative (provides functional LDLR) but high-risk. Heterozygous FH (HeFH): Less severe. LDL 190-400 mg/dL. One mutant allele. Treat with statin + ezetimibe; PCSK9i if inadequate. This patient: LDL 620 mg/dL, xanthomas childhood, both parents affected, aortic stenosis - HoFH. Requires aggressive combination therapy + likely apheresis. C correct.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents with abdominal pain. Labs: Triglycerides 2840 mg/dL, total cholesterol 680 mg/dL, lipemic serum. Amylase/lipase elevated. CT: Acute pancreatitis. No alcohol use. What is MOST appropriate acute and long-term management?
options: A. Acute: NPO, IV fluids, insulin infusion fibrate ،omega-3 fatty acids
B. Statin monotherapy
C. No specific treatment for triglycerides
D. LDL apheresis
questions.explanation: - Severe hypertriglyceridemia: Definitions: Normal: <150 mg/dL. Borderline high: 150-199. High: 200-499. Very high: 500-999. Severe: ≥1000 mg/dL. Complications: Acute pancreatitis: Risk when TG >500 mg/dL, especially >1000 mg/dL. Eruptive xanthomas. Lipemia retinalis. Hepatosplenomegaly. Causes severe hypertriglyceridemia: Primary (genetic): Familial chylomicronemia syndrome (lipoprotein lipase deficiency), Familial hypertriglyceridemia. Secondary: Uncontrolled diabetes, Alcohol abuse, Obesity, Medications (estrogen, tamoxifen, corticosteroids, protease inhibitors, atypical antipsychotics), Hypothyroidism, Nephrotic syndrome, Pregnancy. Often combination primary + secondary. Acute management (pancreatitis): NPO (bowel rest - no oral intake stimulates chylomicron production). IV fluids. Insulin infusion: 0.1-0.3 units/kg/h with dextrose infusion (euglycemic). Activates lipoprotein lipase → rapidly lowers TG. Can decrease TG 50% within 24-48h. Plasmapheresis: If TG remains >2000 mg/dL despite insulin or severe pancreatitis. Long-term management: Lifestyle: Very low-fat diet (<15% calories from fat). Avoid alcohol completely. Weight loss if obese. Exercise. Medications: Fibrates (first-line): Fenofibrate 145mg daily (preferred) or gemfibrozil 600mg BID. Lower TG 30-50%. Omega-3 fatty acids: High-dose (4g daily) - Vascepa (icosapent ethyl), Lovaza. Lower TG 20-30%. Niacin: Less effective for severe hypertriglyceridemia. Side effects limit use. Treat secondary causes: Optimize diabetes control, Stop offending medications, Treat hypothyroidism. Goal: TG <500 mg/dL (prevents pancreatitis). Ideally <150 mg/dL. This patient: TG 2840 mg/dL with acute pancreatitis. Acute: NPO, IV fluids, insulin infusion. Longterm: Fenofibrate + omega-3 + very low-fat diet. Evaluate for secondary causes (diabetes, alcohol, medications). A correct. B wrong: Statins lower TG only 10-30%, insufficient for severe hypertriglyceridemia.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with T2DM, metabolic syndrome. Labs: Total cholesterol 278 mg/dL, LDL-C 168 mg/dL, HDL-C 32 mg/dL, TG 390 mg/dL. 10-year ASCVD risk 18%. What is MOST appropriate lipid management?
options: A. Fibrate monotherapy
B. Niacin monotherapy
C. Omega-3 alone
D. High-intensity statin
questions.explanation: - Mixed dyslipidemia management: Pattern: Elevated LDL + elevated TG + low HDL (typical in metabolic syndrome, diabetes). This patient: LDL 168 mg/dL (high), TG 390 mg/dL (high), HDL 32 mg/dL (low). Primary target: LDL reduction. First-line: High-intensity statin: Atorvastatin 40-80mg or rosuvastatin 20-40mg. Lowers LDL 50%, lowers TG 20-30%, raises HDL 5-10%. Indication: T2DM age 40-75y (regardless of LDL) OR ASCVD risk 18% (≥7.5%). Secondary targets (if TG remains elevated on statin): TG 200-499 mg/dL on statin: Icosapent ethyl (Vascepa) 2g BID: REDUCE-IT trial: 25% reduction CV events when added to statin in patients with TG 135-499 mg/dL despite statin. Mechanism: Omega-3 fatty acid (EPA only). Alternative: Omega-3 mixed (EPA+DHA) 4g daily - less evidence. TG ≥500 mg/dL despite statin: Consider fibrate to reduce pancreatitis risk. Fenofibrate safer than gemfibrozil with statins. Combination therapy controversies: Statin + fibrate: ACCORD Lipid, FIELD trials: No overall CV benefit adding fenofibrate to statin. Possible benefit in subgroup with TG >204 mg/dL + HDL <34 mg/dL. Gemfibrozil + statin: Increased myopathy risk (gemfibrozil inhibits statin metabolism). AVOID combination. Fenofibrate + statin: Safer than gemfibrozil but limited CV benefit data. Statin + niacin: AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE trials: No CV benefit, increased adverse effects. NOT recommended. Low HDL management: No proven therapy to raise HDL and reduce CV events. Focus on LDL reduction. This patient: T2DM, high ASCVD risk, mixed dyslipidemia. Start: High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg). Reassess lipids in 4-12 weeks. If TG remains 200-499 mg/dL → add icosapent ethyl 2g BID. If TG ≥500 mg/dL → consider fenofibrate (pancreatitis prevention). Lifestyle: Weight loss, low-fat diet, exercise (improve all lipid parameters). A wrong: Fibrate monotherapy doesn't address LDL. D correct - statin primary, consider icosapent ethyl if needed.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with HTN on lisinopril 40mg, amlodipine 10mg, chlorthalidone 25mg daily. BP remains 156/94 mmHg (confirmed on home BP monitoring, average of multiple readings). Adherent to medications. No white coat effect. What defines resistant hypertension and next step?
options: A. This is not resistant HTN - need 5 medications
B. Resistant HTN
C. Switch all medications
D. No further workup needed
questions.explanation: - Resistant hypertension: Definition: BP above goal despite adherence to 3 optimally dosed antihypertensives from different classes, one being a diuretic. OR BP controlled but requiring ≥4 medications. Prevalence: 10-15% of hypertensive patients. This patient: On 3 medications (ACE-I, CCB, thiazide) at optimal doses, BP 156/94 (above goal <130/80) → meets definition of resistant HTN. Pseudo-resistant HTN (exclude first): Poor adherence (most common). White coat HTN (office BP elevated, home BP normal). Improper BP measurement technique. Inadequate therapy (suboptimal doses, wrong classes). Volume overload (excessive salt, inadequate diuresis). Evaluation: Confirm true resistant HTN: Home BP monitoring, 24h ambulatory BP monitoring. Assess adherence: Pill counts, pharmacy refills, directly observed therapy, urine drug levels. Evaluate for secondary causes: Renal artery stenosis: Renal ultrasound with Doppler, CTA/MRA, plasma renin. Primary aldosteronism (most common secondary cause): Aldosterone/renin ratio, confirmatory testing. Obstructive sleep apnea: Sleep study if suspected. Pheochromocytoma: Plasma/urine metanephrines (if suggestive symptoms). Cushing syndrome: 24h urine cortisol, dexamethasone suppression test. Thyroid disorders, hyperparathyroidism. Medication/substance review: NSAIDs, decongestants, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, stimulants, alcohol, licorice. Management: Lifestyle optimization: Sodium restriction (<2g/day), weight loss, exercise, limit alcohol, DASH diet. Optimize diuretic: Ensure adequate diuretic (chlorthalidone preferred over HCTZ, longer half-life). Add 4th agent: Spironolactone 25-50mg daily (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist): Most effective 4th agent. PATHWAY-2 trial: Superior to doxazosin or bisoprolol as add-on. Monitor K (risk hyperkalemia especially with ACE-I). Alternative 4th agents: Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol), Alpha-blocker (doxazosin), Centrally-acting (clonidine), Vasodilator (hydralazine, minoxidil). This patient: Confirmed resistant HTN, good adherence. Evaluate secondary causes (aldosterone/renin ratio, renal artery imaging, sleep study). Add spironolactone 25mg daily. Reinforce lifestyle. B correct.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with resistant HTN (BP 168/98 on 4 medications including spironolactone 25mg). Labs: K 3.2 mEq/L (low-normal), random aldosterone 28 ng/dL, plasma renin <0.6 ng/mL/h. Aldosterone-to-renin ratio 47 (elevated). What is next step in evaluation and management?
options: A. Confirmatory testing for primary aldosteronism (salt loading test or fludrocortisone suppression test); if confirmed, adrenal CT; if unilateral adenoma, refer for adrenalectomy; if bilateral hyperplasia, increase spironolactone to 50-100mg or add amiloride
B. No further workup - treat empirically
C. Start beta-blocker
D. Renal artery angioplasty
questions.explanation: - Primary aldosteronism (PA): Most common secondary cause of HTN (5-10% of hypertensives, up to 20% with resistant HTN). Causes: Aldosterone-producing adenoma (30- 40%), Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (60-70%), Unilateral hyperplasia, Familial hyperaldosteronism, Aldosterone-producing carcinoma (rare). Screening: Indications: Resistant HTN, HTN + hypokalemia (spontaneous or diuretic-induced), HTN + adrenal incidentaloma, HTN + family history PA, HTN age <40y. Test: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR). Draw morning sample, patient seated x5min. Positive: ARR >20-40 (varies by assay) AND aldosterone >15 ng/dL. This patient: ARR 47 (elevated), aldosterone 28 ng/dL - SCREEN POSITIVE for PA. Confirmatory testing (required): Salt loading test: Oral (high-salt diet 3 days, 24h urine aldosterone), OR IV (2L saline over 4h, measure aldosterone). Positive: Aldosterone remains elevated despite volume expansion. Fludrocortisone suppression test. Captopril challenge test. Subtype classification (if confirmed PA): Adrenal CT: Identify unilateral adenoma vs bilateral hyperplasia. Adrenal vein sampling (AVS): Gold standard to distinguish unilateral vs bilateral disease. Required before surgery. Treatment: Unilateral adenoma: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy (CURATIVE in 30-60%, improves BP in 90%). Bilateral hyperplasia or non-surgical candidates: Medical therapy: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists: Spironolactone 25-100mg daily (firstline). Side effects: gynecomastia, erectile dysfunction, menstrual irregularities. Eplerenone 50- 100mg daily (more selective, fewer side effects, more expensive). Amiloride 10-20mg daily (Ksparing diuretic, alternative). This patient: Screen positive for PA. Next steps: Confirmatory testing (salt loading), Adrenal CT, Consider AVS if surgery candidate, Increase spironolactone or add amiloride while evaluating. A correct.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman with HTN, flash pulmonary edema episodes x2, renal insufficiency (Cr 1.8 mg/dL, was 1.2 one year ago). Abdominal bruit. Renal ultrasound: Right kidney 8.2 cm, left kidney 11.8 cm (asymmetric). CTA: 80% stenosis right renal artery. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Immediate renal artery stenting for all patients
B. ACE inhibitor as first-line therapy
C. No treatment needed
D. Renal artery revascularization
questions.explanation: - Renal artery stenosis (RAS): Causes: Atherosclerotic (90%): Elderly, CVD risk factors, ostial/proximal stenosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia (10%): Young women, mid-distal stenosis, beaded appearance. Presentation: Resistant HTN, Flash pulmonary edema (bilateral RAS), Progressive renal insufficiency, Asymmetric kidney sizes (>1.5 cm difference), Abdominal bruit. Diagnosis: Renal artery duplex ultrasound (non-invasive screening). CTA or MRA (imaging). Renal angiography (gold standard, invasive). This patient: Flash pulmonary edema, worsening renal function, asymmetric kidneys, significant RAS - concerning features. Medical therapy: Antihypertensives: CCB, beta-blockers, diuretics. ACE-I/ARB: Controversial in RAS. May worsen renal function if bilateral RAS or RAS to solitary kidney (blocks efferent arteriole constriction). Can use cautiously with monitoring if unilateral RAS. Statins, antiplatelet therapy (atherosclerotic RAS). Revascularization: CORAL, ASTRAL trials: No benefit of stenting over medical therapy for atherosclerotic RAS with HTN alone. Possible indications for revascularization (controversial): Flash pulmonary edema (recurrent), Progressive renal insufficiency despite optimal medical therapy, Truly resistant HTN (>3 drugs), RAS and intolerance to medications, Bilateral severe RAS or RAS to solitary kidney with declining function. Fibromuscular dysplasia (angioplasty very effective). Technique: Percutaneous angioplasty ± stenting (atherosclerotic - stent usually needed). Angioplasty alone (fibromuscular dysplasia). Surgical revascularization (rarely needed). This patient: Flash pulmonary edema + progressive renal insufficiency - MAY be reasonable candidate for revascularization. However, optimize medical therapy first. Discuss risk-benefit. If recurrent flash edema despite therapy → consider revascularization. D correct - individualized decision. A wrong: Not for all patients - CORAL showed no routine benefit. B wrong: ACE-I may worsen function in bilateral RAS.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with recurrent typical atrial flutter despite antiarrhythmic therapy (sotalol, amiodarone trials). Multiple cardioversions. AF-free, only flutter. Structurally normal heart. What is MOST appropriate definitive management?
options: A. Continue trying different antiarrhythmic drugs
B. AV node ablation with pacemaker
C. Catheter ablation of cavotricuspid isthmus
D. Surgical maze procedure
questions.explanation: - Atrial flutter management: Typical (cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent) flutter: Most common type (90%). Macroreentrant circuit around tricuspid annulus. ECG: Sawtooth flutter waves, rate 250-350 bpm atrial, usually 2:1 AV conduction (ventricular rate 150 bpm). Acute management: Rate control or cardioversion (similar to AF). Anticoagulation (same as AF - CHA2DS2-VASc). Long-term management: Rhythm control difficult with antiarrhythmics. Catheter ablation PREFERRED: Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation: Creates line of block across isthmus. Success rate >95%. Recurrence <10%. Procedure time 1-2h, same-day discharge. Complications rare (<1%): bleeding, tamponade, AV block. CURATIVE - first-line for symptomatic recurrent typical flutter. Antiarrhythmic drugs less effective for flutter vs AF. Class I: Flecainide, propafenone (avoid if structural heart disease - can slow flutter rate → 1:1 AV conduction → very rapid ventricular rate). Class III: Sotalol, dofetilide, amiodarone (modest efficacy). AV node ablation + pacemaker: For rate control if ablation fails or patient refuses. Not first-line (requires permanent pacing). This patient: Recurrent typical flutter despite multiple antiarrhythmics. Structurally normal heart. CTI ablation HIGHLY appropriate - curative, excellent success rate, low risk. Much better than chronic antiarrhythmics. C correct - ablation first-line for recurrent symptomatic typical flutter.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%), ICD placed 2y ago. Multiple ICD shocks x6 past year for VT despite amiodarone 200mg daily. VT originates from LV scar. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Increase amiodarone dose
B. VT catheter ablation
C. Remove ICD
D. Observation only
questions.explanation: - VT catheter ablation: Indications: Recurrent monomorphic VT despite optimal medical therapy (antiarrhythmics), Multiple ICD shocks (VT storm), Incessant VT, Symptomatic VT in patients who cannot tolerate/refuse medications. Technique: Map VT circuit using electrophysiology study, Ablate critical isthmus (usually in scar border zone), Substrate modification (ablate abnormal potentials in scar). Success rates: Ischemic VT: 50-75% freedom from VT at 1 year, Reduces ICD shocks 50-70%. Non-ischemic VT: Variable (depends on substrate). Complications: Stroke, tamponade, vascular injury, heart block, death (<1%). This patient: Ischemic CMP with LV scar, recurrent VT despite amiodarone, 6 ICD shocks past year - CLEAR indication for VT ablation. Reduces VT burden, ICD shocks, improves QOL. Alternative: Try different antiarrhythmic (sotalol, mexiletine) but ablation preferred if already failed amiodarone.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man with syncope while sleeping. Family history: Brother died suddenly at age 28. ECG: Type 1 Brugada pattern (coved ST-elevation in V1-V2). EP study: Inducible VF. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Beta-blocker therapy
B. Amiodarone only
C. Observation - no intervention
D. ICD implantation - indicated for Brugada with prior syncope, documented VT/VF, or inducible VF with symptoms/family history sudden death; only proven therapy to prevent sudden cardiac death
questions.explanation: - Brugada syndrome: Genetic channelopathy (SCN5A mutation most common). Sodium channel dysfunction. Presentation: Type 1 ECG pattern: Coved ST-elevation ≥2mm in V1-V2 (diagnostic). Syncope, VT/VF, sudden cardiac death (often during sleep or rest). Family history sudden death common. Triggers: Fever, large meals, alcohol, certain medications (sodium channel blockers, vagotonic agents). Risk stratification: High risk: Cardiac arrest survivor, Documented VT/VF, Syncope with Type 1 ECG pattern, Inducible VF on EP study with symptoms/family history. Intermediate/low risk: Asymptomatic with Type 1 ECG, Type 2 or 3 pattern (not diagnostic - need provocation testing). Management: ICD: ONLY proven therapy to prevent SCD. Indicated: Cardiac arrest survivor, Syncope + Type 1 ECG, Documented VT/VF, Inducible VF + symptoms or family history SCD. NOT indicated: Asymptomatic patients (controversial, no proven benefit). Medications: Quinidine (Class Ia) may reduce VF episodes (not widely used, limited data). Isoproterenol for VT storm. Avoid triggers: Treat fevers aggressively, Avoid certain medications (check Brugadadrugs.org). This patient: Syncope, Type 1 ECG, inducible VF, family history SCD - HIGH risk. ICD indicated.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman with severe functional TR (annular dilation from chronic AF, RV dilation). Progressive fatigue, peripheral edema, ascites. Echo: Severe TR, RV dilation, RVSP 38mmHg, LVEF 60%. Symptoms persist despite maximal diuretics. What is management approach?
options: A. Tricuspid valve surgery
B. No intervention - TR is benign
C. Increase diuretics only
D. Beta-blocker therapy
questions.explanation: - Severe tricuspid regurgitation: Etiology: Functional (secondary) 80%: Annular dilation from RV/RA dilation (AF, pulmonary HTN, left heart disease). Primary (organic): Endocarditis, rheumatic, carcinoid, Ebstein anomaly, pacemaker lead. Presentation: Right HF symptoms: Peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly. Fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance. Exam: Holosystolic murmur at left sternal border (increases with inspiration), Pulsatile liver, JVP with prominent V wave. Diagnosis: Echo: Qualitative (color Doppler jet), quantitative (vena contracta, EROA). Severity: Severe if vena contracta >7mm or EROA >40mm². Management: Medical: Diuretics for volume overload. Treat underlying causes (AF rate control, treat pulmonary HTN). Surgery: Indications: Severe TR + symptoms despite medical therapy, Severe TR + undergoing left-sided valve surgery, Severe TR + progressive RV dilation/dysfunction. Repair preferred over replacement (lower mortality, better outcomes). Techniques: Annuloplasty (ring or suture), Leaflet repair, Replacement (bioprosthetic). Transcatheter: Edge-to-edge repair (TriClip), Annuloplasty devices, TTVR (transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement). Emerging therapies for high surgical risk patients. Outcomes: Isolated TR surgery: Higher operative mortality (8-10%) but reasonable if severe symptoms. Concurrent left-sided surgery: Lower incremental risk. This patient: Severe symptomatic TR refractory to diuretics. Consider surgery vs transcatheter intervention.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with mechanical mitral valve (bileaflet) on warfarin presents with progressive dyspnea x1 week. INR today 1.6 (subtherapeutic, goal 2.5-3.5). Echo: Elevated gradient across mitral valve (mean 14mmHg, baseline 4mmHg), reduced leaflet motion. Fluoroscopy: Restricted leaflet opening. Diagnosis: Prosthetic valve thrombosis. NYHA class III symptoms, no cardiogenic shock. What is MOST appropriate management?
options: A. Emergency valve replacement surgery
B. Continue warfarin at current dose
C. Thrombolytic therapy
D. Observation only
questions.explanation: - Prosthetic valve thrombosis: Risk factors: Inadequate anticoagulation (most common), Mitral position > aortic, Older mechanical valves (ball-cage, tilting disk > bileaflet), AF, LV dysfunction, Hypercoagulable states. Presentation: Obstructive: Dyspnea, HF symptoms, elevated gradients, muffled prosthetic sounds, thromboembolic events. Non-obstructive: May be asymptomatic or mild symptoms. Diagnosis: TTE/TEE: Elevated gradients, reduced leaflet motion, visualize thrombus. Fluoroscopy: Restricted leaflet opening. CT if diagnosis unclear. Management: Based on thrombus size, location, symptoms, hemodynamic status. Nonobstructive thrombosis: UFH or LMWH + optimize warfarin (INR goal). Serial echos to assess resolution. Obstructive thrombosis: NYHA I-II, small thrombus (<5mm): Thrombolytic therapy reasonable OR surgery. NYHA III-IV, large thrombus, or failed thrombolysis: Surgery (valve replacement) preferred. Cardiogenic shock/critical: Emergency surgery. Thrombolytic regimens: Standard: Alteplase 25mg IV over 6h, repeat if needed. Low-dose slow: Alteplase 25mg over 25h (lower bleeding risk). Monitor: Serial echos, assess leaflet motion and gradients. Success rate: 70- 80% (higher for right-sided, recent thrombus). Complications: Major bleeding 10-15%, thromboembolism 10-15%, recurrence 10-20%. Surgery: Valve replacement. Higher risk if emergent. Definitive treatment. This patient: NYHA III, mitral valve thrombosis, INR subtherapeutic. Start UFH, consider thrombolysis vs surgery. Given NYHA III (not shock), thrombolysis reasonable. If fails or large thrombus → surgery.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with bicuspid aortic valve, mild AS (peak velocity 2.4 m/s, mean gradient 18mmHg), trace AR. Asymptomatic. Ascending aorta diameter 4.2 cm. What is MOST appropriate surveillance strategy?
options: A. No follow-up needed - valve and aorta normal
B. Serial echocardiography
C. Immediate valve replacement
D. Only check if symptoms develop
questions.explanation: - Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV): Most common congenital cardiac anomaly (1-2% population). Associated conditions: Aortic stenosis (early onset, typically 5th-6th decade), Aortic regurgitation, Ascending aortic aneurysm/dilation (50-60%), Coarctation of aorta (10-15%), Aortic dissection (increased risk). Surveillance: Echocardiography: Assess valve function (AS/AR severity, progression). Assess ascending aorta (diameter, dilation). Frequency: Mild AS/AR + aorta <4.0cm: Every 2-3 years. Moderate AS/AR: Annually. Severe AS/AR: Every 6- 12 months. Aortic imaging: Echo usually adequate for proximal ascending aorta. CT or MRI if: Aortic diameter ≥4.0cm (more accurate measurement), Suspected aortic pathology, Surgical planning. Frequency: Aorta 4.0-4.4cm: Annually. Aorta 4.5-4.9cm: Every 6-12 months. Aorta ≥5.0cm: Consider surgery (see below). Interventions: Valve: AVR for severe symptomatic AS or AR (same as tricuspid valve). Aorta: Surgery indications: Aortic diameter ≥5.5cm (general population), Aortic diameter ≥5.0cm (bicuspid valve - LOWER threshold), Aortic diameter ≥4.5cm if undergoing AVR for valve dysfunction, Rapid growth >0.5cm/year, Family history aortic dissection or sudden death. Family screening: First-degree relatives - echo to screen for BAV and aortic dilation. This patient: Mild AS, trace AR, aorta 4.2cm. Echo annually (aorta ≥4.0cm). Consider CT/MRI for accurate aortic measurement. Monitor for progression.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man 2 weeks post-heart transplant. Standard triple immunosuppression: tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisone. Tacrolimus level 8 ng/mL (goal 10-12 ng/mL first 6 months). Cr 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). What adjustment is needed?
options: A. Decrease tacrolimus - level too high
B. No change needed
C. Switch to cyclosporine
D. Increase tacrolimus
questions.explanation: - Heart transplant immunosuppression: Standard triple therapy: Calcineurin inhibitor: Tacrolimus (first-line) or cyclosporine. Antiproliferative: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) or azathioprine. Corticosteroid: Prednisone (tapered over months). Tacrolimus: Mechanism: Inhibits T-cell activation. Dosing: Initial 0.075mg/kg/day divided BID, adjust to levels. Target levels: 0-6 months: 10-15 ng/mL (varies by center, this case 10-12 ng/mL). >6 months: 8-12 ng/mL (lower to minimize toxicity). Monitoring: Trough levels Q3-7 days initially, then less frequent when stable. Side effects: Nephrotoxicity (dose-dependent, often reversible), Neurotoxicity (tremor, headache), Hyperglycemia (new-onset diabetes 20-30%), Hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, GI upset. Drug interactions: CYP3A4 substrate - many interactions. Increase levels: Azole antifungals, macrolides, CCBs, grapefruit juice. Decrease levels: Rifampin, phenytoin, St. John's wort. This patient: Tacrolimus 8 ng/mL, goal 10-12 ng/mL early posttransplant. SUB-therapeutic - increase dose. Risk acute rejection if inadequate immunosuppression. Monitor Cr (1.4, mild increase - acceptable, monitor).

questions.question: A 48-year-old man post-heart transplant (day 5). Donor CMV-positive, recipient CMVnegative (high-risk D+/R-). On tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisone. What is MOST appropriate CMV prophylaxis strategy?
options: A. Valganciclovir 900mg daily
B. No prophylaxis needed
C. Acyclovir only
D. Wait for symptoms before treating
questions.explanation: - CMV in heart transplant: Risk stratification: High risk (D+/R-): Donor positive, recipient negative. 50-75% develop CMV without prophylaxis. Intermediate risk (D+/R+, D- /R+): 20-40% risk. Low risk (D-/R-): <5% risk. Prophylaxis: High risk (D+/R-): Valganciclovir 900mg PO daily x 3-6 months (most centers use 3-6 months). Dose adjust for CrCl: CrCl 40-59: 450mg daily, CrCl 25-39: 450mg every 2 days, CrCl 10-24: 450mg twice weekly. Intermediate risk: Valganciclovir x 3 months OR preemptive therapy (monitor CMV PCR weekly, treat if positive). Monitoring: CBC weekly x 1 month, then biweekly (neutropenia risk). CMV PCR if symptomatic. Side effects: Neutropenia 5-15% (dose-limiting), GI upset, interactions with immunosuppressants. Alternative: IV ganciclovir 5mg/kg daily if cannot take PO. CMV disease post-transplant: Presents 1-6 months post-transplant (median 2-3 months). Manifestations: CMV syndrome (fever, malaise, leukopenia), GI disease (most common - esophagitis, gastritis, colitis), Pneumonitis, Retinitis. Treatment: IV ganciclovir 5mg/kg Q12h x 2-3 weeks + reduce immunosuppression. This patient: High-risk D+/R-, day 5 post-transplant. Start valganciclovir 900mg daily (adjust for CrCl). Continue x 3-6 months.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman 6 months post-heart transplant. Routine surveillance biopsy: Grade 2R acute cellular rejection (moderate). Asymptomatic, stable hemodynamics. Echo: LVEF 60%, no change. What is MOST appropriate treatment?
options: A. No treatment - asymptomatic
B. Increase oral prednisone only
C. IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy
D. Immediate retransplant
questions.explanation: - Acute cellular rejection grading (ISHLT): Grade 0R: No rejection. Grade 1R: Mild (interstitial/perivascular infiltrate without myocyte damage). Grade 2R: Moderate (one focus with myocyte damage). Grade 3R: Severe (multifocal myocyte damage ± edema, hemorrhage, vasculitis). Clinical significance: Grade 0-1R: Usually no treatment (unless hemodynamically significant). Grade 2R: Treatment recommended (associated with worse outcomes if untreated). Grade 3R: Aggressive treatment required. Treatment grade 2R rejection: IV methylprednisolone: 500-1000mg daily x 3 days (pulse therapy). Repeat biopsy: 1-2 weeks post-treatment to confirm resolution. Optimize maintenance immunosuppression: Ensure adequate tacrolimus/cyclosporine levels, Maximize MMF dose if tolerated. Persistent/recurrent rejection: Rabbit antithymocyte globulin (rATG, thymoglobulin) 1.5mg/kg daily x 5-14 days OR Alemtuzumab (Campath) 30mg x 2 doses. Photopheresis (extracorporeal). Hemodynamically significant rejection: IABP, inotropes, consider mechanical support if severe. Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR): Different entity (antibodies against donor HLA). Treatment: Plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab, bortezomib. This patient: Grade 2R rejection (moderate), asymptomatic. Treat with IV methylprednisolone x 3 days. Repeat biopsy. Optimize immunosuppression.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with acute decompensated HF. Admitted with pulmonary edema, volume overload. Started on IV furosemide. Day 3: Cr increased 1.2 to 2.4 mg/dL despite diuresis. Urine output decreased. BUN/Cr ratio 28. What type of cardiorenal syndrome and management?
options: A. Type 2 - chronic cardiorenal syndrome
B. Type 1 acute cardiorenal syndrome
C. Type 3 - acute renocardiac syndrome
D. Not cardiorenal syndrome
questions.explanation: - Cardiorenal syndrome classification: Type 1 (Acute cardiorenal): Acute worsening cardiac function → acute kidney injury. Example: Acute decompensated HF → AKI. Type 2 (Chronic cardiorenal): Chronic HF → chronic kidney disease. Example: Chronic HFrEF → progressive CKD. Type 3 (Acute renocardiac): AKI → acute cardiac dysfunction. Example: AKI → pulmonary edema, arrhythmias. Type 4 (Chronic renocardiac): CKD → chronic cardiac disease. Example: CKD → LVH, HF. Type 5 (Secondary): Systemic disease → both cardiac and renal dysfunction. Example: Sepsis, amyloidosis. This patient: Acute decompensated HF → AKI during treatment = Type 1. Pathophysiology Type 1: Decreased CO → renal hypoperfusion. Increased venous congestion → increased renal venous pressure. Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, SNS). Diuretic resistance. Management: Optimize hemodynamics: Ensure adequate CO (inotropes if low CO). Reduce congestion (diuretics, ultrafiltration). Balance between decongestion and avoiding AKI. Diuretics: Continue diuresis if still volume overloaded (Cr elevation may be acceptable if achieving decongestion). Consider diuretic combination (loop + thiazide), Higher loop diuretic doses, Continuous IV infusion. Ultrafiltration: If diuretic-resistant, severe volume overload. Removes fluid mechanically. May preserve renal function better than high-dose diuretics. Inotropes: Dobutamine if low CO contributing to renal hypoperfusion. Avoid nephrotoxins: NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides. ACE-I/ARB: May need to hold temporarily if Cr rising significantly. Vasopressors: Low-dose dopamine NOT beneficial (ROSE trial). This patient: Type 1 CRS. Continue gentle diuresis if volume overloaded. Consider ultrafiltration. Monitor closely.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with chronic HFrEF (LVEF 25%) x5 years. Progressive decline in renal function: Cr 1.2 → 1.8 → 2.2 mg/dL over past 2 years. eGFR now 32 mL/min/1.73m2. Proteinuria 2+. What defines this cardiorenal syndrome and management approach?
options: A. Type 1 - acute cardiorenal syndrome
B. Type 3 - acute renocardiac syndrome
C. Type 5 - secondary cardiorenal syndrome
D. Type 2 (chronic cardiorenal syndrome)
questions.explanation: - Type 2 cardiorenal syndrome: Chronic HF → progressive chronic kidney disease. Pathophysiology: Chronic low CO → chronic renal hypoperfusion. Chronic venous congestion → increased renal interstitial pressure. Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, SNS) → glomerular damage. Inflammation, fibrosis. Prevalence: 20-30% of chronic HF patients develop worsening renal function. Prognosis: CKD in HF associated with worse outcomes (increased mortality, hospitalizations). Management: Optimize HF therapy: Continue GDMT despite renal dysfunction: ACE-I/ARB (reduce proteinuria, slow CKD progression despite Cr elevation up to 30%). Beta-blockers (proven benefit in HF, safe in CKD). MRA (spironolactone) - use cautiously, monitor K and Cr closely. SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) - beneficial in HF and CKD, slow CKD progression. Diuretics: Adjust based on CKD stage. Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide) preferred over thiazides in CKD stage 4-5. Higher doses needed as GFR declines. Avoid nephrotoxins: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast (use cautiously with hydration). Monitor: Cr, eGFR, K, Mg regularly. Anemia management: Erythropoiesisstimulating agents if Hgb <10 g/dL. Iron supplementation. CKD-mineral bone disease: Manage hyperphosphatemia, hyperparathyroidism. Renal replacement therapy: Dialysis if ESRD (eGFR <15). Kidney transplant evaluation if appropriate. This patient: Chronic HFrEF with progressive CKD over 2 years = Type 2 CRS. Continue GDMT, add SGLT2i, monitor closely.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man with CKD (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2), DM scheduled for elective coronary angiography tomorrow. What is MOST effective strategy to prevent contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN)?
options: A. IV isotonic saline )
B. No prophylaxis needed
C. Mannitol only
D. Furosemide before procedure
questions.explanation: - Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN): Definition: Cr increase ≥0.5 mg/dL or ≥25% from baseline within 48-72h of contrast exposure. Risk factors: Pre-existing CKD (eGFR <60, especially <30), DM, Volume depletion, CHF, Age >75y, Hypotension, Anemia, High contrast volume (>100-150 mL). Prevention strategies: IV hydration (MOST effective): Isotonic saline 0.9% NaCl: 1-1.5 mL/kg/h x 3-12h before and 6-12h after. OR Sodium bicarbonate 154 mEq/L: 3mL/kg/h x 1h before, then 1mL/kg/h x 6h after. May be superior to saline (controversial). Oral hydration insufficient. Contrast selection: Low-osmolar (LOCM) or isoosmolar (IOCM) contrast. Minimize volume (<100mL if possible). Avoid high-osmolar contrast. Medication adjustments: HOLD: Metformin (restart 48h post if Cr stable - lactic acidosis risk), NSAIDs 24h before/after, Diuretics. CONTINUE: ACE-I/ARB (holding may worsen outcomes). N-acetylcysteine (NAC): 600-1200mg PO BID x 2 days (start day before). Benefit controversial (multiple trials conflicting). Inexpensive, low risk - reasonable to use. Mechanism: Antioxidant. Statins: Continue/start high-dose statin (may reduce CIN). NOT proven interventions: Fenoldopam, Theophylline, Ascorbic acid, Hemofiltration (prophylactic). Post-procedure: Monitor Cr at 48-72h. Hydrate until Cr stable. This patient: CKD + DM (high risk). IV saline hydration 12h before and 12h after. Low-osmolar contrast, minimize volume. NAC 1200mg BID x 2 days. Hold metformin.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman post-CABG day 7. On UFH prophylaxis. Platelets dropped from 250K to 88K (>50% drop). No bleeding. Suspect HIT. 4T score: 6 (high probability). What is MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: A. Continue heparin - platelet drop is normal post-surgery
B. Switch to LMWH

C. STOP all heparin (UFH, LMWH, flushes); start alternative anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux); send HIT antibody testing; avoid platelet transfusions unless bleeding; do NOT wait for antibody results to change therapy
D. Observe only
questions.explanation: - Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT): Pathophysiology: Type I (nonimmune): Early (<4 days), mild drop, benign, no treatment. Type II (immune-mediated, "HIT"): Antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4)-heparin complex. Platelet activation → thrombosis risk 50%. Timing: 5-10 days after heparin start (earlier if prior exposure). Clinical: Platelet drop ≥50% (usually 50-150K, rarely <20K). Thrombosis (arterial or venous) 50%. Skin necrosis at injection sites. 4T score (pretest probability): Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher causes. Score 0-3: Low, 4-5: Intermediate, 6-8: High. This patient: 4T score 6 (high probability), platelet drop >50%, day 7 post-op. HIGH suspicion for HIT. Management: STOP all heparin immediately: UFH, LMWH, heparin flushes, heparin-coated catheters. Do NOT wait for HIT antibody results. Start alternative anticoagulant (direct thrombin inhibitors or factor Xa inhibitors): Argatroban: 2mcg/kg/min IV (reduce in liver disease). Monitor aPTT. Bivalirudin: 0.15mg/kg/h IV. Fondaparinux: 5-10mg SC daily (off-label for HIT). NOT FDA-approved but used. Apixaban, rivaroxaban: Emerging data, off-label. DO NOT use: LMWH (cross-reacts with HIT antibodies 80-90%), Warfarin alone (risk warfarin-induced skin necrosis, paradoxical thrombosis). Wait until platelets recover >150K before starting warfarin, overlap with alternative anticoagulant ≥5 days. Avoid platelet transfusions: Unless active bleeding (may worsen thrombosis). Testing: HIT antibody (ELISA): Sensitive but less specific. Serotonin release assay (SRA): Gold standard, specific. Duration: Anticoagulate x 4 weeks minimum (thrombosis risk persists after platelet recovery). This patient: Stop heparin, start argatroban, send HIT antibodies. p.458-461

questions.question:
AM is a 68-year-old male who presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of severe chest pain that he describes as “a crushing weight.” The pain started approximately 30 minutes ago while he was reading a book in his armchair. It radiates to his left arm and jaw and is accompanied by profuse sweating and shortness of breath. He denies any recent trauma or fever. He states he took three doses of sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg each) at 5-minute intervals, but the medication provided no relief. AM’s medical history includes hypertension and dyslipidemia, for which he takes ramipril 10 mg PO daily and simvastatin 20 mg PO QHS. AM has no personal history of coronary artery disease (CAD), but his father died of a heart attack at age 62. AM is a former smoker but quit 10 years ago. He drinks 1-2 beers per week. On examination, AM appears pale and diaphoretic. His blood pressure is 89/65 mmHg, heart rate is 110 bpm, respiratory rate is 24 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. An immediate 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed, which shows ST-segment elevation of 3 mm in leads V2- V4. Cardiac troponin I levels, drawn upon arrival, are elevated at 0.8 ng/mL (normal < 0.04 ng/mL). AM’s creatinine clearance is 45 ml/min.
Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
options: A. Administer enoxaparin, bisoprolol, Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and ticagrelor immediately and arrange for urgent reperfusion therapy
B. Initiate Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid), ticagrelor and enoxaparin immediately and arrange for coronary angiography within the next 72 hours
C. Administer enoxaparin, Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and ticagrelor immediately and arrange for urgent reperfusion therapy
D. Prescribe a nitroglycerin patch, optimize the existing medication regimens, and advise the patient to avoid strenuous activities
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:C
• Administer enoxaparin, Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and ticagrelor immediately and arrange for urgent reperfusion therapy - An anticoagulant such as enoxaparin, dual antiplatelet therapy (with low-dose Aspirin® and ticagrelor), and immediate reperfusion (either via PCI or fibrinolysis) are all crucial components of the initial management of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
Incorrect Answers:
• Administer enoxaparin, bisoprolol, Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and ticagrelor immediately and arrange for urgent reperfusion therapy - Enoxaparin, dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin® and ticagrelor), and immediate reperfusion are all crucial components of the initial management of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Beta-blockers such as bisoprolol are also a core component, but given the patient’s severe hypotension, therapy should be delayed until hemodynamic stability is achieved.
• Initiate Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid), ticagrelor and enoxaparin immediately and arrange for coronary angiography within the next 72 hours - While anticoagulants and antiplatelets are foundational for managing ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), the timing and urgency of coronary angiography are incorrect. Rapid reperfusion is paramount in STEMI; therefore, coronary angiography must be performed as soon as possible.
• Prescribe a nitroglycerin patch, optimize the existing medication regimens, and advise the patient to avoid strenuous activities - Prescribing a short-acting nitrate alongside a primary prevention medication regimen is appropriate for regimen is appropriate for stable angina, but this patient is experiencing an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). As such, urgent reperfusion therapy is critical.
.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Urgent reperfusion (either via PCI or fibrinolysis), as well as anticoagulation and dual antiplatelet therapy are critical in the acute management of ST-elevation myocardial…

questions.question:
AM successfully underwent revascularization with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and is recovering well. The physician plans to discharge him tomorrow. The hospital discharge prescription is sent to you for review. It includes the following medications: Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg BID, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, ramipril 10 mg daily, simvastatin 20 mg at bedtime and nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual spray 1 dose Q5 min PRN (up to 3 doses). Upon accessing the patient’s lab work, the following findings are noted:
• Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): 95 mL/min/1.73m²
• Sodium: 140 mmol/L (reference range: 135-145 mmol/L)
• Potassium: 4.1 mmol/L (reference range: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L)
• Total Cholesterol: 4.5 mmol/L (reference range: < 5.2 mmol/L)
• Low-density lipoprotein (LDL): 1.8 mmol/L (reference range: < 2.6 mmol/L or individualized target)
• High-density lipoprotein (HDL): 1.5 mmol/L (reference range: > 1.0 mmol/L)
• Serum triglycerides: 1.5 mmol/L (reference range: < 1.7 mmol/L)
• HbA1C: 6.4%
Which of the following is the most appropriate statement?
options: A. Simvastatin should be discontinued and replaced with atorvastatin 10 mg PO QHS
B. Metformin 250 mg PO BID should be added to the discharge prescription since the patient has pre-diabetes
C. The discharge prescription is complete and accurate; the discharge process should proceed
D. The current statin regimen is appropriate since AM’s LDL level is < 2 mmol/L
E. Simvastatin should be discontinued and replaced with rosuvastatin 20 mg PO QHS
questions.explanation:
Answer E
Simvastatin should be discontinued and replaced with rosuvastatin 20 mg PO QHS - A highintensity statin (such as atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) is indicated in patients with STEMI for better cardiovascular outcomes, regardless of LDL levels.
Incorrect Answers:
• Simvastatin should be discontinued and replaced with atorvastatin 10 mg PO QHS - A highintensity statin (such as atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) is indicated in all patients with STEMI for better cardiovascular outcomes, regardless of LDL levels.
