Atorvastatin 10 mg PO daily is considered a moderate-intensity statin regimen.
• Metformin 250 mg PO BID should be added to the discharge prescription since the patient has pre-diabetes - While the A1C reading may suggest pre-diabetes, additional bloodwork and assessment are necessary prior to starting medication. Furthermore, this is not the most urgent intervention.
• The discharge prescription is complete and accurate; the discharge process should proceed - A high-intensity statin (such as atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) is indicated in all patients with STEMI for better cardiovascular outcomes, regardless of LDL levels. The existing statin regimen is considered low intensity.
• The current statin regimen is appropriate since AM’s LDL level is < 2 mmol/L - A high-intensity statin (such as atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) is indicated in all patients with STEMI for better cardiovascular outcomes, regardless of LDL levels.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
A high-intensity statin (such as atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) is indicated in all patients with STEMI for better cardiovascular outcomes, regardless of LDL levels.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with mechanical mitral valve on warfarin, now 8 weeks pregnant. What is anticoagulation management?
options: A. Continue warfarin throughout
B. Switch to aspirin
C. Switch to LMWH (enoxaparin 1mg/kg Q12h) targeting anti-Xa 0.6-1.0; transition to UFH 36h before delivery; resume LMWH or warfarin postpartum
D. No anticoagulation
questions.explanation: - Mechanical valve pregnancy: Switch to LMWH NOW (first trimester). Enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC Q12h. Monitor anti-Xa weekly. Stop LMWH 36h before delivery or switch to UFH. Resume LMWH or warfarin postpartum.

questions.question:
Unfortunately, ticagrelor is not available at your institution and AY will be receiving clopidogrel prior to his procedure.
Which of the following is the maximum loading dose of clopidogrel recommended in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) who are undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)?
options: A. 75 mg
B. 150 mg
C. 300 mg
D. 450 mg
E. 600 mg
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:E
• 600 mg - The maximum recommended loading dose of clopidogrel in patients with STEMI who are receiving PCI is 600 mg.
Incorrect Answers:
• 75 mg - This is the recommended maintenance dose, not a loading dose.
• 150 mg - This is not a recommended loading dose.
• 300 mg - This is an appropriate loading dose but is not the maximum recommended dose.
• 450 mg - This is not a recommended loading dose.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
The maximum recommended loading dose of clopidogrel in patients with STEMI who are receiving PCI is 600 mg.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To identify appropriate dosing for antiplatelet agents in patients who have experienced an STelevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
BACKGROUND:
Aggressive medical therapy is initiated to stabilize the patient and prevent further…

questions.question: Which of the following should NOT be included in AY’s discharge prescription?
options: A. Start Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily
B. Start candesartan 8 mg PO daily
C. Start bisoprolol 5 mg PO daily
D. Continue perindopril/indapamide 8 mg/2.5 mg PO daily
E. Start ticagrelor 90 mg PO BID
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE: Correct Answer:B
• Start candesartan 8 mg PO daily - Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are an appropriate alternative for patients who are unable to tolerate or have a contraindication to ACE inhibitors. However, ARBs should never be combined with ACE inhibitors, due to the increased risk of angioedema and hyperkalemia. Since AY already takes perindopril/indapamide, adding an ARB would not be appropriate.
Incorrect Answers:
• Start Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily - Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily is recommended as part of dual antiplatelet therapy in patients who have experienced a STEMI.
• Start bisoprolol 5 mg PO daily - Bisoprolol 5 mg PO daily is a recommended beta-blocker regimen in patients who have experienced a STEMI, as it lowers the risk of current myocardial infarctions and mortality.
• Continue perindopril/indapamide 8 mg/2.5 mg PO daily - Perindopril 8 mg/indapamide 2.5 mg PO daily is an appropriate antihypertensive regimen for a patient who has experienced a STEMI.
• Start ticagrelor 90 mg PO BID - Ticagrelor 90 mg PO BID is recommended as part of dual antiplatelet therapy in patients who have experienced a STEMI and underwent PCI.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are an appropriate alternative for patients who are unable to tolerate or have a contraindication to ACE inhibitors. However, ARBs should never be combined with ACE inhibitors, due to the increased risk of angioedema and hyperkalemia.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To identify potential drug-drug interactions which may occur in patients treated for an STelevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
BACKGROUND:
Following STEMI treatment, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) typically continues for 1 year.
After 1 year, the P2Y12 inhibitor is generally stopped, whereas low-dose Aspirin®
(acetylsalicylic acid) therapy is continued indefinitely, unless contraindicated.
P2Y12 inhibitors include prasugrel, clopidogrel and ticagrelor.

questions.question:
You are working as an inpatient pharmacist at a local hospital in a small rural community. Unfortunately, patients experiencing an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) in your community are typically not able to reach a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)-capable facility within the 2-hour timeframe. As such, most patients experiencing a STEMI will undergo fibrinolysis.
For which of the following patients would fibrinolysis NOT be contraindicated?
options: A. A 43-year-old female who is currently menstruating
B. A 56-year-old male who experienced a traumatic brain injury 2 months ago as the result of a motor vehicle accident
C. A 65-year-old male patient whose peptic ulcer is actively bleeding
D. A 55-year-old female who has comorbid pericarditis
E. A 73-year-old male who is undergoing treatment for glioblastoma
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:A
• A 43-year-old female who is currently menstruating - Current menstruation is specifically excluded from the list of contraindications to fibrinolysis and should not delay treatment.
Incorrect Answers:
• A 56-year-old male who experienced a traumatic brain injury 2 months ago as the result of a motor vehicle accident - Significant closed head or facial trauma within the last 3 months is an absolute contraindication to the use of fibrinolysis.
• A 65-year-old male patient whose peptic ulcer is actively bleeding - An active gastrointestinal bleed is an absolute contraindication to the use of fibrinolysis.
• A 55-year-old female who has comorbid pericarditis - Pericarditis is an absolute contraindication to the use of fibrinolysis.
• A 73-year-old male who is undergoing treatment for glioblastoma - A malignant intracranial neoplasm is an absolute contraindication to the use of fibrinolysis.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Absolute contraindications for the use of fibrinolytics include pericarditis, previous intracranial hemorrhage, known malignant intracranial neoplasm, known cerebral vascular lesion, ischemic stroke within 3 months except for acute stroke within 3 hours, suspected aortic dissection, active bleeding or bleeding diathesis (excluding menstruation) and significant closed head or facial trauma within 3 months.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To identify the contraindications to drug therapies which are used in ST-elevation myocardial infarctions (STEMI).
BACKGROUND:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the first-line reperfusion therapy for all patients who can access a PCI-capable facility within 2 hours. PCI is indicated in patients with contraindications to thrombolytic therapy or cardiogenic shock and is preferred in patients over 75 years of age but who are at a higher risk of intracranial…
bleeding; pregnancy; active peptic ulcer and current use of anticoagulants.

questions.question:
THE NEXT 2 QUESTIONS RELATE TO THE FOLLOWING CASE:
LW is a 65-year-old male who presents to the emergency department accompanied by his wife. Approximately 45 minutes ago, LW began experiencing chest pain which radiated to his left arm and jaw. LW initially attributed his symptoms to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) but became concerned when his usual dose of Tums® (calcium carbonate) did not alleviate his symptoms. At triage, LW underwent an electrocardiogram (ECG) which showed an ST-segment depression. Bloodwork was drawn, and LW’s troponin levels were elevated. LW’s medical history is significant for dyslipidemia, hypertension and GERD for which he takes atorvastatin 20 mg PO daily, Coversyl Plus® (perindopril/indapamide) 4 mg/1.25 mg 1 tab PO daily and Tums® (calcium carbonate) 500 mg PO PRN.
Which of the following agents should NOT be initiated immediately?
options: A. Nitroglycerin
B. Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and clopidogrel
C. Enoxaparin
D. Alteplase
E. Metoprolol
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:D
• Alteplase - Fibrinolytic agents such as alteplase are not used in patients who are experiencing a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).
Incorrect Answers:
• Nitroglycerin - Nitroglycerin is appropriate for the initial management of non-ST-elevation myocardial infarctions (NSTEMI).
• Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and clopidogrel - Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and clopidogrel are appropriate for the initial management of non-ST-elevation myocardial infarctions (NSTEMI).
• Enoxaparin - Enoxaparin is an appropriate anticoagulant for the initial management of non-STelevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).
• Metoprolol - Metoprolol is an appropriate beta-blocker for the initial management of non-STelevation myocardial infarctions (NSTEMI).
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Fibrinolytic agents are not used in patients experiencing an NSTEMI.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS

questions.question:
Three days later, LW’s clinical condition significantly improved following medical management. LW’s medical history is significant for dyslipidemia, hypertension and GERD. He is currently taking Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily, clopidogrel 300 mg PO daily, atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily, metoprolol 50 mg PO daily, Coversyl Plus® (perindopril/indapamide) 4 mg/1.25 mg 1 tab PO daily, pantoprazole 40 mg PO once daily and nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual tablet Q5 min PRN (maximum of 3 doses).
Which of the following constitutes a drug therapy problem in LW’s case?
options: A. LW is at risk of bleeding as his clopidogrel dose is too high
B. LW is at an increased risk of cardiac events as his Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) dose is too low
C. LW is at risk of increased mortality as his atorvastatin dose is too low
D. LW is at risk of recurrent anginal pain as his metoprolol dose is too low
E. Enoxaparin is missing from LW’s medication list and should be restarted
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:A
• LW is at risk of bleeding as his clopidogrel dose is too high - Clopidogrel 300 mg should only be given as a one-time loading dose in patients experiencing an NSTEMI. The dose should then be decreased to 75 mg PO daily for maintenance.
Incorrect Answers:
• LW is at an increased risk of cardiac events as his Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) dose is too low - Acetylsalicylic acid 81 mg is a sufficient dose for cardioprotective benefits.
• LW is at risk of increased mortality as his atorvastatin dose is too low - Atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily is a high-intensity statin regimen.
• LW is at risk of recurrent anginal pain as his metoprolol dose is too low - Beta blocker dosing is generally titrated to the patient’s heart rate and may differ for each patient.
• Enoxaparin is missing from LW’s medication list and should be restarted - As LW is 3 days post-myocardial infarction, it is appropriate to stop enoxaparin.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
In patients experiencing an NSTEMI, clopidogrel 300 mg should only be given as a one-time loading dose and then the dose should be decreased to 75 mg PO daily as maintenance.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To understand pharmacological treatment options in patients with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarctions (NSTEMI).

questions.question:
THE NEXT 2 QUESTIONS RELATE TO THE FOLLOWING CASE:
TF is a 62-year-old male who has been hospitalized after being diagnosed with an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). TF’s medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, for which he takes metformin 1000 mg PO BID with meals, atorvastatin 20 mg PO daily and ramipril/hydrochlorothiazide 10 mg/12.5 mg 1 tablet PO once daily. TF has no known allergies to medications. He is accompanied by his wife and daughter, who are very concerned.
TF is unable to reach a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)-capable facility within 2 hours, so he will be receiving fibrinolysis. TF’s physician asks for your recommendation regarding enoxaparin dosing. TF has normal renal function and weighs approximately 175 lbs.
Which of the following dosing regimens is most appropriate for TF?
options: A. Enoxaparin 30 mg IV plus 40 mg SC for 1 dose then 40 mg SC q24h
B. Enoxaparin 70 mg SC for 1 dose then 40 mg SC q12h
C. Enoxaparin 100 mg SC for one dose then 80 mg SC q24h
D. Enoxaparin 30 mg IV bolus plus 80 mg SC for one dose then 80 mg SC q12h
E. Enoxaparin 80 mg SC q12h
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:D
• Enoxaparin 30 mg IV bolus plus 80 mg SC for one dose then 80 mg SC q12h - In patients experiencing a STEMI, a one-time IV bolus dose of 30 mg is given in addition to the 1mg/kg weight-based subcutaneous dose, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg SC q12h. Since this patient weighs 175 lbs, which is equivalent to 80 kg, their maintenance dose would be 80 mg SC q12h.
Incorrect Answers:
• Enoxaparin 30 mg IV plus 40 mg SC for 1 dose then 40 mg SC q24h - In patients experiencing a STEMI, a one-time IV bolus dose of 30 mg is given in addition to the 1mg/kg weight-based subcutaneous dose, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg SC q12h. Since this patient weighs 175 lbs, which is equivalent to 80 kg, their maintenance dose would be 80 mg SC q12h, not 40 mg SC q24h.
• Enoxaparin 70 mg SC for 1 dose then 40 mg SC q12h - In patients experiencing a STEMI, a one-time IV bolus dose of 30 mg is given in addition to the 1mg/kg weight-based subcutaneous dose, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg SC q12h. Since this patient weighs 175 lbs, which is equivalent to 80 kg, their maintenance dose would be 80 mg SC q12h, not 40 mg SC q12h. Furthermore, the bolus dose would be given intravenously, not subcutaneously.
• Enoxaparin 100 mg SC for one dose then 80 mg SC q24h - In patients experiencing a STEMI, a one-time IV bolus dose of 30 mg is given in addition to the 1mg/kg weight-based subcutaneous dose, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg SC q12h. Since this patient weighs 175 lbs, which is equivalent to 80 kg, their maintenance dose would be 80 mg SC q12h, not 40 mg SC q12h. Furthermore, the bolus dose would be given intravenously, not subcutaneously.
• Enoxaparin 80 mg SC q12h - This is the correct maintenance dose for this patient. However, they will also require a one-time IV bolus dose of 30 mg, since they are experiencing an STelevation myocardial infarction.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Enoxaparin dosing in patients with normal renal function is 1 mg/kg q12h. In patients with renal dysfunction, the dosage is adjusted to 1 mg/kg q24h. Patients experiencing a STEMI should receive an additional one-time IV bolus dose of 30 mg.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS

questions.question:
JT is a 72-year-old male who presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with complaints of chest pain, shortness of breath and nausea. Upon arrival, an electrocardiogram (ECG) is conducted which shows ST-segment depression. Bloodwork is drawn, the results of which are shown below:
Troponin-I: 150 ng/L (reference range: ≤ 45 ng/L)
C-Reactive Protein: 40 mg/L (reference range: ≤ 10 mg/L)
CrCl: 25 mL/min
JT’s medical history is significant for hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 4 chronic kidney disease (CKD). He takes empagliflozin 10 mg PO daily, metformin 500 mg PO daily, ramipril 5 mg PO daily, atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily and Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily.
The attending physician discusses JT’s treatment options with him, and he opts for non-urgent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). While awaiting PCI, JT’s physician would like to start an anticoagulant.
Which of the following anticoagulants would be most appropriate for JT?
options: A. Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
B. Enoxaparin
C. Fondaparinux
D. Dalteparin
E. Abciximab
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:A
• Unfractionated heparin (UFH) - Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is the drug of choice in patients with significant renal dysfunction (CrCl < 30 ml/min).
Incorrect Answers:
• Enoxaparin - Enoxaparin is not recommended in patients with significant renal dysfunction (CrCl < 30 ml/min), as the risk of bleeding is increased in this population.
• Fondaparinux - The use of fondaparinux should be avoided in patients with CrCl < 30 ml/min because it increases the risk of bleeding.
• Dalteparin - Dalteparin is not recommended in patients with significant renal dysfunction (CrCl < 30 ml/min), as the risk of bleeding is increased in this population.
• Abciximab - Abciximab is an antiplatelet agent, not an anticoagulant, and is not indicated for this disease state.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is the preferred anticoagulant in patients with significant renal dysfunction (CrCl < 30 mL/min).
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS

questions.question:
You are working as a hospital pharmacist at a large institution. You have been asked to conduct a Drug Use Evaluation (DUE) to assess whether antiplatelets are being used appropriately in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarctions (STEMI).
Which of the following patients has NO relative contraindications to prasugrel?
options: A. A 78-year-old male patient, weighing 143 lbs, with no history of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) who is undergoing a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
B. A 65-year-old male patient, weighing 110 lbs, with no history of stroke or TIA who is undergoing PCI
C. A 63-year-old male patient, weighing 132 lbs, with a history of stroke who is undergoing PCI
D. A 54-year-old female patient, weighing 121 lbs, with no history of stroke or TIA who does not require PCI
E. A 45-year-old male patient, weighing 154 lbs, with no history of stroke, who is undergoing PCI
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:E
• A 45-year-old male patient, weighing 154 lbs, with no history of stroke, who is undergoing PCI - This patient does not have any relative contraindications to the use of prasugrel
Incorrect Answers:
• A 78-year-old male patient, weighing 143 lbs, with no history of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) who is undergoing a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) - This patient is over the age of 75, which is a relative contraindication to the use of prasugrel.
• A 65-year-old male patient, weighing 110 lbs, with no history of stroke or TIA who is undergoing PCI - This patient weighs less than 60 kg (=132 lbs), which is a relative contraindication to the use of prasugrel.
• A 63-year-old male patient, weighing 132 lbs, with a history of stroke who is undergoing PCI - This patient has a history of stroke, which is a relative contraindication to the use of prasugrel.
• A 54-year-old female patient, weighing 121 lbs, with no history of stroke or TIA who does not require PCI - This patient weighs less than 60 kg (=132 lbs), which is a relative contraindication to the use of prasugrel.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
The use of prasugrel should be avoided in certain patient populations (age > 75, weight < 60 kg, history of stroke or TIA), and either ticagrelor or clopidogrel should be used as alternatives.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to using non-selective beta-blockers?
options: A. Severe asthma
B. First-degree heart block (no pacemaker)
C. Second-degree heart block (no pacemaker)
D. Third-degree heart block (no pacemaker)
E. Severe bradycardia
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:B
• First-degree heart block (no pacemaker) - Non-selective beta-blockers are not contraindicated in first-degree heart block.
Incorrect Answers:
• Severe asthma - Severe asthma - Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in severe asthma.
• Second-degree heart block (no pacemaker) - Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in second-degree heart block without a pacemaker.
• Third-degree heart block (no pacemaker) - Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in third-degree heart block without a pacemaker.
• Severe bradycardia - Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in severe bradycardia.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in patients with any of the following: severe asthma, second or third-degree heart block without a pacemaker and severe bradycardia.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To understand how to select the most appropriate beta-blocker based on patient factors such as comorbidities.
BACKGROUND:
Beta-blockers decrease heart rate, contractility and blood pressure. They reduce symptoms of angina by decreasing myocardial oxygen demand. In patients with recent prior myocardial infarction and/or depressed left ventricular systolic function, beta-blockers also reduce mortality.
Beta-blockers are subdivided into 2 categories: selective and non-selective, which…

questions.question:
THE NEXT TWO QUESTIONS INCLUSIVE REFER TO THE FOLLOWING CASE:
FC is a 64-year-old female who presents to your community pharmacy. She appears stressed and tells you that she just received a phone call from her cardiologist, who diagnosed her with stable angina. She states that for the past few months, she has been experiencing chest heaviness and discomfort when going up the stairs or walking briskly. The symptoms typically resolve within a few minutes. She saw her primary care provider, who referred her to a cardiologist for an exercise stress test.
FC has an appointment with the cardiologist in 2 weeks, but in the interim, she would like to learn more about her condition.
FC’s medical history is significant for dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus and stable angina (new diagnosis). She takes atorvastatin 20 mg PO daily, metformin 1 g PO BID and empagliflozin 10 mg PO daily.
Her average blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is 1.9 mmol/L and HbA1C is 6.8%.
Which of the following statements is correct regarding drug therapy for stable angina?
options: A. Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are not recommended for stable angina unless the patient has comorbid hypertension
B. Nitroglycerin patches are recommended in patients with stable angina to decrease their risk of myocardial infarctions and cardiovascular-related death
C. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are contraindicated in patients with stable angina as they have been shown to increase the risk of mortality
D. A statin should be initiated in all patients with stable angina, regardless of their lipid panel

E. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with low-dose Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and a P2Y12 inhibitor are recommended for patients with stable angina to decrease their risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:D
• A statin should be initiated in all patients with stable angina, regardless of their lipid panel - A statin should be initiated in all patients with stable angina, with the goal of lowering LDL-C to below 1.8 mmol/L or by at least 50%.
Incorrect Answers:
• ACE inhibitors are not recommended for stable angina unless the patient has comorbid hypertension - ACE inhibitors (or ARBs if ACE inhibitors are not tolerated) are recommended for all patients with stable angina to decrease their risk of cardiovascular events and mortality, regardless of blood pressure.
• Nitroglycerin patches are recommended in patients with stable angina to decrease their risk of myocardial infarctions and cardiovascular-related death - Nitroglycerin patches may be used for symptom management in patients with stable angina but have not shown evidence of mortality reduction.
• Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are contraindicated in patients with stable angina as they have been shown to increase the risk of mortality - ARBs are not contraindicated in patients with stable angina. They can be used if patients cannot tolerate or do not respond to ACE inhibitors.
• Dual antiplatelet therapy with low-dose Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) and a P2Y12 inhibitor are recommended for patients with stable angina to decrease their risk of major adverse cardiovascular events - DAPT is not recommended in patients with stable angina due to limited benefit and increased risk of bleeding. Low-dose Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) is first-line, and if contraindicated or not tolerated, clopidogrel may be used as an alternative.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
In the absence of contraindications, all patients with stable angina should be started on an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, as they have been shown to prevent major cardiovascular events.

questions.question: Which of the following modifications to FC’s medication regimen would NOT be appropriate?
options: A. Add perindopril 2 mg PO daily
B. Add Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily
C. Add nitroglycerin spray 0.4 mg Q 5 minutes PRN (up to 3 doses)
D. Increase dose of atorvastatin to 40 mg PO daily
E. Add nifedipine 10 mg PO TID
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:E
• Add nifedipine 10 mg PO TID - Short-acting nifedipine is not recommended, as it can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure, leading to reflex tachycardia.
Incorrect Answers:
• Add perindopril 2 mg PO daily – Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are indicated in all patients with stable angina, unless there are specific contraindications.
• Add Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily - Low-dose Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) is indicated in all patients with stable angina, unless there are specific contraindications.
• Add nitroglycerin spray 0.4 mg Q 5 minutes PRN (up to 3 doses) - Nitroglycerin spray is indicated for symptom management (to be used as needed) in stable angina.
• Increase dose of atorvastatin to 40 mg PO daily - FC’s current statin regimen is of moderateintensity, whereas a high-intensity regimen is recommended for patients with stable angina.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
If beta-blockers are not tolerated or are contraindicated, calcium channel blockers can be used as an alternative to reduce heart rate and cardiac contractility in patients with stable angina. However, short-acting nifedipine should be avoided due to the risk of sudden hypotension and reflex tachycardia.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To understand the pharmacological options for major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) prevention and symptom management in patients with stable angina.
BACKGROUND:
Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are divided into two classes: non-dihydropyridines and dihydropyridines.

questions.question:
AR is a 58-year-old male who was recently diagnosed with stable angina. His other medical conditions include hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He takes ramipril 5 mg PO daily, atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily and metformin/sitagliptin 1000 mg/50 mg PO BID. He started bisoprolol 5 mg PO daily, Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily and nitroglycerin spray 0.4 mg Q 5 minutes PRN (up to 3 doses) 1 week ago. AR’s most recent A1C was 7.6% and his average blood pressure is 138/90 mmHg.
Which of the following medications should be added to AR’s drug regimen?
options: A. Amlodipine 2.5 mg PO daily
B. Diltiazem 120 mg PO daily
C. Empagliflozin 12.5 mg PO daily
D. Long-acting gliclazide 30 mg PO daily
E. Nitroglycerin patch 0.2 mg/hour apply 1 patch once daily (remove at bedtime)
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:C
• Empagliflozin 12.5 mg PO daily - It is appropriate to start empagliflozin (an SGLT2 inhibitor), given that AR has comorbid diabetes which is not optimally controlled and that empagliflozin has proven cardiovascular benefits, which will help prevent a future myocardial infarction.
Incorrect Answers:
• Amlodipine 2.5 mg PO daily - Amlodipine (a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) should not be started at this time, given that a beta-blocker was started very recently (1 week ago). A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker may be added if the patient continues to experience symptoms despite an adequate trial of beta-blocker therapy.
• Diltiazem 120 mg PO daily - Diltiazem (a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) should not be added to a beta-blocker, given that there is a significant risk of bradycardia and atrioventricular block with this combination.
• Long-acting gliclazide 30 mg PO daily - Gliclazide is not the most optimal antihyperglycemic, since agents with cardiovascular benefit are available and would be more beneficial in a patient with stable angina.
• Nitroglycerin patch 0.2 mg/hr apply 1 patch once daily (remove at bedtime) - A long-acting nitrate is not indicated at this time, given that the patient started a short-acting nitrate very recently (1 week ago). If the patient continues to experience symptoms after an adequate trial of a beta-blocker and/or calcium channel blocker and a short-acting nitrate, a long-acting nitrate may be trialed.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
In patients with comorbid type 2 diabetes mellitus and stable angina, it is recommended to preferentially use antihyperglycemics with proven cardiovascular benefits. An adequate trial of a beta-blocker should be conducted prior to adding a calcium channel blocker or long-acting nitrate.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To understand how to appropriately manage comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes mellitus in patients with higher cardiovascular risk (e.g. patients with stable angina).

questions.question: All of the following are relative contraindications to fibrinolysis, EXCEPT:
options: A. Severe and uncontrolled hypertension
B. Recent major surgery (less than 3 weeks prior)
C. Active peptic ulcer
D. Delay in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
E. Current use of anticoagulants
questions.explanation:
RATIONALE:
Correct Answer:D
• Delay in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) – A delay in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is not a contraindication to fibrinolysis. Patients who are candidates for future non-urgent PCI may still receive fibrinolytic therapy.
Incorrect Answers:
• Severe and uncontrolled hypertension - Severe and uncontrolled hypertension (BP > 180/110 mmHg) is a contraindication to the use of fibrinolysis.
• Recent major surgery (less than 3 weeks prior) - Recent major surgery is a contraindication to the use of fibrinolysis.
• Active peptic ulcer - An active peptic ulcer is a contraindication to the use of fibrinolysis.
• Current use of anticoagulants - Current use of anticoagulants is a contraindication to the use of thrombolysis.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Patients who are candidates for future non-urgent PCI may still receive fibrinolytic therapy.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS
LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
To identify the contraindications to fibrinolysis.
BACKGROUND:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the first-line reperfusion therapy for all patients who can access a PCI-capable facility within 2 hours. PCI is indicated in patients with contraindications to thrombolytic therapy or cardiogenic shock and is preferred in patients over 75 years of age because of a higher risk of intracranial…

questions.question:
RO is a 70-year-old female patient who was diagnosed with stable angina 5 years ago. RO has been experiencing worsening shortness of breath (SOB) with activity such as walking up the stairs. Her SOB typically improves within 3 minutes of using her nitroglycerin spray.
Her medical history is significant for hypertension (diagnosed 10 years ago), dyslipidemia (diagnosed 10 years ago) and stable angina (diagnosed 5 years ago). She takes ramipril 10 mg PO daily, atorvastatin 80 mg PO daily, Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily, metoprolol 100 mg PO BID and nitroglycerin spray 0.4 mg 1 spray every 5 minutes PRN (up to 3 doses).
Which of the following recommendations would be the most appropriate for the management of RO’s stable angina?
options: A. Advise RO to avoid activity that increases shortness of breath
B. Add amlodipine 5 mg PO daily to her medication regimen
C. Add verapamil 80 mg PO daily to her medication regimen
D. Switch Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily to clopidogrel 75 mg PO daily
E. Add nitroglycerin 0.2 mg/hour patch to be applied once daily
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:B
• Add amlodipine 5 mg PO daily to her medication regimen- Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as amlodipine, should be added if symptoms persist despite an optimal betablocker regimen.
Incorrect Answers:
• Advise RO to avoid activity that increases dyspnea - Avoiding activities which increase dyspnea is neither practical nor is it beneficial to patients.
• Add verapamil 80 mg PO daily to her medication regimen - Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as verapamil, should be avoided in combination with beta-blockers, since the combination can lead to severe bradycardia and atrioventricular block.
• Switch Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid) 81 mg PO daily to clopidogrel 75 mg PO daily - Clopidogrel is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate or have a contraindication to Aspirin® (acetylsalicylic acid). This patient does not meet this criterion. Furthermore, antiplatelets are used in stable angina for mortality reduction, not symptom management.
• Add nitroglycerin 0.2 mg/hour patch to be applied once daily - A long-acting nitrate would not be the best option for this patient, as we have not yet optimized their beta-blocker/calcium channel blocker regimen.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as amlodipine, may be added if anginal symptoms, such as chest pain or tightness, persist despite an optimal beta-blocker regimen. However, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as verapamil, should be avoided in combination with beta-blockers, since the combination can lead to severe bradycardia and atrioventricular block.
TOPIC: Stable Angina & ACS

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with persistent AF (3mo), mild symptoms. CHA2DS2-VASc 5, LVEF 55%. HR 88-110 bpm. Management?
options: A. Rhythm control mandatory
B. Immediate cardioversion
C. Rate control preferred in elderly with minimal symptoms
D. No treatment
questions.explanation: - AF elderly: Rate control non-inferior to rhythm control (AFFIRM, RACE). Age 82y, mild symptoms - rate control preferred. Metoprolol or diltiazem. Lenient control <110 bpm acceptable. Anticoagulation ESSENTIAL (CHA2DS2-VASc 5).

questions.question:
RF is a 73-year-old female who was recently diagnosed with stable angina. She presents to your primary care clinic with complaints of ongoing chest pain upon exertion. Her medical history is also significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and asthma, for which she takes sitagliptin/metformin 50/1000 mg PO BID, candesartan/hydrochlorothiazide 16/12.5 mg PO daily, Flovent HFA® (fluticasone propionate) 250 mcg 1 puff once daily and Ventolin HFA® (salbutamol) 100 mcg/actuation 1-2 puffs Q4-6H PRN. RF’s primary care physician would like to initiate a medication regimen for symptom management and has asked for your recommendation.
Which of the following combinations of medications would be most appropriate for RF’s anginal symptoms?
options: A. Diltiazem, verapamil, nitroglycerin
B. Atenolol, diltiazem and nifedipine
C. Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN), bisoprolol and amlodipine
D. Verapamil, amlodipine and propranolol
E. Nifedipine, verapamil and bisoprolol
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:C
• Isosorbide dinitrate (ISD), bisoprolol and amlodipine - Isosorbide dinitrate (ISD), bisoprolol and amlodipine are all appropriate for symptom management in patients with stable angina.
Incorrect Answers:
o Diltiazem, verapamil, nitroglycerin - Diltiazem, verapamil and nitroglycerin would not be an appropriate regimen, as it contains dual therapy with two calcium channel blockers (diltiazem and verapamil).
o Atenolol, diltiazem and nifedipine -Atenolol, diltiazem and nifedipine would not be an appropriate regimen, as it contains immediate-release nifedipine, which is preferably avoided due to its risk of sudden low blood pressure, reflex tachycardia and stroke.
o Verapamil, amlodipine and propranolol - Verapamil, amlodipine and propranolol would not be an appropriate regimen, as it contains both a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker and a beta-blocker, which should not be combined due to additive risk of bradycardia and atrioventricular block. Furthermore, propranolol is a non-selective betablocker which should be avoided due to its risk of aggravating the patient's asthma.
o Nifedipine, verapamil and bisoprolol- Nifedipine, verapamil and bisoprolol would not be an appropriate regimen, as it contains nifedipine, which is preferably avoided due to its risk of sudden low blood pressure and reflex tachycardia.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers should not be combined. Multiple drugs in the same class should not be combined. Immediate-release nifedipine is preferably avoided due to its risk of sudden low blood pressure and reflex tachycardia.

questions.question:
ST is a 71-year-old male who presents to your community pharmacy with complaints of dizziness, fatigue, headache and insomnia. ST's medical history is significant for hypertension, dyslipidemia and a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) 3 months ago. He tells you that at that time, his cardiologist advised him to start a new medication. He cannot recall the name of the drug but tells you that it ends with 'lol'. He also takes perindopril/amlodipine 7/5 mg PO daily and atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily.
Which of the following beta-blockers is most likely to be causing ST's symptoms?
options: A. Bisoprolol
B. Metoprolol.
C. Nadolol
D. Timolol
E. Propranolol
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:E
• Propranolol - Propranolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, is more likely to cause central nervous system (CNS) side effects such as dizziness, fatigue and insomnia than other agents because of its greater lipid solubility.
Incorrect Answers:
o Bisoprolol - Bisoprolol, a cardioselective beta-blocker, is not the most likely to cause CNS side effects.
o Metoprolol - Metoprolol, a cardioselective beta-blocker, is not the most likely to cause CNS side effects.
o Nadolol - Nadolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, is not the most likely to cause CNS side effects.
o Timolol - Timolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, is not the most likely to cause CNS side effects.
TAKEAWAY/KEYPOINTS:
Propranolol is more likely to cause central nervous system (CNS) side effects (e.g. insomnia, depression, vivid dreams) than other agents because of its greater lipid solubility.

questions.question:
You are working your regular shift as a pharmacist when a patient of yours, KP, calls seeking advice on allergy relief. KP reports a two-week history of worsening nasal congestion, which she attributes to a pollen allergy flare-up that occurred after a family picnic two weeks ago. She also experienced frequent sneezing, a runny nose, and itchy, watery eyes. KP states that she has been taking loratadine 10mg daily for the past 14 days, which has helped relieve all her allergy symptoms except the congestion that is now significantly impacting her sleep and work. KP is a 42-year-old female who works as a high school teacher, a role that often involves public speaking and stressful interactions with students and parents. Her medical conditions include hypothyroidism, hypertension, migraines, and anxiety. Her current medications include Synthroid®(levothyroxine) 88 mcg PO daily, Norvasc®(amlodipine) 5 mg PO daily, Maxalt RD®(rizatriptan) 5 mg PO as needed during migraine attacks (KP gets a migraine attack approximately once every 2 months), and Ativan®(lorazepam) 0.5-1 mg PO as needed during stressful situations like parent-teacher meetings. KB lives alone and usually has 1-2 glasses of wine with dinner to unwind after a stressful day at work. She does not use any tobacco or illicit drugs. You check the available over-the-counter allergy options.
Which of the following would be the best recommendation?
options: A. Continue loratadine 10mg daily for another week
B. Oral loratadine plus pseudoephedrine
C. Saline nasal rinse
D. Otrivin® (xylometazoline) nasal spray
E. Oral Sudafed® (pseudoephedrine) and increase the amlodipine dose to 7.5mg daily
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:D
• Otrivin® (xylometazoline) nasal spray - A nasal decongestant is the preferred option because it primarily works locally, with minimal systemic absorption, and therefore has a low probability of affecting blood pressure.
Incorrect Answers:
o Continue loratadine 10mg daily for another week - It is unlikely that loratadine will resolve the patient's nasal congestion, as she has already used
o Oral loratadine plus pseudoephedrine - Loratadine will not resolve the patient's nasal congestion, and oral pseudophedrine can raise the blood pressure and counteract the effect of the antihypertensive medication.
o Saline nasal rinse - A saline nasal rinse may provide minor relief from nasal congestion; however, it is unlikely to resolve the issue completely, considering the severe nature of the congestion.
o Oral Sudafed® (pseudoephedrine) and increase the amlodipine dose to 7.5mg daily - Oral pseudoephedrine can raise blood pressure. Increasing amlodipine solely to counter this effect without a comprehensive assessment is medically inappropriate.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
Due to their limited systemic absorption, nasal decongestants generally have a lower risk of increasing blood pressure compared to oral decongestants. Hence, they are the safer option for the treatment of nasal congestion in patients with hypertension.

questions.question:
You are working in a community pharmacy when one of your patients, SN, drops off a new prescription for 30 capsules of Altace HCT® (ramipril/hydrochlorothiazide) 5 mg/2.5 mg, to be taken 1 capsule daily in the morning. SNis a 51-year-old female who has been diagnosed with hypertension. She says her physician told her that the new medication is a combination of two blood-pressure-lowering drugs. She says she was surprised to hear this because her blood pressure was "not even that high".
She typically measures her blood pressure in the morning, and her average blood pressure reading is 147/95 mmHg. She mentions that her blood pressure tends to be a bit higher when she goes to the physician's office (around 150/98 mmHg). She is wondering why her physician would prescribe her two medications at once. In addition to hypertension, she also has dyslipidemia and depression. Her current medications include Crestor® (rosuvastatin) 20 mg PO daily, Zoloft® (sertraline) 50 mg PO daily, and Champix® (varenicline) 1 mg PO BID for smoking cessation. Despite using Champix®, SN continues to smoke 5 cigarettes a day. SN mentions that her mom has had hypertension for many years and suffered from a myocardial infarction at the age of 50. Given the patient's medical conditions, positive family history, and current smoking status, her Framingham Risk score (FRS) is 15.6%. SN wants to know whether multiple antihypertensive medications are necessary.
Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A. SN should not be on a combination therapy. Monotherapy is recommended initially, and a second antihypertensive should be added only if blood pressure targets are not met with the single agent
B. SN does not require antihypertensive medications since her blood pressure does not exceed the threshold for therapy initiation
C. SN does not require any antihypertensive therapy since her high blood pressure at the physician's office is likely considered white coat hypertension
D. SN does not require combination therapy. Combination therapy should only be considered if her blood pressure is more than 30/20 mmHg above target
E. SN would benefit from combination therapy, as this is a recommended first-O line treatment approach to achieve better blood pressure control
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:E
• SN would benefit from combination therapy, as this is a recommended first-line treatment approach to achieve better blood pressure control - Combination therapy as a single pill is recommended as first-line therapy for hypertension management to achieve earlier and better blood pressure control and improve cardiovascular outcomes.
Incorrect Answers:
o SN should not be on a combination therapy. Monotherapy is recommended initially, and a second antihypertensive should be added only if blood pressure targets are not met with the single agent - In the management of hypertension, recommended initial therapy is low-dose single-pill combination therapy (SPC).
o SN does not require antihypertensive medications since her blood pressure does not exceed the threshold for therapy initiation - SN's blood pressure (both in-office and out-of-office) exceeds the threshold for drug therapy initiation of ≥ 140/90 mmHg and would benefit from pharmacotherapy.
o SN does not require any antihypertensive therapy since her high blood pressure at the physician's office is likely considered white coat hypertension - SN's blood pressure (both in-office and out-of-office) exceeds the threshold for drug therapy initiation of ≥ 140/90 mmHg. White coat hypertension would have been a consideration if her home blood pressure readings were within normal parameters while in-office readings were elevated.
o SN does not require combination therapy. Combination therapy should only be considered if her blood pressure is more than 30/20 mmHg above target - In the management of hypertension, recommended initial therapy is low-dose single-pill combination therapy (SPC) regardless of the degree of blood pressure elevation.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
Low-dose SPCs are recommended as initial therapy for adult patients diagnosed with hypertension. The use of SPCs improves blood pressure control and cardiovascular outcomes while also enhancing patient adherence, lowering treatment costs, and reducing adverse effects.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from a hypertensive urgency?
options: A. The presence of acute target organ damage
B. The degree of blood pressure elevation
C. The presence of alarming symptoms such as severe headache and confusion
D. A past medical history of uncontrolled hypertension
E. At initial presentation, patients with suspected hypertensive emergency require immediate management, whereas diagnosis with a hypertensive urgency requires at least 2 additional readings.
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:A
• The presence of acute target organ damage - This is the critical distinction. A hypertensive emergency involves acute target organ damage (e.g. stroke, myocardial infarction, acute kidney injury), while urgency does
Incorrect Answers:
o The degree of blood pressure elevation - While blood pressure is typically very high in both, the key difference is not the number itself, but what high blood pressure does to the body. Hypertensive emergencies are associated with target organ damage, while hypertensive urgencies are not.
o The presence of alarming symptoms such as severe headache and confusion - Severe headaches and altered mental status can occur in both hypertensive emergency and urgency because the blood pressure is significantly elevated, so these are not distinguishing factors.
o A past medical history of uncontrolled hypertension - While past medical history is important for overall patient assessment, it does not distinguish between an urgency or emergency situation.
o At initial presentation, patients with suspected hypertensive emergency require immediate management, whereas diagnosis with hypertensive urgency requires at least 2 additional readings - Patients demonstrating characteristics indicative of hypertensive urgency or emergency warrant immediate diagnosis and management of hypertension.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
Hypertensive urgencies and emergencies both involve a significant elevation in blood pressure. The key distinction is that hypertensive emergency is associated with acute target organ damage (e.g. stroke, myocardial infarction, acute kidney injury), while a hypertensive urgency is not.

questions.question:
IM is a 69-year-old male with a 10-year history of hypertension. His cardiovascular risk has been classified as low. He is currently being treated with Viacoram® (perindopril/amlodipine) 7 mg/5 mg orally daily, and he is not on any other prescription medications. In addition to his hypertension, IM has been experiencing mild gastrosophageal reflux disease (GERD), which he manages with lifestyle modifications on most days and the occasional use of over-the-counter antacids. He also uses loratadine for his seasonal allergies.
IM's blood work was completed 3 weeks ago, and the results are now available. The serum creatinine Is 0.9 mg/dL (normal: 0.70-1.30 mg/dL), and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 85 mL/min/1.73 m2. Other lab values, including a complete blood count, electrolytes, and liver function tests, are all within normal limits. His most recent blood pressure reading, taken this morning, was 133/92 mmHg. His Framingham Risk Score (FRS) is calculated to be 8%. IM is a retired English literature professor who lives at home with his wife and pet parrot. He has never smoked, but consumes alcohol socially, typically one to two drinks on the weekends when he goes golfing with his friends. He reports engaging in light physical activity, such as 30- minute walks three times a week and a 1-hour Tai Chi class on Sundays.
Which of the following is the appropriate blood pressure (BP) target for IM?
options: A. 140/90 mmHg
B. Less than 120/80 mmHg
C. Less than 130/80 mmHg
D. Systolic blood pressure (SP) less than 130 mmHg
E. SBP less than 120 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:C
• Less than 130/80 mmHg - The appropriate blood pressure target for adult patients diagnosed with hypertension is a SBP < 130 mmHg.
Incorrect Answers:
o 140/90 mmHg - The appropriate blood pressure target for adult patients diagnosed with hypertension is a systolic blood pressure (SP) < 130 mmHg.
o Less than 120/80mmHg - The appropriate blood pressure target for adult patients diagnosed with hypertension is a systolic blood pressure (SP) < 130 mmHg.
o Systolic blood pressure (SP) less than 130 mmHg - The appropriate blood pressure target for adult patients diagnosed with hypertension is a SBP < 130 mmHg.
o SBP less than 120mmHg - The appropriate blood pressure target for adult patients diagnosed with hypertension is a SBP < 130 mmHg.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
The appropriate blood pressure target for adult patients diagnosed with hypertension is a SBP < 130 mmHg.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman, GP, is newly diagnosed with hypertension. GP is pregnant with her first child, currently at 32 weeks of gestation. Her blood pressure readings have been consistently above 140/90 mmHg, averaging 145/91 mmg at home and 147/94 mmHg at the gynecologist's office. GP is otherwise healthy and reports no other significant medical history. The patient's lab values are within normal limits, and a fetal ultrasound shows appropriate growth for gestational age. GP mentions that she is looking after her elderly father and is currently managing his complex medication regimen, which is frequently changing and causing confusion. Given her impending initiation of a new antihypertensive medication and the likelihood of postpartum adjustments, GP prefers a stable treatment plan that can be continued postpartum, especially as she plans to breastfeed. GP is married and lives with her family in a suburban area. She enjoys staying active by hiking and attending yoga classes, although she has had to modify her activity level somewhat in her third trimester.
Which of the following antihypertensive medications is appropriate for long-term management of hypertension in this patient?
options: A. Intravenous labetalol
B. Oral long-acting nifedipine
C. Oral short-acting nifedipine
D. Oral enalapril
E. Oral acebutolol
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:B
• Oral long-acting nifedipine - Long-acting nifedipine, as opposed to short-acting, is an appropriate first-line antihypertensive in both pregnancy and lactation.
Incorrect Answers:
o Intravenous labetalol-Oral labetalol, not intravenous, is an appropriate first-line antihypertensive choice in both pregnancy and lactation.
o Oral short-acting nifedipine - Long-acting nifedipine, as opposed to short-acting, is an appropriate first-line antihypertensive in both pregnancy and lactation.
o Oral enalapril - Oral enalapril is an appropriate antihypertensive choice in lactation, but angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy due to the potential for fetal toxicity.
o Oral acebutolol - Oralacebutolol can be used during pregnancy but not during lactation due to higher levels excreted in breastmilk and risk of adverse effects in the infant.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
During pregnancy, hypertension can be managed with first-line oral therapies including labetalol, methyldopa, long-acting nifedipine, and other beta blockers (e.g. acebutolol, metoprolol, pindolol and propranolol). During lactation, first-line antihypertensive choices include labetalol, methyldopa, long-acting nifedipine, enalapril and captopril.

questions.question: According to Hypertension Canada, individuals with a systolic blood pressure (SBP) between 130–139 mmHg who are at high cardiovascular risk should begin pharmacotherapy. Which of the following is NOT one of those CV risk factors?
options: A. Previous myocardial infarction
B. Chronic kidney disease with an eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m²
C. An estimated 10-year Framingham risk score ≥ 20%
D. Type 1 or 2 diabetes mellitus
E. Age ≥ 65 years
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: E — Age ≥ 65 years
The correct age threshold is ≥ 75 years, not ≥ 65 years. Patients who are 65–74 years old are not automatically classified as high CV risk under this specific criterion. The guideline specifies age ≥ 75 as the cutoff requiring pharmacotherapy initiation when SBP is in the 130–139 mmHg range.
Why the Other Options ARE Valid High-Risk Criteria:
A — Previous MI: Established cardiovascular disease (including prior MI) places a patient in the high-risk category, warranting pharmacotherapy at SBP 130–139 mmHg.
B — CKD with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m²: CKD defined by eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m² or albuminuria ≥ 3 mg/mmol is a recognized high CV risk factor under these guidelines.
C — 10-year Framingham Risk ≥ 20%: This score reflects a high predicted risk of a CV event, qualifying the patient for early pharmacotherapy initiation.
D — Type 1 or 2 Diabetes: Either form of diabetes independently classifies a patient as high CV risk, triggering the lower SBP threshold for treatment.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate goal of therapy in the management of hypertension?
options: A. Control modifiable risk factors Prevent cardiovascular morbidity and mortality associated with uncontrolled hypertension
B. Eliminate the need for antihypertensive medications
C. Lower blood pressure to target levels and improve patient adherence to therapy
D. Prevent damage to target organs such as the heart, kidneys and eyes
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:B
• Eliminate the need for antihypertensive medications - Aiming to avoid medication entirely is not an appropriate goal for hypertension management. While lifestyle changes can help some individuals, many require medication to achieve target blood pressure levels.
Incorrect Answers:
o Control modifiable risk factors - Controlling modifiable risk factors is an appropriate goal of therapy in hypertension management.
o Prevent cardiovascular morbidity and mortality associated with uncontrolled hypertension - Preventing cardiovascular morbidity and mortality associated with uncontrolled hypertension is an appropriate goal of therapy in hypertension management.
o Lower blood pressure to target levels and improve patient adherence to therapy-Lowering blood pressure to target levels and improving patient adherence to therapy are appropriate goals of therapy in hypertension management.
o Prevent damage to target organs such as the heart, kidneys and eyes - Preventing damage to target organs such as the heart, kidneys and eyes is an appropriate goal of therapy in hypertension management.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
Goals of therapy for hypertension management include controlling modifiable risk actors through lifestyle changes, preventing cardiovascular morbidity and complications, and providing convenient and cost-effective treatment to improve patient adherence. Medication use is often required to achieve appropriate blood pressure control.

questions.question:
MR is a 62-year-old retired teacher who comes to the clinic for an appointment to get her blood pressure checked. She has a history of well-controlled hypertension, managed with amlodipine 5mg daily for the past 5 years. She reports feeling well overall but mentions that her home blood pressure readings have been a bit variable lately. MR tells you that she lives alone and enjoys gardening. She usually takes a brisk 30-minute walk in the mornings.
This morning, however, she rushed to get to her appointment on time after spilling her coffee, and arrived slightly flustered. She mentioned having a cup of coffee about 20 minutes before leaving her house. While in the waiting area, she scrolled through news on her phone, which included some concerning political updates that made her feel a bit anxious. When you bring MR into the examination room, you note that she is sitting on the edge of the examination table, her legs dangling. You are preparing to take her blood pressure.
Which of the following is LEAST appropriate for obtaining an accurate blood pressure reading?
options: A. The patient's arm should be bare, supported, and the middle of the blood pressure cuff kept below heart level
B. The patient should sit upright in the chair with the back supported and feet flat on the floor
C. The blood pressure cuff should fit snugly but not too tightly on the arm Measurements should be taken at 1-minute intervals
D. The patient should avoid any caffeine-containing beverages (e.g. coffee or tea for 30 minutes before blood pressure measurement
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:A
• The patient's arm should be bare, supported, and the middle of the blood pressure cuff kept below heart level - For correct blood pressure measurement, the middle of the blood pressure cuff should be kept at heart level, not below.
Incorrect Answers:
o The patient should sit upright in the chair with the back supported and feet flat on the floor - Proper patient positioning during blood pressure measurement is essential for obtaining accurate and consistent readings.
o The blood pressure cuff should fit snugly but not too tightly on the arm - The appropriate selection and application of the blood pressure cuff ensure accurate blood pressure measurement.
o Measurements should be taken at 1-minute intervals - The 1-minute interval between blood pressure measurements is an important step in obtaining accurate and reliable readings.
o The patient should avoid any caffeine-containing beverages (e.g. coffee or tea for 30 minutes before blood pressure measurement - Caffeine is a stimulant that can cause a temporary increase in blood pressure. Avoiding caffeinated beverages for 30 minutes before blood pressure measurement helps prevent false elevations and obtain more reliable readings.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
When measuring blood pressure, some strategies are recommended to maximize the accuracy of blood pressure readings. These include relaxing in a quiet place for 5 minutes before measuring, sitting with back supported and feet flat on the ground, avoiding caffeine, nicotine, or physical activity in the preceding 30 minutes, and ensuring the cuff size fits the patient's arm properly

questions.question:
THE NEXT TWO QUESTIONS INCLUSIVE REFER TO THE FOLLOWING CASE:
JB is a 62-year-old male with a 5-year history of hypertension. He has been Not answered adhering to his daily regimen of Twynsta® (telmisartan 80 mg/amlodipine 10 mg) PO once daily, and his current average blood pressure is 135/87 mmHg.
Question JB works as a high school principal in a demanding, under-resourced urban school district, often working more than 60 hours per week. He reports feeling Send stressed and has difficulty finding time for regular exercise. His family history Feedback is significant for hypertension and stroke in both his parents. Aside from his chronic hypertension, JB is healthy. However, his diet could be improved as he admits to relying on fast food due to his busy schedule. A recent workup shows a normal echocardiogram, but the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 54 mL/min/1.73m4. JB's blood work reveals an A1C of 5.6% and K+ levels of 5.2 mmol/L (normal: 3.5 to 5 mmol/L).
Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A. JB would benefit from the addition of bisoprolol to his current therapy to improve blood pressure control
B. Even though JB's blood pressure is at target, he would benefit from counselling on lifestyle modifications
C. JB would benefit from the addition of spironolactone to his current therapy to improve blood pressure control
D. JB would benefit from the addition of ramipril to his current therapy to improve blood pressure control
E. JB would benefit from the addition of hydrochlorothiazide to his current therapy to improve blood pressure control
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:E
• JB would benefit from the addition of hydrochlorothiazide to his current therapy to improve blood pressure control-JB's blood pressure is not at target. Therefore, he would benefit from combination therapy with a thiazide diuretic.
Incorrect Answers:
A. JB would benefit from the addition of bisoprolol to his current therapy to improve blood pressure control - The use of beta blockers is not recommended for hypertension management in patients 60 years of age and older, unless indicated. Better alternatives exist.
B. Even though JB's blood pressure is at target, he would benefit from counselling on lifestyle modifications - JB's current systolic blood pressure exceeds his target of < 130 mmHg, and so additional pharmacotherapy is advised.
C. JB would benefit from the addition of spironolactone to his current herapy to improve blood pressure control - JB's potassium levels ar igher than normal, so potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone should not be used.
D. JB would benefit from the addition of ramipril to his current therapy to improve blood pressure control - The combination of an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB)
E. is not recommended.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
Triple therapy is advised in patients who continue to experience elevated systolic blood pressure despite dose optimization of two antihypertensives in single-pill combinations of either ACE or ARB, thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic, or long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

questions.question:
Three months after having his blood pressure regimen modified, JB returns for a follow-up. His blood pressure measurements are taken, and the average is 128/90 mmHg.
Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A. JB's blood pressure is now at target, no further interventions are required JB should be counselled on lifestyle modifications to maintain blood pressure under control
B. JB's blood pressure remains elevated above target, so he should be referred for resistant hypertension
C. JB requires additional therapy since his diastolic blood pressure remains elevated, despite normal systolic blood pressure
D. JB's antihypertensive medications should be modified because his blood pressure is now too low
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer:A
• JB should be counselled on lifestyle modifications to maintain blood pressure under control - Although the blood pressure is now at target, non-pharmacological interventions remain crucial for maintaining control.
Incorrect Answers:
A. JB's blood pressure is now at target, no further interventions are required - Although the blood pressure is now at target, non-pharmacological interventions remain crucial for maintaining control.
B. JB's blood pressure remains elevated above target, so he should be referred for resistant hypertension - JB's systolic blood pressure is < 130 mmHg, so it is at target.
C. JB requires additional therapy since his diastolic blood pressure remains elevated, despite normal systolic blood pressure - The systolic blood pressure target according to Hypertension Canada is < 130 mmg. There is no diastolic blood pressure target.
D. JB's antihypertensive medications should be modified because his blood pressure is now too low -JB's blood pressure is not low and is at target.
TAKEAWAY/KEY POINTS:
According to Hypertension Canada, the target systolic blood pressure (SP) is < 130 mmHg, with no diastolic blood pressure target. Patients who maintain a SBP < 130 mmg are at low cardiovascular risk even when diastolic readings are between 70-90 mmhg
